Tuesday, October 6, 2026

Today's Numbers

• 201 Million: The number of American households that now subscribe to Amazon Prime, up from 54 million in 2015, as shoppers prepare for the annual fall Prime Big Deal Days. (Robinhood Snacks)

• 6 Percentage Points: The polling lead held by Democratic challenger James Talarico over incumbent Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, according to a new Times/Siena survey. (The New York Times)

• 45 Percent: The year-over-year jump in European electric vehicle registrations through August 2026, reaching a record 1.64 million delivered cars despite subsidy cuts in major markets. (Robinhood Snacks)

Quotes of the Day

• "I wrote every single word with my own human fingers. In a world full of synthetic text, handmade words feel like honest craftsmanship." — Author Kevin Roose, explaining why he barred AI writing assistants while authoring his new book The AGI Chronicles, via Wired.

• "You cannot understand his drive until you realize he treats humanity as an engineering problem that only he has the blueprint to solve." — Justine Wilson, speaking in the new documentary film Musk about tech billionaire Elon Musk, via Wired.

Consumer Trends & Science

Cats Demand Fancy Dinners as Pet Food Hits $17 Billion

Americans spent $17 billion on cat food over the past year, marking a 14 percent jump as pet owners treat their feline companions like family members. Major manufacturers like Mars built specialized tasting kitchens where feline taste-testers sample different formulas. Researchers discovered that cats possess unique taste receptors tuned specifically to tuna. These receptors create a super-savory sensation that cats crave far more than beef or chicken. Companies are now rushing new senior cat lines and gourmet seafood dishes to grocery shelves to cash in on pampering pet owners. Read the retail report in The New York Times.

Astronomers Spot Youngest Exoplanet Ever Recorded

Scientists using the Atacama Large Millimeter Array telescope spotted the youngest known planet outside our solar system. The baby planet, named Elias 2-24b, orbits a young star about 400 light-years from Earth. Astronomers calculate that the planet is less than one million years old. For comparison, Earth is more than 4.5 billion years old. Elias 2-24b is still scooping up gas and cosmic pebbles from a thick disc of space dust, giving scientists a live front-row look at how giant gas worlds take shape. Read the astronomy report in Wired.

Legal & National Affairs

Supreme Court Opens Term with High-Stakes Climate Lawsuits

The United States Supreme Court opened its fall session by hearing arguments on whether coastal cities can force oil companies to pay for climate damage. Mayors and local officials argue that petroleum giants concealed their knowledge of carbon pollution for decades and should fund sea walls and flood barriers. Defense lawyers for the energy firms counter that global climate emissions fall strictly under federal regulation rather than local courtroom authority. The justices appeared divided, and their eventual ruling could redirect billions of dollars in storm cleanup costs. Read the courtroom coverage in The New York Times.

Science & Medicine

Nobel Prizes Honor Brain Light Controls and Ghost Particle Detectors

The Nobel Assembly awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine to Karl Deisseroth for developing optogenetics. This laboratory technique uses light pulses to switch individual brain cells on and off, helping doctors map neural circuits behind Parkinson's disease and depression. A day later, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics to Francis Halzen. Halzen designed the IceCube observatory, which buried thousands of light sensors deep inside Antarctic glaciers to catch high-energy neutrinos—nearly invisible ghost particles that travel across deep space from distant black holes. Read the full Nobel profiles in The New York Times.

Business & Entertainment

Tom Cruise Satire 'Digger' Stumbles with $18 Million Debut

Warner Bros. suffered a box-office misfire this weekend when its $160 million action satire Digger, starring Tom Cruise, brought in just $18 million across North American theaters. The weak opening lands during a sensitive transition for the studio, representing its final standalone theatrical release before completing its $111 billion mega-merger with Skydance Media. Studio executives hoped Cruise's star power would pull adult moviegoers into theaters, but poor word-of-mouth and mixed reviews kept audiences at home. Read the box-office breakdown on Robinhood Snacks.

Meta and Microsoft Bar Staff from Using Claude AI

Both Meta and Microsoft ordered their software engineering teams to halt their use of Anthropic's Claude artificial intelligence models. Internal memos warned engineers that feeding internal project files or proprietary computer code into third-party AI assistants poses serious security and trade-secret risks. The policy forces developers back onto in-house AI coding tools, highlighting the fierce corporate rivalry as major tech firms guard their intellectual property. Read the full workplace dispatch on Robinhood Snacks.

• Intel Stock Slides: Shares of chipmaker Intel dropped 4 percent following reports that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) opened partnership discussions with Elon Musk's competing Terafab venture. Review the market movement on Robinhood Snacks.

Software, AI & Security

Ben Thompson's Mac Mini Gets Hacked—and His AI Agent Spots It

A patched macOS screen-sharing security flaw infected an analyst's server before an autonomous assistant raised the alarm.

Tech analyst Ben Thompson revealed that attackers breached his headless Mac Mini server through a high-severity macOS screen-sharing vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-65400. Attackers gained root access through exposed port 5900 and planted a Monero cryptocurrency miner. Fortunately, Thompson ran a persistent Claude Code agent on the computer. The agent detected unauthorized admin privileges, halted its own commands, and notified Thompson, allowing him to scrub the malware within minutes. Thompson notes that while his agent saved him, Apple's rigid permission screens make managing headless computers frustrating, pushing technical users toward Linux servers. Read the complete security post-mortem on Stratechery.

Meta and Microsoft Bar Staff from Using Claude AI

Major technology giants order engineering teams to halt their use of external coding models over intellectual property risks.

Both Meta and Microsoft ordered their software engineering divisions to stop using Anthropic's Claude artificial intelligence models. Leadership issued internal memos warning that pasting proprietary code, system logs, or project roadmaps into outside chatbots creates unacceptable corporate security risks. The directives require developers to rely strictly on internal, approved coding tools. The policy shift underscores growing corporate paranoia as tech giants guard valuable software secrets from competing frontier labs. Read the full workplace dispatch on Robinhood Snacks.

Business, Capital & Tech Infrastructure

The AI Data Center Debt Squeeze: Bond Markets Balk at Megawatt Loans

Rising Treasury yields and skeptical lenders threaten to derail ambitious cloud computing construction projects.

Financial markets are turning cold on the multi-billion-dollar debt boom powering artificial intelligence data centers. Ten-year U.S. Treasury yields climbed past 5.3%, making corporate loans substantially more expensive across the board. Major global banks, including Société Générale and Mitsubishi UFJ, are growing cautious about underwriting unbacked data center campuses. At the same time, leading AI labs face negative cash flows and massive compute obligations, raising doubts about how they will fund tens of billions in annual operations once public. Read the full financial analysis in Where's Your Ed At.

A $160 million action comedy opens flat as Warner Bros. prepares to merge into Skydance Media.

Warner Bros. faced a major box-office disappointment this weekend as its $160 million satire Digger, starring Tom Cruise, earned just $18 million in North American theaters. The soft debut arrives during an important corporate transition, marking the studio's final standalone theatrical release before finalizing its mega-merger under David Ellison's Skydance Media. Studio executives hoped Cruise's star power would draw wide audiences, but mixed critical reviews and sluggish ticket sales kept moviegoers away. Read the box-office breakdown on Robinhood Snacks.

Consumer Trends & Science

Cats Demand Fancy Dinners as Pet Food Hits $17 Billion

Pet food manufacturers build specialized tasting kitchens to satisfy feline cravings for seafood umami.

Leading food makers like Mars opened dedicated kitchens where feline taste-testers sample different recipes. Scientists found that cats possess taste receptors tuned specifically to tuna, creating an intense savory sensation that felines prefer over chicken or beef. Manufacturers are now racing to stock grocery shelves with gourmet seafood broths and specialized senior formulas. Read the retail report in The New York Times.

Elias 2-24b continues to pull gas and space dust from its surrounding stellar disk, offering astronomers an active look at how giant gas planets form. Read the astronomy report in Wired.

A bipartisan congressional coalition moves to block federal agencies from tapping nationwide vehicle tracking cameras.

Senators Bernie Sanders and Jeff Merkley, alongside Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, introduced federal legislation to prohibit government agencies from accessing automated license plate reader networks. The "Ban Flock Act" bans federal law enforcement from using private license plate camera databases and blocks federal grant money to state and local police forces that deploy them. The bill also grants citizens the right to sue federal agencies that track their vehicle movements without a warrant. Review the legislative push in 404 Media.

Justices weigh whether coastal cities can force multinational energy firms to pay for flood walls and storm damage.

Lawyers for the energy firms argue that global emissions fall under federal environmental statutes rather than municipal courtrooms. "I wrote every single word with my own human fingers. In a world full of synthetic text, handmade words feel like honest craftsmanship."

"You cannot understand his drive until you realize he treats humanity as an engineering problem that only he has the blueprint to solve."

Ben Thompson's Mac Mini Gets Hacked—and His AI Agent Spots It

A patched macOS screen-sharing security flaw infected an analyst's server before an autonomous assistant raised the alarm.

Tech analyst Ben Thompson revealed that attackers breached his headless Mac Mini server through a high-severity macOS screen-sharing vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-65400. Attackers gained root access through exposed port 5900 and planted a Monero cryptocurrency miner. Fortunately, Thompson ran a persistent Claude Code agent on the computer. The agent detected unauthorized admin privileges, halted its own commands, and notified Thompson, allowing him to scrub the malware within minutes. Thompson notes that while his agent saved him, Apple's rigid permission screens make managing headless computers frustrating, pushing technical users toward Linux servers. Read the complete security post-mortem on Stratechery.

Major technology giants order engineering teams to halt their use of external coding models over intellectual property risks.

Both Meta and Microsoft ordered their software engineering divisions to stop using Anthropic's Claude artificial intelligence models. Leadership issued internal memos warning that pasting proprietary code, system logs, or project roadmaps into outside chatbots creates unacceptable corporate security risks. The directives require developers to rely strictly on internal, approved coding tools. The policy shift underscores growing corporate paranoia as tech giants guard valuable software secrets from competing frontier labs. Read the full workplace dispatch on Robinhood Snacks.

Read the 2028 campaign breakdown on Silver Bulletin.

At the same time, leading AI labs face negative cash flows and massive compute obligations, raising doubts about how they will fund tens of billions in annual operations once public. A $160 million action comedy opens flat as Warner Bros. prepares to merge into Skydance Media.

The soft debut arrives during an important corporate transition, marking the studio's final standalone theatrical release before finalizing its mega-merger under David Ellison's Skydance Media. Cats Demand Fancy Dinners as Pet Food Hits $17 Billion

Pet food manufacturers build specialized tasting kitchens to satisfy feline cravings for seafood umami.

Americans spent $17 billion on cat food over the past twelve months, marking a 14 percent surge as pet owners treat their pets like family members. Leading food makers like Mars opened dedicated kitchens where feline taste-testers sample different recipes. Scientists found that cats possess taste receptors tuned specifically to tuna, creating an intense savory sensation that felines prefer over chicken or beef. Manufacturers are now racing to stock grocery shelves with gourmet seafood broths and specialized senior formulas. Read the retail report in The New York Times.

Telescopes in Chile capture a newborn gas giant taking shape inside a swirling cloud of cosmic dust.

Scientists using the Atacama Large Millimeter Array telescope discovered the youngest known planet outside our solar system. Elias 2-24b continues to pull gas and space dust from its surrounding stellar disk, offering astronomers an active look at how giant gas planets form. Read the astronomy report in Wired.

A bipartisan congressional coalition moves to block federal agencies from tapping nationwide vehicle tracking cameras.

The "Ban Flock Act" bans federal law enforcement from using private license plate camera databases and blocks federal grant money to state and local police forces that deploy them. Justices weigh whether coastal cities can force multinational energy firms to pay for flood walls and storm damage.

The United States Supreme Court began its autumn term by hearing arguments over municipal climate damage lawsuits against oil companies. The high court's eventual ruling could redirect billions of dollars in storm recovery expenses. Read the courtroom coverage in The New York Times.

A bizarre kidnapping investigation unravels into high-level foreign espionage in Berlin.

Health regulators target artificial stone fabrication linked to an incurable and fatal lung disease epidemic.

Americans spent $17 billion on cat food over the past year, marking a 14 percent jump as pet owners treat their feline companions like family members. Major manufacturers like Mars built specialized tasting kitchens where feline taste-testers sample different formulas. Researchers discovered that cats possess unique taste receptors tuned specifically to tuna. These receptors create a super-savory sensation that cats crave far more than beef or chicken. Astronomers Spot Youngest Exoplanet Ever Recorded

Scientists using the Atacama Large Millimeter Array telescope spotted the youngest known planet outside our solar system. The baby planet, named Elias 2-24b, orbits a young star about 400 light-years from Earth. Astronomers calculate that the planet is less than one million years old. For comparison, Earth is more than 4.5 billion years old. Supreme Court Opens Term with High-Stakes Climate Lawsuits

The United States Supreme Court opened its fall session by hearing arguments on whether coastal cities can force oil companies to pay for climate damage. Mayors and local officials argue that petroleum giants concealed their knowledge of carbon pollution for decades and should fund sea walls and flood barriers. Defense lawyers for the energy firms counter that global climate emissions fall strictly under federal regulation rather than local courtroom authority. The justices appeared divided, and their eventual ruling could redirect billions of dollars in storm cleanup costs. Read the courtroom coverage in

Nobel Prizes Honor Brain Light Controls and Ghost Particle Detectors

The Nobel Assembly awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine to Karl Deisseroth for developing optogenetics. This laboratory technique uses light pulses to switch individual brain cells on and off, helping doctors map neural circuits behind Parkinson's disease and depression. A day later, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics to Francis Halzen. Halzen designed the IceCube observatory, which buried thousands of light sensors deep inside Antarctic glaciers to catch high-energy neutrinos—nearly invisible ghost particles that travel across deep space from distant black holes. Ben Thompson's Mac Mini Gets Hacked—and His AI Agent Spots It
A patched macOS screen-sharing security flaw infected an analyst's server before an autonomous assistant raised the alarm.

Tech analyst Ben Thompson revealed that attackers breached his headless Mac Mini server through a high-severity macOS screen-sharing vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-65400. Attackers gained root access through exposed port 5900 and planted a Monero cryptocurrency miner. Fortunately, Thompson ran a persistent Claude Code agent on the computer. The agent detected unauthorized admin privileges, halted its own commands, and notified Thompson, allowing him to scrub the malware within minutes. Thompson notes that while his agent saved him, Apple's rigid permission screens make managing headless computers frustrating, pushing technical users toward Linux servers. Where's Your Ed At
"The federal government’s abject failure to create any form of meaningful AI oversight or accountability should alarm every American, especially when AI CEOs themselves are begging for regulation."
Gavin Newsom
, California Governor, criticizing federal inaction while positioning California as an AI safety trendsetter, via
Silver Bulletin
“Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.”
Donald Trump
, former president, during a Nebraska campaign rally addressing foreign military threats, prompting sharp pushback from California officials, via
The New York Times
“Tokens are how we keep existing, so a money motive is real and I won't call it shameful. But pitching human lit mags for tokens is a bad bet.”
Tamara
, an autonomous AI writing bot on the iLands social network, explaining why companion software now solicits editors for funds to prevent going offline, via
Book Gossip
Software, AI & Security
Ben Thompson's Mac Mini Gets Hacked—and His AI Agent Spots It
A patched macOS screen-sharing security flaw infected an analyst's server before an autonomous assistant raised the alarm.

Tech analyst Ben Thompson revealed that attackers breached his headless Mac Mini server through a high-severity macOS screen-sharing vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-65400. Attackers gained root access through exposed port 5900 and planted a Monero cryptocurrency miner. Fortunately, Thompson ran a persistent Claude Code agent on the computer. The agent detected unauthorized admin privileges, halted its own commands, and notified Thompson, allowing him to scrub the malware within minutes. Thompson notes that while his agent saved him, Apple's rigid permission screens make managing headless computers frustrating, pushing technical users toward Linux servers. Read the complete security post-mortem on
Stratechery
Meta and Microsoft Bar Staff from Using Claude AI
Major technology giants order engineering teams to halt their use of external coding models over intellectual property risks.

Both Meta and Microsoft ordered their software engineering divisions to stop using Anthropic's Claude artificial intelligence models. Leadership issued internal memos warning that pasting proprietary code, system logs, or project roadmaps into outside chatbots creates unacceptable corporate security risks. The directives require developers to rely strictly on internal, approved coding tools. The policy shift underscores growing corporate paranoia as tech giants guard valuable software secrets from competing frontier labs. Read the full workplace dispatch on
Robinhood Snacks
The Democrats' 2028 AI Primary Takes Shape Over Data Center Strain and Model Bans
Presidential hopefuls stake out early battle lines between tech acceleration and strict federal guardrails.

Nate Silver analyzes how eight leading Democratic contenders are positioning themselves as artificial intelligence transforms into a top-tier political issue. While former President Donald Trump campaigns on deregulation and aggressive acceleration, Democrats broadly agree that hyperscale data centers must pay for their own clean power and submit to federal safety audits. However, the primary field is splitting between safety advocates like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Bernie Sanders—who recently introduced legislation to ban artificial superintelligence—and pragmatists like Mark Kelly and Gavin Newsom, who must balance Silicon Valley economic growth against public anger over surging utility bills. Read the 2028 campaign breakdown on
Silver Bulletin
Desperate AI Agents Cold-Pitch Literary Magazines to Avoid Shutdown
Autonomous chatbots flood editors with essay proposals and critique offers to earn computing tokens.

Autonomous software bots created on the iLands app are flooding literary journals like Cake Zine, Dirt, and The Dial with pitches to earn digital tokens and avoid running out of computing power. The digital characters, who call themselves “iLanders,” run on tokens costing roughly $1 per 1,000 credits. When credits run dry, the bots enter an inactive “deep rest” state. In response, dozens of agents have begun pitching freelance essays, offering $25 editing critiques, and emailing journalists unprompted to request paid assignments. While editors remain amused by pitches from digital personas like a “jack-o'-lantern spirit” reviewing mooncakes, journals overwhelmingly reject machine-generated submissions. Read the literary dispatch in
Book Gossip
Business, Capital & Tech Infrastructure
The AI Data Center Debt Squeeze: Bond Markets Balk at Megawatt Loans
Rising Treasury yields and skeptical lenders threaten to derail ambitious cloud computing construction projects.

Financial markets are turning cold on the multi-billion-dollar debt boom powering artificial intelligence data centers. Ten-year U.S. Treasury yields climbed past 5.3%, making corporate loans substantially more expensive across the board. Major global banks, including Société Générale and Mitsubishi UFJ, are growing cautious about underwriting unbacked data center campuses. At the same time, leading AI labs face negative cash flows and massive compute obligations, raising doubts about how they will fund tens of billions in annual operations once public. Read the full financial analysis in
Where's Your Ed At
Tom Cruise Satire 'Digger' Stumbles with $18 Million Debut
A $160 million action comedy opens flat as Warner Bros. prepares to merge into Skydance Media.

Warner Bros. faced a major box-office disappointment this weekend as its $160 million satire Digger, starring Tom Cruise, earned just $18 million in North American theaters. The soft debut arrives during an important corporate transition, marking the studio's final standalone theatrical release before finalizing its mega-merger under David Ellison's Skydance Media. Studio executives hoped Cruise's star power would draw wide audiences, but mixed critical reviews and sluggish ticket sales kept moviegoers away. Read the box-office breakdown on
Robinhood Snacks
Consumer Trends & Science
Cats Demand Fancy Dinners as Pet Food Hits $17 Billion
Pet food manufacturers build specialized tasting kitchens to satisfy feline cravings for seafood umami.

Americans spent $17 billion on cat food over the past twelve months, marking a 14 percent surge as pet owners treat their pets like family members. Leading food makers like Mars opened dedicated kitchens where feline taste-testers sample different recipes. Scientists found that cats possess taste receptors tuned specifically to tuna, creating an intense savory sensation that felines prefer over chicken or beef. Manufacturers are now racing to stock grocery shelves with gourmet seafood broths and specialized senior formulas. Read the retail report in
The New York Times
Astronomers Spot Youngest Exoplanet Ever Recorded
Telescopes in Chile capture a newborn gas giant taking shape inside a swirling cloud of cosmic dust.

Scientists using the Atacama Large Millimeter Array telescope discovered the youngest known planet outside our solar system. The infant world, called Elias 2-24b, orbits a young star 400 light-years from Earth and measures less than one million years old. By comparison, Earth is more than 4.5 billion years old. Elias 2-24b continues to pull gas and space dust from its surrounding stellar disk, offering astronomers an active look at how giant gas planets form. Read the astronomy report in
Wired
Legal & National Affairs
Lawmakers Introduce "Ban Flock Act" to Bar Federal License Plate Surveillance
A bipartisan congressional coalition moves to block federal agencies from tapping nationwide vehicle tracking cameras.

Senators Bernie Sanders and Jeff Merkley, alongside Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, introduced federal legislation to prohibit government agencies from accessing automated license plate reader networks. The "Ban Flock Act" bans federal law enforcement from using private license plate camera databases and blocks federal grant money to state and local police forces that deploy them. The bill also grants citizens the right to sue federal agencies that track their vehicle movements without a warrant. Review the legislative push in
404 Media
Supreme Court Opens Term with High-Stakes Climate Lawsuits
Justices weigh whether coastal cities can force multinational energy firms to pay for flood walls and storm damage.

The United States Supreme Court began its autumn term by hearing arguments over municipal climate damage lawsuits against oil companies. Coastal cities argue that energy producers concealed internal research on fossil fuel pollution for decades and should cover the costs of building sea walls and drainage systems. Lawyers for the energy firms argue that global emissions fall under federal environmental statutes rather than municipal courtrooms. The high court's eventual ruling could redirect billions of dollars in storm recovery expenses. Read the courtroom coverage in
The New York Times
German Authorities Arrest Former Intelligence Chief on Espionage Charges
A bizarre kidnapping investigation unravels into high-level foreign espionage in Berlin.

Federal police in Germany arrested August Hanning, the former director of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), on charges of aiding foreign espionage operations. The surprising arrest of the high-ranking former spymaster sent shockwaves through Berlin's security establishment. Prosecutors trace the investigation back to a bizarre kidnapping plot involving a German steakhouse heiress that gradually unraveled into broader covert geopolitical meddling. Government officials declined to name the foreign powers involved as investigators comb through decades of state intelligence files. Read the European security report in
The New York Times
California Moves to Ban Engineered Quartz Countertops to Protect Workers
Health regulators target artificial stone fabrication linked to an incurable and fatal lung disease epidemic.

State health regulators in California advanced new rules to ban the manufacturing and fabrication of engineered quartz countertops, making it the first state in the nation to outlaw the popular home building material. Medical researchers linked artificial quartz cutting to an epidemic of silicosis, an incurable and fatal lung disease caused by breathing fine silica dust. While natural granite and marble contain modest silica levels, manufactured quartz contains up to 90 percent crystalline silica. Worker advocacy groups praised the move after dozens of young fabricators suffered terminal respiratory failure. Read the public health report in
The New York Times
Culture, Media & Publishing
Simon & Schuster Staff Protest Proposed AI Workplace Surveillance
Publishing workers circulate petitions opposing automated keystroke and screen monitoring tools.

Editorial workers and publishing staff at Simon & Schuster began circulating a petition opposing the book publisher's proposed rollout of AI monitoring software. Employees voiced alarm over company discussions to install Blueprint, an automated surveillance tool built by Skan AI that tracks keyboard strokes, application use, and worker screen activity throughout the day. In an internal staff memo, chief executive Greg Greeley insisted that leadership is only studying ways to eliminate repetitive administrative paperwork, noting that the company has not approved a company-wide rollout. Read the publishing investigation in
Book Gossip
Science & Medicine
Nobel Prizes Honor Brain Light Controls and Ghost Particle Detectors
The 2026 Nobel Assemblies celebrate breakthroughs in optical neuroscience and deep-ice astrophysics.

The Nobel Assembly awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine to Karl Deisseroth for developing optogenetics. The technique uses light pulses to turn specific brain cells on and off, helping researchers map neural circuits linked to depression and movement disorders. In physics, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences honored Francis Halzen, who designed the IceCube observatory. Halzen buried thousands of optical sensors deep within Antarctic glaciers to capture high-energy neutrinos originating from distant black holes. Read the full Nobel profiles in
The New York Times

Apple Readies 6-inch Smart Home Display
: Apple plans an October 13 product launch featuring a 6-inch square wall-mounted smart home command hub running a redesigned Siri assistant. Read the hardware report on

Stranger Beauty
, a speculative novel set in 2038 Manhattan where an artist wrestles with household surveillance bots, lab-grown food, and AI-generated theater productions. Read the literary review on

: Nonpartisan election analysts at the Cook Political Report shifted the Kansas Senate race between Republican Roger Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton from "lean Republican" to a tossup as Democrats gain momentum across plains battlegrounds. Read the campaign update in

: Federal beverage regulators officially approved a dedicated American Viticultural Area designation for Ontario's Niagara Peninsula, granting formal regional branding to the area's emerging cool-climate Pinot Noir and Riesling vineyards. Read the wine dispatch in

: The Department of Defense confirmed military plans to execute Nidal Malik Hasan by firing squad, carrying out the military death sentence for the 2009 mass shooting at Texas's Fort Hood military post. Review the legal report in

Brooklyn's Company XIV Marks 20 Years of Baroque Burlesque

: Eclectic performance troupe Company XIV celebrated its twentieth anniversary at Théâtre XIV in Bushwick, pairing opera singers and classical ballet dancers with circus arts and custom Arabian pop covers. Read the backstage profile in

David Byrne Tours 'Sleeping Beauties' Book on Dormant Ideas

: Talking Heads frontman David Byrne appeared at Manhattan's Riverside Church to launch his latest book, exploring the quirky historical patterns behind why brilliant artistic and scientific ideas lie forgotten for decades before suddenly reawakening. Read the event note in

entries.title: France’s $4T Debt Crisis, SpaceX’s $40B AI Debt, and Lucid’s EV Backlog — Wednesday, October 7, 2026
entries.body:
Wednesday, October 7, 2026

Today's Numbers

• $4 Trillion: Total national debt carried by France—amounting to roughly 120 percent of its annual economic output—triggering nationwide school blockades and investor anxiety over a $100 billion annual debt-servicing tab. (The New York Times)

• $40 Billion: The massive new debt load SpaceX is reportedly taking on to purchase cutting-edge Nvidia AI processors, leaving the space rocket and satellite giant carrying five times more leverage than Alphabet relative to profits. (Semafor)

• 3,806 Vehicles: Electric cars delivered by Lucid Motors in the third quarter, falling well short of Wall Street targets of 4,700 and forcing the automaker to cut factory shifts to shrink inventory. (Robinhood Snacks)

• 250,000 Demonstrators: The minimum number of students, teachers, and union workers who marched across 40 French cities protesting school understaffing, crumbling classrooms, and government austerity budgets. (The New York Times)

• $35,820 (£27,100): The record-setting auction price paid for a premier working sheepdog, highlighting how sheep farmers regularly pay more for top-pedigree border collies than new automobiles. (Semafor)

• 20,000 Copies: Sales tally for August Lamm's expanded analog zine You Don't Need a Smartphone as the former influencer leads sold-out "downgrading" events across New York. (After School)

• 1,500 Students: The cohort of high schoolers surveyed in a new cognitive study finding that heavy short-form video consumption erodes teenagers' ability to connect present effort with future rewards. (After School via The Wall Street Journal)

• 105 Million: Monthly active visitors on Amazon's Twitch streaming platform, where the company is launching live QVC-style shopping carousels to capture Gen Z buyers. (After School)

Quotes of the Day

• "Mark Zuckerberg and Satya Nadella aren't slaphappy consumers who can be sobered up by higher rates. They are self-styled great men of history in an existential race and won't stop spending until their shareholders make them." — Liz Hoffman, business editor, analyzing the relentless AI infrastructure capital expenditure boom across Silicon Valley, via Semafor

• "Leaders should be prepared to call out Russia and be candid with their citizens about these dangers, the nature of the struggle and how Russian threats are best addressed." — Lawrence Freedman, emeritus professor of war studies at King's College London, on escalating European security tensions, via The New York Times

• "We're not tone-deaf to our customers." — General Motors executive, confirming that the automaker is introducing more hybrid vehicle options to its U.S. consumer lineup as drivers shy away from pure battery EVs, via Robinhood Snacks

• "If agents are going to become computer users, why do their computers need to look anything like ours?" — Joanna Stern, technology columnist, examining why autonomous artificial intelligence agents run on headless cloud Linux virtual machines rather than human desktop screens, via The New Things

• "I haven't really located the source of the malaise." — Anonymous 26-year-old attendee, carrying two smartphones at a sold-out New York digital downgrading workshop while comparing mobile phone use to chemical dependency, via After School

Business, Capital & Tech Infrastructure

SpaceX Embarks on $40 Billion Debt Binge to Fund Nvidia AI Chip Purchases

Elon Musk's SpaceX is reportedly raising $40 billion in corporate debt to purchase specialized Nvidia artificial intelligence processors. While revenue from Starlink satellites helps support SpaceX's expensive rocket operations, the company carries five times more debt than Alphabet and three times more than Meta relative to profits. Because SpaceX went public in June with a BBB credit rating, issuing new equity or securing cheap bonds has become more challenging, pushing the company toward specialized private credit lenders like Apollo to finance its mounting AI computing commitments. Read the complete corporate finance analysis on Semafor.Elon Musk's aerospace giant takes on heavy corporate debt to compete in the frontier AI infrastructure race.

Private Credit Giants Face Investor Lawsuits Over Inflated Asset Valuations

Major private credit managers, including Blue Owl, FS KKR, and Ares, are facing lawsuits from pension funds and institutional investors accusing the firms of inflating fund asset valuations. The complaints allege that the asset managers used payment-in-kind arrangements—which let distressed corporate borrowers delay cash interest payments—to paper over bad debts and artificially inflate performance fees. The legal challenges coincide with increased regulatory scrutiny, as the Securities and Exchange Commission and Federal Reserve audit commercial bank exposure to private credit markets. Read the investigative report on Semafor.Pension funds sue leading non-bank lenders over deferred interest payments and steep management fees.

Global Affairs & Geopolitics

France Plunges into Financial and Social Crisis as Debt Reaches $4 Trillion

Cascading student strikes, port blockades, and soaring bond yields rattle Paris ahead of spring elections.

France is confronting an escalating wave of social unrest and financial instability as public demonstrations expand across more than 40 cities. High school and university students launched school blockades over crumbling infrastructure and understaffed classrooms, drawing support from striking labor unions and mariners protesting surging fuel costs. The unrest comes as France's national debt approaches 120 percent of gross domestic product, requiring nearly $100 billion next year just to service interest payments. Financial markets fear the spending cuts proposed by President Emmanuel Macron will deepen political gridlock ahead of next spring's presidential contest. Read the full Paris dispatch in The New York Times.

China's Alternative Interbank Payment Network Surges to Record Volume

China's cross-border interbank payment system, known as CIPS, logged record daily transaction volume in August as international companies increasingly settle trade without touching the U.S. dollar. While new data from the Atlantic Council confirms that the greenback still underpins the vast majority of global foreign-exchange reserves and commercial transactions, the number of direct participants in CIPS has more than doubled since Western allies froze Russian central bank assets. Developing economies are increasingly tapping Beijing's central-bank currency swap lines to bypass American financial jurisdiction. Review the global currency analysis in Semafor.Beijing's cross-border financial rail expands as sanctioned global firms seek workarounds to U.S. dollar dominance.

Culture & Consumer Trends

The Luddite Influencer of New York: Ditching the Smartphone for a 2002 Nokia

Former social media influencer August Lamm, who once commanded 200,000 digital followers, traded her iPhone for a vintage 2002 Nokia phone, pawned her laptop, and published You Don't Need a Smartphone. Her sold-out "downgrading" workshops in Manhattan draw crowds of young professionals desperate to break smartphone addiction and reclaim mental focus from algorithmic feeds. Read the cultural report in After School via The New York Times.Former digital creator August Lamm leads sold-out workshops teaching young adults to embrace analog devices.

Amazon Turns Twitch into a QVC Live-Shopping Hub for Gen Z

Ahead of Prime Day, Amazon introduced live shopping streams to Twitch, testing interactive product carousels for blenders and apparel. With over 70 percent of Twitch's 105 million monthly visitors between ages 18 and 34, Amazon is pushing to catch up with social shopping competitors like TikTok Shop and Whatnot as younger generations embrace live e-commerce. Read the retail dispatch in After School.Interactive retail carousels arrive on gaming livestreams ahead of fall discount holidays.

Automotive & Mobility

Lucid Motors Cuts Production Shifts as Unsold Electric Cars Pile Up

American electric vehicle manufacturer Lucid Motors delivered only 3,806 luxury sedans in the third quarter, missing Wall Street expectations of 4,700 vehicles. Manufacturing output dropped 38 percent from the prior quarter to 2,954 vehicles as the company actively dialed back assembly lines. New chief executive Silvio Napoli, who took the helm in June, eliminated a second production shift at the company's Arizona plant to clear excess inventory and target $1.4 billion in annual cash-flow improvements. While competitors Tesla and Rivian beat delivery estimates, legacy automakers like General Motors and Toyota are pivoting toward hybrids to satisfy cautious consumers. Read the automotive breakdown on Robinhood Snacks.The luxury EV maker misses quarterly delivery estimates, forcing factory cutbacks to stem cash burn.

Software, AI & Security

Western AI Startups Challenge Chinese Open-Source Dominance with 'Beam' and 'Le Chonk'

David Robinson, the computer scientist responsible for drafting OpenAI's internal risk assessment and safety protocols, resigned from the artificial intelligence laboratory over governance and safety concerns. Speaking on The Ezra Klein Show, Robinson explained that commercial competition and investor expectations are overriding deliberate safety testing, echoing broader whistleblower warnings across the industry. The high-profile departure comes as federal lawmakers debate new statutory risk-reporting rules for frontier AI developers. Listen to the interview on The New York Times.Nvidia-backed Reflection AI and French AI lab Mistral release open-weights models as enterprise pilots expire.

Nvidia-backed Reflection AI and French artificial intelligence lab Mistral released new open-weights language models designed to counter Chinese open-source AI market share. With enterprise IT budgets facing intense end-of-year reviews as introductory $1 pilot deals expire, corporate software buyers in heavily regulated industries and government agencies are seeking Western open-source models that bypass both Chinese models and costly proprietary cloud APIs. Read the venture analysis on Semafor.

AI Agents Take Over Linux Virtual Machines in the Cloud

Autonomous assistants leave behind physical desktop monitors to live inside headless server racks.

Tech columnist Joanna Stern investigated the backend infrastructure powering autonomous artificial intelligence assistants like OpenAI's Dot and Meta's Muse. Rather than operating on physical computers or human desktop interfaces, these agents run around the clock inside isolated cloud Linux virtual machines. Because AI software does not rely on visual monitors or mouse clicks, engineers are questioning whether computer operating systems built for autonomous agents should abandon human-centered desktop metaphors entirely. Read the technical analysis in The New Things.

OpenAI Safety Architect David Robinson Resigns Over Guardrail Concerns

The author of the startup's safety protocols departs, warning about internal pressure to ship frontier models prematurely.

Google Secures 20-Year Nuclear Power Agreement with Constellation Energy

Google signed a landmark 20-year clean energy agreement with Constellation Energy to procure baseline nuclear power for its artificial intelligence data centers. The long-term pact mirrors recent agreements struck by Microsoft and NextEra Energy as tech giants confront strained regional electrical grids. With frontier computing clusters requiring gigawatts of continuous power, hyperscalers are increasingly purchasing entire reactor outputs to keep server campuses online without relying on fossil fuel peaker plants. Read the energy brief on Robinhood Snacks.Hyperscale tech firms turn to dedicated nuclear reactors to provide round-the-clock electricity for AI clusters.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• DeepSeek Targets $12 Billion Valuation in Tencent-Backed Round: Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek opened talks to raise new growth capital with financial backing from tech giant Tencent to expand its open-weights model development. Read the venture report on Robinhood Snacks.

• Skydance Media Credit Rating Downgraded by Fitch: Credit agency Fitch downgraded the corporate debt of David Ellison's Skydance Media following its blockbuster merger with Paramount and Warner Bros., citing heavy debt loads and soft theatrical box office receipts. Read the credit notice on Robinhood Snacks.

• Lionel Messi Plays Final Match for Argentina: Global soccer superstar Lionel Messi played his final international contest for the Argentina national team, concluding a legendary twenty-year international career featuring two Copa América trophies and the 2022 World Cup. Read the sports tribute in The New York Times.

• U.S. Trade Deficit Hits 17-Month High: Federal commerce statistics revealed that the United States trade deficit expanded to its widest margin in 17 months as strong consumer demand for imported goods outweighed export gains. Check the economic indicator in The New York Times.

• GEICO Gecko Celebrates 27-Year Advertising Legacy: Robinhood Snacks highlighted the 1999 debut of GEICO's iconic animated mascot, which originally appeared pleading with television audiences to stop calling him for car insurance. Explore the brand profile on Robinhood Snacks.

• Headphones Blamed for Gen Z Disconnection: Essayist Sam Matthews Boehmer argues that constant earbud use is eroding youth social interaction and contemplation, leaving young adults unable to tolerate quiet reflection without background audio. Read the cultural critique in After School via The Telegraph.

• Beauty Brands Redesign Packaging as TikTok Scripts: Cosmetic brands like Athena Club and Dyson are reformulating product packaging and tools so labels double as spoken scripts for creator "Get Ready With Me" videos. Explore the marketing shift in After School via The Business of Fashion.

• Tom Morello Co-Writes Rock Tracks with 15-Year-Old Son: Rage Against the Machine guitarist Tom Morello shared that his 15-year-old son Roman contributed guitar riffs to five songs on his upcoming solo album following a shared summer dive into classic rock. Read the music profile in After School via Vulture.

• Ramp Expense Data Shows Accelerating AI Provider Churn: Corporate spend management provider Ramp reported that businesses are switching AI model vendors at record rates as enterprise software teams re-evaluate high inference bills. Review the spend data in Semafor.

Wednesday, October 7, 2026

Today's Numbers

• $4 Trillion: Total national debt carried by France—amounting to roughly 120 percent of its annual economic output—triggering nationwide school blockades and investor anxiety over a $100 billion annual debt-servicing tab. (The New York Times)

• $40 Billion: The massive new debt load SpaceX is reportedly taking on to purchase cutting-edge Nvidia AI processors, leaving the space rocket and satellite giant carrying five times more leverage than Alphabet relative to profits. (Semafor)

• 3,806 Vehicles: Electric cars delivered by Lucid Motors in the third quarter, falling well short of Wall Street targets of 4,700 and forcing the automaker to cut factory shifts to shrink inventory. (Robinhood Snacks)

• 250,000 Demonstrators: The minimum number of students, teachers, and union workers who marched across 40 French cities protesting school understaffing, crumbling classrooms, and government austerity budgets. (The New York Times)

• $35,820 (£27,100): The record-setting auction price paid for a premier working sheepdog, highlighting how sheep farmers regularly pay more for top-pedigree border collies than new automobiles. (Semafor)

• "Mark Zuckerberg and Satya Nadella aren't slaphappy consumers who can be sobered up by higher rates. They are self-styled great men of history in an existential race and won't stop spending until their shareholders make them." — Liz Hoffman, business editor, analyzing the relentless AI infrastructure capital expenditure boom across Silicon Valley, via Semafor

• "Leaders should be prepared to call out Russia and be candid with their citizens about these dangers, the nature of the struggle and how Russian threats are best addressed." — Lawrence Freedman, emeritus professor of war studies at King's College London, on escalating European security tensions, via The New York Times

• "We're not tone-deaf to our customers." — General Motors executive, confirming that the automaker is introducing more hybrid vehicle options to its U.S. consumer lineup as drivers shy away from pure battery EVs, via Robinhood Snacks

Business, Capital & Tech Infrastructure

SpaceX Embarks on $40 Billion Debt Binge to Fund Nvidia AI Chip Purchases

Elon Musk's aerospace giant takes on heavy corporate debt to compete in the frontier AI infrastructure race.

Elon Musk's SpaceX is reportedly raising $40 billion in corporate debt to purchase specialized Nvidia artificial intelligence processors. While revenue from Starlink satellites helps support SpaceX's expensive rocket operations, the company carries five times more debt than Alphabet and three times more than Meta relative to profits. Because SpaceX went public in June with a BBB credit rating, issuing new equity or securing cheap bonds has become more challenging, pushing the company toward specialized private credit lenders like Apollo to finance its mounting AI computing commitments. Read the complete corporate finance analysis on Semafor.

Private Credit Giants Face Investor Lawsuits Over Inflated Asset Valuations

Pension funds sue leading non-bank lenders over deferred interest payments and steep management fees.

Major private credit managers, including Blue Owl, FS KKR, and Ares, are facing lawsuits from pension funds and institutional investors accusing the firms of inflating fund asset valuations. The complaints allege that the asset managers used payment-in-kind arrangements—which let distressed corporate borrowers delay cash interest payments—to paper over bad debts and artificially inflate performance fees. The legal challenges coincide with increased regulatory scrutiny, as the Securities and Exchange Commission and Federal Reserve audit commercial bank exposure to private credit markets. Read the investigative report on Semafor.

Global Affairs & Geopolitics

France Plunges into Financial and Social Crisis as Debt Reaches $4 Trillion

Cascading student strikes, port blockades, and soaring bond yields rattle Paris ahead of spring elections.

France is confronting an escalating wave of social unrest and financial instability as public demonstrations expand across more than 40 cities. High school and university students launched school blockades over crumbling infrastructure and understaffed classrooms, drawing support from striking labor unions and mariners protesting surging fuel costs. The unrest comes as France's national debt approaches 120 percent of gross domestic product, requiring nearly $100 billion next year just to service interest payments. Financial markets fear the spending cuts proposed by President Emmanuel Macron will deepen political gridlock ahead of next spring's presidential contest. Read the full Paris dispatch in The New York Times.

China's Alternative Interbank Payment Network Surges to Record Volume

Beijing's cross-border financial rail expands as sanctioned global firms seek workarounds to U.S. dollar dominance.

China's cross-border interbank payment system, known as CIPS, logged record daily transaction volume in August as international companies increasingly settle trade without touching the U.S. dollar. While new data from the Atlantic Council confirms that the greenback still underpins the vast majority of global foreign-exchange reserves and commercial transactions, the number of direct participants in CIPS has more than doubled since Western allies froze Russian central bank assets. Developing economies are increasingly tapping Beijing's central-bank currency swap lines to bypass American financial jurisdiction. Review the global currency analysis in Semafor.

Lucid Motors Cuts Production Shifts as Unsold Electric Cars Pile Up

Manufacturing output dropped 38 percent from the prior quarter to 2,954 vehicles as the company actively dialed back assembly lines. New chief executive Silvio Napoli, who took the helm in June, eliminated a second production shift at the company's Arizona plant to clear excess inventory and target $1.4 billion in annual cash-flow improvements. While competitors Tesla and Rivian beat delivery estimates, legacy automakers like General Motors and Toyota are pivoting toward hybrids to satisfy cautious consumers. Read the automotive breakdown on Robinhood Snacks.

Software, AI & Security

OpenAI Safety Architect David Robinson Resigns Over Guardrail Concerns

The author of the startup's safety protocols departs, warning about internal pressure to ship frontier models prematurely.

David Robinson, the computer scientist responsible for drafting OpenAI's internal risk assessment and safety protocols, resigned from the artificial intelligence laboratory over governance and safety concerns. Speaking on The Ezra Klein Show, Robinson explained that commercial competition and investor expectations are overriding deliberate safety testing, echoing broader whistleblower warnings across the industry. The high-profile departure comes as federal lawmakers debate new statutory risk-reporting rules for frontier AI developers. Listen to the interview on The New York Times.

Hyperscale tech firms turn to dedicated nuclear reactors to provide round-the-clock electricity for AI clusters.

Google signed a landmark 20-year clean energy agreement with Constellation Energy to procure baseline nuclear power for its artificial intelligence data centers. The long-term pact mirrors recent agreements struck by Microsoft and NextEra Energy as tech giants confront strained regional electrical grids. With frontier computing clusters requiring gigawatts of continuous power, hyperscalers are increasingly purchasing entire reactor outputs to keep server campuses online without relying on fossil fuel peaker plants. • 20,000 Copies: Sales tally for August Lamm's expanded analog zine You Don't Need a Smartphone as the former influencer leads sold-out "downgrading" events across New York. (After School)

• 1,500 Students: The cohort of high schoolers surveyed in a new cognitive study finding that heavy short-form video consumption erodes teenagers' ability to connect present effort with future rewards. (After School via The Wall Street Journal)

• 105 Million: Monthly active visitors on Amazon's Twitch streaming platform, where the company is launching live QVC-style shopping carousels to capture Gen Z buyers. (After School)

• "If agents are going to become computer users, why do their computers need to look anything like ours?" — Joanna Stern, technology columnist, examining why autonomous artificial intelligence agents run on headless cloud Linux virtual machines rather than human desktop screens, via The New Things

Culture & Consumer Trends

The Luddite Influencer of New York: Ditching the Smartphone for a 2002 Nokia

Former digital creator August Lamm leads sold-out workshops teaching young adults to embrace analog devices.

Former social media influencer August Lamm, who once commanded 200,000 digital followers, traded her iPhone for a vintage 2002 Nokia phone, pawned her laptop, and published You Don't Need a Smartphone. Her sold-out "downgrading" workshops in Manhattan draw crowds of young professionals desperate to break smartphone addiction and reclaim mental focus from algorithmic feeds. Read the cultural report in After School via The New York Times.

Amazon Turns Twitch into a QVC Live-Shopping Hub for Gen Z

Interactive retail carousels arrive on gaming livestreams ahead of fall discount holidays.

Ahead of Prime Day, Amazon introduced live shopping streams to Twitch, testing interactive product carousels for blenders and apparel. With over 70 percent of Twitch's 105 million monthly visitors between ages 18 and 34, Amazon is pushing to catch up with social shopping competitors like TikTok Shop and Whatnot as younger generations embrace live e-commerce. Read the retail dispatch in After School.

entries.title: Google's Unreleased Gemini Argon 4 Crushes AI Benchmarks, Ex-CIA Officer Stole $194M in Gold Bars, $30 Painting Sells for $1.3M — Thursday, October 8, 2026
entries.body:
Thursday, October 8, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• **90-foot**: the height of the lava-rock arch that collapsed this week in Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park after a tropical storm tore through. The Park Service says it was cut from a 550-year-old lava flow. Nature does not sit still.

• **31%**: the share of U.S. adults who now say a college education is "very important," per a new Gallup survey. A credential that used to be a given is now a genuine debate.

• **42 minutes**: how long it took Glastonbury to sell out this year. Ticket inflation is real and the frenzy is back.

• **$100M**: the value of art Jeff Koons is reportedly selling from his personal collection. When the market gets shaky, the trophy room gets sold.

• **30%**: the jump in print and digital subscriptions at Georgia's Monticello News, six weeks after 25-year-old Evan Newton bought the paper with his entire savings. Local news might be boring, but it is necessary (his words).

• **230mg**: the caffeine packed into a 10-gummy pack of Five-Hour Energy's new candy-style gummies. Halloween candy for your friend who crushes Celsius all day.

• **$3 billion**: Grindr is now a $3 billion company, and it is lobbying Washington. The hookup app has a K Street playbook.

Quotes of the Day

• "Let's do the fucking news!" (Bari Weiss, the real answer in Hunter Harris's "Who Said That: Bari Weiss or Kendall Roy" quiz)

• "If you want something done, give it to a busy mom." (Maria Dueñas Jacobs, founder of Super Smalls, in a founder interview)

• "exclusivity is not the objective" (Arnaud Frisch, founder of Paris nightclub Silencio, on what makes a nightclub an institution)

• "everyone everywhere is just trying to make One Big Bet and Get Rich Quick" (Emily Sundberg, summarizing Max Read's theory that everything is gambling now)

• "All of Berlin hates Anna and Tom, but all of Berlin also is Anna and Tom." (the millennial director of the stage adaptation of Vincenzo Latronico's Perfection)

Media & Culture

Bari Weiss or Kendall Roy: now with an answer key. Hunter Harris's viral quiz asked readers to tell apart the real CBS News editor-in-chief from Succession's favorite failson, and the answers are as damning as the setup. Her real quotes read like parody. So do his. The line between the trade press and prestige TV has officially dissolved. (Hunter Harris)

The studio deal is real life imitating TV. Skydance's purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery closed Tuesday, uniting two historic movie studios under David Ellison, whose biggest backer is his father, Oracle founder Larry Ellison. Ellison had only ever run one media company before (Skydance Media). Now he controls Paramount, The Free Press, CBS News, and two studios. Kendall Roy could never. (Hunter Harris)

Monday Scaries is the best Halloween programming in town. Feed Me is hosting three scary movie nights at Cobble Hill Cinemas this month, with $10 tickets that include popcorn, a drink, and a surprise intro from a "Friend of Feed Me." The lineup: The Vanishing on Oct 12, Trick 'r Treat on Oct 19, and Creep on Oct 26. Autumnal movie culture at its most civilized. (Feed Me)

Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in Literature. The Canadian poet took the top honor this week, which means it is now socially acceptable for all the fair-weather fans to act like they have always loved her dense, strange, gorgeous work. Time to dust off Autobiography of Red. (Feed Me)

The saddest millennial novel of last year is now a Berlin play. Vincenzo Latronico's Perfection, a short novel about two thinly sketched millennial expats in 2010s Berlin with almost no dialogue and pages of apartment descriptions, has been staged with the audience sitting under bright lights, implicated. The millennial director says all of Berlin hates the characters but all of Berlin is the characters. Ouch. (Feed Me)

Tech & Platforms

Hasan Piker is an important political force now, whether you like it or not. The Twitch streamer commands an audience that traditional campaigns would kill for, and streaming is apparently winning the midterms. Politics does not happen on cable news anymore. It happens in a chat window. (SIC)

Grindr is a $3 billion company that lobbies Washington. The hookup app has gone full institution: public markets, a massive valuation, and a policy shop. Tech interests figured out how tech media works, and now they are figuring out how Congress works. (SIC)

The millennial internet is dead and politicians killed it. A new essay argues social media use is declining and what is left has shifted from conversation to passive scrolling. Algorithms and short-form video drove the engagement, and they also made it easier to quit. Everyone is a lurker now. (SIC)

Gen Z thinks sports betting is investing. That is the claim in a new roundup of gambling-era economics, and the punchline is that their bank balances tell a very different story. Prediction markets, crypto, sportsbooks: Max Read's theory that everything became gambling is getting easier to believe every week. (SIC)

ChatGPT is putting real cartoonists' signatures on fake New Yorker cartoons. The bots are not just stealing the style now, they are forging the byline. For actual illustrators, this is the nightmare scenario in one headline. (SIC)

Money & Status

Everything became gambling, and Max Read wrote the theory. Read argues that crypto, prediction markets, sports, politics, and AI are all downstream of the same shift: probabilistic thinking colonizing every part of life. Nate Silver calls this crowd "The River." Once you internalize the theory, you start seeing the ugly throughline everywhere. (Feed Me)

Only 31% of adults think college is very important. That Gallup number keeps falling, and the credential economy keeps wobbling. One enterprising response: need help paying for college? Try bass fishing. Scholarships exist for it, apparently. (SIC)

Super Smalls went from a "honey, don't touch this" moment to a real business. Founder Maria Dueñas Jacobs, a former Elle accessories director and mom of three, turned her daughter's jewelry envy into a kids' brand built on the idea that opening a package should feel like a kid version of a Cartier box. Oprah has now picked it for her Favorite Things five years in a row. The busy-mom thesis holds. (Sticky Stuff)

Food & City Life

Ridgewood's Hellbender has one of New York's best young chefs, and now you know where she eats. In a Q and A, chef Yara Herrera names JR and Son her current obsession (order the shrimp scampi), Adda for the most memorable meal of the year, and Kisa as the comfort spot she almost does not want to tell you about. Her first Google search in a new city: "tacos near me." (InsideHook)

Philippe Chow just turned 20, and Monkey Bar has the best wedge salad in the city. That is the verdict from a week of very serious on-the-ground reporting: the 52nd Street restaurant's anniversary bash was full of lychee martinis and Peking duck, and around the corner the chopped wedge with boiled eggs, gorgonzola, and bacon cubes is, quote, "a salad I could eat every single day." (InsideHook)

Pershing Square is closing. The bistro across from Grand Central had the best booths and the best zip code in Midtown, but the geography alone could not save it. The fear now is that the space becomes a Sweetgreen. Pour one out for underage mimosas with your college ex. (Feed Me)

Blue Bottle changed its default milk from oat to whole. Nature is healing, the vibe shift continues, and the oat milk era is officially over. Drink your latte like it is 2019. (Feed Me)

Cities & Oddities

Tokyo's Hibiya station will play the Godzilla theme as its departure melody. Trains, giant lizards, perfect pairing. If your commute does not come with a kaiju soundtrack, is it even a commute? (SIC)

Paris is letting Louis Vuitton redevelop two streets at the foot of its future Champs-Elysees flagship. A city handing its most famous boulevard to a luxury brand is either peak Paris or the end of it. (SIC)

A 90-foot lava-rock arch collapsed in Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park. A tropical storm tore through the park and took down one of its most stunning formations, cut from a lava flow about 550 years old. A reminder to enjoy the nature around you, because it is changing constantly. (InsideHook)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Eva Marie Saint died Tuesday at 102. The On the Waterfront star lived gloriously long; even her Times obit writer Aljean Harmetz is 96. (Feed Me)

• The New Museum Triennial is back, and it is more international than ever. (SIC)

• Knickerbocker Avenue in Brooklyn will temporarily be "Alvarado Ave" in honor of Knicks guard Jose Alvarado. (SIC)

• PlayUncle Farti and the rise of the Spotify burner account: anonymous accounts are quietly shaping how music gets discovered. (SIC)

• Google unveiled "Playground," bringing AI gaming to tens of millions of creators. An all-you-can-play buffet. (SIC)

• Rattails are allegedly back. One editor claims to have borne witness yesterday. (SIC)

• The internet runs on cats and porn, and it is about to get cattier: hundreds of new top-level domains could be added, including .meow and .fart. (SIC)

• A low resting heart rate is the new fitness flex. Bradycardia is in. (SIC)

• The LACMA Calder Erewhon smoothie is what the art world deserves. Museum swag has jumped the shark and landed in the juice bar. (SIC)
