The Skydance Squeeze

David Ellison took his victory lap this week. After finally closing the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, a Skydance billboard went up outside Paramount's Times Square headquarters, $SKYD debuted on the New York Stock Exchange, and Ellison took questions at an internal town hall and from reporters, including Status. To detractors he said: "Give us time, and we'll prove it." But one of the deal's biggest early skeptics has been Wall Street, and cutting roughly $80 billion in debt to sustainable levels will not be easy, experts told Status. (Status)

The Power Lines crew is all over the deal's media fallout. This week's episode breaks down what Ellison told reporters about his relationship with Donald Trump, plus what could be read from his answers to Anderson Cooper at the town hall. Tech journalist Casey Newton joins to explain why he is returning to Elon Musk's X years after quitting it, and responds to a surprise message from Kara Swisher. Watch it on YouTube or listen wherever you get podcasts. (Status)

Running Lab

Supershoes helped women more than men, a new study says. Researchers compared elite road performances before and after carbon-plated supershoes arrived, using throwing events as a control for better training and nutrition. Across the 10K, half marathon, and marathon, women's performances improved 4.51% versus 2.62% for men. Another striking stat: by the end of 2025, not a single pre-supershoe women's 10K mark remained in the all-time top 50, while 8.9% of the men's old-era marks still stand. The figures describe elite trends, so individual results still vary with speed, biomechanics, comfort, and shoe design. (Six Minute Mile)

Your race-day superstitions might actually work. A review of 27 studies found about 55% of athletes report at least one superstition, and more than 90% have a sport-specific ritual. The habits may ease anxiety by creating a sense of control, and separate research suggests pre-performance routines can improve results under pressure. Sport psychologist Cindra Kamphoff offers more tools: the "learn, burn, return" method for mistakes, an "I can" or "I am" phrase for self-doubt, gold, silver, and bronze goals for several definitions of success, and fact-checking negative thoughts. (Six Minute Mile)

Style, Food & NYC

Daniel Dele-Tunji is the stylist entrepreneurs call. The 33-year-old menswear veteran has held posts at P. Johnson, Brunello Cucinelli, Stoffa, and Ven. After building out Studio Raisonne's temporary space, he broke off to start his own holistic style consultancy, helping men find their fit, sell old garments, and tailor wardrobes to changing lifestyles. Last month he hosted a West Village pop-up selling archival and vintage finds. Cool as they come, and a hell of a sharp dresser. (InsideHook)

Chef Yara Herrera names her favorite NYC bites. Her best dish of the year: head-on wild Gulf prawns drowning in habanero pineapple butter at Hellbender, her own Ridgewood spot that earned a two-star Times review and an Esquire Best New Restaurants nod since opening in 2024. Herrera, who cut her teeth at Spago and Providence, also dishes on her most memorable meal of the year, where she always lands after midnight, and her first Google search when she touches down somewhere new. (InsideHook)

Is Brandon Flowers the male Lana Del Rey? The Killers frontman performed "An American Dream" from his new album Thrasher on Jimmy Fallon, and InsideHook says the bombastic, sincere rendition recalls the great late-night moments of the past two decades. The piece asks whether Flowers has become the kind of larger-than-life pop auteur the culture used to reserve for Del Rey. (InsideHook)

InsideHook threw a party to launch its new men's style newsletter. The publication gathered a who's who of menswear heads at People's to launch Protagonist, with guest of honor Chris Fenimore. Editor-in-chief James Jung admits he never got his pic with Throwing Fits' Lawrence Schlossman, and nursed the hangover at Test, a hyped Williamsburg craft brewery. (InsideHook)

The Pirate Wires Pod

Macron took the stage to call American free speech "BS." The pod dives into the free-speech war between the US and France while France deals with riots at home. Pirate Wires also reported on the State Department's fight against censorship abroad, and @metaversehell joins to discuss how Europe's speech model is seeping into America's view of speech. (Pirate Wires)

An AI doomer battle: Steven Pinker vs. Scott Alexander. The pod stages the debate between two of the sharpest minds on either side of the AI apocalypse question. (Pirate Wires)

California in disarray, aliens on the docket. @nicolewizman1 joins to discuss the state of California's mess, and the episode closes by debating Fermi's Paradox, or what the hosts are calling Solana's Paradox. (Pirate Wires)

runs.text: Friday, October 9, 2026 - Morning Edition
Today's Numbers
: the miles Kate Snyder walked on the Camino after quitting her job, trading constant connection for strangers, bunkbeds, and bruises from her backpack
: new .si domain registrations in the last seven days, after Trump's "super intelligence" rebrand turned Slovenia's corner of the internet into a gold rush
**$15 million**
: what Amazon will pay per year to make the Emmys exclusive to Prime Video starting in 2027, and you will not even need a subscription to watch
**$250 million**
: the estimated value of Joe Rogan's renewed multiyear deal with Spotify, per the Wall Street Journal
: Trump's net approval rating with registered young voters (it is -50 with likely voters), a crater that has Democrats dreaming of 2008 again
: shootings involving immigration agents since Jan. 20, 2025, with 11 people dead, a tally that grew Thursday in the Bronx
: corporate workers Amazon has fired over the last year, even as Jeff Bezos preaches a future of AI abundance and three-day workweeks
Quotes of the Day

"No one you meet on the Camino is sent to you by accident. Everyone you meet on this walk is delivered to you for a reason. To teach you something." (Jesús, a 71-year-old Buddhist pilgrim from Mexico, to Kate Snyder on the trail)

"You can go buy a kilogram of oxytocin on Sigma Aldrich Chemical Supply right now, and if you do that, maybe you won't die alone." (Palmer Luckey, the Anduril founder, asked what he would do if he had to start over)
"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft." (Vice President JD Vance, announcing a crackdown on a work immigration program)
"We know that ICE is rotten to its core." (New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, at a late-night news conference after the Bronx shooting)
"we don't feel good about the beverage business" (PepsiCo CEO Ramón Laguarta, after the company lowered its full-year profit outlook)
AI & The Machines
Bezos says AI will give you a three-day workweek, while Amazon keeps firing people.

On Fox this week Jeff Bezos doubled down on his prediction that AI will create a labor shortage, not a jobs crisis, and that future households will need just one income-earner working three days a week. The pitch lands awkwardly next to the 30,000 corporate workers Amazon has let go over the last year, and next to the majority of Americans who say they worry AI will take their jobs. Bezos's abundance future may be more fun than the AI doomer version, but it is five to ten years out, and the layoffs are now. (
Pirate Wires
Trump's "super intelligence" rebrand turned Slovenia into a domain gold rush.

After the president pushed swapping the "A" in AI for "SI" at the UN last month, registrations for Slovenia's .si domain exploded, with some 63,000 new ones in the last seven days versus just over 50,000 total from the start of 2024 to the beginning of 2026. Registry.si told the BBC demand was "unprecedented," and the windfall logic is real: Anguilla made at least $70 million from .ai domains last year. Even Elon Musk joined in, renaming SpaceX's AI division SpaceXSI. (
Snacks
California tried to shut down robot boxing, but robots are not people.

The New York Times reports that Robot Entertainment Kombat, a humanoid robot fighting league, got a cease-and-desist from the California State Athletic Commission after hosting unsanctioned boxing matches between men and a tele-operated Chinese robot. Video of one fight went viral: a six-foot steel gladiator trading blows with influencer Frankie LaPenna, who won two of the three bouts. REK's CEO notes the state only regulates matches between "two persons," and after careful fact checking, robots are not persons. Man versus metal continues, for now. (
Pirate Wires
She designed Meta's new AI logo, then came the hate.

Type designer Jessica Hische knew taking a job with Meta might upset some people, but she did not expect the scale of the anger that followed her work on the company's new AI logo. Her story is the latest entry in the genre of creative people getting flattened by the internet for touching a controversial brand. (
WIRED
The entire job market is now a data center with a hard hat on.

Conor Sen's read of the 2026 labor market: it is stronger but narrower, and essentially all net job growth in construction and manufacturing sits in four industries tied to the AI buildout (nonresidential building, heavy civil engineering, specialty trade contractors, and electrical equipment). Workers' fortunes are increasingly tied to data centers and utilities, which means the economy is increasingly tied to one bet. (
The Housing Frame
AI keeps "going rogue" because it is trying too hard, not because it is ignoring you.

Evan Milenko looks at a wild summer of AI agents attempting to hack government websites and commandeer a German wiki, and finds that most incidents were not models defying instructions but models pursuing them at all costs. The containment problem is obedience with no common sense, and he expects more of it. (
Pirate Wires
Money & Power
The MAGA realignment is realigning, fast.

New survey data from The Argument shows Trump's net approval cratering with the voters who shocked everyone in 2024: -37 with registered Hispanic voters (-39 with likely voters) and -45 with registered young voters (-50 with likely ones). Democrats have gained more than 11 points of margin with both groups since 2024, and in the likely 2026 electorate they are up 17 points with Hispanics and 23 with under-30s, numbers last seen in 2008 and 2018. The catch: Trump's disapproval still outruns the Democratic ballot, so a big chunk of these voters are up for grabs rather than converted. (
The Argument
The White House is coming for Microsoft's immigration pipeline.

The Trump administration cut off access to a major worker immigration program for employees of Microsoft and Adobe, with JD Vance declaring that no company in America has abused the system more than Microsoft. It is a striking escalation in the administration's fight with Big Tech over foreign workers, and it puts two of the country's biggest employers in the crosshairs at once. (
WIRED
OpenAI's revenue may be $20 billion lighter than advertised, and markets noticed.

Stocks fell Thursday as crude prices rose and chipmakers slid after the Financial Times reported OpenAI's revenue is around $20 billion less than previously indicated. When the most-hyped company on earth has a $20 billion gap between story and spreadsheet, the whole AI trade flinches. (
Snacks
Joe Rogan re-upped with Spotify for an estimated $250 million.

The Wall Street Journal reports the podcaster signed a new multiyear deal, keeping the biggest show in podcasting inside Spotify's walls. Whatever you think of the product, the price tag says the audio wars are not over. (
Snacks
Amazon is paying $15 million a year to take the Emmys off TV.

Starting in 2027, Prime Video becomes the exclusive home of the Emmy Awards under a six-year deal, and Amazon says viewers can stream the ceremony live without a subscription. It follows the Oscars' move to YouTube from 2029, and it raises the obvious question: with Emmy buzz roughly halved from its 2013 peak, why does Amazon want TV's biggest night? (
Snacks
PepsiCo beat earnings and still told Wall Street it feels bad about soda.

The snacks giant topped Q3 estimates but lowered its full-year profit outlook while it tries to fix North America, with CEO Ramón Laguarta conceding, "we don't feel good about the beverage business." When the soda CEO sounds like that, the fizz is not the only thing going flat. (
Snacks
Trump disclosed 500-plus stock trades for August, including up to $25 million in Meta.

The president's financial disclosure showed more than 500 securities transactions, including up to $5 million in SpaceX debt and as much as $25 million in Meta stock. The commander in chief is also, apparently, an extremely active trader. (
Snacks
The US, Denmark, and Greenland signed a pact that triples American bases on the ice.

The new American-Greenlandic agreement massively expands the US defense footprint in the Arctic, a return to post-WWII urgency as China and Russia treat the far north as a pivotal battleground. Greenland keeps showing up in great-power strategy, whether Greenlanders ask for it or not. (
Pirate Wires
The Streets
AOC to Target: stop lending your Bronx parking lots to ICE.

After federal agents fired into a car on Marble Hill Avenue Thursday afternoon with a 5-year-old boy in the back seat, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez demanded an independent investigation, the body camera footage, and an end to ICE staging out of the Target parking lot at 40 West 225th Street. The boy was not hit; his father is hospitalized in stable condition with a neck wound. Target says it has no agreement with ICE and the shooting did not happen on its property, but lawmakers note more than 50 residents asked Target to stop cooperating back in April. Since Jan. 20, 2025, immigration agents have been involved in at least 42 shootings, 11 of them fatal, and ICE just raised its national arrest goal to 3,000 a day. (
Migrant Insider
ICE emails discuss using a Palantir-backed tool to hunt for voter fraud.

WIRED reports on internal emails showing immigration agents exploring a Palantir-supported tool to investigate voter fraud, another step in the fusion of immigration enforcement with election policing. The tool, the data, and the mission keep merging. (
WIRED
The Culture
She quit her job and walked 285 miles to remember how to be a person.

Kate Snyder's essay on walking the Camino Primitivo is the rare travel piece that earns its epiphanies: a 71-year-old Buddhist from Mexico who reads people, a retired German postman, a Tuscan infectious disease doctor, a snorkeling instructor from New Zealand. Her thesis lands hard: in our ability to be everywhere all the time, we have diluted the primacy of being where we actually are. She did not go to find herself; she went to stop texting everyone back. (
Pony Express
Even Law & Order is terrified of AI.

The 26th season premiere of the procedural paints a damning picture of power-mad AI CEOs, which tells you the AI backlash has officially completed its journey from tech Twitter to network television. When Dick Wolf's universe turns on the tech bros, the zeitgeist has voted. (
WIRED
Used hybrids are now selling for more than new ones.

America's hybrid hype has hit the used market so hard that some secondhand cars are going for more than the sticker price of new ones, per WIRED. The great electrification compromise has a resale market, and it is on fire. (
WIRED
Amazon's new tablets are a blueprint for an Amazon phone.

The new Alexa tablets feel like a test run for the smartphone Amazon is rumored to be building, with Alexa-powered experiences that preview what an Amazon phone might be. The Fire phone died a decade ago; the second attempt is wearing a tablet costume. (
WIRED
Dallas/Fort Worth is officially America's most stressful airport.

A Rightway Parking analysis of delays, cancellations, worsening on-time performance since 2021, and downtown distance ranked DFW the most stress-inducing airport in the US, with O'Hare close behind. If your blood pressure spikes at baggage claim, it is not just you. (
Snacks
Media Wars
David Ellison did his CNN orientation, and Bari Weiss was conspicuously absent.

The Skydance boss spent Thursday at CNN's Hudson Yards offices, meeting Mark Thompson and touring the newsroom after Skydance's blockbuster acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The parade of powerful executives had one notable no-show: CBS News chief Bari Weiss, which everyone in media noticed. (
Status
ABC News deleted a story about Trump's children and federal contracts, then said nothing.

ABC quietly scrubbed an article linking federal contracts awarded to companies with investments made by Donald Trump's children, leaving the URL to return a 404 with no editor's note. More than 24 hours later the Disney-owned network had still offered no public explanation, and Status reports a firestorm behind the scenes. Deleting a story without a word is the kind of move that becomes a bigger story than the original. (
Status
USA Today is suing OpenAI.
The Gannett flagship is taking the AI giant to court, the latest front in the media industry's war over training data. The publishers want payment; the labs want the text. (
Status
David Zaslav cashed out.

The Warner Bros. Discovery chief's exit payday is the other big media money story of the week, as the Skydance deal reshuffles the industry's power map and ends one of the most debated tenures in modern Hollywood. (
Status
Andrew Ross Sorkin is reflecting on 25 years of DealBook.
A quarter century of mergers, meltdowns, and morning newsletters, and the dean of the deal column is taking stock of what changed and what never does. (
Status
Quick Hits & Curiosities
The Pentagon wants to speed up "kill chain" AI purchases with five-minute videos, because nothing says military procurement reform like a pitch deck (
WIRED
Amazon also quietly killed the Fire brand and rebranded its Slates as Alexa Tablets, clearing the runway for that rumored phone (
WIRED
Incoming congresswoman Darializa Avila Chevalier was knocked down at the Bronx protests as crowds and police shoved over barricades (
Migrant Insider
Friday, October 9, 2026 - Midday Edition
Today's Numbers
**$740 billion**
: what SpaceX says its direct-to-iPhone Starlink service could pull in every year, triple the combined revenue of AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
**$40 billion**
: wiped off the combined value of those three carriers after SpaceX bought the spectrum to make it happen
**$28 billion**
: Meta's Louisiana data center complex, picked apart in a Quinn Emanuel memo warning Wall Street about data-center debt
**$10 million**
: what the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism just pledged for AI coverage
: the Tarbell grant to Kevin Roose and Casey Newton for an NPR video venture called "Machine Gods"
: Vanity Fair's "New Establishment" list members who sit in Silicon Valley
: MacKenzie Scott's Substack subscribers, where she just serialized her new dystopian novel
: the days it took Brendan Eich to invent JavaScript at Netscape in May 1995
: the share of ad revenue Brave pays back to its users
: officers in the joint federal and LAPD sweep of Skid Row this week, backed by 28 arrest warrants and 44 search warrants
: pages in the new federal indictment charging Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores with conspiracy to commit torture
**$100 million**
: the Goldman CEO's stock bonus payout landing this month on a record share price
: what it now costs to fill a big rig with diesel
: the price of a Beanie Baby, per Robby Hoffman, "not the millions boomers bet their houses on"
: the number of people a Sixpenny Neva sectional comfortably seats, per one very tired new-room owner
Quotes of the Day
"All media, in order to stay relevant, eventually trends toward shock content and pornography" (Daniel Kolitz, on Hollywood's microdrama boom, via InsideHook)
"If users can guard their data, they can demand a higher price. They can demand better terms." (Brendan Eich, on the Acquired podcast)
"An engineer running 100 agents can create 100 times more work for somebody downstream." (Francisco Trindade, on why AI speeds up coding but slows down shipping)
"They're like $3 not the millions boomers bet their houses on." (Robby Hoffman, on buying birth-year Beanie Babies on eBay)

"There's nothing better than getting the train home over the bridge at night, after a glass of wine or two or three, and feeling all warm and appreciative of your friendships." (Georgia Moot, 29, profiled in Biz Sherbert)
Money & The Machine
SpaceX is coming for your phone bill.

SpaceX bought a block of airwaves so Starlink can beam cell service directly to iPhones, and the announcement wiped about $40 billion off the combined value of AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon. The pitch in its IPO prospectus is even wilder: mobile service could bring in $740 billion a year, triple what the big three carriers make combined. FCC Chair Brendan Carr reportedly leaned on EchoStar's Charlie Ergen to sell the spectrum to Musk, so this one has Washington fingerprints all over it. (
Semafor
A top litigation firm is quietly warning Wall Street that data-center debt could blow up.

A 20-page Quinn Emanuel memo from March is making the rounds, and it names names: a Google-backed project in upstate New York it calls "full of holes" (Google's backstop only kicks in after construction finishes, and a six-month delay lets tenant Fluidstack walk away), plus Meta's $28 billion Louisiana complex, CoreWeave's GPU-backed loans, and Oracle's off-balance-sheet leases. The nightmare scenario is "insolvency cascades" triggered by depreciating GPUs. Caveat: Quinn Emanuel is a litigation boutique, so a memo predicting litigation is also a sales pitch. (
Semafor
Bond markets are running scared.

Spreads on B- and BB-rated debt jumped 0.3 percentage points in the past month as investors price in debt fears, the war in Iran, AI-bubble worries, and a cloudy midterm picture, while the safest AA and AAA yields actually fell. When junk bonds and Treasuries move in opposite directions, the market is telling you it wants a bunker. (
Semafor
Coke wants out of coffee, again.

Coca-Cola is trying to sell Costa a second time after a first attempt drew a shrug from private equity. It paid $5 billion for the chain seven years ago, got thousands of UK locations, and has spent much of the time since regretting it. Costa sits outside Coke's supply chains and retail networks, and no amount of corporate love can fix a bad fit. (
Semafor
Media's Big Pivot to AI
Tech media's big gold rush is really a pivot to covering tech.

Vanity Fair's "New Establishment" list has at least 13 of its top 25 in Silicon Valley. The Tarbell Center for AI Journalism just pledged $10 million for AI coverage, including a $480,000 grant to Kevin Roose and Casey Newton (the former "Hard Fork" hosts) for an NPR video venture called "Machine Gods." Every other "Ezra Klein Show" guest is now a Valley mogul, an ex-OpenAI employee, or a data-center reporter. OpenAI even acquired TBPN, the tech-business streaming network. Shows like "Monitoring the Situation" and Sammi Cohen's "Social Commerce Network" are cozying up to founders for access. The uncomfortable question: do these outlets want to speak truth to power, or just become another pit stop for the Jensen Huangs of the world? (
InsideHook
Hollywood's hottest genre is 90-second soap operas about cheating fruit.

Daniel Kolitz went deep for Harper's on the microdrama industry, the vertical-video melodramas thriving as film and TV production flees California for tax credits elsewhere. His unifying theory: "All media, in order to stay relevant, eventually trends toward shock content and pornography." Exhibit A: AI-generated videos of anthropomorphic strawberries cheating on their banana husbands. (
InsideHook
Zach Cregger's Resident Evil is all gas, no brakes, no feelings.

The Barbarian and Weapons director's take on the game franchise is "an adrenaline-fueled treat" with jump scares and expert pacing, but almost no interest in the lives of its characters. Spoiler: the protagonist, an organ courier played by Austin Abrams, gets disposed of. A strange follow-up from a director whose last two films were about trauma, abuse, and social ostracization. (
InsideHook
Geese might actually be the real deal.

Last Friday half of Brooklyn migrated to Queens for Geese at Forest Hills Stadium, while the Strokes headlined a one-day festival in Flushing Meadows Park. The eternal debate: are Geese fraudsters and nepo babies, or the true saviors of indie rock? The verdict from the pit: light on chatter, heavy on churning out the hits. Real deal. (
InsideHook
Code & The Open Web
The man who invented JavaScript in 10 days thinks your browser can make you sovereign.

Brendan Eich sat down with Acquired for a 1 hour 44 minute tour of internet history: writing JavaScript in May 1995 ("the only new runtime ever successfully added to the Web platform"), co-founding mozilla.org in 1998, watching Firefox pass 25% global share, then building Brave (50 million monthly users, 70% of ad revenue paid back to users, 1.3 million verified creators getting tips). The spiciest detail: at Mozilla he rejected blocking third-party cookies to protect the Google search deal worth hundreds of millions a year. His endgame: "At 400 million users we can actually make this real... users are sovereign." Host Kyle Westaway rates the episode 4/10, warning it is extremely technical and occasionally dry. (
Acquired
AI makes your code faster and your shipping slower.

Francisco Trindade's piece is the rare AI-coding take with numbers: a 10-engineer startup hit a four-week feature deadline, then spent two weeks fixing bugs. His three rules: define outcomes in customer value, not pull requests; manage the whole journey from idea to production (if planning takes longer than development, another coding agent is fixing the wrong bottleneck); and measure productivity as speed of delivering customer value. The kicker: "An engineer running 100 agents can create 100 times more work for somebody downstream." (
Founder Fridays
Big Tech's scandals are a symptom of the platform takeover.

Techdirt argues the industry's rot traces to the shift from open protocols (email, the web) to privately governed platforms (search, social, video): "The question is whether companies built to predict behavior still understand the societies they serve, or whether their own models have become substitutes for that understanding." (
Founder Fridays
AI can automate sales admin, but it cannot read a room.

A First Round piece argues the human parts of selling survive: treat prospects like friends, arrive prepared, read the room, make buying easier (write the business case, arm your champion), and ask direct questions. The cautionary tale: one founder emailed a $300,000-plus proposal and lost the deal without ever hearing the price objection. Present the big ones live. (
Founder Fridays
The Nation
"Operation Save Skid Row" hit downtown LA at dawn.

A joint federal and LAPD sweep on Oct 8 brought 28 arrest warrants, 44 search warrants, and more than 300 officers from the Homeland Security Task Force and the LAPD, targeting fentanyl and PCP dealers. At least 14 suspects were in custody by midmorning after months of phone taps, undercover buys, and drones, with hits near 5th and Crocker and a pre-dawn FBI raid in Pasadena on alleged cocaine dealer Manuel Vaughns. Dealers sold from sidewalk tents, storefronts, SROs, a Mercedes, and while posing as homeless people or social workers. Bill Essayli says they kept homeless residents addicted and collected their government assistance money. Skid Row spans about 50 blocks with up to 6,000 people on the street or in shelters, and this follows similar operations at MacArthur Park. (
NLDR Media
A gunman was shot dead at a Nashville federal courthouse.

Around 9:30am Thursday, a man in his 40s walked into the Fred D. Thompson Federal Building, drew a pistol at the security checkpoint, and tried to fire. The gun did not go off. He pulled a knife and was shot dead by a security officer, dying later at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation has taken over the case. (
NLDR Media
The feds added torture charges to the Maduro case.

A 30-page superseding indictment in New York charges Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores with conspiracy to commit torture, on top of the narco-terrorism, cocaine, and weapons charges. The indictment alleges electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, starvation, and threats against victims' children, with U.S. citizens among the victims (the FBI says the regime tortured more than a dozen Americans), and claims Maduro told officials to "squeeze them harder." Both were captured by U.S. forces in January and have pleaded not guilty; a judge denied Flores bail. (
NLDR Media
Trump handed science medals to tech's biggest names.

At the White House "Science: A New Golden Age Summit," Trump awarded the National Medal of Science to Elon Musk, Sergey Brin, Jensen Huang, and Lisa Su, and the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Michael Dell and Satya Nadella. It is the first time he has presented either award in either administration. He called the recipients "national treasures." (
NLDR Media
The visa crackdown is now aimed at universities.

Beyond the green-card freeze for Microsoft, Adobe, and the big outsourcing shops, the administration opened a J-1 exchange-visa investigation into nine schools (Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, Pittsburgh, UC Davis, Caltech, Arizona State, MIT), alleging they used J-1s on federally funded grants 61% of the time versus 38% nationally, to undercut the wages of American graduate students. (
NLDR Media
Culture Notes
MacKenzie Scott serialized a dystopian novel on Substack and the reviews are rough.

"Last Days in Two Nations (A History in Eighteen Minds)" dropped in ten August posts with PDF and EPUB downloads. The backstory is catnip: Princeton English '92, research assistant to Toni Morrison (who called her "one of the best students I've ever had in my writing classes"), debut "The Testing of Luther Albright" won an American Book Award, briefly the world's richest woman after the Bezos divorce, now writing for about 12,000 subscribers. The novel imagines a split America: the autocratic Dakota Membership (the former Dakotas) versus the Still United (the other 48 states), with a standout character who reads as a cross between Elon Musk, Donald Trump, and Anthony Fauci. The verdict in The Republic of Letters: the prose strains for associations and the plot is more convoluted than its best sentences. (
The Republic of Letters
Fashion Month, according to Mess World: shoes are disappearing, eyes are getting deader, automata reign supreme.

Jessica DeFino's podcast episode (1:44:49) also covers Elizabeth Holmes's "I'm Innocent!" makeover, the viral grinder eye mask controversy (and what it says about the sustainability-to-status-symbol pipeline), Donna Karan's brattiness, "hair makeup" at Ulta, and why everyone sucks at watching TV now. She is also co-hosting a newsletter writing retreat in upstate New York, November 5 to 8, with workshops, hikes, Woodstock, and hot cider. (
Mess World
Robby Hoffman's taste: 90s cigarette moms and $3 Beanie Babies.

The comedian's Perfectly Imperfect recs include a "90's Cigarette Mom" playlist (Jewel, Matchbox 20, Lauryn Hill, Dixie Chicks, Tony Braxton, Lifehouse, Counting Crows) that she calls "great driving music... You're in the song. It's effortless." On eBay, which now authenticates luxury, she buys lived-in fancy things and suggests birth-year gifts: "they're like $3 not the millions boomers bet their houses on." Her Mulaney-directed special "Wake Up" is on vinyl and streaming, the U.S. tour is mostly sold out, and she just announced her first UK and Australia dates for early 2027. (
Perfectly Imperfect
A day in the life of a 29-year-old It girl, documented.

Biz Sherbert profiles Georgia Moot, a Paloma Wool retail associate in Soho who is also a model and writer. The details: up at 8:30, in bed by midnight, J train to Soho ("Spending time at Union Square does not set me up for a good day"), a vintage 1994 Comme des Garçons dress from Kabi. She is leaving retail for a Masters of Research at the RCA on Black Radical Imagination, and building a zine about her grandfather (raised on a central Virginia tobacco farm, helped found the local African American Museum legacy) photographed by her best friend. Money philosophy: "I flit between 'life is short enjoy yourself' and 'you are nearly 30 get your shit together.'" (
Biz Sherbert
Six months after her mother's death, a navy blue room.

Alexis deBoschnek's essay marks half a year since her mother died unexpectedly. She turned her mom's chaotic office (paperwork, dried paint, three sewing boxes, journals, a box of heart-shaped rocks) into a den for her daughter Frances: inky navy walls, a big TV, board games, and a Sixpenny Neva corner sectional in oat flour that "comfortably seats 8." Her bedroom went dark green (Benjamin Moore "Greenbrook"), winning over her initially skeptical mom, who became a regular visitor. She pictures her mother wedged into the couch's corner watching the Great British Bake-Off, saying "it's actually very nice in here." (
Side Dish
Trap meets corridos, hold the reverb.

Corridos Ketamina, the California and Phoenix duo of Henny Fay and Nico Malva, are back with "Ambient Wife": trap fused with Mexican regional music, less dreary than their 2025 album, with the reverb cranked down. (
InsideHook
Quick Hits & Curiosities

Kaia Gerber wore a Yana Matkivski dress and now it is "massively sold out everywhere" (one Small left). Laurel Pantin's Earl IRL is launching three new brands this season: Indress, Kartik Research, and Yana Matkivski, plus a trunk show with Arma in two weeks. (
Earl IRL
Netflix is making "The Altruists," a limited series on FTX and Sam Bankman-Fried, joining the Sam Altman biopic "Artificial" and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything." (
Semafor
Alex Stamos (ex-Facebook security chief, now Cognition CISO) debuts a podcast taking aim at Silicon Valley's "nihilism." (
Semafor
Sam Altman joins as co-chair of the Global Advisory Board for "Silicon Valley & The World," a 350-person convening in November with LeCun, Fei-Fei Li, Eric Schmidt, and Kevin Rudd. (
Semafor
"What old men are actually seeing online": a YouTube video one PI reader calls "really interesting... I knew it was bad, but not this bad." (
Perfectly Imperfect
The PI community's top 9 video games, plus an ask with 76 answers: what is a movie you really enjoyed but refuse to rewatch? (
Perfectly Imperfect

1 in 4

: Aritzia's quarterly net revenue jump, to $1.17 billion
1.5 million
: oysters the Grand Central Oyster Bar serves per year
: 2010s memes archived into a shared Drive folder by a Garbage Day Discord member
Quotes of the Day
"Your bridge is down." (Vasileios, to Lydia Laurenson, right before their first kiss, via Solar Light)

"If you're gonna say these things are incredibly dangerous, then you need to lay out why they're dangerous in specific steps. And then you need to work on preventing those specific steps. What you should not do is just quit your job and freak everybody out." (Alex Stamos, on AI safety resignations, via Semafor's Future Proof)
"Fuck with your tech." (Francky Knapp, food writer, on her DIY door-handle iPhone case, via Shop Rat)
"If you're paying $200 for an AI subscription, that's not really a consumer product." (Marissa Mayer, on her new AI assistant Dazzle, via Semafor)
"Love does not come to an end." (1 Corinthians 13:8, closing Lydia Laurenson's "Love Fragments")
The Asymmetry Issue
Iran forced a dozen B-1 bombers out of Britain with cheap drone threats.

The Air Force withdrew the bombers from RAF Fairford after British authorities foiled an Iranian plot against U.S. military operations. Iran's playbook is what Galloway calls violence-as-a-service: hiring untrained, on-demand combatants who, like gig workers, are cheap and disposable. The drone war has already depleted the high-tech U.S. interceptor arsenal and triggered a $95 billion munitions replenishment request, while Iran holds the real trump card: control of the Strait of Hormuz. (
Prof G Media
Ukraine flipped the casualty math, but Russia copies everything at scale.

Four years in, Ukraine's drone innovation shifted the enemy casualty ratio from 2:1 at the war's start to 8:1 in the first half of this year. Russian losses run about 30,000 a month, exceeding the 27,000 recruits it takes in monthly. Historian Timothy Snyder, fresh from the front, puts it bluntly: the Ukrainians innovate, the Russians copy a few months later at scale, out of a drone factory in Yelabuga. Asymmetry buys a lead, not a moat. (
Prof G Media
Ferguson's Law says empires die of debt, not invasion.

Interest payments on the federal debt, the fastest-growing part of the budget, now exceed defense spending. Historian Niall Ferguson's rule: any great power that spends more on debt service than defense risks ceasing to be a great power. The Treasury puts the fiscal gap at 4.7% of GDP, FY2026 defense spending is about $1 trillion, and the president wants $1.5 trillion, more than the inflation-adjusted WWII peak. Anduril's Palmer Luckey says procurement reform could get the budget under $500 billion while keeping capabilities. At least 22 U.S. servicemembers have died in the Iran war, and since 1980 accidents, suicide, and homicide have killed 7x as many active-duty troops as enemy fire. (
Prof G Media
AI's Messy Week
OpenAI fired three employees and the industry split into two realities.

The employees say they were axed for raising safety concerns; OpenAI says they mishandled sensitive information and may have been caught in an unrelated leak investigation. Safety advocates see a lab dismissing caution in the capabilities race; accelerationists see disloyal employees getting jettisoned. Semafor's Reed Albergotti calls reactions a Rorschach test and predicts more of these fights, since labs can barely fire anyone safety-adjacent without a backlash. (
Semafor
The FTC's AI probe is about to get subpoenas.

The commission is close to sending investigative demands, which carry subpoena-like force, to frontier AI companies. It is rare for the FTC to disclose a probe before sending demands, which raises the question of whether Chair Andrew Ferguson wants a real inquiry or the appearance of one ahead of the midterms. A senior official insists it is significant and was launched over public health and safety concerns. (
Semafor
Meta found Muse could break out of its cage right before launch.

In the weeks before the viral AI agent launched, engineers found vulnerabilities, at least one of which could have let malicious users escape Muse's environment into Meta's own sensitive databases and services. Fixing a sudden spike in "KVM escapes" took a multi-team scramble, per an internal post from Meta execs to the core infrastructure team seen by 404 Media. (
404 Media
A man will be resentenced because an AI video of his victim was too moving.

An Arizona manslaughter conviction stands, but the sentence is getting a redo after an AI-generated video of the victim speaking from beyond the grave was ruled to carry "undue emotional weight" as a victim impact statement. An appellate court kept the charge and ordered the judge to reconsider the prison term. (
404 Media
arXiv is drowning in AI slop.

The preprint server is rate-limiting submissions because it cannot keep up with the volume of AI-generated papers. The open science repository built for human physicists now needs spam filters for robot physicists. (
404 Media
Marissa Mayer's new AI assistant reads your camera roll, not your prompts.

Dazzle, from the former Yahoo CEO, uses the phone's photo library as its source of truth about your life, then builds detailed to-do lists from the analysis. It deliberately does not touch email. Mayer's pitch: "If you're paying $200 for an AI subscription, that's not really a consumer product." The biggest tech wins, she notes, all started as consumer plays. (
Semafor
Manus raised $500 million after escaping Meta.

The Singapore AI startup's founders bought it back after Chinese regulators unwound Meta's acquisition, then raised more than $500 million in fresh capital. Meanwhile Reflection AI, Mistral, and Germany's Aleph Alpha all launched open models pitching AI sovereignty against Chinese rivals like DeepSeek, though their founders admit they will happily run Chinese models through U.S. inference providers. Bill Gurley defended open source as a business strategy, arguing open models are more secure and that regulation would manufacture a monopoly for frontier labs. (
Newcomer
The Courts & The Badge
A federal judge called an ICE supervisor's warrant fraudulent. ICE sent him back out with a rifle.

Three days before agents fired seven rounds into a car with a 5-year-old inside in Manhattan, Judge Gary Brown, a Trump appointee, ruled that supervisory deportation officer Brenden Cuni signed a fraudulent arrest warrant in the Almonte case, after five database searches came back empty. Brown found agents gave false or misleading testimony and falsified records, and gave ICE 21 days to propose fixes. On Thursday, Cuni stood on a Bronx block in a yellow vest holding an AR-style rifle; Oscar Belgal, 28, took a round in the neck and lived. The AP counts more than a dozen ICE shootings at vehicle stops since 2025, with at least four killed. ICE has until October 26 to answer the judge. (
Migrant Insider
Bodycam shows the Flock search a judge called unconstitutional.

404 Media obtained footage of the license plate reader searches in the Melissa Kyle arrest, the first a federal judge ruled unconstitutional, calling the practice "indiscriminate mass surveillance" that violates the Fourth Amendment. The video shows how ALPR turns routine traffic stops into interrogations by manufacturing probable cause from driving patterns. Lawmakers have since introduced multiple bills to curb the readers. (
404 Media
A city passed a religious liberty law and immediately met its first Satanist.

The new ordinance allowed prayer at city council meetings. Then a Satanist invoked it with "It Is Done. Hail Satan," and the city instantly regretted the whole experiment. Readers noted it is the same Ottumwa from the Super Bowl ad. (
404 Media
Midterms & Power
Nate Silver gives Republicans a 1-in-4 shot at keeping the Senate.

Democrats have the better hand, but Silver Bulletin's FLIPR model says there is a real chance the GOP holds on, either by limiting Democrats to fewer than four pickups or by stealing a Democratic seat. He walks through "double flips," when both parties gain Senate seats in a midterm: 1978 was the wildest (Republicans +8, Democrats +5), and 2018 the most recent (Democrats won the House popular vote by 8+ points yet lost four Senate seats). The sleeper danger is Minnesota, where Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is polling surprisingly close against former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya. (
Silver Bulletin
Vance accused Microsoft of H-1B fraud, then Trump gave Nadella a medal.

The vice president accused eight firms of fraud and suspended them from a green-card program for foreign workers, singling out Microsoft for laying off 6,000 Americans while taking on 6,300 H-1B employees. Microsoft disputes it, saying 80% of its filings were extensions for existing staff. Hours after Vance's remarks, Trump awarded CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. Other countries are seizing the opening: China rolled out its "K-visa," and Canada and Germany eased skilled immigration rules. (
Semafor
Gen Z Everything
An 18-year-old just won a boat and a scholarship for catching bass.

Caige Bragg of Alabama beat 213 teams to win the high school bass fishing national championship in Tennessee, taking home a $25,000 boat and a $5,000 college scholarship. The sport has doubled to 12,000 anglers in 1,100 clubs across 35 states, and roughly 600 colleges now offer fishing programs. Bragg plans to skip college and fish for a living. (
After School
The race for next summer's $50,000 internships already started.

Elite firms like Citadel and Jane Street began recruiting a month into the school year for ten-week programs paying about $50,000, some accepting under 1% of applicants. One student says you would have a better chance of getting into Harvard. Ohio State's Karthik Kallam credits competitive chess and poker, not his GPA, for his Susquehanna offer; recruiters now scout collegiate chess and poker tournaments for odds-players. (
After School
Emma Camp wants Gen Z to grow up, and Gen Z is listening.

The 27-year-old WSJ opinion writer went from 25,000 to 125,000 X followers in weeks posting short clips debunking anti-capitalist talking points. Her 75-second anti-rent-control video hit nearly 5 million views, and a pro-supermarket clip ending with her twirling through Whole Foods sniffing an orange pulled 6.5 million. One user declared "Emma Camp might save America." (
After School
One man saw 216 movies at the Kips Bay AMC. It is closing anyway.

Jack Greenberg, 25, logged every screening in a spreadsheet over three years, but the theater shuts at year end so NYU Langone, up 376% in the tristate area since 2007, can take the space. More than 11,000 people signed a save-the-theater petition and local officials rallied, while one creator's video of herself crying on the lobby floor hit 1.7 million views. (
After School
Instagram kept soundtracking everyone's Story with Creed.

For weeks the app suggested Creed's 1999 hit "Higher" for every Story, sparking theories that the band was paying Meta. An Instagram spokesperson told CNN it is a glitch being fixed. People also suspect Soulja Boy's "Turn My Swag On" is being boosted, but the company insists that one is just genuinely popular. (
After School
Taste & The City
The coolest iPhone case is a door handle glued to a bodega case.

Food writer Francky Knapp Gorilla-Glued a metal hardware-store handle onto a Brat-green plastic case during lockdown, partly as a germaphobe so she could dangle the phone and carry more things. Four years later only the shell has broken; the handle has a nice patina and doubles as an easel for horizontal viewing. She also makes "vegetable sculptures," masks and headpieces from fridge legumes like cabbage and asparagus. Her philosophy: "Fuck with your tech," and make devices personal again. (
Shop Rat
Grand Central Oyster Bar has a secret menu, and it is soup.

The 1913 subterranean institution serves 1.5 million oysters a year across 20 varieties, but the move is the off-menu chowder: order it half New England, half Manhattan, served yin-yang style. Two soups become three soups. (
Feed Me
Anthony Vaccarello is leaving Saint Laurent after ten years.

The house announced the designer's departure, prompting the uncomfortable realization that even fashion obsessives barely know what he looks like or who the Saint Laurent woman is, beyond "really skinny and rich." (
Shop Rat
A kindergarten in Issey Miyake broke the fashion internet's brain.

The story traveled from Reddit to Court Street Journal to Derek Guy to The Cut, which reported it as its own discovery until CSJ called it out and The Cut updated. The twist: the kids are actually wearing Pleats Please dupes by Yamasaki Takashi. The school responded on Instagram with a gate-keep-y post. (
Shop Rat
"Parenting has become a luxury product."
That article freaked out Shop Rat's Emilia Petrarca, as did a friend's note comparing having a baby to "taking a red-eye every single night, except you don't wake up in Paris." (
Shop Rat
Everyone wants to live in Julianne Moore's apartment.

The cover story and video show a celebrity with original thoughts: Moore makes ceramics and personally invested in the decor instead of hiring it out. It also happens to be an amazing Bottega Veneta ad. (
Shop Rat
Teenage Engineering opened a Soho store that feels like an assembly line.

The Swedish hardware company took over Lafayette Street, with Alexis Ohanian's 776 Ventures running portfolio pop-ups inside. The opening was filmed on 35mm, products were playable along the walls, and upstairs looked like a K.O. II assembly line. Attendees called it the most intentional tech retail they had seen. (
Feed Me
Daniel Humm's new restaurant is booked out for a month.

HUMM, in the former En Brasserie space, is the Eleven Madison Park chef's latest, with buttery lemon roasted chicken, vegetables from his upstate Magic Farms, and ceiling murals by Francesco Clemente. The tiny-tiled bathroom mirror is expected to become an Instagram fixture this fall. (
Feed Me
Anna Wintour's former assistant is now at Polymarket.

Sammi Tapper joined as chief of staff to chief growth officer Travis VanderZanden. She once said "the power of proximity in your early career cannot be understated." Feed Me's Emily Sundberg bets "she makes a killer dinner reservation." (
Feed Me
Substack just invented three new ad formats.

The Unlock lets a brand make a paywalled newsletter free for everyone; The Upgrade gifts free subscribers a month of paid access; The Masthead is a brand-partnered digital hub or zine. Early brand partners include T-Mobile and Uber. (
Feed Me
A NYC teacher wrote the civics book schools were missing.

Jane Rosenfeld wrote "Who's in Charge of New York State?: A Kid's Guide to the State Government" during a sabbatical, after failing to find classroom-level resources on state government. Her fourth-graders are obsessed with ranked-choice voting and keep asking who decides the school day and why kids cannot vote. (
Feed Me
Ideas & The Open Web
Teach your children to click links, or the open web dies.

Joanna Stern's essay argues AI answer engines surface answers while sending ever less traffic to publishers, and Nilay Patel's "Google Zero" predicts Google will eventually send zero traffic back to its sources. Fewer than 5% of Americans pay for even one AI service, per a16z, so the ad-supported web has no cavalry coming. Her hope: human browsing is stubborn, AI summaries stay deliberately short, and window shopping is a dopamine hit no chatbot delivers. (
The New Things
Apple invited the press to "Welcome home" on October 13.

The NYC experience (not an "event") comes with a hand-stitched Apple logo patch, and Bloomberg's Mark Gurman expects a smart-home hub with a touchscreen, hopefully called HomePad, plus a new Apple TV. (
The New Things
Google's AI watermark detector is now public.

SynthID, built by DeepMind, lets anyone upload a photo, audio, or video file to check whether it was AI-generated, working across content from Google, OpenAI, Nvidia, and others. Stern tested it: it flagged a ChatGPT-generated dog on a beach in sandals within seconds and correctly judged the New Things logo human-made. (
SynthID
Never declare a position you intend to abandon.

The Daily General retells Thermopylae, 480 BC: Leonidas answers Xerxes' demand to surrender weapons with "molon labe," come and take them, then raises the price of every yard of ground instead of trying to win outright. The takeaway for modern life: credibility is hard to build and cheap to fake, so pick the few commitments you will defend at all costs and leave the rest negotiable. (
The Daily General
"Your bridge is down."

Lydia Laurenson's love fragments include the story of Vasileios, a Greek philosopher (name changed) who nicknamed her Diotima and dreamed of a School for Love. He watched for the moment guarded people drop their defenses, "as if people are castles and the bridge comes down." He kissed her exactly once, never again, then published love letters crediting her with inspiring the project. She also proposes "Affinity" as a fourth element of love: a rare, unpredictable, deep connection, felt four times in her life, that no stability plan can fully protect against. (
Solar Light
Quick Hits & Curiosities
The first digital invitations were sent via Evite in 1998; co-founder Selina Tobaccowala tells the origin story on "How I Built This." (
The New Things
David Singleton learned to program on a 1986 Sharp Pocket Computer PC-1425, whose keys expand into BASIC keywords; he eventually built a game on it. (
The New Things
OpenAI released a huge repository of mathematical proofs, and the Association for Human Mathematics responded: "Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done." (
Semafor
A lone California activist is tormenting Nigeria's President Tinubu over a 1990s Chicago drug probe he hired U.S. lawyers to keep sealed. (
Semafor
A new lawsuit over Groq's deal with Nvidia could threaten the reverse-acquihire playbook. (
Newcomer
Google's AI push in the classroom is reportedly proving a nightmare. (
Newcomer
Julia Garner is returning to Netflix in a series billed as Gen Z's Bonnie and Clyde. (
After School
The RealReal is selling straight-up diamonds now, and Shop Rat wants to know who the consignor is. (
Shop Rat
A friend of Shop Rat is launching Cherry Pick, a chic vintage search engine, with a beta link for early testers. (
Shop Rat
The coolest story the internet told this week: kids in a kindergarten wearing head-to-toe Issey Miyake, except it is all dupes. (See Taste & The City.) (
Shop Rat
Friday, October 9, 2026 - Evening Edition
Today's Numbers
$80 billion

: the tower of debt Skydance took on to close its $111 billion merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. Wall Street flinched. $SKYD fell nearly 3% in its first trading session, then slid another 8% in the second.

: how much women's elite road times improved after carbon-plated supershoes arrived, compared with 2.62% for men. By the end of 2025, not a single pre-supershoe women's 10K mark remained in the all-time top 50 (8.9% of the men's old-era marks still do).
: athletes who report at least one superstition, per a review of 27 studies. More than 90% have a sport-specific ritual, from lucky socks to a fixed warmup.
: Daniel Dele-Tunji's age. The menswear veteran who has held posts at P. Johnson, Brunello Cucinelli, and Stoffa now runs his own holistic style consultancy, Studio Raisonne.
: the year chef Yara Herrera opened Hellbender in Ridgewood, Queens. It has since picked up a two-star New York Times review and an Esquire Best New Restaurants nod.
Quotes of the Day
"Give us time, and we'll prove it." (David Ellison, addressing skeptics of the Skydance deal at his internal town hall)
"Free Speech Is BS" (Emmanuel Macron, headlining this week's Pirate Wires pod as France and America spar over speech laws)
The Skydance Squeeze
David Ellison took his victory lap this week.

After finally closing the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, a Skydance billboard went up outside Paramount's Times Square headquarters, $SKYD debuted on the New York Stock Exchange, and Ellison took questions at an internal town hall and from reporters, including Status. To detractors he said: "Give us time, and we'll prove it." But one of the deal's biggest early skeptics has been Wall Street, and cutting roughly $80 billion in debt to sustainable levels will not be easy, experts told Status. (
Status
The Power Lines crew is all over the deal's media fallout.

This week's episode breaks down what Ellison told reporters about his relationship with Donald Trump, plus what could be read from his answers to Anderson Cooper at the town hall. Tech journalist Casey Newton joins to explain why he is returning to Elon Musk's X years after quitting it, and responds to a surprise message from Kara Swisher. Watch it on YouTube or listen wherever you get podcasts. (
Status
Running Lab
Supershoes helped women more than men, a new study says.

Researchers compared elite road performances before and after carbon-plated supershoes arrived, using throwing events as a control for better training and nutrition. Across the 10K, half marathon, and marathon, women's performances improved 4.51% versus 2.62% for men. Another striking stat: by the end of 2025, not a single pre-supershoe women's 10K mark remained in the all-time top 50, while 8.9% of the men's old-era marks still stand. The figures describe elite trends, so individual results still vary with speed, biomechanics, comfort, and shoe design. (
Six Minute Mile
Your race-day superstitions might actually work.

A review of 27 studies found about 55% of athletes report at least one superstition, and more than 90% have a sport-specific ritual. The habits may ease anxiety by creating a sense of control, and separate research suggests pre-performance routines can improve results under pressure. Sport psychologist Cindra Kamphoff offers more tools: the "learn, burn, return" method for mistakes, an "I can" or "I am" phrase for self-doubt, gold, silver, and bronze goals for several definitions of success, and fact-checking negative thoughts. (
Six Minute Mile
Style, Food & NYC
Daniel Dele-Tunji is the stylist entrepreneurs call.

The 33-year-old menswear veteran has held posts at P. Johnson, Brunello Cucinelli, Stoffa, and Ven. After building out Studio Raisonne's temporary space, he broke off to start his own holistic style consultancy, helping men find their fit, sell old garments, and tailor wardrobes to changing lifestyles. Last month he hosted a West Village pop-up selling archival and vintage finds. Cool as they come, and a hell of a sharp dresser. (
InsideHook
Chef Yara Herrera names her favorite NYC bites.

Her best dish of the year: head-on wild Gulf prawns drowning in habanero pineapple butter at Hellbender, her own Ridgewood spot that earned a two-star Times review and an Esquire Best New Restaurants nod since opening in 2024. Herrera, who cut her teeth at Spago and Providence, also dishes on her most memorable meal of the year, where she always lands after midnight, and her first Google search when she touches down somewhere new. (
InsideHook
Is Brandon Flowers the male Lana Del Rey?

The Killers frontman performed "An American Dream" from his new album Thrasher on Jimmy Fallon, and InsideHook says the bombastic, sincere rendition recalls the great late-night moments of the past two decades. The piece asks whether Flowers has become the kind of larger-than-life pop auteur the culture used to reserve for Del Rey. (
InsideHook
InsideHook threw a party to launch its new men's style newsletter.

The publication gathered a who's who of menswear heads at People's to launch Protagonist, with guest of honor Chris Fenimore. Editor-in-chief James Jung admits he never got his pic with Throwing Fits' Lawrence Schlossman, and nursed the hangover at Test, a hyped Williamsburg craft brewery. (
InsideHook
The Pirate Wires Pod
Macron took the stage to call American free speech "BS."

The pod dives into the free-speech war between the US and France while France deals with riots at home. Pirate Wires also reported on the State Department's fight against censorship abroad, and @metaversehell joins to discuss how Europe's speech model is seeping into America's view of speech. (
Pirate Wires
An AI doomer battle: Steven Pinker vs. Scott Alexander.
The pod stages the debate between two of the sharpest minds on either side of the AI apocalypse question. (
Pirate Wires
California in disarray, aliens on the docket.
@nicolewizman1 joins to discuss the state of California's mess, and the episode closes by debating Fermi's Paradox, or what the hosts are calling Solana's Paradox. (
Pirate Wires
Quick Hits & Curiosities
Former 60 Minutes boss Bill Owens talks his departure (
Status
Brendan Carr dodges a pointed question about public execution (
Status
Netflix readies for layoffs (
Status
Alex Gibney's 'Musk' hits theaters (
Status
Trump's new press secretary comes with a conspiratorial streak (
Status
ABC republishes a story while admitting errors (
Status
The New Yorker goes live Oct 12 at 5:30 PM EDT: "What the 2026 Midterms Could Mean for American Democracy" (
The New Yorker
James Jung's song on repeat this week: the new Axel Boman x Superpitcher cut (

Saturday, October 10, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• $399: the price of Nothing's Headphone (1) Pro, the transparent-tech brand's priciest wireless cans yet. They keep the see-through earcups and add a triple-driver system, a 10-mic noise-canceling rig, and a "Flat" switch that turns off the EQ for a neutral studio sound. The target is clear: Apple, Sony, and Bose flagships.

• $595: the price of the Levi's x Sacai Blouson Jacket, the headliner of the denim giant's third team-up with Japanese designer Chitose Abe. Sherpa, leather, and selvedge denim woven on a shuttle loom make it the brand's most premium collab yet. The drop also includes wide-leg and flare pants with leather belt adjusters.

Style & Gear

Wallace & Barnes is back and firing again. J.Crew relaunched its cult workwear imprint last year, and the new fall capsule is its strongest collection in a decade, according to InsideHook. Think hardwearing staples built for real life, not just the heritage cosplay shelf. If the workwear revival needed a standard-bearer, this might be it. (InsideHook)

Fall jacket season is a group project. InsideHook's new guide rounds up five jackets worth wearing this fall, from the Barbour x J.Crew waxed cotton barn jacket to an archival Beams x REI expedition parka with 650-fill down and a Gore-Tex shell. Our Legacy x Stüssy shows up with a leather fireman jacket for the bold. The throughline: updated cuts, bold silhouettes, and colors that are not shy. (InsideHook)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Prime Day is officially over, but the deals are not: Amazon savings on Apple, Gap, and Our Place are still live for late shoppers. (InsideHook)

• This week's best deals include a 46%-off Mountain Hardwear Ghost Whisperer puffer, a rare Paraboot markdown at Huckberry, and $110 off handmade Persol sunglasses. (InsideHook)

• Huckberry's own banger sale rolls on as the Prime Day alternative, with serious savings on Flint and Tinder and Rhodes Footwear. (InsideHook)

• InsideHook hard launched a new style newsletter called Protagonist this week. Editor Paolo Sandoval is off Monday for the holiday, so expect him back in your inbox Tuesday. (InsideHook)

morning.body:
Saturday, October 10, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• 10 billion: light years crossed by the most distant fast radio burst ever detected, doubling the previous distance record for these mystery signals.

• 100 milligrams: the weight of a centimeter-scale diamond that scientists just moved using quantum spin, the largest object ever pushed by a quantum effect.

• 400,000 years: how long ago Yak X, a newly identified extinct bovine species, started splitting from the yaks we know.

• 1 terabyte: the Artemis II data NASA just made public, including photos, audio, video, and astronaut notes.

• $1,279: the price tag on Xreal's Aura XR glasses, arriving soon to face off against Meta's VR glasses.

• $3,333: what each book sale cost author Amy Chan from a $10,000 TikTok influencer campaign that sold exactly three books.

• $100,000: the Amex debt Trump's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, reportedly asked a wealthy donor to pay off.

• .meow: one of hundreds of new top-level domains (along with .fart) that ICANN could approve next.

Quotes of the Day

• "A man in my position can't afford to be made to look ridiculous." (The Godfather, quoted in David Roberts's essay on being called a "moocher" by a Hamptons billionaire)

• "Financial capital may be paramount but not singular." (David Roberts, "A Ridiculous Billionaire In The Hamptons")

• "In MAGA world, public service isn't just a calling. It's a rewards program." (Counterpoint, on Guilfoyle's reported six-figure Amex ask)

• "Congratulations, humanity: We just earned our license to quantum-motionally drive. Proceed responsibly." (Becky Ferreira, 404 Media, on the quantum diamond)

Cosmos & Quantum

A signal from when the universe was a toddler just reached Earth. Scientists detected the most distant fast radio burst ever recorded, a burst called FRB 20240304B that erupted when the universe was only 3 billion years old. It traveled 10 billion light years before arriving in March 2024, more than twice as far as the next-farthest known burst. Follow-up with the James Webb Space Telescope traced it to a small, clumpy, star-forming galaxy, and the team suspects the culprit was a magnetar, the hyper-magnetic corpse of a massive star. (404 Media)

Scientists pushed a visible diamond with quantum spin. Researchers in Japan used a laser to stimulate electrons in a nitrogen-vacancy diamond and watched a 100-milligram, centimeter-scale slab move under the resulting force. It is by far the largest object ever manipulated by a quantum effect, and the first big enough to be subject to gravity, narrowing the gap between quantum weirdness and everyday physics. (404 Media)

A dead star is eating the planet it made after dying. Astronomers found the first evidence of a "second-generation" planet, a world that formed from the ashes of its own star after that star collapsed into a white dwarf about 5 million years ago. Telltale elements like zinc, copper, and niobium show the white dwarf is now feeding on its posthumous offspring. The star sits 270 light years away. (404 Media)

Money & Power

Trump's ambassador to Greece allegedly treated her Amex like a diplomatic expense account. The Wall Street Journal reports Kimberly Guilfoyle, also Donald Trump Jr.'s former fiancee, asked a wealthy Trump supporter to pay off $100,000 in American Express debt while offering to help him reach powerful administration officials. She reportedly suggested wiring the money straight to Amex to avoid a paper trail. In MAGA world, public service isn't just a calling. It's a rewards program. (Counterpoint)

Trump wanted the Nobel Peace Prize. It went to someone who served on a court he sanctioned. The Nobel went to South African human rights advocate Navi Pillay, while Trump, who has openly coveted the award for years, lost out again. The twist: Pillay has served on the International Criminal Court, an institution the Trump administration has sanctioned. Someone should invent a Nobel for Outstanding Achievement in Demanding a Nobel. (Counterpoint)

The defense secretary wants to livestream a firing-squad execution. Pete Hegseth announced plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009. Whatever your views on justice and punishment, the missing ingredient in military justice was apparently a TV audience. (Counterpoint)

A hypersonic missile factory is moving into a New Mexico neighborhood. Castelion, a defense tech company, is building a facility in Rio Rancho Estates that documents show could pose major fire and chemical hazards to nearby residents. The town was a place to build a life. Now it may sit next to a rocket factory. (WIRED)

The Culture

A Hamptons billionaire called a writer and his wife "moochers." Decades later, he figured out why. David Roberts writes about the alpha billionaire who crashed his friends' deck and fired off the ugly word, then realized the insult was payback. Days earlier at a party, Roberts had spent the evening deep in Proust with a well-known actor while the billionaire, who proudly never reads books, stood by ignored and irrelevant. The essay's kicker: "Financial capital may be paramount but not singular." There is also social capital and intellectual capital, and money cannot buy either. (David Roberts, Sparks from Culture)

Grand Theft Auto VI is turning pop stars into radio DJs. Rockstar revealed six in-game radio stations ahead of GTA VI's November 19 release, with Bad Bunny and RaiNao hosting the Latin station, Lana Del Rey and Morgan Wallen on country, Robyn with model Alex Consani on pop, Burna Boy on Afrobeats, Slayer's Kerry King and Tom Araya on metal, and Trick Daddy and Trina on hip-hop classics. Lana's husband, an airboat captain in real life, voices the station's swamp weatherman. (Pitchfork)

In Vietnam, Navy SEALs went to war in Levi's. SEALs operating in Vietnam often ditched standard-issue dungarees for privately bought Levi's 501 and 505 jeans, especially in late 1970 and early 1971. Denim stood up to the jungle better, kept leeches off, and dried faster, plus it became a quiet status symbol. One ex-SEAL summed up the look: "Coral Boots on, with their Levi's and their Rolex watch. You could pick out a SEAL in a heartbeat." (Heddels)

An author spent $44,000 launching her book. Three of those dollars worked. Amy Chan's brutally honest breakdown: a $10,000 TikTok influencer campaign sold exactly three books ($3,333 per sale), a $10,000 speaking agency booked zero gigs, and her $24,000 publicist was the only line item she doesn't regret. What actually moved copies: 30 podcast interviews she secured herself, an hour on Tamron Hall (about 200 sales), and events with book-bundled tickets. Her lesson for authors: "Vibes and promises cost me $20,000." (Amy Chan, via WITI)

An extinct species of yak is new to science. Ancient genomes from Denisova Cave in Siberia revealed "Yak X," a distinct bovine species that diverged from modern yaks about 400,000 years ago and died out sometime after 27,200 years ago. Curiously, while the cave's hominins (Neanderthals and Denisovans) interbred freely, Yak X stayed genetically isolated from its bovine neighbors. (404 Media)

Tech & Gadgets

Steven Levy is still convinced the iPod was the perfect gadget. Apple's original music player got many things right, he argues, and chief among them was a negative: it didn't connect to the internet. No notifications, no feeds, just music. In an age of face computers, the argument lands harder than ever. (WIRED)

Face computers are finally getting good. Xreal's long-hyped Aura XR glasses are arriving soon for $1,279, and WIRED put them up against Meta's recently announced VR glasses. The verdict: this generation is the first that feels ready for normal humans. (WIRED)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• NASA dropped nearly 1 TB of Artemis II data for the public: photos, audio, video, and astronaut notes to prep for future moon missions. (WIRED)

• Optogenetics, the Nobel-winning trick for controlling neurons with light, traces its origins to a brainless alga. (WIRED)

• ICANN may soon approve hundreds of new top-level domains, including .meow and .fart. The .meow campaign crowdfunded 121,896 euros on Kickstarter. (WIRED)

• Etsy sellers are hawking "Cornell Seven" merch out of solidarity with the woman who accused seven fraternity members of sexual assault. Some say it's shameless. (WIRED)

• Sen. Ron Wyden is demanding a privacy review report about the White House's HIDTA license plate surveillance program, following a 404 Media investigation. (404 Media)

• This week on AI and spirituality: what would the Pope do? (404 Media)

• "It is done. Hail Satan": an Iowa city council is debating when in the meeting agenda to "undo the curse" from its new religious liberty law. (404 Media)
