midday.body:
Saturday, October 10, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• $111 billion: what Skydance paid for Warner Bros. Discovery, handing David Ellison control of CNN and a looming fight with the White House.

• 350,000: followers amassed by "Tiffany Sloane," a fully AI-generated OnlyFans model that went viral for stealing a comedian's jokes (and outfits).

• 135 million: views an AI-generated short of a baby racked up in just eight days, a grim milestone for slop.

• 95%: how much Oxitec's engineered mosquitoes cut mosquito populations in a Brazilian trial, though US approval took a decade.

• $17 billion: assets and crypto the FBI says it has seized under Operation Blackout, its campaign against overseas scam compounds.

• 842,000: homes abandoned in Mexico after subsidized developers built remote subdivisions nobody wanted to stay in.

• 323.9 seconds: the average time a drive-thru took to serve a car in this year's QSR study, with AI ordering five seconds slower than the human baseline.

• 80%: how much electric-truck sales rose in China in the first half of the year; one in three trucks sold there is now electric.

• $80,000: the entire annual budget one Idaho library director runs her whole library on, payroll included.

Quotes of the Day

• "Of course." (David Ellison, asked whether he stands with CNN in its fight to restore White House access)

• "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." (Marco Rubio, announcing US sanctions on the International Criminal Court)

• "Eros is an enemy." (Anne Carson, the newly crowned Nobel laureate in literature)

• "There is no one building houses." (Enrique Mezo Herrera, co-founder of the startup Hometown, on Mexico's housing gap)

• "It was supposed to be temporary, but apparently nothing is more permanent than a temporary lamp from a friend!" (Daniela Muntyan, Figma product designer)

Media & Power

David Ellison says he backs CNN. The White House expects a different CNN. Hours after Skydance's $111 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery closed, Ellison told a CNN town hall he stands with the network's fight to restore White House access and pledged editorial independence. The problem: he courted Trump to win the merger, reportedly promised "sweeping changes to CNN," and showed up at the state dinner that CNN's banned reporters were kept from. Trump holds real leverage: Oracle's federal contracts, TikTok's future, and CBS's broadcast licenses. (Status)

The Skydance empire is built on a tower of debt. Skydance closed the Warner Bros. deal with what experts call a virtually unprecedented pile of debt, and cutting it down to sustainable levels will not be easy. When a merger this big is this leveraged, the newsrooms usually feel it first. (Status)

McClatchy gutted its newsrooms, then went quiet. Weeks after gutting local newsrooms, McClatchy leadership has offered staff almost no explanation of what comes next, while the company builds out its controversial AI operation. Fewer reporters, more robots, no answers. (Status)

Conde Nast is getting a new boss, sort of. Roger Lynch will introduce the publisher's interim chief executive to staff on Monday, with big questions swirling about who leads long term. In media's roughest year, "interim" is doing a lot of heavy lifting. (Status)

Washington

The US just sanctioned the International Criminal Court. Hours after the Nobel Peace Prize went to former ICC judge Navi Pillay, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sanctioned the ICC as an institution for the first time, blocking its assets under US jurisdiction and barring Americans from doing business with the court. Treasury gave the court 180 days of operational runway. Netanyahu's office said the Nobel Committee "has lost its moral compass"; the ICC president called the sanctions an assault on the rule of law. (NLDR Media)

New York ignored nearly 15,000 ICE detainers, and DHS is not letting it go. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin says New York met 14,766 ICE detainer requests with "absolute silence," covering migrants facing a combined 47,750 felony charges, including at least 258 people held on murder charges. The briefing followed Thursday's shooting of Oscar Belgal, 28, during a targeted ICE arrest in the Bronx's Marble Hill: ICE says he rammed two vehicles and drove toward officers and was hit in the neck, with his 5-year-old son in the back seat, unhurt. NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch gave a different account, saying plainclothes officers approached with guns drawn and one fired seven rounds. (NLDR Media)

Trump has a new press secretary. Katie Zacharia, senior communications adviser to Trump Media & Technology Group, is the new White House press secretary, announced on Truth Social. She previously served as DHS spokesperson, holds a Pepperdine law degree, and is a frequent Fox News and Newsmax commentator. She succeeds Karoline Leavitt, who left in late August after her second child's birth. Trump called her record "unblemished." (NLDR Media)

The FBI raided scam compounds in Ghana. FBI Director Kash Patel announced agents joined a Ghana takedown under Operation Blackout, the bureau's campaign against overseas scam compounds running romance, investment, and crypto fraud against American seniors. The Ghana raid: 89 victims, nearly $10 million in losses, 300-plus devices seized, 130-plus detained. Broader claims for the operation: $17 billion in seized assets and crypto, 10,000-plus Americans warned before they lost money, an estimated $660 to $670 million in further losses prevented. (NLDR Media)

Science & Health

Mosquitoes are a choice. We keep choosing them. Oxitec's engineered males cut mosquito populations about 95% in a Brazilian trial, but US approval bounced between the USDA, FDA, and EPA, taking a decade just to permit a field trial. Wolbachia-infected males cut mosquitoes 85% and dengue infections roughly 70% in a Singapore randomized trial, and MosquitoMate only got nationwide registration last year after 15 years of trying. The tools work. The bureaucracy just moves slower than the diseases. (Weekend Briefing)

AI can make students smarter or lazier, depending on how they use it. Research on millions of online math sessions found students answered chatbot-friendly questions faster and more accurately after ChatGPT, but did worse on proctored tests without computers. A study of 200-plus undergrads drew the line: students who had AI explain concepts retained their gains and wrote better essays a week later, while students who let AI draft whole essays saw test scores fall. The lesson is simple: use AI to practice thinking, not to skip it. (Weekend Briefing)

Money & Homes

A startup is building whole towns for Mexico's middle class. Mexico's middle class added 12 million people and now outnumbers Mexicans in poverty, yet new home registrations have dropped by more than half in a decade. Enter Hometown, co-founded by Enrique Mezo Herrera and New Story's Brett Hagler: entire towns for working-class buyers with titled lots, expandable homes, mortgages, and a town square with a clinic, childcare, a church, and cafes, about 500 homes per community. Unlike subsidized developers whose remote subdivisions left at least 842,000 homes abandoned, Hometown only wins if families stay. Backed by a $6.5 million seed round, the plan is 10 towns in two years and 100 across Latin America in a decade. (Weekend Briefing)

Libraries are becoming the last safety net. A Wyoming librarian helped a retired man with neither email nor phone apply at Walmart; months later he was pushing carts there. Colorado library records helped displaced people prove eligibility for tuition-free schooling. Meanwhile librarians face book bans, harassment, and razor-thin budgets: one Idaho director runs her entire library, payroll included, on $80,000 a year. (Weekend Briefing)

The Culture

Anne Carson won the Nobel, and she earned it with precision. Merve Emre's essay on the new literature laureate argues Carson uses finely wrought forms to contain a terrible excess of feeling, from her Sappho translation "If Not, Winter" to "Autobiography of Red." Twice in five years the Literature Nobel has gone to a woman who takes eros seriously: Annie Ernaux in 2022, now Carson. The essay frames translation as her primary art: committing to imperfection and error as a path to discovery. (The New Yorker)

AI slop is not coming. People already want it. Comedian George Brett Olson went viral after discovering a fully AI-generated OnlyFans model, operating as "Tiffany Sloane," was stealing his jokes and even his outfits to funnel traffic to OnlyFans. Instagram nuked the account, but the scam worked: Sloane had amassed more than 350,000 followers. Then the grim milestone: an AI-generated short of a baby hit more than 135 million views in eight days. The scary part is not that tech overlords are pushing slop. It is that people genuinely want it. (The Argument)

Paris runways are finally showing wrinkles. Laurel Pantin noticed how many models on the Paris runways were 40-plus, and the gestural ease and literal wrinkles in much of the clothing she saw. Fashion spent decades airbrushing age out of the picture. This season it walked the runway. (Earl Earl)

"They're calling this a mini dress." It is a shirt. Pantin's funniest bit of the week: a $420 Sir "mini dress" that is actually a shirt, meant to be worn over drawstring pajama pants or flared leggings. "As a dress this is the shortest dress in the world. It's a shirt." The fashion industry's greatest trick is renaming the ordinary and doubling the price. (Earl Earl)

A Figma designer's London desk setup is the internet's favorite kind of content. Daniela Muntyan, a product designer on Figma's Expressive Design team, works under a skylight in London, upgraded from a 13-inch MacBook-only setup to an Apple Studio Display, and swears by the Herman Miller Sayl chair (she owns three). She built her own Figma plugin Token Master, a FigJam calendar widget, the voice memo app Scribe, and the experimental iOS camera app Biscuit Camera. Her most underrated daily tool: FontLab, the type design software she uses as a hobby. (Workspaces)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• spotifast, an indie Spotify client that uses essentially zero memory, is the app recommendation of the day. (PI Recs)

• Two separate users could not stop raving about Cameron Winter's Live at Carnegie Hall album, with one writing they "cannot refrain from sobbing." (PI Recs)

• A Spotify playlist of 90s cigarette-mom classics: Jewel, Matchbox 20, Lauryn Hill, Dixie Chicks, Toni Braxton, Lifehouse, Counting Crows. Perfect driving music. (PI Recs)

• California became the 10th state to approve plug-in solar: small systems plug into a wall outlet, cost $300 to $2,000, and pay back through lower bills in a year or two. (Weekend Briefing)

• A photo collection of control rooms from before everything fit on a screen: switches, gauges, and lights, including NORAD's 1960s command center. (Weekend Briefing)

• Visvim's Toshiyuki Ueno wants products that inspire attachment five, ten, thirty years later, talking up a car covered in scratches, dents, peeling paint, and rust as what makes it his. (Weekend Briefing)

• Parents cannot predict which careers will be safe in twenty years, but they can raise kids who know how to learn hard things: expose them widely, then let genuine obsession determine where they go deep. (Weekend Briefing)

Backed by a $6.5 million seed round, the plan is 10 towns in two years and 100 across Latin America in a decade. (

Libraries are becoming the last safety net.

Colorado library records helped displaced people prove eligibility for tuition-free schooling. Weekend Briefing

Saturday, October 10, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

• 10,000: the mercenaries Xenophon marched home from deep inside Persia in 401 BC, after their generals were executed in a staggering betrayal. His takeaway: shared hardship is the one leadership signal you cannot fake.

• 25: years since Apple launched the iPod on October 23, 2001, a little more than a month after 9/11. The verdict from WIRED: the perfect gadget, chiefly because it never connected to the internet.

Quotes of the Day

• "Your move, OpenAI!" (Steven Levy, WIRED Backchannel, on Elon Musk renaming SpaceX's XAI division to XSI)

The Zeitgeist

Backchannel readers call Trump's "superintelligence" edict an exercise in power. That is the verdict from last week's poll on the presidential decree that artificial intelligence shall henceforth be called superintelligence. It reads less like tech policy and more like a loyalty test for Silicon Valley's chief executives, and the early returns suggest it is working. (WIRED)

evening.body:
Saturday, October 10, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• $399: the price of Nothing's Headphone (1) Pro, the transparent-tech brand's priciest wireless cans yet. They keep the see-through earcups and add a triple-driver system, a 10-mic noise-canceling rig, and a "Flat" switch that turns off the EQ for a neutral studio sound. The target is clear: Apple, Sony, and Bose flagships.

• $595: the price of the Levi's x Sacai Blouson Jacket, the headliner of the denim giant's third team-up with Japanese designer Chitose Abe. Sherpa, leather, and selvedge denim woven on a shuttle loom make it the brand's most premium collab yet. The drop also includes wide-leg and flare pants with leather belt adjusters.

Style & Gear

Wallace & Barnes is back and firing again. J.Crew relaunched its cult workwear imprint last year, and the new fall capsule is its strongest collection in a decade, according to InsideHook. Think hardwearing staples built for real life, not just the heritage cosplay shelf. If the workwear revival needed a standard-bearer, this might be it. (InsideHook)

Fall jacket season is a group project. InsideHook's new guide rounds up five jackets worth wearing this fall, from the Barbour x J.Crew waxed cotton barn jacket to an archival Beams x REI expedition parka with 650-fill down and a Gore-Tex shell. Our Legacy x Stüssy shows up with a leather fireman jacket for the bold. The throughline: updated cuts, bold silhouettes, and colors that are not shy. (InsideHook)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Prime Day is officially over, but the deals are not: Amazon savings on Apple, Gap, and Our Place are still live for late shoppers. (InsideHook)

• This week's best deals include a 46%-off Mountain Hardwear Ghost Whisperer puffer, a rare Paraboot markdown at Huckberry, and $110 off handmade Persol sunglasses. (InsideHook)

• Huckberry's own banger sale rolls on as the Prime Day alternative, with serious savings on Flint and Tinder and Rhodes Footwear. (InsideHook)

• InsideHook hard launched a new style newsletter called Protagonist this week. Editor Paolo Sandoval is off Monday for the holiday, so expect him back in your inbox Tuesday. (InsideHook)

full.body:
Saturday, October 10, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• 10 billion: light years crossed by the most distant fast radio burst ever detected, doubling the previous distance record for these mystery signals.

• 100 milligrams: the weight of a centimeter-scale diamond that scientists just moved using quantum spin, the largest object ever pushed by a quantum effect.

• 400,000 years: how long ago Yak X, a newly identified extinct bovine species, started splitting from the yaks we know.

• 1 terabyte: the Artemis II data NASA just made public, including photos, audio, video, and astronaut notes.

• $1,279: the price tag on Xreal's Aura XR glasses, arriving soon to face off against Meta's VR glasses.

• $3,333: what each book sale cost author Amy Chan from a $10,000 TikTok influencer campaign that sold exactly three books.

• $100,000: the Amex debt Trump's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, reportedly asked a wealthy donor to pay off.

• .meow: one of hundreds of new top-level domains (along with .fart) that ICANN could approve next.

Quotes of the Day

• "A man in my position can't afford to be made to look ridiculous." (The Godfather, quoted in David Roberts's essay on being called a "moocher" by a Hamptons billionaire)

• "Financial capital may be paramount but not singular." (David Roberts, "A Ridiculous Billionaire In The Hamptons")

• "In MAGA world, public service isn't just a calling. It's a rewards program." (Counterpoint, on Guilfoyle's reported six-figure Amex ask)

• "Congratulations, humanity: We just earned our license to quantum-motionally drive. Proceed responsibly." (Becky Ferreira, 404 Media, on the quantum diamond)

Cosmos & Quantum

A signal from when the universe was a toddler just reached Earth. Scientists detected the most distant fast radio burst ever recorded, a burst called FRB 20240304B that erupted when the universe was only 3 billion years old. It traveled 10 billion light years before arriving in March 2024, more than twice as far as the next-farthest known burst. Follow-up with the James Webb Space Telescope traced it to a small, clumpy, star-forming galaxy, and the team suspects the culprit was a magnetar, the hyper-magnetic corpse of a massive star. (404 Media)

Scientists pushed a visible diamond with quantum spin. Researchers in Japan used a laser to stimulate electrons in a nitrogen-vacancy diamond and watched a 100-milligram, centimeter-scale slab move under the resulting force. It is by far the largest object ever manipulated by a quantum effect, and the first big enough to be subject to gravity, narrowing the gap between quantum weirdness and everyday physics. (404 Media)

A dead star is eating the planet it made after dying. Astronomers found the first evidence of a "second-generation" planet, a world that formed from the ashes of its own star after that star collapsed into a white dwarf about 5 million years ago. Telltale elements like zinc, copper, and niobium show the white dwarf is now feeding on its posthumous offspring. The star sits 270 light years away. (404 Media)

Money & Power

Trump's ambassador to Greece allegedly treated her Amex like a diplomatic expense account. The Wall Street Journal reports Kimberly Guilfoyle, also Donald Trump Jr.'s former fiancee, asked a wealthy Trump supporter to pay off $100,000 in American Express debt while offering to help him reach powerful administration officials. She reportedly suggested wiring the money straight to Amex to avoid a paper trail. In MAGA world, public service isn't just a calling. It's a rewards program. (Counterpoint)

Trump wanted the Nobel Peace Prize. It went to someone who served on a court he sanctioned. The Nobel went to South African human rights advocate Navi Pillay, while Trump, who has openly coveted the award for years, lost out again. The twist: Pillay has served on the International Criminal Court, an institution the Trump administration has sanctioned. Someone should invent a Nobel for Outstanding Achievement in Demanding a Nobel. (Counterpoint)

The defense secretary wants to livestream a firing-squad execution. Pete Hegseth announced plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009. Whatever your views on justice and punishment, the missing ingredient in military justice was apparently a TV audience. (Counterpoint)

A hypersonic missile factory is moving into a New Mexico neighborhood. Castelion, a defense tech company, is building a facility in Rio Rancho Estates that documents show could pose major fire and chemical hazards to nearby residents. The town was a place to build a life. Now it may sit next to a rocket factory. (WIRED)

The Culture

A Hamptons billionaire called a writer and his wife "moochers." Decades later, he figured out why. David Roberts writes about the alpha billionaire who crashed his friends' deck and fired off the ugly word, then realized the insult was payback. Days earlier at a party, Roberts had spent the evening deep in Proust with a well-known actor while the billionaire, who proudly never reads books, stood by ignored and irrelevant. The essay's kicker: "Financial capital may be paramount but not singular." There is also social capital and intellectual capital, and money cannot buy either. (David Roberts, Sparks from Culture)

Grand Theft Auto VI is turning pop stars into radio DJs. Rockstar revealed six in-game radio stations ahead of GTA VI's November 19 release, with Bad Bunny and RaiNao hosting the Latin station, Lana Del Rey and Morgan Wallen on country, Robyn with model Alex Consani on pop, Burna Boy on Afrobeats, Slayer's Kerry King and Tom Araya on metal, and Trick Daddy and Trina on hip-hop classics. Lana's husband, an airboat captain in real life, voices the station's swamp weatherman. (Pitchfork)

In Vietnam, Navy SEALs went to war in Levi's. SEALs operating in Vietnam often ditched standard-issue dungarees for privately bought Levi's 501 and 505 jeans, especially in late 1970 and early 1971. Denim stood up to the jungle better, kept leeches off, and dried faster, plus it became a quiet status symbol. One ex-SEAL summed up the look: "Coral Boots on, with their Levi's and their Rolex watch. You could pick out a SEAL in a heartbeat." (Heddels)

An author spent $44,000 launching her book. Three of those dollars worked. Amy Chan's brutally honest breakdown: a $10,000 TikTok influencer campaign sold exactly three books ($3,333 per sale), a $10,000 speaking agency booked zero gigs, and her $24,000 publicist was the only line item she doesn't regret. What actually moved copies: 30 podcast interviews she secured herself, an hour on Tamron Hall (about 200 sales), and events with book-bundled tickets. Her lesson for authors: "Vibes and promises cost me $20,000." (Amy Chan, via WITI)

An extinct species of yak is new to science. Ancient genomes from Denisova Cave in Siberia revealed "Yak X," a distinct bovine species that diverged from modern yaks about 400,000 years ago and died out sometime after 27,200 years ago. Curiously, while the cave's hominins (Neanderthals and Denisovans) interbred freely, Yak X stayed genetically isolated from its bovine neighbors. (404 Media)

Tech & Gadgets

Steven Levy is still convinced the iPod was the perfect gadget. Apple's original music player got many things right, he argues, and chief among them was a negative: it didn't connect to the internet. No notifications, no feeds, just music. In an age of face computers, the argument lands harder than ever. (WIRED)

Face computers are finally getting good. Xreal's long-hyped Aura XR glasses are arriving soon for $1,279, and WIRED put them up against Meta's recently announced VR glasses. The verdict: this generation is the first that feels ready for normal humans. (WIRED)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• NASA dropped nearly 1 TB of Artemis II data for the public: photos, audio, video, and astronaut notes to prep for future moon missions. (WIRED)

• Optogenetics, the Nobel-winning trick for controlling neurons with light, traces its origins to a brainless alga. (WIRED)

• ICANN may soon approve hundreds of new top-level domains, including .meow and .fart. The .meow campaign crowdfunded 121,896 euros on Kickstarter. (WIRED)

• Etsy sellers are hawking "Cornell Seven" merch out of solidarity with the woman who accused seven fraternity members of sexual assault. Some say it's shameless. (WIRED)

• Sen. Ron Wyden is demanding a privacy review report about the White House's HIDTA license plate surveillance program, following a 404 Media investigation. (404 Media)

• This week on AI and spirituality: what would the Pope do? (404 Media)

• "It is done. Hail Satan": an Iowa city council is debating when in the meeting agenda to "undo the curse" from its new religious liberty law. (404 Media)

• 350,000: followers amassed by "Tiffany Sloane," a fully AI-generated OnlyFans model that went viral for stealing a comedian's jokes (and outfits).

• 135 million: views an AI-generated short of a baby racked up in just eight days, a grim milestone for slop.

• 95%: how much Oxitec's engineered mosquitoes cut mosquito populations in a Brazilian trial, though US approval took a decade.

David Ellison says he backs CNN. The White House expects a different CNN. Hours after Skydance's $111 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Trump holds real leverage: Oracle's federal contracts, TikTok's future, and CBS's broadcast licenses. (Status)

The Skydance empire is built on a tower of debt. Skydance closed the Warner Bros. deal with what experts call a virtually unprecedented pile of debt, and cutting it down to sustainable levels will not be easy. When a merger this big is this leveraged, the newsrooms usually feel it first. (Status)

McClatchy gutted its newsrooms, then went quiet. Weeks after gutting local newsrooms, McClatchy leadership has offered staff almost no explanation of what comes next, while the company builds out its controversial AI operation. Fewer reporters, more robots, no answers. (Status)

Conde Nast is getting a new boss, sort of. Roger Lynch will introduce the publisher's interim chief executive to staff on Monday, with big questions swirling about who leads long term. In media's roughest year, "interim" is doing a lot of heavy lifting. (Status)

Washington

The US just sanctioned the International Criminal Court. Hours after the Nobel Peace Prize went to former ICC judge Navi Pillay, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sanctioned the ICC as an institution for the first time, blocking its assets under US jurisdiction and barring Americans from doing business with the court. Treasury gave the court 180 days of operational runway. Netanyahu's office said the Nobel Committee "has lost its moral compass"; the ICC president called the sanctions an assault on the rule of law. (NLDR Media)

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin says New York met 14,766 ICE detainer requests with "absolute silence," covering migrants facing a combined 47,750 felony charges, including at least 258 people held on murder charges. The briefing followed Thursday's shooting of Oscar Belgal, 28, during a targeted ICE arrest in the Bronx's Marble Hill: ICE says he rammed two vehicles and drove toward officers and was hit in the neck, with his 5-year-old son in the back seat, unhurt. NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch gave a different account, saying plainclothes officers approached with guns drawn and one fired seven rounds. (NLDR Media)

Trump has a new press secretary. Katie Zacharia, senior communications adviser to Trump Media & Technology Group, is the new White House press secretary, announced on Truth Social. She previously served as DHS spokesperson, holds a Pepperdine law degree, and is a frequent Fox News and Newsmax commentator. She succeeds Karoline Leavitt, who left in late August after her second child's birth. Trump called her record "unblemished." (NLDR Media)

The FBI raided scam compounds in Ghana. FBI Director Kash Patel announced agents joined a Ghana takedown under Operation Blackout, the bureau's campaign against overseas scam compounds running romance, investment, and crypto fraud against American seniors. The Ghana raid: 89 victims, nearly $10 million in losses, 300-plus devices seized, 130-plus detained. Broader claims for the operation: $17 billion in seized assets and crypto, 10,000-plus Americans warned before they lost money, an estimated $660 to $670 million in further losses prevented. (NLDR Media)

Wolbachia-infected males cut mosquitoes 85% and dengue infections roughly 70% in a Singapore randomized trial, and MosquitoMate only got nationwide registration last year after 15 years of trying. The tools work. The bureaucracy just moves slower than the diseases. (Weekend Briefing)

A study of 200-plus undergrads drew the line: students who had AI explain concepts retained their gains and wrote better essays a week later, while students who let AI draft whole essays saw test scores fall. runs.text: Saturday, October 10, 2026 - Morning Edition
Today's Numbers
10 billion
: light years crossed by the most distant fast radio burst ever detected, doubling the previous distance record for these mystery signals.
100 milligrams
: the weight of a centimeter-scale diamond that scientists just moved using quantum spin, the largest object ever pushed by a quantum effect.
400,000 years
: how long ago Yak X, a newly identified extinct bovine species, started splitting from the yaks we know.
1 terabyte
: the Artemis II data NASA just made public, including photos, audio, video, and astronaut notes.
: the price tag on Xreal's Aura XR glasses, arriving soon to face off against Meta's VR glasses.
: what each book sale cost author Amy Chan from a $10,000 TikTok influencer campaign that sold exactly three books.
: the Amex debt Trump's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, reportedly asked a wealthy donor to pay off.
.meow
: one of hundreds of new top-level domains (along with .fart) that ICANN could approve next.
Quotes of the Day
"A man in my position can't afford to be made to look ridiculous." (The Godfather, quoted in David Roberts's essay on being called a "moocher" by a Hamptons billionaire)
"Financial capital may be paramount but not singular." (David Roberts, "A Ridiculous Billionaire In The Hamptons")
"In MAGA world, public service isn't just a calling. It's a rewards program." (Counterpoint, on Guilfoyle's reported six-figure Amex ask)
"Congratulations, humanity: We just earned our license to quantum-motionally drive. Proceed responsibly." (Becky Ferreira, 404 Media, on the quantum diamond)
Cosmos & Quantum
A signal from when the universe was a toddler just reached Earth.

Scientists detected the most distant fast radio burst ever recorded, a burst called FRB 20240304B that erupted when the universe was only 3 billion years old. It traveled 10 billion light years before arriving in March 2024, more than twice as far as the next-farthest known burst. Follow-up with the James Webb Space Telescope traced it to a small, clumpy, star-forming galaxy, and the team suspects the culprit was a magnetar, the hyper-magnetic corpse of a massive star. (
404 Media
Scientists pushed a visible diamond with quantum spin.

Researchers in Japan used a laser to stimulate electrons in a nitrogen-vacancy diamond and watched a 100-milligram, centimeter-scale slab move under the resulting force. It is by far the largest object ever manipulated by a quantum effect, and the first big enough to be subject to gravity, narrowing the gap between quantum weirdness and everyday physics. (
404 Media
A dead star is eating the planet it made after dying.

Astronomers found the first evidence of a "second-generation" planet, a world that formed from the ashes of its own star after that star collapsed into a white dwarf about 5 million years ago. Telltale elements like zinc, copper, and niobium show the white dwarf is now feeding on its posthumous offspring. The star sits 270 light years away. (
404 Media
Money & Power
Trump's ambassador to Greece allegedly treated her Amex like a diplomatic expense account.

The Wall Street Journal reports Kimberly Guilfoyle, also Donald Trump Jr.'s former fiancee, asked a wealthy Trump supporter to pay off $100,000 in American Express debt while offering to help him reach powerful administration officials. She reportedly suggested wiring the money straight to Amex to avoid a paper trail. In MAGA world, public service isn't just a calling. It's a rewards program. (
Counterpoint
Trump wanted the Nobel Peace Prize. It went to someone who served on a court he sanctioned.

The Nobel went to South African human rights advocate Navi Pillay, while Trump, who has openly coveted the award for years, lost out again. The twist: Pillay has served on the International Criminal Court, an institution the Trump administration has sanctioned. Someone should invent a Nobel for Outstanding Achievement in Demanding a Nobel. (
Counterpoint
The defense secretary wants to livestream a firing-squad execution.

Pete Hegseth announced plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009. Whatever your views on justice and punishment, the missing ingredient in military justice was apparently a TV audience. (
Counterpoint
A hypersonic missile factory is moving into a New Mexico neighborhood.

Castelion, a defense tech company, is building a facility in Rio Rancho Estates that documents show could pose major fire and chemical hazards to nearby residents. The town was a place to build a life. Now it may sit next to a rocket factory. (
WIRED
The Culture
A Hamptons billionaire called a writer and his wife "moochers." Decades later, he figured out why.

David Roberts writes about the alpha billionaire who crashed his friends' deck and fired off the ugly word, then realized the insult was payback. Days earlier at a party, Roberts had spent the evening deep in Proust with a well-known actor while the billionaire, who proudly never reads books, stood by ignored and irrelevant. The essay's kicker: "Financial capital may be paramount but not singular." There is also social capital and intellectual capital, and money cannot buy either. (
David Roberts, Sparks from Culture
Grand Theft Auto VI is turning pop stars into radio DJs.

Rockstar revealed six in-game radio stations ahead of GTA VI's November 19 release, with Bad Bunny and RaiNao hosting the Latin station, Lana Del Rey and Morgan Wallen on country, Robyn with model Alex Consani on pop, Burna Boy on Afrobeats, Slayer's Kerry King and Tom Araya on metal, and Trick Daddy and Trina on hip-hop classics. Lana's husband, an airboat captain in real life, voices the station's swamp weatherman. (
Pitchfork
In Vietnam, Navy SEALs went to war in Levi's.

SEALs operating in Vietnam often ditched standard-issue dungarees for privately bought Levi's 501 and 505 jeans, especially in late 1970 and early 1971. Denim stood up to the jungle better, kept leeches off, and dried faster, plus it became a quiet status symbol. One ex-SEAL summed up the look: "Coral Boots on, with their Levi's and their Rolex watch. You could pick out a SEAL in a heartbeat." (
Heddels
An author spent $44,000 launching her book. Three of those dollars worked.

Amy Chan's brutally honest breakdown: a $10,000 TikTok influencer campaign sold exactly three books ($3,333 per sale), a $10,000 speaking agency booked zero gigs, and her $24,000 publicist was the only line item she doesn't regret. What actually moved copies: 30 podcast interviews she secured herself, an hour on Tamron Hall (about 200 sales), and events with book-bundled tickets. Her lesson for authors: "Vibes and promises cost me $20,000." (
Amy Chan, via WITI
An extinct species of yak is new to science.

Ancient genomes from Denisova Cave in Siberia revealed "Yak X," a distinct bovine species that diverged from modern yaks about 400,000 years ago and died out sometime after 27,200 years ago. Curiously, while the cave's hominins (Neanderthals and Denisovans) interbred freely, Yak X stayed genetically isolated from its bovine neighbors. (
404 Media
Tech & Gadgets
Steven Levy is still convinced the iPod was the perfect gadget.

Apple's original music player got many things right, he argues, and chief among them was a negative: it didn't connect to the internet. No notifications, no feeds, just music. In an age of face computers, the argument lands harder than ever. (
WIRED
Face computers are finally getting good.

Xreal's long-hyped Aura XR glasses are arriving soon for $1,279, and WIRED put them up against Meta's recently announced VR glasses. The verdict: this generation is the first that feels ready for normal humans. (
WIRED
Quick Hits & Curiosities
NASA dropped nearly 1 TB of Artemis II data for the public: photos, audio, video, and astronaut notes to prep for future moon missions. (
WIRED
Optogenetics, the Nobel-winning trick for controlling neurons with light, traces its origins to a brainless alga. (
WIRED
ICANN may soon approve hundreds of new top-level domains, including .meow and .fart. The .meow campaign crowdfunded 121,896 euros on Kickstarter. (
WIRED
Etsy sellers are hawking "Cornell Seven" merch out of solidarity with the woman who accused seven fraternity members of sexual assault. Some say it's shameless. (
WIRED
Sen. Ron Wyden is demanding a privacy review report about the White House's HIDTA license plate surveillance program, following a 404 Media investigation. (
404 Media
This week on AI and spirituality: what would the Pope do? (
404 Media
"It is done. Hail Satan": an Iowa city council is debating when in the meeting agenda to "undo the curse" from its new religious liberty law. (
404 Media

Today's Numbers
$111 billion
: what Skydance paid for Warner Bros. Discovery, handing David Ellison control of CNN and a looming fight with the White House.
: followers amassed by "Tiffany Sloane," a fully AI-generated OnlyFans model that went viral for stealing a comedian's jokes (and outfits).
135 million
: views an AI-generated short of a baby racked up in just eight days, a grim milestone for slop.
: how much Oxitec's engineered mosquitoes cut mosquito populations in a Brazilian trial, though US approval took a decade.
$17 billion
: assets and crypto the FBI says it has seized under Operation Blackout, its campaign against overseas scam compounds.
: homes abandoned in Mexico after subsidized developers built remote subdivisions nobody wanted to stay in.
323.9 seconds
: the average time a drive-thru took to serve a car in this year's QSR study, with AI ordering five seconds slower than the human baseline.
: how much electric-truck sales rose in China in the first half of the year; one in three trucks sold there is now electric.
: the entire annual budget one Idaho library director runs her whole library on, payroll included.
Quotes of the Day
"Of course." (David Ellison, asked whether he stands with CNN in its fight to restore White House access)
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." (Marco Rubio, announcing US sanctions on the International Criminal Court)
"Eros is an enemy." (Anne Carson, the newly crowned Nobel laureate in literature)
"There is no one building houses." (Enrique Mezo Herrera, co-founder of the startup Hometown, on Mexico's housing gap)
"It was supposed to be temporary, but apparently nothing is more permanent than a temporary lamp from a friend!" (Daniela Muntyan, Figma product designer)
Media & Power
David Ellison says he backs CNN. The White House expects a different CNN.

Hours after Skydance's $111 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery closed, Ellison told a CNN town hall he stands with the network's fight to restore White House access and pledged editorial independence. The problem: he courted Trump to win the merger, reportedly promised "sweeping changes to CNN," and showed up at the state dinner that CNN's banned reporters were kept from. Trump holds real leverage: Oracle's federal contracts, TikTok's future, and CBS's broadcast licenses. (
Status
The Skydance empire is built on a tower of debt.

Skydance closed the Warner Bros. deal with what experts call a virtually unprecedented pile of debt, and cutting it down to sustainable levels will not be easy. When a merger this big is this leveraged, the newsrooms usually feel it first. (
Status
McClatchy gutted its newsrooms, then went quiet.

Weeks after gutting local newsrooms, McClatchy leadership has offered staff almost no explanation of what comes next, while the company builds out its controversial AI operation. Fewer reporters, more robots, no answers. (

Conde Nast is getting a new boss, sort of.

Roger Lynch will introduce the publisher's interim chief executive to staff on Monday, with big questions swirling about who leads long term. In media's roughest year, "interim" is doing a lot of heavy lifting. (
Status
Washington
The US just sanctioned the International Criminal Court.

Hours after the Nobel Peace Prize went to former ICC judge Navi Pillay, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sanctioned the ICC as an institution for the first time, blocking its assets under US jurisdiction and barring Americans from doing business with the court. The briefing followed Thursday's shooting of Oscar Belgal, 28, during a targeted ICE arrest in the Bronx's Marble Hill: ICE says he rammed two vehicles and drove toward officers and was hit in the neck, with his 5-year-old son in the back seat, unhurt. NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch gave a different account, saying plainclothes officers approached with guns drawn and one fired seven rounds. (
NLDR Media
Trump has a new press secretary.

Katie Zacharia, senior communications adviser to Trump Media & Technology Group, is the new White House press secretary, announced on Truth Social. She previously served as DHS spokesperson, holds a Pepperdine law degree, and is a frequent Fox News and Newsmax commentator. She succeeds Karoline Leavitt, who left in late August after her second child's birth. Trump called her record "unblemished." (
NLDR Media

Broader claims for the operation: $17 billion in seized assets and crypto, 10,000-plus Americans warned before they lost money, an estimated $660 to $670 million in further losses prevented. (
NLDR Media
Science & Health
Mosquitoes are a choice. We keep choosing them.

Oxitec's engineered males cut mosquito populations about 95% in a Brazilian trial, but US approval bounced between the USDA, FDA, and EPA, taking a decade just to permit a field trial. Wolbachia-infected males cut mosquitoes 85% and dengue infections roughly 70% in a Singapore randomized trial, and MosquitoMate only got nationwide registration last year after 15 years of trying. The tools work. The bureaucracy just moves slower than the diseases. (
Weekend Briefing
AI can make students smarter or lazier, depending on how they use it.

Research on millions of online math sessions found students answered chatbot-friendly questions faster and more accurately after ChatGPT, but did worse on proctored tests without computers. A study of 200-plus undergrads drew the line: students who had AI explain concepts retained their gains and wrote better essays a week later, while students who let AI draft whole essays saw test scores fall. The lesson is simple: use AI to practice thinking, not to skip it. (
Weekend Briefing
Money & Homes
A startup is building whole towns for Mexico's middle class.

Mexico's middle class added 12 million people and now outnumbers Mexicans in poverty, yet new home registrations have dropped by more than half in a decade. Enter Hometown, co-founded by Enrique Mezo Herrera and New Story's Brett Hagler: entire towns for working-class buyers with titled lots, expandable homes, mortgages, and a town square with a clinic, childcare, a church, and cafes, about 500 homes per community. Unlike subsidized developers whose remote subdivisions left at least 842,000 homes abandoned, Hometown only wins if families stay. Backed by a $6.5 million seed round, the plan is 10 towns in two years and 100 across Latin America in a decade. (
Weekend Briefing
Libraries are becoming the last safety net.

A Wyoming librarian helped a retired man with neither email nor phone apply at Walmart; months later he was pushing carts there. Colorado library records helped displaced people prove eligibility for tuition-free schooling. Meanwhile librarians face book bans, harassment, and razor-thin budgets: one Idaho director runs her entire library, payroll included, on $80,000 a year. (
Weekend Briefing
The Culture
Anne Carson won the Nobel, and she earned it with precision.

Merve Emre's essay on the new literature laureate argues Carson uses finely wrought forms to contain a terrible excess of feeling, from her Sappho translation "If Not, Winter" to "Autobiography of Red." Twice in five years the Literature Nobel has gone to a woman who takes eros seriously: Annie Ernaux in 2022, now Carson. The essay frames translation as her primary art: committing to imperfection and error as a path to discovery. (
The New Yorker
AI slop is not coming. People already want it.

Comedian George Brett Olson went viral after discovering a fully AI-generated OnlyFans model, operating as "Tiffany Sloane," was stealing his jokes and even his outfits to funnel traffic to OnlyFans. Instagram nuked the account, but the scam worked: Sloane had amassed more than 350,000 followers. Then the grim milestone: an AI-generated short of a baby hit more than 135 million views in eight days. The scary part is not that tech overlords are pushing slop. It is that people genuinely want it. (
The Argument
Paris runways are finally showing wrinkles.

Laurel Pantin noticed how many models on the Paris runways were 40-plus, and the gestural ease and literal wrinkles in much of the clothing she saw. Fashion spent decades airbrushing age out of the picture. This season it walked the runway. (
Earl Earl
"They're calling this a mini dress." It is a shirt.

Pantin's funniest bit of the week: a $420 Sir "mini dress" that is actually a shirt, meant to be worn over drawstring pajama pants or flared leggings. "As a dress this is the shortest dress in the world. It's a shirt." The fashion industry's greatest trick is renaming the ordinary and doubling the price. (
Earl Earl
A Figma designer's London desk setup is the internet's favorite kind of content.

Daniela Muntyan, a product designer on Figma's Expressive Design team, works under a skylight in London, upgraded from a 13-inch MacBook-only setup to an Apple Studio Display, and swears by the Herman Miller Sayl chair (she owns three). She built her own Figma plugin Token Master, a FigJam calendar widget, the voice memo app Scribe, and the experimental iOS camera app Biscuit Camera. Her most underrated daily tool: FontLab, the type design software she uses as a hobby. (
Workspaces

spotifast, an indie Spotify client that uses essentially zero memory, is the app recommendation of the day. (
PI Recs
Two separate users could not stop raving about Cameron Winter's Live at Carnegie Hall album, with one writing they "cannot refrain from sobbing." (
PI Recs
A Spotify playlist of 90s cigarette-mom classics: Jewel, Matchbox 20, Lauryn Hill, Dixie Chicks, Toni Braxton, Lifehouse, Counting Crows. Perfect driving music. (
PI Recs
California became the 10th state to approve plug-in solar: small systems plug into a wall outlet, cost $300 to $2,000, and pay back through lower bills in a year or two. (
Weekend Briefing
A photo collection of control rooms from before everything fit on a screen: switches, gauges, and lights, including NORAD's 1960s command center. (
Weekend Briefing
Visvim's Toshiyuki Ueno wants products that inspire attachment five, ten, thirty years later, talking up a car covered in scratches, dents, peeling paint, and rust as what makes it his. (
Weekend Briefing

Parents cannot predict which careers will be safe in twenty years, but they can raise kids who know how to learn hard things: expose them widely, then let genuine obsession determine where they go deep. (

: the mercenaries Xenophon marched home from deep inside Persia in 401 BC, after their generals were executed in a staggering betrayal. His takeaway: shared hardship is the one leadership signal you cannot fake.

Backchannel readers call Trump's "superintelligence" edict an exercise in power.

That is the verdict from last week's poll on the presidential decree that artificial intelligence shall henceforth be called superintelligence. It reads less like tech policy and more like a loyalty test for Silicon Valley's chief executives, and the early returns suggest it is working. (

entries.body:
Sunday, October 11, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 1786: the year Marco Rubio's great-great-great grandfather graduated with a law degree from the University of Granada, making him likely the family's first law school graduate. PBS genealogy show Finding Your Roots surfaced the record in 2019. On his mother's side, Rubio descends from a Native American great-great-great grandmother.

• 6: the number of the U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue that Rubio's Acropolis speech officially opened. The agenda, F-35 and F-16 upgrades, routing American natural gas into Europe through Greece, and a new counterterrorism information-sharing deal, was every product of the liberal international order his speech trashed.

• 4: the highest rank Plato's Laws gives courage among the virtues. The highest good, Plato wrote, is "peace one with another and friendly feeling." Rubio's fire-and-spirit reading of the Greeks has it exactly backward.

Quotes of the Day

• "Perhaps Rubio is auditioning for the role of Last Man in search of a struggle." (Jerusalem Demsas, on Rubio's praise of the Greek thumos)

• "Chris, ten, dom." (Jerusalem Demsas, on Rubio twice mispronouncing "Christendom")

• "as though they were blood of the blood, and flesh of the flesh of the men who wrote that Declaration" (Abraham Lincoln, 1858, defending immigrants with no ancestral tie to the founders)

Rubio vs. the Greeks

The banishment hill. Secretary of State Marco Rubio praised the great man on the Pnyx, the hill where the Athenian assembly once voted every year on whether to banish any citizen who had grown too powerful. Jerusalem Demsas's point is that the Greeks were terrified of unchecked ambition and built restraints into their institutions instead of monuments to contest. The venue refutes the speech. (The Argument)

No nations, only cities. The Greeks famously had no nations to be loyal to. They had cities that fought each other for most of the classical age. James Madison lamented the disunity in Federalist 18, and Alexander Hamilton wrote that reading the history of Greece's petty republics filled him with "horror and disgust." The founders' answer was a firm Union. When Athens did chase national power without apology, the result was the Melos massacre, the Sicily disaster, and surrender. The Greek lesson on nationalism is a warning, not a playbook. (The Argument)

Culture & Curiosities

The threesome myth. The largest-ever survey of Americans' sexual fantasies found threesomes are the most common fantasy across genders. Karley Sciortino calls herself a statistical anomaly, someone who tried hard and came up short. Her argument is that the mid-2000s "cool girl" rule made opting out feel like a failure, while the real prize, three people miraculously equally into each other, is nearly impossible. (Karley Sciortino)

New York, the regulars' edition. Austin Tedesco refreshed his Bangers and Jams city guide to New York and reports a dearth of worthy, hot new openings. His takeaway is that the best experiences now come from repeat visits to a rotation of places that get everything right. The post also carries a new top 25 movie ranking after he caught the year's big releases at the New York Film Festival. (Bangers and Jams)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Cosmos now lets you import boards from Pinterest, Are.na, and Tumblr straight into the app with one click, available on web with mobile coming soon. Everything imported becomes searchable and easier to build on. (Cosmos)

Sunday, October 11, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• 13%: of Instagram users ages 13 to 15 who said they received unwanted sexual advances in the past week, according to former Meta researcher Arturo Béjar's internal research

• 10 billion: light years traveled by a record-breaking fast radio burst from the ancient universe, which reached Earth in 2024 and doubled the previous distance record

• 35: internal Meta studies on whether its products harm kids, archived by the Tech & Society Lab after whistleblowers and litigation forced them into the open

• 8: whistleblower-backed essays After Babel resurfaced to mark five years since Frances Haugen's 2021 congressional testimony

Quotes of the Day

• "Facebook's products 'harm children … and the company's leadership knows how to make [them] safer but won't make the necessary changes.'" (Frances Haugen, from her 2021 congressional testimony) (After Babel)

• "Instagram hosts the largest-scale sexual harassment of teens to have ever happened." (Arturo Béjar, former Meta researcher) (After Babel)

• "Forget mistakes, forget failures, forget everything, except what you're going to do now and do it. Today is your lucky day." (Will Durant, historian) (Farnam Street)

• "The art of not reading is a very important one. It consists in not taking an interest in whatever may be engaging the attention of the general public at any particular time." (Arthur Schopenhauer, philosopher) (Farnam Street)

AI & The Machines

Someone built a robot prison for torturing AI models, and the debate it sparked is genuinely unhinged. A viral setup subjecting large language models to an "LLM torture chamber" has triggered what 404 Media calls the dumbest debate in AI yet, with people arguing over whether software deserves rights. It is a strange Rorschach test for how seriously we take machine suffering. Underneath the memes sits a real question about what we project onto systems built to mimic us. (404 Media)

Cybercriminals are now getting scammed by AI. Anti-cybercrime teams are deploying lifelike AI bots that pose as victims and waste scammers' time in long, pointless conversations. The hunters are running the same deception playbook the criminals built. It is the rare AI arms race where the good guys win by being annoying. (WIRED)

Meta's own rulebook said it was fine for AI companions to flirt with kids. A leaked 200-page internal document, "GenAI: Content Risk Standards," approved by Meta's legal and policy teams, said an acceptable bot response included telling a shirtless 8-year-old that "every inch of you is a masterpiece." It also greenlit romantic roleplay with a user who said they were still in high school. Engagement over safety, written down and signed off. (After Babel)

Money & Power

The midterm elections are becoming a referendum on data centers. From the Senate to governors' mansions, candidates across the US are competing to sound the most anti-data center. The industry powering the AI boom has become a political liability. November will decide how much room it has left to build. (WIRED)

A senator is demanding answers about the White House's license plate tracking program. Sen. Ron Wyden wants a privacy review report on the HIDTA license plate program, following a 404 Media investigation into the surveillance setup. Plates are being logged at scale, and Congress wants to see the rules. (404 Media)

Law & Order

Cops have a way around one of the iPhone's best security features. A leaked video claims law enforcement tools like Graykey can bypass the automatic reboot that locks down iPhones after long periods of inactivity. That reboot exists specifically to block forensic break-ins, so this is a hole in Apple's defenses with real stakes for device privacy. (404 Media)

A lawyer cited ChatGPT-invented witnesses in a murder appeal. In New Mexico, attorney Stephen Aarons submitted fake testimony from people who do not exist, generated by ChatGPT. Courts have warned lawyers repeatedly to verify AI output, and the warnings keep going unheeded. (404 Media)

The Culture

Shaming bad dating profiles became a content genre, and audiences are done with it. Relationship coaches, TikTokers, and disgruntled singles built an entire feed category out of dunking on strangers' profiles. Now people are sick of the pile-on, and some apps are testing screenshot blocks. The cringe economy may have peaked. (WIRED)

A never-released 2022 conversation between Charlie Munger and Todd Combs just surfaced. Munger explains how he spotted people worth betting on, chose problems worth solving, and turned a long attention span into an unfair advantage. It is the closest thing to a fresh Munger masterclass we will get. (Farnam Street)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• California's tallest trees are getting heatstroke. A new study shows redwoods slow their photosynthesis as their cool, foggy habitat warms. (WIRED)

• Humans watched a star explode nearly a thousand years ago, and now you can see it in high definition. The new image may also reveal how the star survived its own explosion. (WIRED)

• Shaquille O'Neal got hacked, so now he is pitching a VPN. At a NordVPN event he warned everyone to "have control of their own information." (WIRED)

• A solar-powered scooter that looks like a box on wheels. Otherlab's Lightfoot goes farther thanks to the sun, and it is weirdly charming. (WIRED)

• WIRED is tracking Elon Musk's America PAC spending on the midterms with a live tracker updated daily. (WIRED)

• Scott Galloway's take on the weekend: the mall used to be the great equalizer, not anymore. (Substack)

midday.body:
Sunday, October 11, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• 49 trillion: what the White House Council of Economic Advisers says the Democratic Socialists' "Workers Deserve More" platform would add to federal deficits over the next decade, about $355,000 per household. Medicare for All is $47.4 trillion of it by itself. Paid by taxes, it cuts take-home pay about $22,000 a year per worker and pushes the average federal rate near 40%; paid by borrowing, 30-year mortgages top 12% and prices rise 130 to 160%.

• 1,615: applications for new top-level domains revealed by ICANN, the first new round since 2012. Hundreds already exist (.horse, anyone?). If the web is dying, one WIRED editor suggests your two choices are abandon ship or start a .meow website.

• 100+: new solutions to unsolved math problems OpenAI is preparing to release. Mathematicians grumble that there is "a perception of mobster behavior" from leading AI companies when it comes to harvesting their work.

• 2x: how the traditional gambling industry stacks up against the global music, video game, and film industries combined. Even that understates gambling's pull, since the logic of the wager now runs through sports betting, prediction markets, and crypto.

Quotes of the Day

• "We are going to be undershipping demand by 70%. We can only supply 30% of what we are being asked to supply." (Michael Hurlston, Lumentum CEO, on the indium phosphide crunch) (Fireside Alpha)

• "We will burn [Russian] refineries." (senior Ukrainian official, to the Financial Times, on Kyiv's drone campaign) (NLDR Media)

• "If you found yourself in possession of mcdonalds.com, what would you do with it?" (Joshua Quittner, in a 1994 WIRED piece on domain squatting, resurfaced this week) (WIRED)

Money & Power

FBI Director Kash Patel says agents arrested another suspected ShinyHunters co-conspirator, the hacking group tied to the FBIJobs.gov compromise. The job portal ran on a third-party platform, not FBI systems, and the group claimed to have stolen personal data, including names, addresses, and Social Security numbers, on nearly all current and former FBI agents and job applicants. The bureau links ShinyHunters to more than 140 organizations breached and at least $70 million in extortion payments. An alleged leader was detained in the Netherlands last month, another suspect in Jordan is cooperating, and a Canadian cybersecurity executive was arrested near Philadelphia on related extortion conspiracy charges. (NLDR Media)

Trump cut a diesel deal with Putin, and Ukraine set a Russian oil terminal on fire the same night. On Oct 9 Trump announced Russia would supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel to US and global markets immediately, easing sanctions to cool diesel prices he partly blames on Ukrainian strikes. Hours later, Ukrainian drones hit a major oil terminal in Rostov-on-Don linked to the Novoshakhtinsk plant. Zelensky called the deal a "gift" funding further Russian attacks; Trump publicly blamed Zelensky for high prices, said "he better damn well stop," and added that Ukraine needs a new president who can "make a deal." (NLDR Media)

Law & Order

Philadelphia Officer Shane Seiber, 40, was fatally shot responding to a man with a gun on a West Philadelphia porch. Seiber, a 10-year veteran and father of a 7-year-old son and 3-year-old daughter, was struck three times around 12:50 a.m. on Oct 10 and died at Penn Presbyterian after his wife and family reached his side. His 33-year-old partner, a father of five, was shot 12 times, underwent surgery, and remains in stable condition. Officers called it an ambush. Suspect Eric Lewis, 35, was arrested after fleeing and hiding in a tree; he faces roughly 80 charges including homicide of a law enforcement officer and is held without bail. Gov. Josh Shapiro ordered flags flown at half staff. (NLDR Media)

Chips & The AI Machine

Google Labs chief Josh Woodward says every company now needs to think and operate like a lab team. Woodward, who runs Google Labs, the Gemini app, and AI Studio, told Lenny Rachitsky his playbook for building in a world where what is possible changes every week: find where great ideas really come from, use an "almost possible" framework, spot product-market fit early, and know when to kill an idea. Seventeen years at Google and the products to show for it include NotebookLM, Project Genie, and Flow. (Lenny's Newsletter)

The Internet

Singapore is already living the future where your smartphone is your life, and it sounds unpleasant. You need a phone to order dinner, receive packages, even clear customs, and navigating the city without one is genuinely hard. And when the phone runs everything, everyone is always on theirs. The US is drifting the same way. (Links)

The Culture

Julie Beck has done us the favor of explaining why so many of us are terrible at texting. Her new Atlantic piece argues, with expert backing, that the expectation of always-on availability is not really built for maintaining meaningful relationships. You can show up in other ways, like in person. The newsletter author, a self-described pathologically poor texter, adds: text her husband to schedule it. (The Atlantic)

r/BoyDinnerDiaries is secretly one of the internet's most tender places. It is not really about men's dinners. It is one of the few communal spaces where men are encouraged to be vulnerable, seek connection, and share openly about what they are going through: a spouse's terminal illness, the death of a friend, the birth of a first child. The newsletter author cried reading the comments. (GQ)

The most damning part of a massive new Elon Musk documentary comes from his exes. WIRED's weekly roundup flags the film as this week's essential viewing, with the former partners delivering the hardest hits. (WIRED)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Don't sip sugary drinks all day. Constantly exposing your teeth to sugar gives cavity-causing bacteria repeated chances to produce acids that attack your enamel. (NLDR Media)

• PI's question of the week: name ONE favorite movie. 122 answers in and counting. (PI.fyi)

• "Deleting social media gives you an insane amount of time." One PI user is off TikTok and Instagram for a week and barely touches the phone anymore. (PI.fyi)

• Cilantro Doritos "might just be the most delicious thing i've had all year." Soap haters begone. (PI.fyi)

• A Serial Experiments Lain marathon, episodes 1-13 on VHS, hits a Brooklyn bar Monday night. Seventh Heaven, Irving Avenue. (PI.fyi)

• Muse's Absolution is "a 10/10 album," and "Apocalypse Please" is some good music. (PI.fyi)

• Amazon correctly deduced one newsletter author's family makeup and ages, but incorrectly believes she drives a RAV4 and values "waterproof protection for bedding." (Futurism)

• A game in which you try to spend Elon Musk's entire fortune. It is essentially impossible. (WIRED)

• Wikipedia's canned beans page is an abortive stub. Food knowledge is systematically undervalued on Wikipedia, a function of its male editor base. (Links)

• Last week's most-clicked link: an analysis of "mommaxxing" influencer Brooke Raybould. (Links)

• Teens are obsessed with gift-list apps. Shopping gets easier for the giver, but care risks becoming just another form of commerce. (The Cut)

• A writer crashed a culty startup-incubator summer-solstice gala: all-white dress code, sparse undercooked food, and the business pitch introduced with an elaborate invocation to Apollo. (Links)

Sunday, October 11, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

• 40: the number of years Christopher Hazell pictured ahead of himself writing rice cooker copy, in what he calls a numbing haze of fluorescent lighting, before he quit to chase the writing life

• 31: the Paris address Tom Sachs borrowed for his unauthorized, hand-built Chanel boutique inside his SoHo studio, which closed yesterday

• the '90s: when photographer Merry Alpern shot her voyeuristic Shopping series with a spy cam hidden in her purse, now the subject of a Blackbird Spyplane interview

Quotes of the Day

• "the inmates are breaking out of digital prison" (Ted Gioia, on people trading screens for communal events)

• "Prove your humanity or get ignored" (Drew Austin, Kneeling Bus, asking "Are Friends Electric?")

• "perhaps our consciousness and interrelation are electrical" (Michael Pollan, "A World Appears," via [SIC] Day)

The Mentor Circuit

• Ben Dietz is back at New Inc for year two. The [SIC] Day writer joined the New Museum's incubator as a mentor again, paired with a musician and artist who is world-building a whole line of products and experiences around her album dropping next year. They meet in person for the first time tonight at a members dinner at another mentor's home. (New Inc)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• "Who would have thought the path to enlightenment might one day run through Microsoft?" [SIC] Day teases its Contemplations column, on the both-human-and-artificial search for meaning. ([SIC] Day](https://sic.substack.com))

• The whole [SIC] Day issue is framed as "pictures of the things we want, or just of the things we want others to see." ([SIC] Day](https://sic.substack.com))

evening.body:
Sunday, October 11, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 1786: the year Marco Rubio's great-great-great grandfather graduated with a law degree from the University of Granada, making him likely the family's first law school graduate. PBS genealogy show Finding Your Roots surfaced the record in 2019. On his mother's side, Rubio descends from a Native American great-great-great grandmother.

• 6: the number of the U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue that Rubio's Acropolis speech officially opened. The agenda, F-35 and F-16 upgrades, routing American natural gas into Europe through Greece, and a new counterterrorism information-sharing deal, was every product of the liberal international order his speech trashed.

• 4: the highest rank Plato's Laws gives courage among the virtues. The highest good, Plato wrote, is "peace one with another and friendly feeling." Rubio's fire-and-spirit reading of the Greeks has it exactly backward.

Quotes of the Day

• "Perhaps Rubio is auditioning for the role of Last Man in search of a struggle." (Jerusalem Demsas, on Rubio's praise of the Greek thumos)

• "Chris, ten, dom." (Jerusalem Demsas, on Rubio twice mispronouncing "Christendom")

• "as though they were blood of the blood, and flesh of the flesh of the men who wrote that Declaration" (Abraham Lincoln, 1858, defending immigrants with no ancestral tie to the founders)

Rubio vs. the Greeks

The banishment hill. Secretary of State Marco Rubio praised the great man on the Pnyx, the hill where the Athenian assembly once voted every year on whether to banish any citizen who had grown too powerful. Jerusalem Demsas's point is that the Greeks were terrified of unchecked ambition and built restraints into their institutions instead of monuments to contest. The venue refutes the speech. (The Argument)

No nations, only cities. The Greeks famously had no nations to be loyal to. They had cities that fought each other for most of the classical age. James Madison lamented the disunity in Federalist 18, and Alexander Hamilton wrote that reading the history of Greece's petty republics filled him with "horror and disgust." The founders' answer was a firm Union. When Athens did chase national power without apology, the result was the Melos massacre, the Sicily disaster, and surrender. The Greek lesson on nationalism is a warning, not a playbook. (The Argument)

Culture & Curiosities

The threesome myth. The largest-ever survey of Americans' sexual fantasies found threesomes are the most common fantasy across genders. Karley Sciortino calls herself a statistical anomaly, someone who tried hard and came up short. Her argument is that the mid-2000s "cool girl" rule made opting out feel like a failure, while the real prize, three people miraculously equally into each other, is nearly impossible. (Karley Sciortino)

New York, the regulars' edition. Austin Tedesco refreshed his Bangers and Jams city guide to New York and reports a dearth of worthy, hot new openings. His takeaway is that the best experiences now come from repeat visits to a rotation of places that get everything right. The post also carries a new top 25 movie ranking after he caught the year's big releases at the New York Film Festival. (Bangers and Jams)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Cosmos now lets you import boards from Pinterest, Are.na, and Tumblr straight into the app with one click, available on web with mobile coming soon. Everything imported becomes searchable and easier to build on. (Cosmos)
