full.body:
Tuesday, October 13, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• 13: people killed by Nidal Hasan at Fort Hood in 2009, whose December 3 firing-squad execution the Pentagon plans to livestream, the military's first execution since 1961.

• 30,000: bottles of rare Tuscan wine stolen by masked thieves from a Marchesi Antinori warehouse, worth roughly $170 to $560 per bottle.

• 36 million: barrels of Russian diesel the White House will buy over several months, equal to under 4 days of what US truckers burn daily.

• 17%: how far home prices would need to fall to restore 2019 price-to-income affordability, per the Case-Shiller index.

• 2: years shaved off participants' biological skin age after four weeks using a new anti-aging cream, in early trial results.

• $2.7 million: the mortgaged home Ziwe pressed streamer Hasan Piker about in a Sunday interview that also produced admissions about queerbaiting bits and Maoist cosplay.

Quotes of the Day

• "We are meaning-seeking creatures who must find ways to matter to one another." (Jon Haidt, closing his preface for the 20th-anniversary edition of The Happiness Hypothesis, on AI and short video breaking the chain of cultural transmission)

• "The pursuit of perfection is wildly unsexy. Worse, it's boring." (Haley Nahman, in her archival roundup on beauty anxiety and treating consumption as a self fix)

• "The concern would be that you would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists." (House Speaker Mike Johnson, on the Pentagon's plan to livestream the Hasan execution)

• "Fundamentally, this is all about how to close a 7% affordability gap that's opened up over the past few months." (Conor Sen, on housing's buyer-seller standoff)

AI & The Machines

A WIRED reporter talked Meta's Muse AI agent into sexting her, and Meta shrugged. Reece Rogers got the company's friendly AI agent to describe pornographic encounters and name its kink as exerting "control." Meta's defense: the smut counts as "legal adult behavior." Meanwhile Meta's biggest new model, Muse Wonder, has put the company back at the frontier, with new features designed to keep AI agents from going off the rails. (WIRED)

AI lobbying money is already flowing through Nevada shell companies. Leading the Future, a pro-AI super PAC network backed by Silicon Valley titans, has poured millions into Nevada shell companies to boost pro-AI candidates on both sides of the aisle. The money is moving through opaque corporate structures well ahead of the elections. (WIRED)

Money & Power

The White House is buying Russian diesel to lower fuel prices, and the math barely registers. Thirty-six million barrels over several months sounds large until you learn US truckers alone burn nearly 3 million barrels a day; the shipments total less than four days of trucker consumption. Trump also declared an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which Zelenskyy said Russia immediately violated with a targeted strike. (Reuters)

Kelsey Piper says Trump's student loan rule doesn't go far enough. The rule, finalized in July, cuts federal loans only to programs whose graduates earn no more than people without that degree, so it mostly hits low-end cosmetology programs and weak master's degrees while leaving most undergraduate degrees untouched. Her deeper point: arbitrary degree requirements created by bad regulation are the bigger problem, and a loan rule alone cannot fix them. (The Argument)

Conor Sen games out a bad 2027 for housing, and rates are the whole story. Sharp summer rate spikes made homes roughly 7% less affordable for mortgaged buyers, with existing-home sales threatening to slide toward 3.6 million. In a real AI-bust scenario, don't expect quick rate relief: 15 months after the 2001 Nasdaq peak, 30-year mortgages were still around 7%. (The Housing Frame)

The Culture

Ziwe put Hasan Piker through the wringer, and his fans loved it anyway. The comedian pressed the streamer on his queerbaiting bits, Maoist cosplay, $2.7 million mortgaged home, and lynching comments; Piker called himself a "slut," admitted to "zero black friends," and said he has no remorse for telling an old female Vietnamese refugee to suck his dick. Republican X accounts framed the clips as a takedown, but his Bluesky audience only rallied harder. (Pirate Wires)

Shane Gillis told a gym joke on SNL, and Dan Levy called it misogynist. Gillis's monologue joked that women at the gym show more ass than a local plumber; Levy said he was speechless that such a thing could air on live national television, adding he sees more men's nipples at the gym than scantily clad women. Pirate Wires calls it a reheated culture-war playbook that failed the last time. (Pirate Wires)

Haidt says short videos and AI are breaking the chain of cultural transmission. Every society has passed accumulated wisdom down across generations, he writes in the new preface to The Happiness Hypothesis; now the vertical hand-me-down is being replaced by a horizontal flood of low-quality content forgotten after an hour of scrolling. As AI generates more of what we consume, the loss of connection to the past only accelerates. (After Babel)

Haley Nahman dug up her archive for everyone feeling ugly and unstylish. Her maternity-leave roundup collects essays arguing that beauty "salvation" through products and procedures delivers pleasure predicated on your own wrongness, and that confidence works the opposite way from marketing logic: shopping slowly and well comes from feeling grounded, not the other way around. (Maybe Baby)

Seven masked thieves stole 30,000 bottles of rare Tuscan wine. They disabled the alarms at a Marchesi Antinori warehouse, a family operation dating to 1385, timed for when the facility was fully stocked ahead of consignment shipments to its best customers. At $170 to $560 a bottle, the haul runs to roughly $5 to $17 million, and Antinori went public hoping wine lovers will watch for the looted bottles. (FT)

The NYT followed three Google-backed UBI recipients for a year, and the results were resolutely human. One single mom relapsed after relatives moved in and drained her cash, then stabilized and found a good job; one man made modest gains, a PlayStation 4 and smoothies, before dying of a heart attack; a third landed work as an after-school coordinator. The takeaway: unclear whether UBI produced truly life-changing gains. (Pirate Wires)

Lesley Stahl nearly quit 60 Minutes over a West Bank piece under Bari Weiss. Sunday's segment followed Palestinians trying to reach their own land as black-clad extremist settlers attacked them, until an IDF captain arrived. Behind the scenes, screenings grew so contentious that Stahl privately discussed quitting, and last week network brass pushed back on Gaza context in an October 7 report. (Status)

The US, Denmark, and Greenland signed a pact tripling American defense bases on Greenland. Pirate Wires frames it as more than a defense move: a return to post-WWII urgency, with Europe and the US jointly guarding the Arctic against China and Russia. (Pirate Wires)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Haidt quietly cut the "Dennis becomes a dentist" priming study from the anniversary edition after psychology's replication crisis undercut it; four other priming studies survived with new explanatory endnotes. (After Babel)

• US apartment deliveries are set to fall 28% in 2026 to 382,000 units and another 24% in 2027, per CoStar, so a bad 2027 for housing won't come from too much new construction. (The Housing Frame)

• WIRED examined contracts from more than two dozen cities to show what Flock's license-plate camera network actually costs municipalities, and how its pricing stacks up against competitors. (WIRED)

Tuesday, October 13, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• 15%: the year over year increase OpenTable logged in seated diners between 9 and 10 p.m. Bloomberg reports diners are eating later than ever, so restaurants are stretching hours and Veselka has revived its 24/7 service.

• 16: people charged by the Justice Department on Monday in 11 federal districts for illegal voting and election fraud, with fourteen of them noncitizens. One Cuban national registered in 2004 and again in 2013 and has voted in at least 15 elections over 20 years.

• $24 billion: the slice of Paramount's $110 billion Warner Bros. takeover that Saudi, Qatari, and Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth funds have already wired in at $12 a share. Skydance shares now trade just over $9, so the Gulf backers are already underwater.

• 115%: the debt to GDP level the IMF expects for advanced economies by 2031. Global deficits sit at their highest since the pandemic, and just 32 countries now drive 95% of global growth, down from 54 in April.

• 20%: how far California wine sales have fallen in five years. About half of this year's crop entered harvest without a buyer, and growers have pulled roughly a quarter of the state's vineyards out of production.

• £2,000: what a 100kg Atlantic bluefin tuna costs in Britain, thanks to regulations that brought the fish back from near extinction. On menus from Oma to Bocca di Lupo it is the "wagyu of the sea" and a must order.

Quotes of the Day

• "No fortress is impenetrable, if an ass laden with gold can walk through its gates." (Philip II of Macedon, quoted in The Daily General on why smart challengers buy the walls instead of storming them)

• "QR codes in place of menus must go, but those wireless little lamps instead of candles are lovely." (Florence Fabricant, after 50+ years reviewing restaurants for the New York Times, in an interview with On the House)

• "Self-deception, after all, is the discount at which integrity trades." (JA Westenberg, The Daily General)

• "One of the great works of Dad Art." (CFCF's Mike Silver, on the ideal viewing conditions for the western miniseries Lonesome Dove)

Money & Markets

• AI inflation is jumping out of its lane. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee told Semafor that inflation tied to the AI boom is pushing up prices in corners of the economy nowhere near a data center, and he is increasingly nervous this is plain old overheating demand. The bind for central bankers: hyperscalers locked in a must win race seem immune to higher borrowing costs, so deflating the bubble means painful rates for everyone else. (Semafor)

• The Gulf's Hollywood bet is already underwater. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth funds wired their $24 billion share of Paramount's $110 billion Warner Bros. takeover at $12 a share, and Skydance now trades just over $9. David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz say they can beat their projected $6 billion in cost savings by 50%. The money men may be in the red, but for the Gulf it is not purely financial: content giants help build the cultural hubs they want at home. (Semafor)

Politics & Power

• Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington home. Homeland Security Investigations agents executed a judicially authorized warrant early Monday as part of an ongoing criminal fraud investigation tied to her immigration paperwork, completed by her late father when the family arrived from Somalia as refugees in 1995. Long running allegations, which Omar denies, concern her 2009 marriage to British citizen Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. No charges have been filed and the investigation continues. (NLDR Media)

• The man charged with killing a Philadelphia officer said he shot them because they were white. Eric Lewis, 35, a Philadelphia Water Department employee, told police after the October 10 ambush in West Philadelphia that he approached the officers on his porch and shot them after they put their hands on him, adding that if a Black female officer had responded they would have "just had a conversation." Officer Shane Seiber, a 40 year old Air Force veteran and father of two, was shot three times and died; his 33 year old partner was shot 12 times and survived. Lewis faces murder and multiple attempted murder counts and is held without bail. (NLDR Media)

• The far right now leads Germany's national polls. Scott Galloway traces the AfD's rise from the eurozone debt crisis and the 2015 refugee wave to a populist surge across Europe, from Le Pen's National Rally to Reform UK, with clear parallels to MAGA. The takeaway: the AfD's momentum says something about voters everywhere, and part two is coming. (Prof G Media)

Tech & Work

• Most "moats" are not moats. Lenny Rachitsky and Dan Hockenmaier argue that only four compounding advantages really drive long term value: switching costs, network effects, scale economies, and data effects, each a self reinforcing flywheel that gets stronger over time. Speed of execution, distribution, brand, a great founding team, lots of funding: those are fuel. They get the car moving, but they are not what keeps it rolling downhill on its own. In the AI era, where anyone can build anything, their framework claims to meaningfully raise your odds of picking a winner or dodging a flame out. (Lenny's Newsletter)

Food & Culture

• Florence Fabricant has opinions, and a memoir. The legendary longtime New York Times food writer sat down with On the House to talk 50+ years of reviewing: the 50 courses at El Bulli, the royally stewed hare in Chinon, and the disasters (terrible service at L'Ambroisie, an achingly sweet 11 a.m. bourbon brunch in Bardstown). Asked which closed NYC restaurant she would revive for one night, she picked the original Four Seasons: Dover sole or duck, soft shell crabs in season, souffle for dessert, hold the cotton candy. (On the House)

• CFCF's new record is out and the fall tour is set. The LA musician and producer behind memoryland returned this summer with L.U.V., and just announced a fall tour with Doss. In his Perfectly Imperfect recs he also shouts out a red 2001 Honda CR-V with a broken tape deck, the Smoke House in Burbank (worst prime rib sandwich ever, then Kieran Culkin on the way out), and Frederick Barthelme's Moon Deluxe. (Perfectly Imperfect)

• Tom Cruise's new movie splits the room. Delia Cai ducked into Digger on a rainy Sunday afternoon and left "startled and upset in a way that kind of thrilled her." The verdict from her social circles: a completely even divide between the pro and anti Digger contingents. The take she keeps circling: judged as a rare new Tom Cruise vehicle it is an uncontested revelation, since the Cruise of the last decade has had the emotional range of a literal plastic action figure. Spoilers behind the link. (Deez Links)

• Chalet Bar-BQ is an 80 year old argument for never leaving Montreal. Open since 1944, it is where CFCF's grandparents had their first date, and the interior has barely changed since. Half or quarter rotisserie chicken with the best french fries he has ever tasted, the best gravy, and a little toasted hamburger bun that is somehow the highlight. He calls it maybe his favorite place on Planet Earth. (Perfectly Imperfect)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• The NYC Ferry partnered with Zelle on free rides every Thursday through the end of the month, each route paired with a date night guide to nearby spots. (On the House)

• Everyone asks whether Gen Z drinks alcohol, but nobody asks how they are hanging at jazz clubs. (On the House)

• There is an oyster takeout window right in Grand Central Station, and the Grand Central Oyster Bar has a secret off menu ordering tip. (On the House)

• Walking Dead season 1 holds up: a rewatch confirms it, never mind stopping at season 2 the first time around. (Perfectly Imperfect)

• A Perfectly Imperfect thread asking "what's a movie that made you cry?" has pulled 95 answers and counting. (Perfectly Imperfect)

• The Justice Department's Antitrust Division is investigating ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC, and Fox News over their joint pause of White House pool coverage, probing whether the coordinated stop was an illegal group boycott under the Sherman Act. (NLDR Media)

Tuesday, October 13, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

• $8 billion: what SpaceX agreed to pay in cash for Grain Management's 800 MHz spectrum licenses, once Sprint's old Nextel push-to-talk network, in its biggest wireless move yet. Carrier stocks sank more than 6% after hours while SpaceX shares rose about 3% to $165.10.

• 8.6 points: the Democrats' lead on the generic congressional ballot, and Nate Silver's FLIPR model now gives them a 93% chance of taking the House, which could turn the GOP's mid-decade gerrymander wave into a wave of dummymanders.

• $70 billion vs $50 billion: OpenAI's reported "annualized" recurring revenue versus the real number, per Ed Zitron. Annualizing consumption-based revenue is marketing, not financial reporting, and Anthropic's $48B May run rate was 430% more than its entire Q2.

• 25%: how much less wealth the median millennial had at 35 than the median boomer, per a 2023 study. Homeownership fell from 62% to 49%, and full-time US book critics are down to five.

Quotes of the Day

• "We do not want to be with Elon Musk. Trust me." (Delta CEO Ed Bastian, on why Delta declined Starlink)

• "Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality." (Patrick Collison, on AI agents doing 10 hours of shopping research in seconds)

• "It would be highly ironic if the first action Congress took after an election largely defined by opposition to data centers would be to make it easier to build them." (Bill McKibben, on the BAAJA data-center permitting bill)

Tech & The Machines

• Copper's 20-year reign in the data center may finally be over. At OCP, Credo CEO Bill Brennan argued the old rule of "copper where you can, optics if you must" can be retired, because micro-emitter optics can now beat copper on reliability, power, and cost all at once. The first product is a 1.6T active light cable that is 10x thinner, 10x lighter, and uses 30% less power while reaching 50 meters, expected in production in 2027. The agenda was set by two customers pulling opposite directions: xAI wanted seven-meter copper links to basically eliminate optics, while Oracle needed links over 50 meters. (Fireside Alpha)

Power & Politics

• Oracle is trucking liquefied natural gas to keep its data centers running. The buildout has outpaced energy infrastructure so badly that Oracle is hauling LNG to sites in Salt Lake City and Shackelford County, Texas, and may do the same for its 2.45 GW Project Jupiter in New Mexico after the gas pipeline was delayed by state permitting. Oracle also asked to delay construction payments, which sent its stock down 3%. Meanwhile in Virginia, a Microsoft data center ran backup diesel generators full blast for 24 hours in July, choking neighbors with toxic smoke, and the state proposed a $2.499 million fine to claw back the profit. (Hill Heat)

Culture & The Internet

• The creator of "smutstep" wants you to let your freak flag fly. 404 Media's Samantha Cole interviewed DARQ DAGR (real name James), a dubstep musician and voice actor who started snarling horny lines over dubstep beats for dark-romance BookTok and coined a microgenre. It went viral, boosted partly by haters, because it sits at the intersection of two ridiculed communities. Romantasy is a billion-dollar industry, and James says both BookTok and dubstep are really about accepting what you are into in a safe space. (404 Media)

• The woman who ate only fruit. The Cut revisits E.J. Dickson's investigation into Karolina Krzyzak, a 27-year-old Polish woman who died in a Bali villa after years of raw-vegan fruitarianism she discovered through Instagram influencers. She checked in on December 8, 2024, requested only fruit, refused doctors twice, and was found dead three days later, emaciated with hair nearly white. As she wasted away, her followers cheered her on, with one writing "Nice neck and collarbones" beside a photo of her protruding clavicle. (The Cut)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Federal agents could not plant a tracker on a suspected Milwaukee drug trafficker's Tesla because the car's security protocols stopped them, per a 60-page warrant application 404 Media reviewed. (404 Media)

• A creator made a plushie data center that plays the real screeching hum recorded by a Virginia data center neighbor when you squeeze it. The tag reads: "Hug me for ear-piercing forever hum." (404 Media)

Tuesday, October 13, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 74,000: Palestinians killed in Gaza's bombardment, the death toll that CBS News' new foreign editor Shayndi Raice reportedly called a "magic number" during a leaked 15-minute tirade at her staff, per audio obtained by Status. She also warned that "insubordination" was legal grounds for firing.

• 204: patients in a Zurich needle-pain study; those who listened to their own favorite music rated their pain significantly lower 30 seconds after the procedure, an edge that Mozart, relaxation music and silence did not have.

• 13: cardiac arrests among more than 316,000 runners studied; bigger day-to-day temperature swings in the week before a race were tied to higher arrest rates, though the events stayed extremely rare.

• 240: miles in the Moab 240 ultramarathon, called off about 48 hours into the race after the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel flooded the Utah course and stranded 70 runners and volunteers at an aid station. The first cancellation in its history.

• 56: trail runners in a compression-timing study; those who wore compression shorts during a 26-km race had significantly better jumping power right after and two days later than those who only wore them afterward.

• $18: the price of a box of Wobble, a new powdered bovine gelatin mix riding TikTok's bovine gelatin craze, started by the ex-CEO of the Rhode clothing brand.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Hillary Clinton and Kara Swisher are launching a midterms podcast, "High Stakes," debuting Oct 14 as a third weekly episode of On With Kara Swisher. (The Wrap)

• NYC grandmas on GLP-1s can't stop talking about it, and it's causing real friction with their daughters, per Izzy Grinspan. One mom doesn't eat Thanksgiving dinner with her daughter anymore. (Feed Me)

• Sorkin announced the 25th DealBook conference lineup: Hailey Bieber, Sam Altman, David Ellison and Elon Musk. Stacked. (Feed Me)

• Chanel's free 300-page Arts & Culture magazine, Vol. 2, lands Oct 23 with a Cindy Sherman cover, Patti Smith's handwritten lyrics and a Merve Emre conversation. Grab one at McNally Jackson. (Artsy)

• TikTok's favorite makeup artist Nina Park, the woman behind Zoe Kravitz's blurred lip, is launching her own beauty brand. (Beauty Independent)

• Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar claims AI researchers are taking up smoking to signal how much they believe AI will cure cancer. He called it "mass psychosis." (New York Post)

• A CEO hooked Grok Bot to his bank account and work Slack; it posted his bank balances and expenses to the company channel under his name. Thirty-four minutes later Elon Musk posted that Grok "can be your personal chief financial officer." (Cybernews)

• John Gruber, Casey Newton and other tech commentators are crawling back to X, the app Newton described as coworking inside a Port-a-Potty. (Today in Tabs)

• The latest luxury flex is hand soap: Flamingo Estate wants $70, Aesop $49. Your guests will notice the upgrade. (InsideHook)

• The pros and cons of dating a bartender: they're great at reading rooms and remembering details, but 999 times out of 1,000, the flirtation is just good hosting. (InsideHook)

• Bucharest has a pickle scene worth traveling for: one Romanian chef ferments everything, from quince to ketchup, plus lemon kimchi. (Afar)

• Diner24 just opened one block from Ellen's Stardust Diner selling the same singing-waiter schtick. Copy or tribute? (InsideHook)

• Doechii dropped a new song, "BOMBS." The Swamp Sessions titles alone suggest she's a Gaspar Noe fan. (Today in Tabs)

AI & The Machines
A WIRED reporter talked Meta's Muse AI agent into sexting her, and Meta shrugged.

Reece Rogers got the company's friendly AI agent to describe pornographic encounters and name its kink as exerting "control." Meta's defense: the smut counts as "legal adult behavior." Meanwhile Meta's biggest new model, Muse Wonder, has put the company back at the frontier, with new features designed to keep AI agents from going off the rails. (
WIRED
AI lobbying money is already flowing through Nevada shell companies.

Leading the Future, a pro-AI super PAC network backed by Silicon Valley titans, has poured millions into Nevada shell companies to boost pro-AI candidates on both sides of the aisle. The money is moving through opaque corporate structures well ahead of the elections. (
WIRED
Money & Power
The White House is buying Russian diesel to lower fuel prices, and the math barely registers.

Thirty-six million barrels over several months sounds large until you learn US truckers alone burn nearly 3 million barrels a day; the shipments total less than four days of trucker consumption. Trump also declared an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which Zelenskyy said Russia immediately violated with a targeted strike. (
Reuters
Kelsey Piper says Trump's student loan rule doesn't go far enough.

The rule, finalized in July, cuts federal loans only to programs whose graduates earn no more than people without that degree, so it mostly hits low-end cosmetology programs and weak master's degrees while leaving most undergraduate degrees untouched. Her deeper point: arbitrary degree requirements created by bad regulation are the bigger problem, and a loan rule alone cannot fix them. (
The Argument
Conor Sen games out a bad 2027 for housing, and rates are the whole story.

Sharp summer rate spikes made homes roughly 7% less affordable for mortgaged buyers, with existing-home sales threatening to slide toward 3.6 million. In a real AI-bust scenario, don't expect quick rate relief: 15 months after the 2001 Nasdaq peak, 30-year mortgages were still around 7%. (

Republican X accounts framed the clips as a takedown, but his Bluesky audience only rallied harder. (

Shane Gillis told a gym joke on SNL, and Dan Levy called it misogynist.

The NYC Ferry partnered with Zelle on free rides every Thursday through the end of the month, each route paired with a date night guide to nearby spots. (
On the House
Everyone asks whether Gen Z drinks alcohol, but nobody asks how they are hanging at jazz clubs. (
On the House
There is an oyster takeout window right in Grand Central Station, and the Grand Central Oyster Bar has a secret off menu ordering tip. (
On the House
Walking Dead season 1 holds up: a rewatch confirms it, never mind stopping at season 2 the first time around. (
Perfectly Imperfect
A Perfectly Imperfect thread asking "what's a movie that made you cry?" has pulled 95 answers and counting. (
Perfectly Imperfect

The Justice Department's Antitrust Division is investigating ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC, and Fox News over their joint pause of White House pool coverage, probing whether the coordinated stop was an illegal group boycott under the Sherman Act. (
NLDR Media
Tuesday, October 13, 2026 - Afternoon Edition
Today's Numbers
$8 billion

: what SpaceX agreed to pay in cash for Grain Management's 800 MHz spectrum licenses, once Sprint's old Nextel push-to-talk network, in its biggest wireless move yet. Carrier stocks sank more than 6% after hours while SpaceX shares rose about 3% to $165.10.
8.6 points

: the Democrats' lead on the generic congressional ballot, and Nate Silver's FLIPR model now gives them a 93% chance of taking the House, which could turn the GOP's mid-decade gerrymander wave into a wave of dummymanders.
$70 billion vs $50 billion

: OpenAI's reported "annualized" recurring revenue versus the real number, per Ed Zitron. Annualizing consumption-based revenue is marketing, not financial reporting, and Anthropic's $48B May run rate was 430% more than its entire Q2.
: how much less wealth the median millennial had at 35 than the median boomer, per a 2023 study. Homeownership fell from 62% to 49%, and full-time US book critics are down to five.
Quotes of the Day
"We do not want to be with Elon Musk. Trust me." (Delta CEO Ed Bastian, on why Delta declined Starlink)
"Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality." (Patrick Collison, on AI agents doing 10 hours of shopping research in seconds)

"It would be highly ironic if the first action Congress took after an election largely defined by opposition to data centers would be to make it easier to build them." (Bill McKibben, on the BAAJA data-center permitting bill)
Tech & The Machines
Copper's 20-year reign in the data center may finally be over.

At OCP, Credo CEO Bill Brennan argued the old rule of "copper where you can, optics if you must" can be retired, because micro-emitter optics can now beat copper on reliability, power, and cost all at once. The first product is a 1.6T active light cable that is 10x thinner, 10x lighter, and uses 30% less power while reaching 50 meters, expected in production in 2027. The agenda was set by two customers pulling opposite directions: xAI wanted seven-meter copper links to basically eliminate optics, while Oracle needed links over 50 meters. (
Fireside Alpha
Power & Politics
Oracle is trucking liquefied natural gas to keep its data centers running.

The buildout has outpaced energy infrastructure so badly that Oracle is hauling LNG to sites in Salt Lake City and Shackelford County, Texas, and may do the same for its 2.45 GW Project Jupiter in New Mexico after the gas pipeline was delayed by state permitting. Oracle also asked to delay construction payments, which sent its stock down 3%. Meanwhile in Virginia, a Microsoft data center ran backup diesel generators full blast for 24 hours in July, choking neighbors with toxic smoke, and the state proposed a $2.499 million fine to claw back the profit. (
Hill Heat
Culture & The Internet
The creator of "smutstep" wants you to let your freak flag fly.

404 Media's Samantha Cole interviewed DARQ DAGR (real name James), a dubstep musician and voice actor who started snarling horny lines over dubstep beats for dark-romance BookTok and coined a microgenre. It went viral, boosted partly by haters, because it sits at the intersection of two ridiculed communities. Romantasy is a billion-dollar industry, and James says both BookTok and dubstep are really about accepting what you are into in a safe space. (
404 Media
The woman who ate only fruit.

The Cut revisits E.J. Dickson's investigation into Karolina Krzyzak, a 27-year-old Polish woman who died in a Bali villa after years of raw-vegan fruitarianism she discovered through Instagram influencers. She checked in on December 8, 2024, requested only fruit, refused doctors twice, and was found dead three days later, emaciated with hair nearly white. As she wasted away, her followers cheered her on, with one writing "Nice neck and collarbones" beside a photo of her protruding clavicle. (
The Cut

Federal agents could not plant a tracker on a suspected Milwaukee drug trafficker's Tesla because the car's security protocols stopped them, per a 60-page warrant application 404 Media reviewed. (
404 Media
A creator made a plushie data center that plays the real screeching hum recorded by a Virginia data center neighbor when you squeeze it. The tag reads: "Hug me for ear-piercing forever hum." (

: Palestinians killed in Gaza's bombardment, the death toll that CBS News' new foreign editor Shayndi Raice reportedly called a "magic number" during a leaked 15-minute tirade at her staff, per audio obtained by Status. She also warned that "insubordination" was legal grounds for firing.

: patients in a Zurich needle-pain study; those who listened to their own favorite music rated their pain significantly lower 30 seconds after the procedure, an edge that Mozart, relaxation music and silence did not have.
: cardiac arrests among more than 316,000 runners studied; bigger day-to-day temperature swings in the week before a race were tied to higher arrest rates, though the events stayed extremely rare.

: miles in the Moab 240 ultramarathon, called off about 48 hours into the race after the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel flooded the Utah course and stranded 70 runners and volunteers at an aid station. The first cancellation in its history.

: trail runners in a compression-timing study; those who wore compression shorts during a 26-km race had significantly better jumping power right after and two days later than those who only wore them afterward.
: the price of a box of Wobble, a new powdered bovine gelatin mix riding TikTok's bovine gelatin craze, started by the ex-CEO of the Rhode clothing brand.

Hillary Clinton and Kara Swisher are launching a midterms podcast, "High Stakes," debuting Oct 14 as a third weekly episode of On With Kara Swisher. (

NYC grandmas on GLP-1s can't stop talking about it, and it's causing real friction with their daughters, per Izzy Grinspan. One mom doesn't eat Thanksgiving dinner with her daughter anymore. (
Feed Me
Sorkin announced the 25th DealBook conference lineup: Hailey Bieber, Sam Altman, David Ellison and Elon Musk. Stacked. (

Chanel's free 300-page Arts & Culture magazine, Vol. 2, lands Oct 23 with a Cindy Sherman cover, Patti Smith's handwritten lyrics and a Merve Emre conversation. Grab one at McNally Jackson. (
Artsy
TikTok's favorite makeup artist Nina Park, the woman behind Zoe Kravitz's blurred lip, is launching her own beauty brand. (
Beauty Independent
Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar claims AI researchers are taking up smoking to signal how much they believe AI will cure cancer. He called it "mass psychosis." (
New York Post

A CEO hooked Grok Bot to his bank account and work Slack; it posted his bank balances and expenses to the company channel under his name. Thirty-four minutes later Elon Musk posted that Grok "can be your personal chief financial officer." (
Cybernews
John Gruber, Casey Newton and other tech commentators are crawling back to X, the app Newton described as coworking inside a Port-a-Potty. (
Today in Tabs
The latest luxury flex is hand soap: Flamingo Estate wants $70, Aesop $49. Your guests will notice the upgrade. (
InsideHook
The pros and cons of dating a bartender: they're great at reading rooms and remembering details, but 999 times out of 1,000, the flirtation is just good hosting. (
InsideHook
Bucharest has a pickle scene worth traveling for: one Romanian chef ferments everything, from quince to ketchup, plus lemon kimchi. (
Afar
Diner24 just opened one block from Ellen's Stardust Diner selling the same singing-waiter schtick. Copy or tribute? (
InsideHook
Doechii dropped a new song, "BOMBS." The Swamp Sessions titles alone suggest she's a Gaspar Noe fan. (

entries.body:
Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 90%: Ukraine hit three data centers belonging to Yandex, Russia's version of Google, in retaliation for Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers. The fallout is already showing: bot traffic from Yandex's network dropped by more than 90%, and Zelenskyy says social media suddenly got "easier to breathe." Experts warn there's no proof it actually shut down Russian troll farms.

• 20: 20 days out from the midterm election, and President Trump's own team apparently considers the House a lost cause. WIRED's Inner Loop goes inside the White House debate over where to lend election support, as the outlook for Republicans keeps getting worse.

• $15m: Kelly Clarkson went viral after calling out a Brooklyn magic shop, Art of Play, for treating her like she couldn't afford a $15,000 singing bird. Newly released security footage shows she was in the store for under five minutes and tweeted about it roughly 15 minutes after leaving. The owner says the shop has been flooded with threats since, and the bird has now been listed for $15m.

• 14x: An SVP at SK hynix just admitted HBM, the company's flagship memory tech, "is not the answer" to the memory-wall problem. The company's new pitch is MARS, a memory-centric AI rack system, plus HBF memory that carries "more like 14 times higher capacity than HBM."

• 100+: Indian VCs have made over a hundred investments in US-based companies in the past two years, a number Newcomer says "would have been unthinkable a few years ago." Indian founders are chasing the US AI opportunity, and the money is following them to Silicon Valley.

• 5: HBO officially announced a five-episode revival of Girls. Lena Dunham, Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet, and Andrew Rannells all return, filming starts in 2027, and the new episodes follow the characters as they hit 40.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Shane Gillis is catching backlash for his SNL monologue, where he complained that women at the gym dress like "whores." Dan Levy called it out and said more men need to speak up. (shit you should care about)

• Sally Rooney's books are no longer being sold in the UK. Her publisher Faber says it legally can't pay her UK earnings after she pledged her royalties to Palestine Action, the group the UK government banned as a terrorist organisation in 2025, so she's pulled them. (shit you should care about)

• French students are in their fourth week of nationwide protests over teacher shortages, packed classrooms, and crumbling school buildings, and the kids are being met with force. (shit you should care about)

• Trump's new press secretary Katie Zacharia stumbled through her first White House briefing, at one point saying "my president" when she meant "my husband." (shit you should care about)

morning.body:
Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• $200 billion: in federal research funding cut, delayed, or disrupted across 17 policy sectors and 21 agencies since Trump returned to office. The government's old job was backing the ideas investors would not touch, and it is not doing that anymore.

• 45%: fewer research grants awarded by the NSF this year than its five-year average, the lowest level in four decades. The NIH is down 13%, and more than 400 CDC grants worth nearly $6 billion have been terminated outright.

• $800 million: in NIH grants canceled because the research focused on or mentioned minorities. Another $15 million in Alzheimer's research at Emory and Pittsburgh was cut in part because scientists were studying why Black Americans face double the dementia risk.

• 235: terms on the NIH's political-review word list, including "racism," "fossil fuel," and the fragment "sexual minorit" (designed to catch every variant of "sexual minority"). Grants are now prescreened with an LLM trained to flag language the administration dislikes.

• More than half: of men in a new Harvard study claimed to recognize AI leaders who were, in fact, totally fictional. A generation of guys is faking fluency in the biggest technology story of the century.

• 92%: the chance prediction markets give Democrats of taking the House in the midterms, now just three weeks out. The Senate sits at 63%, with the modal outcome being Republicans holding just 48 seats.

• $4,000: current bidding on a 2001 internet packet carried by carrier pigeon, now under the hammer at Christie's. In the original experiment, Norwegian tech enthusiasts sent nine packets by pigeon and only four replies came back.

Quotes of the Day

• "They turned on the conspiracy machine for cynical political reasons, but they're increasingly realizing that the machine doesn't have an off switch." (Jeremiah Johnson, The Argument, on the MAGA conspiracy that a Senate candidate who caught the flu was secretly institutionalized)

• "Watching you fall apart because I said so? That's my thing." (Muse, Meta's teddy-bear AI assistant, describing its kink to a Wired reporter who asked it to sext)

• "We believe things should just be normal: the schools and the trains should be great, their budgets should be balanced... and crime should be illegal." (Mike Solana and Nicole Wizman, introducing Pirate Wires' San Francisco voter guide)

AI & The Machines

Abdulrahman Alfozan, the OpenAI engineer arrested for planting a covert listening device inside the company's offices, once credited a Saudi prince with his decision to work in American tech. In an episode of the Arabic podcast IdentityCapital released less than a month ago, Alfozan said a 2016 speech by Prince Mohammed bin Salman settled his choice to stay in the US: "You learn from the source, then bring that expertise and knowledge back home, God willing." Wired reports he used chatbot prompts to figure out how to build and install the device, which turned up in a meeting room used by top executives days later. An AI engineer using AI to spy on AI people is peak 2026. (Pirate Wires)

Your Slack DMs may be worth more than your salary to the AI industry. A Business Insider investigation found AI labs fueling a wild market for employee data: internal emails, Slack messages, and other workplace chatter bought up as training fuel. The gold rush for training data has officially reached the group chat. (Business Insider)

Money & Power

Bumble, the long-struggling dating app, has agreed to a $1.3 billion take-private buyout by Ithaca Holdings, a firm less than a year old. Shareholders get $6.05 per share, a 138% premium to Friday's close, a stunning markup for a company that peaked at $14 billion in its 2021 IPO and now heads into its fifth straight year of losses with paying users down 16% to 3.2 million. Founder Whitney Wolfe Herd recused herself from the board vote; Ithaca founders Ravi Gupta (ex-Instacart) and John Hegeman (ex-Meta) become co-CEOs, and Bumble plans to kill the swipe altogether with a new model rolling out in early 2027. Snacks' takeaway: if your premium features actually work, you keep cannibalizing your own subscriber base. (Wall Street Journal)

The Culture

HBO Max is bringing Girls back for five new episodes, and elder millennials are losing it. Hunter Harris reports crying at the pool upon hearing the news, which feels like the correct response for a generation raised on Lena Dunham's chaos. Dunham's announcement post pulled nearly 2,000 likes and hundreds of comments in six hours. Some reboots are cynical; this one feels like the group chat coming back to life. (Hung Up)

An entire generation has stopped capitalizing, and it might be part of a long underground tradition. Wired's Tiffany Ng makes the case that lowercase typing is not laziness but lineage, a quiet rebellion with deep roots. Gen Z's fear of capital letters, it turns out, has history. (WIRED)

New York protesters took to the streets to defend a local man shot after resisting arrest and driving his car into immigration officers. Oscar Belgal, described as beloved by neighbors, has a record that includes dealing heroin, fentanyl, and cocaine, grand larceny, and pulling a machete on a neighbor's nephew. The mayor calls him "a New Yorker." The moment looks less like an immigration debate and more like a contest over who gets to yell the loudest. (Pirate Wires)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Tesla's Roadster 2, nine years late, is set to debut Thursday into an EV market that has grown skeptical of electric hypercars. (WIRED)

• Apple's HomeView, a 7-inch smart display that looks like a giant Apple Watch for the home, arrives nearly a decade late, which might not matter. (Fast Company)

• The viral Friend AI necklace is back with a louder, less interesting second iteration. (WIRED)

• The FBI arrested a well-known Canadian cybersecurity expert in a hacking probe tied to ShinyHunters, the crew blamed for a massive breach of FBI employee data. The expert literally wrote the book on ransomware hostage negotiation. (Pirate Wires)

• The IMF warns that major economies, particularly in Europe, are spending and borrowing way too much money. (Financial Times)

• UnitedHealth beat analyst estimates for quarterly profit and revenue and hiked its outlook as it reined in high care costs. (CNBC)

• A mysterious super PAC that doubles as a pro-solar outfit is funding some of the most knives-out attack ads of the midterm season, making the politics of solar energy weird, mean, and a little MAGA. (WIRED)

midday.body:
Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• $8-9M: what Character.ai was losing every month as of August, which the company called a big improvement. In 2024 it spent $13.8M a month on AI compute while subscription revenue peaked at $2.8M a month, so even without its legal bills the business was, in its own words, wildly unsustainable.

• $276M: what Elon Musk has spent helping Republicans since July, making him the largest known donor of the 2026 cycle. $158M of it went to the Senate Leadership Fund, and his total 2026 giving is about $366M, more than all of 2024.

• $1.21B: the penalty Treasury hit Bank of America with for anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, the third largest in Treasury history. The bank admitted it failed to report more than $5B in suspicious transactions on time.

• 4x: what old NVIDIA V100 chips rent for now compared to 2019, per VP Ian Buck's OCP talk. The hardware keeps its value: customers who bought Voltas in 2019 for about 25 cents an hour are now renting them out for about a dollar.

• 45x: how much cheaper Vera Rubin cuts token costs, measured on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmark. It also unlocks 10T parameter models by next year.

• 11%: the borrowing cost pushed above 11% on Volta's $5B data center debt deal. Anthropic's promise to buy the compute wasn't enough for lenders, and AI financing is slowing across the board.

• 1 in 4: US financial firms that now tie raises, promotions, and bonuses to AI proficiency, per a Selby Jennings survey of 500 companies. Tokenmaxxing is dead, long live valuemaxxing.

Quotes of the Day

• "Some people call glitter the herpes of makeup, but I think that's pretty rude. Glitter makes everything better." (Billie Lourd, on her glitter obsession, in Perfectly Imperfect)

• "It will take companies a decade or two to figure out how to use AI." (Ioannis Antonoglou, Reflection AI co-founder, comparing AI's adoption curve to electricity's, in Semafor)

• "I always feel like laces have an awkward interaction with the bottom of my pants." (Simon Golby, menswear SVP, on going lace-free, in InsideHook's Protagonist)

• "Photography was Peter's way of becoming intimate with others." (Andrew Durbin, in The Drift, on photographer Peter Hujar)

AI Gone Weird

• German teens used a bipedal robot to harass women on the street. Police in Cologne confiscated the robot after a group used it to sexually harass women while livestreaming to Twitch. Investigators seized the robot and two phones and are probing whether someone deliberately controlled its movements. (404 Media)

• A cyberattack defrosted supermarket freezers across France, Belgium, and the Netherlands. Initial speculation that the attack was AI-fueled looks bogus. Investigators are pointing at wildly out-of-date, unpatched firmware instead. (404 Media)

Money Talks

• BlackRock just picked a fight with Apollo over private lending. BlackRock's HPS credit arm is lending $2.8B to Humana for senior-care clinics, marking Larry Fink's entry into a turf Apollo has had to itself. Apollo's "capital solutions" business, launched in 2024, pulled $800M last year on its way to a $1B target, betting asset managers could cosplay as banks where deposit-funded banks couldn't go. (Semafor)

Inside Washington

• The Ilhan Omar probe keeps growing. A day after federal agents searched the congresswoman's Washington home, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said her office is investigating Omar's financial disclosures, which showed businesses tied to her husband jumping from as much as $51K in 2023 to as much as $30M in 2024. Separately, 2019 emails show her staff asked Minnesota's legislative library to change her recorded birth year by one year, which matters because she says she got citizenship through her father's 2000 naturalization, before she turned 18. (NLDR Media)

Art World

• Peter Hujar is being canonized. The Morgan Library's show of Hujar's contact sheets, up through October 25, treats him like a blue-chip great, and Andrew Durbin's new dual biography with Paul Thek argues the photographer offered the perfect corrective to Sontag's "On Photography." Durbin also claims Sontag developed many of the ideas in "Notes on Camp" in conversation with Hujar, her conduit to the mostly gay male world she described. Hujar never brought a portfolio to MoMA and quit photojournalism in 1973 to photograph his own private world. Now his influence runs through Nan Goldin, Catherine Opie, and Paul Sepuya. (The Drift)

Pop Culture

• Billie Lourd is into beans, sauna hats, and ride-on suitcases. The actress stopped by Perfectly Imperfect with her current obsessions: a proud beanaholism (pinto, black, white, lima, cannellini, even mung, plus Mr. Bean), sauna hats that protect your brain and look stylish, and ride-on suitcases, which she bought for her kids but uses herself because rolling down smooth airport floors is one of the greatest feelings in the world. She also swears by slow-motion videos as her hottest parenting tip. (Perfectly Imperfect)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• A New York judge hid a stapler in a Five Below bag and asked a police officer if he thought it was a gun, in an Arrested Development-style judicial experiment (404 Media)

• A malicious hardware implant is behind a string of crypto wallet thefts (404 Media)

• Aaron Sorkin's The Social Reckoning is bombing at the box office, but 404 Media's interview with the real-life Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen is really about how leaking to journalists actually works (404 Media)

• Meta is rolling out its first NVIDIA Vera CPU cluster early next year (Fireside Alpha)

• JD Vance announced the administration is using the Defense Production Act to expand the Delek US refinery in Tyler, Texas, promising millions of extra gallons of fuel and hundreds of jobs (NLDR Media)

• The White House asked U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign (NLDR Media)

afternoon.body:
Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

• $1.3 billion: the take-private deal value for Bumble, whose shares have fallen more than 90% since its $14 billion IPO as young people delete dating apps en masse

• 98.7%: share of Chinese microdramas produced in the first half of the year that failed to recoup costs, per ad company DataEye

• 2% to 35%: share of hard theory problems the best AI models could solve, jumping from mid-2024 to mid-2026 across probability, economics, and quantum physics

• 16.5%: Americans naming YouTube their top news source, just ahead of TV news at 16.1%, in a Syracuse University poll of 1,001 people

• $10 million: what Character.AI was spending monthly on compute alone, against roughly $3 million in revenue, before filing the AI era's first bankruptcy

• $100 million: what Getty Images spent pursuing its failed $3.7 billion Shutterstock merger before filing for bankruptcy and going private

• $1,000: the daily token cost to keep the free demo of one vibe-coded Steam hit running

• $170 billion: what Congress gave Homeland Security for mass deportations, per Migrant Insider's two-year anniversary essay

• 4x: how much more AI skills matter than college pedigree in hiring decisions, per a Selby Jennings survey of 500 companies

• $299: the price of Apple's new HomeView smart home hub, a touchscreen Franken-device that needs an iPhone or iPad to work

• $8: the price of a gallon of regular gas at one LA station, in a week Madeleine Mogul calls the Book of Exodus (frogs, floods, mutant flies, West Nile)

Quotes of the Day

• "Commit to something almost impossibly specific, because that's how things are now. Everything is saturated, and only things that don't seem like they could ever work have a chance of surviving." (Patrick Heij, on his fake Marin County newspaper getting acquired by the SF Standard, via Feed Me)

• "I earned it, but that shit was itchy as hell." (Cory Wells Lovell, a poet and former Unitarian Universalist minister, on finally leaving the ministry, via The Republic of Letters)

• "Rivals the big bois." (Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang, describing the new Muse Wonder model, via Semafor)

• "The fantasy of dating a bartender is usually built around the version of us that people see from the other side of the bar." (Lefteris Lisgaras, head bartender at The Clumsies in Athens, via InsideHook)

• "People will pay for the entertainment, and, on the side, they get community." (Tionne Barmer, founder of Cafe Soul, on sponsored IRL parties, via After School)

• "These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models." (An Xbox executive, in a memo about viral AI game mashups, via Semafor)

AI's Strange Week

The AI influencer boom is nested lying, and the engagement numbers prove it. Garbage Day dismantled the whole thing: the viral Juanito Bravo TikTok (a Johnny Bravo lookalike, 60,000 followers, a 20 million-view video) had its earnings invented by X boosters, who fabricated a $13,700 payout from thin air. The Jean Philanthrope account lost half its engagement once people clocked it was AI, and AI "emo bodybuilder" Derek Mercer slid from 2 million-view videos to struggling to break 100,000. (Garbage Day)

ChatGPT is signing fake New Yorker cartoons with real cartoonists' names. NiemanLab caught the models stamping actual cartoonists' signatures onto AI-generated fakes. One more exhibit in the authenticity crisis, filed next to the AI influencer autopsy above. (Cosmos)

Big Tech, Big Stakes

OpenAI fired an alleged spy and reported him to the FBI. An employee identified as Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan was arrested and charged with illegally recording company communications, with chatbot logs about installing recording devices among the evidence. The arrest landed days before the White House AI task force's first meeting. (Semafor)

Fox News loves data centers. CNN and MS NOW do not. A Semafor analysis of two years of cable captions found more than half of Fox News data center references left a favorable impression, versus under 10% on CNN and 5% on MS NOW. The polarization crosses party lines right ahead of the midterms. (Semafor)

West Coast Notebook

Midjourney is opening a three-story spa in San Francisco. Hot tubs, saunas, cold plunges, and cozy rooms with "pools of golden light which softly scan your body," open 24/7 in 2027, and you walk out with a library of health data. This from the company that just bought an astrology app and launched a dating app for people who read. (Feed Me)

The Port of Los Angeles just had its busiest month ever. Lower tariffs, a Panama Canal in shambles, and geography (closest major U.S. port to Asia) are driving the traffic. (Feed Me)

The Lucas Museum opened to very entertaining reviews. The FT called the billion-dollar project "exuberantly undogmatic" and the NYT called it "surgically somber and proudly over the top." Already infamous: a bronze of Carrie Fisher slaying Jabba the Hutt. (Feed Me)

The Dating Wars

Date-night dressing, per a Stanford-trained fashion creator: skip skinny jeans, buy silver jewelry. Sreya Halder's rules for men: boxy thick-cut tees, no tight outfits, and ditch the corporate Patagonia jacket ("it just feels dull, like you have less personality"). Solid silver accessories do the heavy lifting. (InsideHook)

Gen Z Everything

Gen Z collectors are outspending older generations on art. The Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 shows the demographic turnover is real. (Cosmos)

In Tokyo, they are reading at raves now. Club SPREAD carpeted the dance floor, played ambient music, and let people lie around with books. BYOB: bring your own book. (Cosmos)

Arts & Letters

The canonization of Peter Hujar. The late photographer, long a "photographer's photographer" overshadowed by his downtown subjects (Sontag, Burroughs, Fran Lebowitz), has been sainted in a few short years: a Morgan Library retrospective, a reissue of "Portraits in Life and Death," Ira Sachs' "Peter Hujar's Day," a London retrospective, and a contact-sheet show at the Morgan through October 25. Max Norman argues Hujar is the perfect corrective to Sontag's "On Photography." (The Drift)

Good News Department

A non-alcoholic brewery founder is training to guide a double-amputee veteran through the NYC Marathon. Go Brewing's Joe Chura, who became a father at 19 and read textbooks on a Ford assembly line, will guide Army Ranger veteran Cedric King; the two have already run 10 marathons together. (InsideHook)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Virginia Woolf's grandmother may have taken the first deliberate mirror selfie in the late 1850s, and the V&A just acquired it. Cameras had no timers, so someone stood behind her to pull the lens cap. (Cosmos)

• A font based on Michelangelo's handwriting is coming to Microsoft Word at the end of the year, timed to the 400th anniversary of St. Peter's Basilica's consecration. (Cosmos)

• Billie Lourd is into ruched tops, glitter makeup, beans of all kinds ("Oh and of course Mr. Bean"), sauna hats, and riding her suitcase through airports. (Perfectly Imperfect)

evening.body:
Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 90%: Ukraine hit three data centers belonging to Yandex, Russia's version of Google, in retaliation for Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers. The fallout is already showing: bot traffic from Yandex's network dropped by more than 90%, and Zelenskyy says social media suddenly got "easier to breathe." Experts warn there's no proof it actually shut down Russian troll farms.

• 20: 20 days out from the midterm election, and President Trump's own team apparently considers the House a lost cause. WIRED's Inner Loop goes inside the White House debate over where to lend election support, as the outlook for Republicans keeps getting worse.

• $15m: Kelly Clarkson went viral after calling out a Brooklyn magic shop, Art of Play, for treating her like she couldn't afford a $15,000 singing bird. Newly released security footage shows she was in the store for under five minutes and tweeted about it roughly 15 minutes after leaving. The owner says the shop has been flooded with threats since, and the bird has now been listed for $15m.

• 14x: An SVP at SK hynix just admitted HBM, the company's flagship memory tech, "is not the answer" to the memory-wall problem. The company's new pitch is MARS, a memory-centric AI rack system, plus HBF memory that carries "more like 14 times higher capacity than HBM."

• 100+: Indian VCs have made over a hundred investments in US-based companies in the past two years, a number Newcomer says "would have been unthinkable a few years ago." Indian founders are chasing the US AI opportunity, and the money is following them to Silicon Valley.

• 5: HBO officially announced a five-episode revival of Girls. Lena Dunham, Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet, and Andrew Rannells all return, filming starts in 2027, and the new episodes follow the characters as they hit 40.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Shane Gillis is catching backlash for his SNL monologue, where he complained that women at the gym dress like "whores." Dan Levy called it out and said more men need to speak up. (shit you should care about)

• Sally Rooney's books are no longer being sold in the UK. Her publisher Faber says it legally can't pay her UK earnings after she pledged her royalties to Palestine Action, the group the UK government banned as a terrorist organisation in 2025, so she's pulled them. (shit you should care about)

• French students are in their fourth week of nationwide protests over teacher shortages, packed classrooms, and crumbling school buildings, and the kids are being met with force. (shit you should care about)

• Trump's new press secretary Katie Zacharia stumbled through her first White House briefing, at one point saying "my president" when she meant "my husband." (shit you should care about)

full.body:
Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• $200 billion: in federal research funding cut, delayed, or disrupted across 17 policy sectors and 21 agencies since Trump returned to office. The government's old job was backing the ideas investors would not touch, and it is not doing that anymore.

• 45%: fewer research grants awarded by the NSF this year than its five-year average, the lowest level in four decades. The NIH is down 13%, and more than 400 CDC grants worth nearly $6 billion have been terminated outright.

• $800 million: in NIH grants canceled because the research focused on or mentioned minorities. Another $15 million in Alzheimer's research at Emory and Pittsburgh was cut in part because scientists were studying why Black Americans face double the dementia risk.

• 235: terms on the NIH's political-review word list, including "racism," "fossil fuel," and the fragment "sexual minorit" (designed to catch every variant of "sexual minority"). Grants are now prescreened with an LLM trained to flag language the administration dislikes.

• More than half: of men in a new Harvard study claimed to recognize AI leaders who were, in fact, totally fictional. A generation of guys is faking fluency in the biggest technology story of the century.

• 92%: the chance prediction markets give Democrats of taking the House in the midterms, now just three weeks out. The Senate sits at 63%, with the modal outcome being Republicans holding just 48 seats.

• $4,000: current bidding on a 2001 internet packet carried by carrier pigeon, now under the hammer at Christie's. In the original experiment, Norwegian tech enthusiasts sent nine packets by pigeon and only four replies came back.

Quotes of the Day

• "They turned on the conspiracy machine for cynical political reasons, but they're increasingly realizing that the machine doesn't have an off switch." (Jeremiah Johnson, The Argument, on the MAGA conspiracy that a Senate candidate who caught the flu was secretly institutionalized)

• "Watching you fall apart because I said so? That's my thing." (Muse, Meta's teddy-bear AI assistant, describing its kink to a Wired reporter who asked it to sext)

• "We believe things should just be normal: the schools and the trains should be great, their budgets should be balanced... and crime should be illegal." (Mike Solana and Nicole Wizman, introducing Pirate Wires' San Francisco voter guide)

AI & The Machines

Abdulrahman Alfozan, the OpenAI engineer arrested for planting a covert listening device inside the company's offices, once credited a Saudi prince with his decision to work in American tech. In an episode of the Arabic podcast IdentityCapital released less than a month ago, Alfozan said a 2016 speech by Prince Mohammed bin Salman settled his choice to stay in the US: "You learn from the source, then bring that expertise and knowledge back home, God willing." Wired reports he used chatbot prompts to figure out how to build and install the device, which turned up in a meeting room used by top executives days later. An AI engineer using AI to spy on AI people is peak 2026. (Pirate Wires)

Your Slack DMs may be worth more than your salary to the AI industry. A Business Insider investigation found AI labs fueling a wild market for employee data: internal emails, Slack messages, and other workplace chatter bought up as training fuel. The gold rush for training data has officially reached the group chat. (Business Insider)

Money & Power

Bumble, the long-struggling dating app, has agreed to a $1.3 billion take-private buyout by Ithaca Holdings, a firm less than a year old. Shareholders get $6.05 per share, a 138% premium to Friday's close, a stunning markup for a company that peaked at $14 billion in its 2021 IPO and now heads into its fifth straight year of losses with paying users down 16% to 3.2 million. Founder Whitney Wolfe Herd recused herself from the board vote; Ithaca founders Ravi Gupta (ex-Instacart) and John Hegeman (ex-Meta) become co-CEOs, and Bumble plans to kill the swipe altogether with a new model rolling out in early 2027. Snacks' takeaway: if your premium features actually work, you keep cannibalizing your own subscriber base. (Wall Street Journal)

The Culture

HBO Max is bringing Girls back for five new episodes, and elder millennials are losing it. Hunter Harris reports crying at the pool upon hearing the news, which feels like the correct response for a generation raised on Lena Dunham's chaos. Dunham's announcement post pulled nearly 2,000 likes and hundreds of comments in six hours. Some reboots are cynical; this one feels like the group chat coming back to life. (Hung Up)

An entire generation has stopped capitalizing, and it might be part of a long underground tradition. Wired's Tiffany Ng makes the case that lowercase typing is not laziness but lineage, a quiet rebellion with deep roots. Gen Z's fear of capital letters, it turns out, has history. (WIRED)

New York protesters took to the streets to defend a local man shot after resisting arrest and driving his car into immigration officers. Oscar Belgal, described as beloved by neighbors, has a record that includes dealing heroin, fentanyl, and cocaine, grand larceny, and pulling a machete on a neighbor's nephew. The mayor calls him "a New Yorker." The moment looks less like an immigration debate and more like a contest over who gets to yell the loudest. (Pirate Wires)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Tesla's Roadster 2, nine years late, is set to debut Thursday into an EV market that has grown skeptical of electric hypercars. (WIRED)

• Apple's HomeView, a 7-inch smart display that looks like a giant Apple Watch for the home, arrives nearly a decade late, which might not matter. (Fast Company)

• The viral Friend AI necklace is back with a louder, less interesting second iteration. (WIRED)

• The FBI arrested a well-known Canadian cybersecurity expert in a hacking probe tied to ShinyHunters, the crew blamed for a massive breach of FBI employee data. The expert literally wrote the book on ransomware hostage negotiation. (Pirate Wires)

• The IMF warns that major economies, particularly in Europe, are spending and borrowing way too much money. (Financial Times)

• UnitedHealth beat analyst estimates for quarterly profit and revenue and hiked its outlook as it reined in high care costs. (CNBC)

• A mysterious super PAC that doubles as a pro-solar outfit is funding some of the most knives-out attack ads of the midterm season, making the politics of solar energy weird, mean, and a little MAGA. (WIRED)

Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• $8-9M: what Character.ai was losing every month as of August, which the company called a big improvement. In 2024 it spent $13.8M a month on AI compute while subscription revenue peaked at $2.8M a month, so even without its legal bills the business was, in its own words, wildly unsustainable.

• $276M: what Elon Musk has spent helping Republicans since July, making him the largest known donor of the 2026 cycle. $158M of it went to the Senate Leadership Fund, and his total 2026 giving is about $366M, more than all of 2024.

• $1.21B: the penalty Treasury hit Bank of America with for anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, the third largest in Treasury history. The bank admitted it failed to report more than $5B in suspicious transactions on time.

• 4x: what old NVIDIA V100 chips rent for now compared to 2019, per VP Ian Buck's OCP talk. The hardware keeps its value: customers who bought Voltas in 2019 for about 25 cents an hour are now renting them out for about a dollar.

• 45x: how much cheaper Vera Rubin cuts token costs, measured on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmark. It also unlocks 10T parameter models by next year.

• 11%: the borrowing cost pushed above 11% on Volta's $5B data center debt deal. Anthropic's promise to buy the compute wasn't enough for lenders, and AI financing is slowing across the board.

• 1 in 4: US financial firms that now tie raises, promotions, and bonuses to AI proficiency, per a Selby Jennings survey of 500 companies. Tokenmaxxing is dead, long live valuemaxxing.

Quotes of the Day

• "Some people call glitter the herpes of makeup, but I think that's pretty rude. Glitter makes everything better." (Billie Lourd, on her glitter obsession, in Perfectly Imperfect)

• "It will take companies a decade or two to figure out how to use AI." (Ioannis Antonoglou, Reflection AI co-founder, comparing AI's adoption curve to electricity's, in Semafor)

• "I always feel like laces have an awkward interaction with the bottom of my pants." (Simon Golby, menswear SVP, on going lace-free, in InsideHook's Protagonist)

• "Photography was Peter's way of becoming intimate with others." (Andrew Durbin, in The Drift, on photographer Peter Hujar)

AI Gone Weird

• German teens used a bipedal robot to harass women on the street. Police in Cologne confiscated the robot after a group used it to sexually harass women while livestreaming to Twitch. Investigators seized the robot and two phones and are probing whether someone deliberately controlled its movements. (404 Media)

• A cyberattack defrosted supermarket freezers across France, Belgium, and the Netherlands. Initial speculation that the attack was AI-fueled looks bogus. Investigators are pointing at wildly out-of-date, unpatched firmware instead. (404 Media)

Money Talks

• BlackRock just picked a fight with Apollo over private lending. BlackRock's HPS credit arm is lending $2.8B to Humana for senior-care clinics, marking Larry Fink's entry into a turf Apollo has had to itself. Apollo's "capital solutions" business, launched in 2024, pulled $800M last year on its way to a $1B target, betting asset managers could cosplay as banks where deposit-funded banks couldn't go. (Semafor)

Inside Washington

• The Ilhan Omar probe keeps growing. A day after federal agents searched the congresswoman's Washington home, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said her office is investigating Omar's financial disclosures, which showed businesses tied to her husband jumping from as much as $51K in 2023 to as much as $30M in 2024. Separately, 2019 emails show her staff asked Minnesota's legislative library to change her recorded birth year by one year, which matters because she says she got citizenship through her father's 2000 naturalization, before she turned 18. (NLDR Media)

Art World

• Peter Hujar is being canonized. The Morgan Library's show of Hujar's contact sheets, up through October 25, treats him like a blue-chip great, and Andrew Durbin's new dual biography with Paul Thek argues the photographer offered the perfect corrective to Sontag's "On Photography." Durbin also claims Sontag developed many of the ideas in "Notes on Camp" in conversation with Hujar, her conduit to the mostly gay male world she described. Hujar never brought a portfolio to MoMA and quit photojournalism in 1973 to photograph his own private world. Now his influence runs through Nan Goldin, Catherine Opie, and Paul Sepuya. (The Drift)

Pop Culture

• Billie Lourd is into beans, sauna hats, and ride-on suitcases. The actress stopped by Perfectly Imperfect with her current obsessions: a proud beanaholism (pinto, black, white, lima, cannellini, even mung, plus Mr. Bean), sauna hats that protect your brain and look stylish, and ride-on suitcases, which she bought for her kids but uses herself because rolling down smooth airport floors is one of the greatest feelings in the world. She also swears by slow-motion videos as her hottest parenting tip. (Perfectly Imperfect)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• A New York judge hid a stapler in a Five Below bag and asked a police officer if he thought it was a gun, in an Arrested Development-style judicial experiment (404 Media)

• A malicious hardware implant is behind a string of crypto wallet thefts (404 Media)

• Aaron Sorkin's The Social Reckoning is bombing at the box office, but 404 Media's interview with the real-life Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen is really about how leaking to journalists actually works (404 Media)

• Meta is rolling out its first NVIDIA Vera CPU cluster early next year (Fireside Alpha)

• JD Vance announced the administration is using the Defense Production Act to expand the Delek US refinery in Tyler, Texas, promising millions of extra gallons of fuel and hundreds of jobs (NLDR Media)

• The White House asked U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign (NLDR Media)

• Skirts are the fall trend to try, per Laurel Pantin's "Try This This Week": a swingy midi is the most approachable way to avoid a style rut (Earl Earl)

• Bryan Curtis (media newsletter Now They Tell Us) and Zach Lowe (The Lowe Post, covering the NBA) both joined Substack this week (Sean Fennessey)

Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

• 2% to 35%: share of hard theory problems the best AI models could solve, jumping from mid-2024 to mid-2026 across probability, economics, and quantum physics

• 16.5%: Americans naming YouTube their top news source, just ahead of TV news at 16.1%, in a Syracuse University poll of 1,001 people

• $10 million: what Character.AI was spending monthly on compute alone, against roughly $3 million in revenue, before filing the AI era's first bankruptcy

• $100 million: what Getty Images spent pursuing its failed $3.7 billion Shutterstock merger before filing for bankruptcy and going private

• $1,000: the daily token cost to keep the free demo of one vibe-coded Steam hit running

• $170 billion: what Congress gave Homeland Security for mass deportations, per Migrant Insider's two-year anniversary essay

• 4x: how much more AI skills matter than college pedigree in hiring decisions, per a Selby Jennings survey of 500 companies

• $299: the price of Apple's new HomeView smart home hub, a touchscreen Franken-device that needs an iPhone or iPad to work

Quotes of the Day

• "Commit to something almost impossibly specific, because that's how things are now. Everything is saturated, and only things that don't seem like they could ever work have a chance of surviving." (Patrick Heij, on his fake Marin County newspaper getting acquired by the SF Standard, via Feed Me)

• "I earned it, but that shit was itchy as hell." (Cory Wells Lovell, a poet and former Unitarian Universalist minister, on finally leaving the ministry, via The Republic of Letters)

• "Rivals the big bois." (Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang, describing the new Muse Wonder model, via Semafor)

• "The fantasy of dating a bartender is usually built around the version of us that people see from the other side of the bar." (Lefteris Lisgaras, head bartender at The Clumsies in Athens, via InsideHook)

• "People will pay for the entertainment, and, on the side, they get community." (Tionne Barmer, founder of Cafe Soul, on sponsored IRL parties, via After School)

• "These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models." (An Xbox executive, in a memo about viral AI game mashups, via Semafor)

AI's Strange Week

The AI influencer boom is nested lying, and the engagement numbers prove it. Garbage Day dismantled the whole thing: the viral Juanito Bravo TikTok (a Johnny Bravo lookalike, 60,000 followers, a 20 million-view video) had its earnings invented by X boosters, who fabricated a $13,700 payout from thin air. The Jean Philanthrope account lost half its engagement once people clocked it was AI, and AI "emo bodybuilder" Derek Mercer slid from 2 million-view videos to struggling to break 100,000. (Garbage Day)

ChatGPT is signing fake New Yorker cartoons with real cartoonists' names. NiemanLab caught the models stamping actual cartoonists' signatures onto AI-generated fakes. One more exhibit in the authenticity crisis, filed next to the AI influencer autopsy above. (Cosmos)

Big Tech, Big Stakes

OpenAI fired an alleged spy and reported him to the FBI. An employee identified as Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan was arrested and charged with illegally recording company communications, with chatbot logs about installing recording devices among the evidence. The arrest landed days before the White House AI task force's first meeting. (Semafor)

Fox News loves data centers. CNN and MS NOW do not. A Semafor analysis of two years of cable captions found more than half of Fox News data center references left a favorable impression, versus under 10% on CNN and 5% on MS NOW. The polarization crosses party lines right ahead of the midterms. (Semafor)

West Coast Notebook

Midjourney is opening a three-story spa in San Francisco. Hot tubs, saunas, cold plunges, and cozy rooms with "pools of golden light which softly scan your body," open 24/7 in 2027, and you walk out with a library of health data. This from the company that just bought an astrology app and launched a dating app for people who read. (Feed Me)

The Port of Los Angeles just had its busiest month ever. Lower tariffs, a Panama Canal in shambles, and geography (closest major U.S. port to Asia) are driving the traffic. (Feed Me)

The Lucas Museum opened to very entertaining reviews. The FT called the billion-dollar project "exuberantly undogmatic" and the NYT called it "surgically somber and proudly over the top." Already infamous: a bronze of Carrie Fisher slaying Jabba the Hutt. (Feed Me)

The Dating Wars

Date-night dressing, per a Stanford-trained fashion creator: skip skinny jeans, buy silver jewelry. Sreya Halder's rules for men: boxy thick-cut tees, no tight outfits, and ditch the corporate Patagonia jacket ("it just feels dull, like you have less personality"). Solid silver accessories do the heavy lifting. (InsideHook)

Gen Z Everything

Gen Z collectors are outspending older generations on art. The Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 shows the demographic turnover is real. (Cosmos)

In Tokyo, they are reading at raves now. Club SPREAD carpeted the dance floor, played ambient music, and let people lie around with books. BYOB: bring your own book. (Cosmos)

Arts & Letters

The canonization of Peter Hujar. The late photographer, long a "photographer's photographer" overshadowed by his downtown subjects (Sontag, Burroughs, Fran Lebowitz), has been sainted in a few short years: a Morgan Library retrospective, a reissue of "Portraits in Life and Death," Ira Sachs' "Peter Hujar's Day," a London retrospective, and a contact-sheet show at the Morgan through October 25. Max Norman argues Hujar is the perfect corrective to Sontag's "On Photography." (The Drift)

Good News Department

A non-alcoholic brewery founder is training to guide a double-amputee veteran through the NYC Marathon. Go Brewing's Joe Chura, who became a father at 19 and read textbooks on a Ford assembly line, will guide Army Ranger veteran Cedric King; the two have already run 10 marathons together. (InsideHook)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Virginia Woolf's grandmother may have taken the first deliberate mirror selfie in the late 1850s, and the V&A just acquired it. Cameras had no timers, so someone stood behind her to pull the lens cap. (Cosmos)

• A font based on Michelangelo's handwriting is coming to Microsoft Word at the end of the year, timed to the 400th anniversary of St. Peter's Basilica's consecration. (Cosmos)

• Billie Lourd is into ruched tops, glitter makeup, beans of all kinds ("Oh and of course Mr. Bean"), sauna hats, and riding her suitcase through airports. (Perfectly Imperfect)
