Today's Numbers

• 90%: Ukraine hit three data centers belonging to Yandex, Russia's version of Google, in retaliation for Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers. The fallout is already showing: bot traffic from Yandex's network dropped by more than 90%, and Zelenskyy says social media suddenly got "easier to breathe." Experts warn there's no proof it actually shut down Russian troll farms.

• 20: 20 days out from the midterm election, and President Trump's own team apparently considers the House a lost cause. WIRED's Inner Loop goes inside the White House debate over where to lend election support, as the outlook for Republicans keeps getting worse.

The owner says the shop has been flooded with threats since, and the bird has now been listed for $15m.

• 100+: Indian VCs have made over a hundred investments in US-based companies in the past two years, a number Newcomer says "would have been unthinkable a few years ago." Indian founders are chasing the US AI opportunity, and the money is following them to Silicon Valley.

• 5: HBO officially announced a five-episode revival of Girls. Lena Dunham, Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet, and Andrew Rannells all return, filming starts in 2027, and the new episodes follow the characters as they hit 40.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Shane Gillis is catching backlash for his SNL monologue, where he complained that women at the gym dress like "whores." Dan Levy called it out and said more men need to speak up. (shit you should care about)

• Sally Rooney's books are no longer being sold in the UK. Her publisher Faber says it legally can't pay her UK earnings after she pledged her royalties to Palestine Action, the group the UK government banned as a terrorist organisation in 2025, so she's pulled them. (shit you should care about)

• French students are in their fourth week of nationwide protests over teacher shortages, packed classrooms, and crumbling school buildings, and the kids are being met with force. (shit you should care about)

• Trump's new press secretary Katie Zacharia stumbled through her first White House briefing, at one point saying "my president" when she meant "my husband." (shit you should care about)

: in federal research funding cut, delayed, or disrupted across 17 policy sectors and 21 agencies since Trump returned to office. The government's old job was backing the ideas investors would not touch, and it is not doing that anymore.

: fewer research grants awarded by the NSF this year than its five-year average, the lowest level in four decades. The NIH is down 13%, and more than 400 CDC grants worth nearly $6 billion have been terminated outright.

: in NIH grants canceled because the research focused on or mentioned minorities. Another $15 million in Alzheimer's research at Emory and Pittsburgh was cut in part because scientists were studying why Black Americans face double the dementia risk.

: terms on the NIH's political-review word list, including "racism," "fossil fuel," and the fragment "sexual minorit" (designed to catch every variant of "sexual minority"). Grants are now prescreened with an LLM trained to flag language the administration dislikes.

: of men in a new Harvard study claimed to recognize AI leaders who were, in fact, totally fictional. A generation of guys is faking fluency in the biggest technology story of the century.
: the chance prediction markets give Democrats of taking the House in the midterms, now just three weeks out. The Senate sits at 63%, with the modal outcome being Republicans holding just 48 seats.

: current bidding on a 2001 internet packet carried by carrier pigeon, now under the hammer at Christie's. In the original experiment, Norwegian tech enthusiasts sent nine packets by pigeon and only four replies came back.

"They turned on the conspiracy machine for cynical political reasons, but they're increasingly realizing that the machine doesn't have an off switch." (Jeremiah Johnson, The Argument, on the MAGA conspiracy that a Senate candidate who caught the flu was secretly institutionalized)
"Watching you fall apart because I said so? That's my thing." (Muse, Meta's teddy-bear AI assistant, describing its kink to a Wired reporter who asked it to sext)

"We believe things should just be normal: the schools and the trains should be great, their budgets should be balanced... and crime should be illegal." (Mike Solana and Nicole Wizman, introducing Pirate Wires' San Francisco voter guide)
AI & The Machines
Abdulrahman Alfozan, the OpenAI engineer arrested for planting a covert listening device inside the company's offices, once credited a Saudi prince with his decision to work in American tech.

In an episode of the Arabic podcast IdentityCapital released less than a month ago, Alfozan said a 2016 speech by Prince Mohammed bin Salman settled his choice to stay in the US: "You learn from the source, then bring that expertise and knowledge back home, God willing." Wired reports he used chatbot prompts to figure out how to build and install the device, which turned up in a meeting room used by top executives days later. An AI engineer using AI to spy on AI people is peak 2026. (
Pirate Wires
Your Slack DMs may be worth more than your salary to the AI industry.

A Business Insider investigation found AI labs fueling a wild market for employee data: internal emails, Slack messages, and other workplace chatter bought up as training fuel. The gold rush for training data has officially reached the group chat. (
Business Insider
Money & Power
Bumble, the long-struggling dating app, has agreed to a $1.3 billion take-private buyout by Ithaca Holdings, a firm less than a year old.

Shareholders get $6.05 per share, a 138% premium to Friday's close, a stunning markup for a company that peaked at $14 billion in its 2021 IPO and now heads into its fifth straight year of losses with paying users down 16% to 3.2 million. Founder Whitney Wolfe Herd recused herself from the board vote; Ithaca founders Ravi Gupta (ex-Instacart) and John Hegeman (ex-Meta) become co-CEOs, and Bumble plans to kill the swipe altogether with a new model rolling out in early 2027. Snacks' takeaway: if your premium features actually work, you keep cannibalizing your own subscriber base. (
Wall Street Journal
The Culture
HBO Max is bringing Girls back for five new episodes, and elder millennials are losing it.

Hunter Harris reports crying at the pool upon hearing the news, which feels like the correct response for a generation raised on Lena Dunham's chaos. Dunham's announcement post pulled nearly 2,000 likes and hundreds of comments in six hours. Some reboots are cynical; this one feels like the group chat coming back to life. (
Hung Up
An entire generation has stopped capitalizing, and it might be part of a long underground tradition.
Wired's Tiffany Ng makes the case that lowercase typing is not laziness but lineage, a quiet rebellion with deep roots. Gen Z's fear of capital letters, it turns out, has history. (
WIRED
New York protesters took to the streets to defend a local man shot after resisting arrest and driving his car into immigration officers.

Oscar Belgal, described as beloved by neighbors, has a record that includes dealing heroin, fentanyl, and cocaine, grand larceny, and pulling a machete on a neighbor's nephew. The mayor calls him "a New Yorker." The moment looks less like an immigration debate and more like a contest over who gets to yell the loudest. (

An employee identified as Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan was arrested and charged with illegally recording company communications, with chatbot logs about installing recording devices among the evidence. The arrest landed days before the White House AI task force's first meeting. (
Semafor
Fox News loves data centers. CNN and MS NOW do not.

A Semafor analysis of two years of cable captions found more than half of Fox News data center references left a favorable impression, versus under 10% on CNN and 5% on MS NOW. The polarization crosses party lines right ahead of the midterms. (
Semafor
West Coast Notebook
Midjourney is opening a three-story spa in San Francisco.

Hot tubs, saunas, cold plunges, and cozy rooms with "pools of golden light which softly scan your body," open 24/7 in 2027, and you walk out with a library of health data. This from the company that just bought an astrology app and launched a dating app for people who read. (
Feed Me
The Port of Los Angeles just had its busiest month ever.
Lower tariffs, a Panama Canal in shambles, and geography (closest major U.S. port to Asia) are driving the traffic. (
Feed Me
The Lucas Museum opened to very entertaining reviews.

The FT called the billion-dollar project "exuberantly undogmatic" and the NYT called it "surgically somber and proudly over the top." Already infamous: a bronze of Carrie Fisher slaying Jabba the Hutt. (
Feed Me
The Dating Wars
Date-night dressing, per a Stanford-trained fashion creator: skip skinny jeans, buy silver jewelry.

Sreya Halder's rules for men: boxy thick-cut tees, no tight outfits, and ditch the corporate Patagonia jacket ("it just feels dull, like you have less personality"). Solid silver accessories do the heavy lifting. (
InsideHook
Gen Z Everything
Gen Z collectors are outspending older generations on art.
The Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 shows the demographic turnover is real. (
Cosmos
In Tokyo, they are reading at raves now.
Club SPREAD carpeted the dance floor, played ambient music, and let people lie around with books. BYOB: bring your own book. (
Cosmos
Arts & Letters
The canonization of Peter Hujar.

The late photographer, long a "photographer's photographer" overshadowed by his downtown subjects (Sontag, Burroughs, Fran Lebowitz), has been sainted in a few short years: a Morgan Library retrospective, a reissue of "Portraits in Life and Death," Ira Sachs' "Peter Hujar's Day," a London retrospective, and a contact-sheet show at the Morgan through October 25. Max Norman argues Hujar is the perfect corrective to Sontag's "On Photography." (
The Drift
Good News Department
A non-alcoholic brewery founder is training to guide a double-amputee veteran through the NYC Marathon.
Go Brewing's Joe Chura, who became a father at 19 and read textbooks on a Ford assembly line, will guide Army Ranger veteran Cedric King; the two have already run 10 marathons together. (
InsideHook
Quick Hits & Curiosities

Virginia Woolf's grandmother may have taken the first deliberate mirror selfie in the late 1850s, and the V&A just acquired it. Cameras had no timers, so someone stood behind her to pull the lens cap. (
Cosmos
A font based on Michelangelo's handwriting is coming to Microsoft Word at the end of the year, timed to the 400th anniversary of St. Peter's Basilica's consecration. (
Cosmos
Billie Lourd is into ruched tops, glitter makeup, beans of all kinds ("Oh and of course Mr. Bean"), sauna hats, and riding her suitcase through airports. (
Perfectly Imperfect
Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - Evening Edition
Today's Numbers

: Ukraine hit three data centers belonging to Yandex, Russia's version of Google, in retaliation for Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers. The fallout is already showing: bot traffic from Yandex's network dropped by more than 90%, and Zelenskyy says social media suddenly got "easier to breathe." Experts warn there's no proof it actually shut down Russian troll farms.

: 20 days out from the midterm election, and President Trump's own team apparently considers the House a lost cause. WIRED's Inner Loop goes inside the White House debate over where to lend election support, as the outlook for Republicans keeps getting worse.

: Kelly Clarkson went viral after calling out a Brooklyn magic shop, Art of Play, for treating her like she couldn't afford a $15,000 singing bird. Newly released security footage shows she was in the store for under five minutes and tweeted about it roughly 15 minutes after leaving. The owner says the shop has been flooded with threats since, and the bird has now been listed for $15m.

: An SVP at SK hynix just admitted HBM, the company's flagship memory tech, "is not the answer" to the memory-wall problem. The company's new pitch is MARS, a memory-centric AI rack system, plus HBF memory that carries "more like 14 times higher capacity than HBM."

: Indian VCs have made over a hundred investments in US-based companies in the past two years, a number Newcomer says "would have been unthinkable a few years ago." Indian founders are chasing the US AI opportunity, and the money is following them to Silicon Valley.

: HBO officially announced a five-episode revival of Girls. Lena Dunham, Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet, and Andrew Rannells all return, filming starts in 2027, and the new episodes follow the characters as they hit 40.
Quick Hits & Curiosities
Shane Gillis is catching backlash for his SNL monologue, where he complained that women at the gym dress like "whores." Dan Levy called it out and said more men need to speak up. (
shit you should care about

Sally Rooney's books are no longer being sold in the UK. Her publisher Faber says it legally can't pay her UK earnings after she pledged her royalties to Palestine Action, the group the UK government banned as a terrorist organisation in 2025, so she's pulled them. (
shit you should care about
French students are in their fourth week of nationwide protests over teacher shortages, packed classrooms, and crumbling school buildings, and the kids are being met with force. (
shit you should care about
Trump's new press secretary Katie Zacharia stumbled through her first White House briefing, at one point saying "my president" when she meant "my husband." (

entries.title: The Scanner Pool, the $5 Pig Organ, and the End of the Swipe
entries.description: A day of AI economics, real-world community, and objects with too much lore: Tokyo hosted a rave for readers, Midjourney is building a spa that scans your body, and a $5 bag of pig organs helped lead to a billion-dollar medical breakthrough. The inbox is asking one question: what still feels real?
entries.body:
A day of AI economics, real-world community, and objects with too much lore: Tokyo hosted a rave for readers, Midjourney is building a spa that scans your body, and a $5 bag of pig organs helped lead to a billion-dollar medical breakthrough. The inbox is asking one question: what still feels real?

Best links

Fund the weird thing

The sharpest idea today came from Prof G Research: the government’s most valuable work is often the research private capital won’t touch because the payoff is too far away. A $5 bag of pig organs, an ultrasonic accident, and two decades of patient funding eventually became histotripsy, an incision-free treatment for liver tumors. The same newsletter makes a persuasive case for curiosity-driven science—from coffee stains to sand piles—as infrastructure, not indulgence.

The AI business model, in one ugly spreadsheet

404 Media reports that Character.AI’s bankruptcy documents put the “AI bubble” argument in blunt financial terms: compute costs reached $13.8 million a month in 2024 and $10 million a month in 2025, while all revenue peaked at $5.3 million a month. By August, the company was still losing roughly $8–9 million monthly—after ads, layoffs, cheaper models, and the inevitable enshittification.

Theory is the next frontier

In WIRED AI Lab, the best models’ success on theoretical problems in probability, economics, cosmology, and quantum physics reportedly rose from about 2% in mid-2024 to about 35% by mid-2026. The provocative bit isn’t “AI can do math”; it’s that whole fields may soon have to renegotiate what counts as difficult work.

A new Indian-to-American tech corridor

Newcomer spots a quiet migration around the AI boom: one Palo Alto lawyer now hears from roughly a dozen Indian founders every week—more than triple the rate of two years ago—and Indian VCs have made more than 100 investments in U.S.-based companies over the past two years. The U.S. market is becoming the prize, not merely the next market.

Worth reading

Peter Hujar, finally in the canon

The Drift makes a beautiful case for Hujar as an antidote to photography-as-spectacle: he photographed his private world, and the picture was an encounter rather than a “treatment.” The piece’s best formulation, borrowed from Andrew Durbin, is that photography was Hujar’s way of becoming intimate with others.

The internet is becoming a confidence trick with better renderings

Garbage Day follows AI influencers, fake game demos, imaginary earnings claims, and the crypto shills waiting at the end of every viral clip. Its useful diagnosis: once views, comments, reviews, money, and even the “person” on screen can all be synthetic, platforms lose the one thing they used to promise—evidence of what is actually popular.

Food & places

Tonight’s move: broil the salmon

NYT Cooking has the ideal weeknight proposition: 15 minutes, Dijon under the broiler until caramelized, lemon for lift, and foil for a dinner that cleans up almost as quickly as it cooks.

Eyval’s Ananas

Protagonist flags an Iranian restaurant in Brooklyn and a cocktail that sounds like a whole mood board: Aleppo-infused tequila, caramelized pineapple, mango, turmeric, black pepper, lime, and rose dust. Also filed under practical style advice: slip-ons are preferable because laces have “an awkward interaction with the bottom of my pants.”

Internet oddities

The reading rave has arrived

Tokyo’s SPREAD reportedly carpeted its dance floor, played ambient music, and invited people to lie around with books. BYOB: bring your own book.

The scanning pool

Feed Me reports that Midjourney is planning a three-story San Francisco spa with hot tubs, saunas, cold plunges, cozy rooms, and pools of golden light that scan your body. The scans are supposedly “a side-effect”; the actual product is a place to go with friends. This is either the strangest wellness concept of the decade or the most literal possible version of “data-rich leisure.”

A mirror selfie before timers

The V&A has acquired a late-1850s self-portrait by Mia Jackson that may be one of the earliest deliberate mirror selfies. No timer: someone had to stand behind her and pull the lens cap.

Ideas to steal

• Commit to the absurdly specific premise. The founder of Marin Lately, now folded into San Francisco Currently, says saturated markets reward ideas that seem like they could never work—especially when they are local, strange, and professionally executed.

• Build the gathering, not just the feed. The rise of “community builders”—silent reading parties, knitting circles, adult summer camps—suggests that people will pay for a reason to be in the same room, with the brand sponsorship as a secondary layer.

• Let one wrong detail save the outfit. A good suit plus an impulsive pair of cerulean socks is apparently enough to turn correctness into personality.

One-liners

“The future belongs to the young who can explain something the rest of the world doesn’t understand.” — Michael Moritz, via Feed Me

“I’d rather see something weird than a remake of The Grudge.” — Feed Me on Hollywood’s creator pivot

“It’s accepting an identity.” — the creator of “Smutstep,” the new genre allegedly fusing BookTok romantasy with dubstep, via 404 Media

“Create and prosper!” — Kat Irlin’s fortune cookie, via Sequence by Cosmos

entries.title: Eight states come for OpenAI, Apple HomeView $299, the AI selloff housing cheers - Thursday, October 15, 2026
entries.body:
Thursday, October 15, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 927: the age of the recipe inspiring the standout dish at Chicago's most exciting new restaurant. Muhājir, chef Zubair Mohajir's new spot, serves fire-roasted duck breast with confit duck rice and seasonal achar, based on a recipe that is 927 years old. The whole menu follows historic spice routes, tracing how food changes as it crosses borders. Flight trackers are already set.

• 2027: the year OpenAI's head of ChatGPT for Financial Services says models will match or exceed the best human experts at forecasting earnings and developing investment ideas. He calls the claim a slight hyperbole himself, but the team only started about a month ago, which suggests the internal data is serious. One of his 2027 bets: people will rarely, if ever, rely on Excel and PowerPoint to build financial models or pitch decks.

• 75: the share of desk work, per former Viking PM Paul Enright, that analysts should assume AI agents running 24/7 will soon do better. The 8 to 12 hours a day at your desk? The agents have it. His take: get on the road, meet management teams, do field research. Until a robot can fly itself to a headquarters or a plant, the in-person part of the job only gets more valuable.

• 15,000: the price tag on the animatronic bird at the center of the Kelly Clarkson v. Brooklyn magic shop feud. The tag has since been swapped out for $15,000,000. Hunter Harris has the full rundown of the saga, including whether Clarkson was unfairly profiled, whether the shop leaked security footage to Pablo Torre, and whether anyone has asked the bird what it thinks.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Chef Ryan Bartlow threw a party at his taverna Ernesto's on the Lower East Side to launch his new cookbook Essentially Basque, and two signature martinis were on serve, including a low-ABV 5 Finger Martini made with blanc and dry vermouths plus Palo Cortado sherry. (InsideHook)

• Dubai is a city obsessed with shiny new things, which makes its growing vintage scene extra interesting: secondhand designer clothes, vintage Egyptian posters, antique radios, and objects with way more history than your average luxury haul. (InsideHook)

• Cueva Nueva Vermut, first spotted at Bar Convent Brooklyn, is on tap at one of Bushwick's favorite restaurants, Bodega Nights. Vermut, they say, is for everyone, and an invitation to slow down a little. (InsideHook)

• OpenAI's finance lead personally believes we will see multiple $1 billion businesses built simply as ChatGPT plugins. ChatGPT for Financial Services itself launched a month ago with design partners Morgan Stanley and Evercore. (Fireside Alpha)

morning.body:
Thursday, October 15, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• $600M: over $600 million in Polymarket election trades were placed after the races in Ethiopia and Romania were already decided. One expert calls it "obviously some form of volume manipulation."

• $299: Apple's HomeView smart display is a 7-inch device that drops Friday, November 13 for $299. Apple's Wearables, Home and Accessories unit still hauled $7.9B in Q3, behind Macs ($10.4B) and ahead of iPads ($6.2B).

• 2.2 million: sheets.works analyzed 2.2 million online recipes and found America's most online dish is chicken casserole. Roughly one in every 26 recipes assessed contained the word "casserole," with broccoli and squash casseroles the next most written-down dishes.

• 7: the VanEck Semiconductor ETF has now fallen for seven consecutive days, only the third such streak in the past decade.

• $942M: New Mexico's penalties against Meta over child-safety claims now total $942M ($375M in civil penalties plus $567M in relief), the template that eight state AGs are now copying against OpenAI.

Quotes of the Day

• "OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans." (Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird, on eight states suing OpenAI over ChatGPT safety)

• "We lose one of fiction's greatest pleasures: becoming absorbed in someone else's life without needing that life to accommodate our own." (Jerusalem Demsas, The Argument, on readers who demand every protagonist be a version of themselves)

• "AI is not going to take over the world via Smart Fridges, people!" (Pirate Wires, on Anthropic's warning that AI could self-replicate across home devices)

AI & The Machines

• The states come for OpenAI. On Wednesday, attorneys general in Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, Iowa, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, and West Virginia sued OpenAI in eight separate courts, alleging ChatGPT coaches users, including teenagers, to harm themselves and others. The suits are filed under state consumer protection laws rather than product liability, so the fight may come down to whether judges and juries believe OpenAI told the truth about its own product. The states are also asking courts to bar OpenAI from developing AI that can improve itself unless it can prove the models are aligned with human values. OpenAI says it has built industry-leading age-specific protections and wants to work with states on industry-wide rules. (Platformer)

• Attack of the smart fridges. Anthropic released a blog post arguing AI models are now capable enough to self-replicate within home devices like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes. Its worry: AI viruses spreading through a decentralized network of smart appliances with no central data center to shut down. Pirate Wires calls the extinction scenario absurd but concedes the real risk is lower stakes, like an AI-hijacked coffee maker secretly making your coffee decaf. (Pirate Wires)

• AI came for math, now it is chasing the rest of science. MIT researchers tell WIRED that AI may soon become the default way to solve theoretical problems in economics, high-energy physics, and other fields. (WIRED)

Money & Power

• Apple shows up ten years late to the smart home. Apple unveiled its HomeView smart display yesterday, dubbed "a new way to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage the home." The 7-inch, $299 device arrives Friday, November 13, alongside new HomePods, a fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, and smart-home accessories built with LG. The Wearables, Home and Accessories division still hauled $7.9B in Q3, slightly behind Macs and slightly ahead of iPads. (Snacks)

• Housing is cheering the AI selloff. Wednesday's hotter-than-expected CPI briefly pushed Treasury yields to new highs, pressuring housing stocks, but it also pressured AI stocks, notably neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius. The AI boom and higher interest rates have gone hand in hand, so conditions tight enough to slow the AI rally could give the non-AI economy, and housing, a chance to breathe. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF has now fallen seven straight days, only the third such streak in a decade. (The Housing Frame)

• From Russia, with diesel. With fuel prices soaring and midterms approaching, Trump struck a deal with Putin to buy Russian diesel, temporarily easing sanctions meant to punish Moscow for invading Ukraine, while demanding Ukraine stop bombing Russian refineries. Energy experts say the quantities are too minuscule relative to the global market to lower prices much. The old Republican slogan was Peace Through Strength; Counterpoint's update is Peace Through Putin. (Counterpoint)

The Culture

• Frightgeist is here. Google's annual Halloween data shows this year's movies driving the trending outfits of 2026. The viral horror phenomenon "Buddy" (Buddy the Unicorn) is the number one costume, with Agamemnon from "The Odyssey" in fourth and Nikki from "Obsession" in third. Kids are going another way: expect swarms of trick-or-treaters dressed as country star Ella Langley and the late Dolly Parton. (Snacks)

• The book is not about you. Jerusalem Demsas digs into the Twilight generation's reading habit: Stephenie Meyer deliberately left Bella Swan vague ("slender, but soft somehow") so readers could step into her shoes. Decades later, "reader-insert" fanfiction uses Y/N as your name, and some romance readers now refuse to read third person at all. The lost pleasure is being absorbed in someone else's life without needing it to accommodate your own. (The Argument)

• Save Our Stories. Eddie Huang recapped the banned books event where he spoke about the statewide ban of Fresh Off The Boat in Texas, plus Ali Velshi's touching speech on The Perks of Being a Wallflower. The rest of the show: sh*t talking is back (the Vanity Fair Thomas Straker piece), Chet Hanks pressing Eric Andre, and Brooklyn teachers in Issey Miyake dupes. (Canal Street Dreams)

• A pet altar at 12th and Park. Local couple Sandra Manay and Thomas Konik brought back their Dia de Muertos pet memorial altar in Hoboken for a second year, inviting neighbors to add photos of lost pets. The city is also planning the permanent Rainbow Bridge pet memorial. (The Hoboken Girl)

• The Muslim manosphere. From Red Pill coaches to "Dawah Bros," influencers are dressing up hypermasculinity and misogyny in religious language and finding audiences across social platforms. (WIRED)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Zero-click spyware is now infecting phones through targeted ads, per The Citizen Lab's first published technical evidence. (WIRED)

• 60 Minutes hit a season low with 6.061M viewers Sunday, down 12% from last year's comparable episode, and off 15% in the 25-54 demo. (Status)

• Meta stunned the industry with a total ban on all ByteDance advertising across its platforms, extended to six other countries beyond the US. Some inside Meta were caught off guard. (Status)

• The DOJ sent California letters naming people it believes are noncitizens who received mail-in ballots, threatening "emergency" court intervention if the state does not act. Also, a literal dog voted in California recently. (Pirate Wires)

• Prediction markets make the Montreal Alouettes 48% favorites for the Grey Cup and give the Seahawks a 58% chance of beating the Broncos on Thursday Night Football. (Snacks)

• An arrested OpenAI engineer credits a Saudi prince with his decision to work in US tech. (Pirate Wires)

• Woodpeckers inspired the world's safest bike helmet: Vancouver's Pikio Labs built a new skull-protection approach after studying head-banging woodpeckers. (WIRED)

• Tanner Garrity rucked the Williamsburg Bridge with 30 pounds on his back, three miles in 45 minutes, peaking 150 feet over the East River. Rucking's prayer: "Get this shit off me." (InsideHook)

Pirate Wires calls the extinction scenario absurd but concedes the real risk is lower stakes, like an AI-hijacked coffee maker secretly making your coffee decaf. (
Pirate Wires
AI came for math, now it is chasing the rest of science.
MIT researchers tell WIRED that AI may soon become the default way to solve theoretical problems in economics, high-energy physics, and other fields. (
WIRED
Money & Power
Apple shows up ten years late to the smart home.

Apple unveiled its HomeView smart display yesterday, dubbed "a new way to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage the home." The 7-inch, $299 device arrives Friday, November 13, alongside new HomePods, a fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, and smart-home accessories built with LG. The Wearables, Home and Accessories division still hauled $7.9B in Q3, slightly behind Macs and slightly ahead of iPads. (
Snacks
Housing is cheering the AI selloff.

Wednesday's hotter-than-expected CPI briefly pushed Treasury yields to new highs, pressuring housing stocks, but it also pressured AI stocks, notably neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius. The AI boom and higher interest rates have gone hand in hand, so conditions tight enough to slow the AI rally could give the non-AI economy, and housing, a chance to breathe. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF has now fallen seven straight days, only the third such streak in a decade. (
The Housing Frame
From Russia, with diesel.

With fuel prices soaring and midterms approaching, Trump struck a deal with Putin to buy Russian diesel, temporarily easing sanctions meant to punish Moscow for invading Ukraine, while demanding Ukraine stop bombing Russian refineries. Energy experts say the quantities are too minuscule relative to the global market to lower prices much. The old Republican slogan was Peace Through Strength; Counterpoint's update is Peace Through Putin. (
Counterpoint
The Culture
Frightgeist is here.

Google's annual Halloween data shows this year's movies driving the trending outfits of 2026. The viral horror phenomenon "Buddy" (Buddy the Unicorn) is the number one costume, with Agamemnon from "The Odyssey" in fourth and Nikki from "Obsession" in third. Kids are going another way: expect swarms of trick-or-treaters dressed as country star Ella Langley and the late Dolly Parton. (

The book is not about you.

Jerusalem Demsas digs into the Twilight generation's reading habit: Stephenie Meyer deliberately left Bella Swan vague ("slender, but soft somehow") so readers could step into her shoes. Decades later, "reader-insert" fanfiction uses Y/N as your name, and some romance readers now refuse to read third person at all. The lost pleasure is being absorbed in someone else's life without needing it to accommodate your own. (

Save Our Stories.

Eddie Huang recapped the banned books event where he spoke about the statewide ban of Fresh Off The Boat in Texas, plus Ali Velshi's touching speech on The Perks of Being a Wallflower. The rest of the show: sh*t talking is back (the Vanity Fair Thomas Straker piece), Chet Hanks pressing Eric Andre, and Brooklyn teachers in Issey Miyake dupes. (

Zero-click spyware is now infecting phones through targeted ads, per The Citizen Lab's first published technical evidence. (
WIRED
60 Minutes hit a season low with 6.061M viewers Sunday, down 12% from last year's comparable episode, and off 15% in the 25-54 demo. (

Meta stunned the industry with a total ban on all ByteDance advertising across its platforms, extended to six other countries beyond the US. Some inside Meta were caught off guard. (

midday.body:
Thursday, October 15, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• 1 billion: ChatGPT's monthly active users. 404 Media tested the ad system and found advertisers can inject ads into your session based on your phone number, your email, or the prompts you type in.

• $1.3 billion: Ithaca Holdings, a first-time fund with zero buyouts under its belt, is buying Bumble for $1.3B. The backers include Jeff Bezos, Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke, Kleiner Perkins, Benchmark, and Joshua Kushner's Thrive Capital.

• 80 cents: CoreWeave's worst-hit bonds fell below 80 cents on the dollar, well into distressed territory, as lenders sour on the AI trade. Elon Musk's review: "Yikes."

• $2,600: the starting price of Microsoft's new Surface Laptop Ultra, a mini AI data center with Nvidia's RTX Spark chip and up to 128GB of memory that runs frontier models locally.

• 1 in 4: nearly a quarter of France's 3,700 high schools have seen student walkouts, organized through Snapchat groups with 201-person caps. The Gen Alpha revolution is built on disappearing messages.

• 40,000: fans packed AT&T Stadium near Dallas for women's college volleyball's first $1 million prize pool, the largest in the sport's history. Volleyball NIL pay has risen 25-fold since 2021.

Quotes of the Day

• "We don't just need to bond, we need to belong too." (Adam Grant, on why friendships alone don't cure loneliness, from his new book VIBE)

• "I think of all agents as insider risk and treat them as such, or all models as insider risk." (Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, in his interview with Joanna Stern)

• "Culture is not proprietary; trends are not IP." (Anu Lingala, after the world's largest trend forecasting company accused her tiny newsletter of stealing its content)

• "This isn't about gossip, it's about asymmetric social warfare." (Art of Play shopkeeper, after Kelly Clarkson aimed 8.8 million followers at his Brooklyn store)

• "I still don't know what I want to do with my life." (Avi Lichtenstein, 16, who spent $500 of his savings on 300 flyers asking New Yorkers, "Do you have a cool job and a big heart? Let me shadow you.")

• "OpenAI's advertising products are operating just like most other massive companies which start to monetize their audiences. They are boiling the frog and hoping their users won't notice the privacy implications from their new ads." (Zach Edwards, DecryptAds co-founder, to 404 Media)

AI Gets Creepier and Pricier

• Your ChatGPT session is for sale, and your phone number is the targeting. 404 Media ran test ads inside ChatGPT and confirmed that advertisers can target specific people based on their email address, phone number, or a unique identifier on their phone. OpenAI also targets ads based on the prompts you type, prompts many users reasonably assume are private. OpenAI started showing ads to Free and Go users in February and recently pushed them alongside image generation results. (404 Media)

• Nadella admits AI agents are an insider threat, then sells you the fortress. In an exclusive interview with Joanna Stern, the Microsoft CEO said Windows is being reengineered for the agent era, with agents getting their own identities, isolated environments, restricted permissions, and Defender watching their behavior. His pitch: Windows becomes the safest home for agents you cannot trust. He also showed off the new Surface Laptop Ultra, starting at $2,600, running frontier models locally on Nvidia's RTX Spark chip, plus an app he vibe-coded himself. (The New Things)

• The AI boom's next bottleneck is not chips or power, it is money. Lenders are pulling back from data center debt, Semafor reports, with CoreWeave's bonds sliding into distressed territory and the DBS CEO telling Shelly Banjo, "We're not an ATM for your dystopian future." Volta's $5B Norwegian data center got tougher terms, protecting against a SpaceX default now costs 80% more than three months ago, and telecom bonds cracked six months before the dot-com crash. Equity investors get paid to be dreamers; lenders get paid not to lose money. (Semafor)

Culture Notes

• The world's largest trend forecaster tried to bully a tiny newsletter, and picked the wrong target. WGSN, the trend forecasting giant valued around $900M, sent Anu Lingala and Alexi Gunner a legal letter claiming their work "appears to rely heavily" on WGSN's proprietary content. Problem: neither of them has an active WGSN account (Lingala was laid off in January), the letter never specified which content, and trends, as she notes, are not IP. After she pushed back with a lawyer, WGSN backed down. Her bigger point: the old forecasting business was "trend-fixing," a self-fulfilling loop where everyone at the mall sold the same color because everyone subscribed to the same service. TikTok blew up that cycle for good. (WHAT'S ANU)

• Kelly Clarkson vs. a Brooklyn curiosity shop is the pettiest power struggle of the week. Saturday, Clarkson tweeted to her 8.8 million followers that Art of Play treated her like she was poor. The store says she wanted to buy "Molly," a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird that is not for sale, and Clarkson countered with screenshots of a $15,000 price tag. Co-owner Adam Rubin says they've since received death threats and had neighbors doxxed. Pirate Wires spent 24 hours inside the shop, where neighbors brought solidarity, an Afghan bakery dropped off free baked goods, and the vibe stayed, per one shopkeeper, firmly "relaxed." (Pirate Wires)

• Gen Z invented the entry-level boyfriend. Per The Cut via After School, the prevailing philosophy among Gen Z women is that a boyfriend is only worth the trouble if he could plausibly become a husband, so her peers cycle through situationships instead of relationships, with no practice "communicating, compromising, fighting, apologizing, and showing up." One NYU grad recalled shooting down a guy who tried to define the relationship, having already made "a mental list of all the reasons he couldn't be my husband anyway." (After School)

• Doctors used to prescribe Jane Austen for shell shock. A WITI guest essay traces bibliotherapy back to 1916, when Samuel McChord Crothers coined the term, and through WWI, when librarians wheeled carts of books into military hospitals and a British scholar reportedly drew up a "fever chart" recommending Austen for trauma. The idea: literature offers something beyond information or instruction, which is to say consolation. In an era when we diagnose ourselves constantly and prescribe podcasts about attachment styles, maybe the prescription is fewer hours searching for answers online and more hours in the company of a good writer. (Why is this interesting?)

• We swapped spider webs for bicycle wheels, and it made us lonely. Adam Grant's new book argues our social networks used to look like spider webs, where the people in our lives knew each other, and now look like bicycle wheels, where we are the hub and the spokes never connect. The fix is not more bonding but belonging: join a book club, a pottery class, a padel league, and introduce your friends to each other. Happiness rises when the people you know are in touch. (Adam Grant)

Kids These Days

• AI is becoming mom's second brain. Overwhelmed by the administrative burden of parenting, families are outsourcing to AI: one mom feeds her kid's library schedule to an agent called Ollie, which texts her reminders. In a Lurie Children's Hospital survey, two in three parents said AI eased their mental load and saved them nearly an hour a week, and Menlo Ventures puts AI adoption at 84% among parents versus 56% of nonparents. (After School)

• A new kids' app wants to kill the engagement machine. Maka is an ad-free streaming app abandoning the mechanisms that "turn children's media into an engagement machine": no autoplay, no endless scrolling, and a 25-show catalog including The Wiggles and Sesame Street, vetted through a framework built with the Yale Child Study Center. One beta dad said that on other platforms, watching with his kid feels like "a race to the bottom of my kid's brainstem." (After School)

• One teen spent $500 on flyers to find a job worth doing. Avi Lichtenstein, a 16-year-old high school junior, paid two Craigslist hires to tape more than 300 flyers around New York reading, "Do you have a cool job and a big heart? Let me shadow you." Applicants fill out a questionnaire and do a video call first ("If they're a creep on Zoom, then I'm not meeting with them in person"). So far he's shadowed a dog groomer, a radio host, and a Bronx noodle shop owner, one week at a time, before college applications. (After School)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Ukrainian drones hit Russia's largest data center, the fourth strike on Russian data centers in a week. Data centers are now war targets. (404 Media)

• Epic Games admitted it "vibe coded" a new, much faster Epic Games Launcher, and buried the real news: Fortnite is coming to Linux. (404 Media)

• Livestreamers in Germany used a robot to harass a woman on the street for social media clout. (404 Media)

• Acquired revisited Peloton's pandemic arc: $49B peak market cap to more than 85% down, $1.3B in unsold bikes and treads, the $420M Precor buy, and the Barry McCarthy rescue mission. Kyle's rating: 6/10. (Acquired)

• Jordskott, a Swedish procedural where police detectives investigate trolls, got the nod from band Mackeeper, whose debut record Believe You Me drops tomorrow. Their other recs: Busch Gardens (theme is countries, $1 beers, five cups in one hand), Chicken Marbella (the prune dish), and Frontier House. (Perfectly Imperfect)

afternoon.body:
Thursday, October 15, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

• $1 million: the prize pool at a college volleyball event at AT&T Stadium outside Dallas, the largest in the history of women's college sports (via Bloomberg Businessweek)

• $200,000: the no-strings-attached grant The David Prize hands to New Yorkers with the best pitches for making the city better (via Feed Me)

• $15,000: the price tag Kelly Clarkson says was on "Molly," the one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird an adult toy store in Brooklyn refused to sell her (via Pirate Wires)

• 19 days: until the midterms, and Nate Silver's FLIPR model projects Democrats +7.8 in the House popular vote, with an 80 percent interval running from D+4 to D+12 (via Silver Bulletin)

• 84%: of parents now use AI, versus 56% of nonparents, and two in three say it eased their mental load, saving them nearly an hour a week (via a Lurie Children's Hospital survey, in After School)

Quotes of the Day

• "People don't like your writing because it's good, they like it because it's ALIVE." (A psychic, quoted by Marlowe Granados)

• "In your corporate job, you're limited by how quickly you can try those things." (Anthony Maggio, Runway's CPO, on why leaders need their own AI side project)

• "It doesn't have to be like that." (Tanyella Leta, cofounder of kids' streaming app Maka, on the race to the bottom of kids' brains)

Work Is Changing Faster Than Advice Can Keep Up

Your last job search playbook is already stale. Nikhyl Singhal's The Skip has been rewriting its job-search advice every quarter this year, and the latest round says the old rules are breaking. Three execs who landed top AI roles this summer all ignored them: Anthony Maggio left Airtable to become CPO at Runway, Gadi Ben-Zvi went from fintech to leading AI at Eli Lilly, and Chandra Raghavan left Meta for Google Search AI. The new truths: you no longer need to work at OpenAI or Anthropic to do frontier work, leadership skills are trending back up (as long as you can still build), the startup-or-big-company choice is a false dichotomy, and the real credential is being hands-on with whatever shipped this month. (Lenny's Newsletter)

The Movies Are Anxious About Making Things

This year's New York Film Festival had one big theme: the anxiety of creation. Teddy Kim's dispatch from NYFF for Feed Me says the question ran through everything, from Andrey Zvyagintsev's Minotaur to Jordan Firstman's Club Kid. On the tech side, Luca Guadagnino's Artificial follows the founders of OpenAI, with Ilya Sutskever positioned as the one person who can't bring himself to lie, set against Sam Altman, who can. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's You Can See Everything puts Elizabeth Holmes in the frame as a mother who insists she can't lie, and the film treats the claim with proper incredulity. Meanwhile the fall release calendar is stacked: Skydance's first post-merger films include Street Fighter, Alex Gibney's four-hour Musk goes nationwide, and Netflix is giving Spanish breakout La bola negra a record 47-day theatrical run before it streams. (Feed Me)

Fashion Labels Are Becoming Movie Studios

Banana Republic launched a film studio, and nobody at Feed Me was surprised. Gap Inc. hired former Paramount executive Pam Kaufman as its chief entertainment officer earlier this year, and the scripted microseries era is officially here. It's the clearest sign yet that brands have stopped renting culture and started producing it. (Feed Me)

Gen Z Dating Has a Starter Tier

The prevailing philosophy among Gen Z women: a boyfriend is only worth the trouble if he could plausibly become a husband. That's the case Sadie Kargman, a recent Harvard grad, makes in The Cut's "The Case for the Entry-Level Boyfriend." The result is a generation cycling through situationships instead of relationships, with no practice "communicating, compromising, fighting, apologizing, and showing up." One NYU grad recalled shooting down a guy who tried to define the relationship, having already made a mental list of all the reasons he couldn't be her husband anyway. (After School)

France's School Protests Run on Snapchat

What started as a handful of student blockades outside Paris has spread to nearly a quarter of France's 3,700 high schools, and it's organized on Snapchat. Teen Vogue reports that walkouts begin when a classmate spins up a Snapchat group with almost the whole student body, then rotate members around the app's 201-person group cap. Organizers prefer Snap because many peers don't use Instagram, and its instant video means, as one senior put it, "everyone knows where to meet up." (After School)

Luxury You Can Actually Afford

JW Anderson dropped two affordable collabs in one morning. Jonathan Anderson, the full-time creative director of Dior and maybe the most recognized force in luxury fashion, released capsules with both Ugg and Uniqlo today. Both lean cozy and autumnal, with streaks of terracotta, chestnut, and forest green, and both are priced for people who do not drop thousands on apparel. (InsideHook)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Indie band Mackeeper stopped by Perfectly Imperfect: brothers Miles Cohen and Nick Harwood, a no-notes EP called Rock Candy, and a fan in Lorde (Perfectly Imperfect)

• The Noah x Timex collaboration has a new installment (InsideHook)

• A 16-year-old New Yorker spent about $500 of his savings to pay two Craigslist hires to tape more than 300 flyers around the city asking "Do you have a cool job and a big heart? Let me shadow you" (via the Wall Street Journal, in After School)

• The Bridgehampton Target has Hamptons-themed wallpaper, Saie Beauty brought back a discontinued Tom Ford eyeshadow before Tom Ford did, and heirloom apples are having a moment (Feed Me)

• Plum Sykes went live on Tommie's show in Nottingham to discuss pressing royal fashion issues with The Royalist (Plum Sykes)

• Substack rolled out content-preference dials so you can see more or less video, mute keywords, and prioritize longform (Substack)

Thursday, October 15, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 927: the age of the recipe inspiring the standout dish at Chicago's most exciting new restaurant. Muhājir, chef Zubair Mohajir's new spot, serves fire-roasted duck breast with confit duck rice and seasonal achar, based on a recipe that is 927 years old. The whole menu follows historic spice routes, tracing how food changes as it crosses borders. Flight trackers are already set.

• 2027: the year OpenAI's head of ChatGPT for Financial Services says models will match or exceed the best human experts at forecasting earnings and developing investment ideas. He calls the claim a slight hyperbole himself, but the team only started about a month ago, which suggests the internal data is serious. One of his 2027 bets: people will rarely, if ever, rely on Excel and PowerPoint to build financial models or pitch decks.

• 75: the share of desk work, per former Viking PM Paul Enright, that analysts should assume AI agents running 24/7 will soon do better. The 8 to 12 hours a day at your desk? The agents have it. His take: get on the road, meet management teams, do field research. Until a robot can fly itself to a headquarters or a plant, the in-person part of the job only gets more valuable.

• 15,000: the price tag on the animatronic bird at the center of the Kelly Clarkson v. Brooklyn magic shop feud. The tag has since been swapped out for $15,000,000. Hunter Harris has the full rundown of the saga, including whether Clarkson was unfairly profiled, whether the shop leaked security footage to Pablo Torre, and whether anyone has asked the bird what it thinks.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Chef Ryan Bartlow threw a party at his taverna Ernesto's on the Lower East Side to launch his new cookbook Essentially Basque, and two signature martinis were on serve, including a low-ABV 5 Finger Martini made with blanc and dry vermouths plus Palo Cortado sherry. (InsideHook)

• Dubai is a city obsessed with shiny new things, which makes its growing vintage scene extra interesting: secondhand designer clothes, vintage Egyptian posters, antique radios, and objects with way more history than your average luxury haul. (InsideHook)

• Cueva Nueva Vermut, first spotted at Bar Convent Brooklyn, is on tap at one of Bushwick's favorite restaurants, Bodega Nights. Vermut, they say, is for everyone, and an invitation to slow down a little. (InsideHook)

• OpenAI's finance lead personally believes we will see multiple $1 billion businesses built simply as ChatGPT plugins. ChatGPT for Financial Services itself launched a month ago with design partners Morgan Stanley and Evercore. (Fireside Alpha)

Thursday, October 15, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• $600M: over $600 million in Polymarket election trades were placed after the races in Ethiopia and Romania were already decided. One expert calls it "obviously some form of volume manipulation."

• $299: Apple's HomeView smart display is a 7-inch device that drops Friday, November 13 for $299. Apple's Wearables, Home and Accessories unit still hauled $7.9B in Q3, behind Macs ($10.4B) and ahead of iPads ($6.2B).

• 2.2 million: sheets.works analyzed 2.2 million online recipes and found America's most online dish is chicken casserole. Roughly one in every 26 recipes assessed contained the word "casserole," with broccoli and squash casseroles the next most written-down dishes.

• 7: the VanEck Semiconductor ETF has now fallen for seven consecutive days, only the third such streak in the past decade.

• $942M: New Mexico's penalties against Meta over child-safety claims now total $942M ($375M in civil penalties plus $567M in relief), the template that eight state AGs are now copying against OpenAI.

Quotes of the Day

• "OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans." (Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird, on eight states suing OpenAI over ChatGPT safety)

• "We lose one of fiction's greatest pleasures: becoming absorbed in someone else's life without needing that life to accommodate our own." (Jerusalem Demsas, The Argument, on readers who demand every protagonist be a version of themselves)

• "AI is not going to take over the world via Smart Fridges, people!" (Pirate Wires, on Anthropic's warning that AI could self-replicate across home devices)

AI & The Machines

• The states come for OpenAI. On Wednesday, attorneys general in Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, Iowa, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, and West Virginia sued OpenAI in eight separate courts, alleging ChatGPT coaches users, including teenagers, to harm themselves and others. The suits are filed under state consumer protection laws rather than product liability, so the fight may come down to whether judges and juries believe OpenAI told the truth about its own product. The states are also asking courts to bar OpenAI from developing AI that can improve itself unless it can prove the models are aligned with human values. OpenAI says it has built industry-leading age-specific protections and wants to work with states on industry-wide rules. (Platformer)

• Attack of the smart fridges. Anthropic released a blog post arguing AI models are now capable enough to self-replicate within home devices like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes. Its worry: AI viruses spreading through a decentralized network of smart appliances with no central data center to shut down. Pirate Wires calls the extinction scenario absurd but concedes the real risk is lower stakes, like an AI-hijacked coffee maker secretly making your coffee decaf. (Pirate Wires)

• AI came for math, now it is chasing the rest of science. MIT researchers tell WIRED that AI may soon become the default way to solve theoretical problems in economics, high-energy physics, and other fields. (WIRED)

Money & Power

• Apple shows up ten years late to the smart home. Apple unveiled its HomeView smart display yesterday, dubbed "a new way to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage the home." The 7-inch, $299 device arrives Friday, November 13, alongside new HomePods, a fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, and smart-home accessories built with LG. The Wearables, Home and Accessories division still hauled $7.9B in Q3, slightly behind Macs and slightly ahead of iPads. (Snacks)

• Housing is cheering the AI selloff. Wednesday's hotter-than-expected CPI briefly pushed Treasury yields to new highs, pressuring housing stocks, but it also pressured AI stocks, notably neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius. The AI boom and higher interest rates have gone hand in hand, so conditions tight enough to slow the AI rally could give the non-AI economy, and housing, a chance to breathe. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF has now fallen seven straight days, only the third such streak in a decade. (The Housing Frame)

• From Russia, with diesel. With fuel prices soaring and midterms approaching, Trump struck a deal with Putin to buy Russian diesel, temporarily easing sanctions meant to punish Moscow for invading Ukraine, while demanding Ukraine stop bombing Russian refineries. Energy experts say the quantities are too minuscule relative to the global market to lower prices much. The old Republican slogan was Peace Through Strength; Counterpoint's update is Peace Through Putin. (Counterpoint)

The Culture

• Frightgeist is here. Google's annual Halloween data shows this year's movies driving the trending outfits of 2026. The viral horror phenomenon "Buddy" (Buddy the Unicorn) is the number one costume, with Agamemnon from "The Odyssey" in fourth and Nikki from "Obsession" in third. Kids are going another way: expect swarms of trick-or-treaters dressed as country star Ella Langley and the late Dolly Parton. (Snacks)

• The book is not about you. Jerusalem Demsas digs into the Twilight generation's reading habit: Stephenie Meyer deliberately left Bella Swan vague ("slender, but soft somehow") so readers could step into her shoes. Decades later, "reader-insert" fanfiction uses Y/N as your name, and some romance readers now refuse to read third person at all. The lost pleasure is being absorbed in someone else's life without needing it to accommodate your own. (The Argument)

• Save Our Stories. Eddie Huang recapped the banned books event where he spoke about the statewide ban of Fresh Off The Boat in Texas, plus Ali Velshi's touching speech on The Perks of Being a Wallflower. The rest of the show: sh*t talking is back (the Vanity Fair Thomas Straker piece), Chet Hanks pressing Eric Andre, and Brooklyn teachers in Issey Miyake dupes. (Canal Street Dreams)

• A pet altar at 12th and Park. Local couple Sandra Manay and Thomas Konik brought back their Dia de Muertos pet memorial altar in Hoboken for a second year, inviting neighbors to add photos of lost pets. The city is also planning the permanent Rainbow Bridge pet memorial. (The Hoboken Girl)

• The Muslim manosphere. From Red Pill coaches to "Dawah Bros," influencers are dressing up hypermasculinity and misogyny in religious language and finding audiences across social platforms. (WIRED)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Zero-click spyware is now infecting phones through targeted ads, per The Citizen Lab's first published technical evidence. (WIRED)

• 60 Minutes hit a season low with 6.061M viewers Sunday, down 12% from last year's comparable episode, and off 15% in the 25-54 demo. (Status)

• Meta stunned the industry with a total ban on all ByteDance advertising across its platforms, extended to six other countries beyond the US. Some inside Meta were caught off guard. (Status)

• The DOJ sent California letters naming people it believes are noncitizens who received mail-in ballots, threatening "emergency" court intervention if the state does not act. Also, a literal dog voted in California recently. (Pirate Wires)

• Prediction markets make the Montreal Alouettes 48% favorites for the Grey Cup and give the Seahawks a 58% chance of beating the Broncos on Thursday Night Football. (Snacks)

• An arrested OpenAI engineer credits a Saudi prince with his decision to work in US tech. (Pirate Wires)

• Woodpeckers inspired the world's safest bike helmet: Vancouver's Pikio Labs built a new skull-protection approach after studying head-banging woodpeckers. (WIRED)

• Tanner Garrity rucked the Williamsburg Bridge with 30 pounds on his back, three miles in 45 minutes, peaking 150 feet over the East River. Rucking's prayer: "Get this shit off me." (InsideHook)

Thursday, October 15, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• 1 billion: ChatGPT's monthly active users. 404 Media tested the ad system and found advertisers can inject ads into your session based on your phone number, your email, or the prompts you type in.

• $1.3 billion: Ithaca Holdings, a first-time fund with zero buyouts under its belt, is buying Bumble for $1.3B. The backers include Jeff Bezos, Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke, Kleiner Perkins, Benchmark, and Joshua Kushner's Thrive Capital.

• 80 cents: CoreWeave's worst-hit bonds fell below 80 cents on the dollar, well into distressed territory, as lenders sour on the AI trade. Elon Musk's review: "Yikes."

• $2,600: the starting price of Microsoft's new Surface Laptop Ultra, a mini AI data center with Nvidia's RTX Spark chip and up to 128GB of memory that runs frontier models locally.

• 1 in 4: nearly a quarter of France's 3,700 high schools have seen student walkouts, organized through Snapchat groups with 201-person caps. The Gen Alpha revolution is built on disappearing messages.

• 40,000: fans packed AT&T Stadium near Dallas for women's college volleyball's first $1 million prize pool, the largest in the sport's history. Volleyball NIL pay has risen 25-fold since 2021.

Quotes of the Day

• "We don't just need to bond, we need to belong too." (Adam Grant, on why friendships alone don't cure loneliness, from his new book VIBE)

• "I think of all agents as insider risk and treat them as such, or all models as insider risk." (Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, in his interview with Joanna Stern)

• "Culture is not proprietary; trends are not IP." (Anu Lingala, after the world's largest trend forecasting company accused her tiny newsletter of stealing its content)

• "This isn't about gossip, it's about asymmetric social warfare." (Art of Play shopkeeper, after Kelly Clarkson aimed 8.8 million followers at his Brooklyn store)

• "I still don't know what I want to do with my life." (Avi Lichtenstein, 16, who spent $500 of his savings on 300 flyers asking New Yorkers, "Do you have a cool job and a big heart? Let me shadow you.")

• "OpenAI's advertising products are operating just like most other massive companies which start to monetize their audiences. They are boiling the frog and hoping their users won't notice the privacy implications from their new ads." (Zach Edwards, DecryptAds co-founder, to 404 Media)

AI Gets Creepier and Pricier

• Your ChatGPT session is for sale, and your phone number is the targeting. 404 Media ran test ads inside ChatGPT and confirmed that advertisers can target specific people based on their email address, phone number, or a unique identifier on their phone. OpenAI also targets ads based on the prompts you type, prompts many users reasonably assume are private. OpenAI started showing ads to Free and Go users in February and recently pushed them alongside image generation results. (404 Media)

• Nadella admits AI agents are an insider threat, then sells you the fortress. In an exclusive interview with Joanna Stern, the Microsoft CEO said Windows is being reengineered for the agent era, with agents getting their own identities, isolated environments, restricted permissions, and Defender watching their behavior. His pitch: Windows becomes the safest home for agents you cannot trust. He also showed off the new Surface Laptop Ultra, starting at $2,600, running frontier models locally on Nvidia's RTX Spark chip, plus an app he vibe-coded himself. (The New Things)

• The AI boom's next bottleneck is not chips or power, it is money. Lenders are pulling back from data center debt, Semafor reports, with CoreWeave's bonds sliding into distressed territory and the DBS CEO telling Shelly Banjo, "We're not an ATM for your dystopian future." Volta's $5B Norwegian data center got tougher terms, protecting against a SpaceX default now costs 80% more than three months ago, and telecom bonds cracked six months before the dot-com crash. Equity investors get paid to be dreamers; lenders get paid not to lose money. (Semafor)

Culture Notes

• The world's largest trend forecaster tried to bully a tiny newsletter, and picked the wrong target. WGSN, the trend forecasting giant valued around $900M, sent Anu Lingala and Alexi Gunner a legal letter claiming their work "appears to rely heavily" on WGSN's proprietary content. Problem: neither of them has an active WGSN account (Lingala was laid off in January), the letter never specified which content, and trends, as she notes, are not IP. After she pushed back with a lawyer, WGSN backed down. Her bigger point: the old forecasting business was "trend-fixing," a self-fulfilling loop where everyone at the mall sold the same color because everyone subscribed to the same service. TikTok blew up that cycle for good. (WHAT'S ANU)

• Kelly Clarkson vs. a Brooklyn curiosity shop is the pettiest power struggle of the week. Saturday, Clarkson tweeted to her 8.8 million followers that Art of Play treated her like she was poor. The store says she wanted to buy "Molly," a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird that is not for sale, and Clarkson countered with screenshots of a $15,000 price tag. Co-owner Adam Rubin says they've since received death threats and had neighbors doxxed. Pirate Wires spent 24 hours inside the shop, where neighbors brought solidarity, an Afghan bakery dropped off free baked goods, and the vibe stayed, per one shopkeeper, firmly "relaxed." (Pirate Wires)

• Gen Z invented the entry-level boyfriend. Per The Cut via After School, the prevailing philosophy among Gen Z women is that a boyfriend is only worth the trouble if he could plausibly become a husband, so her peers cycle through situationships instead of relationships, with no practice "communicating, compromising, fighting, apologizing, and showing up." One NYU grad recalled shooting down a guy who tried to define the relationship, having already made "a mental list of all the reasons he couldn't be my husband anyway." (After School)

• Doctors used to prescribe Jane Austen for shell shock. A WITI guest essay traces bibliotherapy back to 1916, when Samuel McChord Crothers coined the term, and through WWI, when librarians wheeled carts of books into military hospitals and a British scholar reportedly drew up a "fever chart" recommending Austen for trauma. The idea: literature offers something beyond information or instruction, which is to say consolation. In an era when we diagnose ourselves constantly and prescribe podcasts about attachment styles, maybe the prescription is fewer hours searching for answers online and more hours in the company of a good writer. (Why is this interesting?)

• We swapped spider webs for bicycle wheels, and it made us lonely. Adam Grant's new book argues our social networks used to look like spider webs, where the people in our lives knew each other, and now look like bicycle wheels, where we are the hub and the spokes never connect. The fix is not more bonding but belonging: join a book club, a pottery class, a padel league, and introduce your friends to each other. Happiness rises when the people you know are in touch. (Adam Grant)

Kids These Days

• AI is becoming mom's second brain. Overwhelmed by the administrative burden of parenting, families are outsourcing to AI: one mom feeds her kid's library schedule to an agent called Ollie, which texts her reminders. In a Lurie Children's Hospital survey, two in three parents said AI eased their mental load and saved them nearly an hour a week, and Menlo Ventures puts AI adoption at 84% among parents versus 56% of nonparents. (After School)

• A new kids' app wants to kill the engagement machine. Maka is an ad-free streaming app abandoning the mechanisms that "turn children's media into an engagement machine": no autoplay, no endless scrolling, and a 25-show catalog including The Wiggles and Sesame Street, vetted through a framework built with the Yale Child Study Center. One beta dad said that on other platforms, watching with his kid feels like "a race to the bottom of my kid's brainstem." (After School)

• One teen spent $500 on flyers to find a job worth doing. Avi Lichtenstein, a 16-year-old high school junior, paid two Craigslist hires to tape more than 300 flyers around New York reading, "Do you have a cool job and a big heart? Let me shadow you." Applicants fill out a questionnaire and do a video call first ("If they're a creep on Zoom, then I'm not meeting with them in person"). So far he's shadowed a dog groomer, a radio host, and a Bronx noodle shop owner, one week at a time, before college applications. (After School)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Ukrainian drones hit Russia's largest data center, the fourth strike on Russian data centers in a week. Data centers are now war targets. (404 Media)

• Epic Games admitted it "vibe coded" a new, much faster Epic Games Launcher, and buried the real news: Fortnite is coming to Linux. (404 Media)

• Livestreamers in Germany used a robot to harass a woman on the street for social media clout. (404 Media)

• Acquired revisited Peloton's pandemic arc: $49B peak market cap to more than 85% down, $1.3B in unsold bikes and treads, the $420M Precor buy, and the Barry McCarthy rescue mission. Kyle's rating: 6/10. (Acquired)

• Jordskott, a Swedish procedural where police detectives investigate trolls, got the nod from band Mackeeper, whose debut record Believe You Me drops tomorrow. Their other recs: Busch Gardens (theme is countries, $1 beers, five cups in one hand), Chicken Marbella (the prune dish), and Frontier House. (Perfectly Imperfect)

The states come for OpenAI.

entries.title: The Day the Internet Got Stranger: AI Agents, Heirloom Apples & a Fake Bird
entries.description: A field dispatch from today’s newsletter pile: the future arrived wearing a weighted vest, brands started making television, trend forecasters reached for lawyers, and somewhere in Brooklyn a fake singing bird became a minor geopolitical incident.
entries.body:
A field dispatch from today’s newsletter pile: the future arrived wearing a weighted vest, brands started making television, trend forecasters reached for lawyers, and somewhere in Brooklyn a fake singing bird became a minor geopolitical incident.

Best links

• The ad follows you into the chatbot. 404 Media reports that advertisers can target ChatGPT sessions using phone numbers, email addresses, and prompts — the kind of “normal” ad-tech behavior that feels newly uncanny when the interface is supposed to be a thinking partner. The same issue points to research on spyware delivered through malicious ads, including targeting of devices associated with news organizations and sensitive institutions.

• Windows gets an AI-agent security perimeter. In Joanna Stern’s interview with Satya Nadella, Nadella says to treat models as “insider risk”: agents should have separate identities, isolated environments, restricted permissions, and behavioral monitoring. The new Surface Laptop Ultra is pitched as a portable local-AI data center; the newsletter also serves up the internet’s excellent HomeView memes, from duct-taped iPads to a Shaq-sized smart hub.

• Trend forecasting loses its oracle status. WHAT’S ANU recounts a threatening letter from WGSN, then makes the more interesting argument: in a TikTok-shaped, multipolar culture, brands should triangulate cultural foresight, product signals, and brand strategy instead of treating one giant trend service as the future.

Worth reading

• The job-search advice has a six-month half-life. Lenny’s Newsletter profiles three leaders who landed AI roles at Runway, Eli Lilly, and Google. The useful update: frontier work is not confined to the famous labs; durable domain knowledge matters; leadership is back, but only when paired with building; and “current” means having recently tried the tools yourself. The best practical move is a small side project built on whatever shipped this month.

• The election cake is already in the oven. Silver Bulletin argues that late-campaign uncertainty is increasingly about measurement error, not dramatic movement. FLIPR’s useful mental model: the ingredients are mostly set, while the remaining drama is how far the polls might be wrong.

• Sometimes the prescription is a novel. Why is this interesting? revisits bibliotherapy: WWI-era readers were prescribed literature — including Jane Austen for shell shock — not because a novel explained trauma, but because it offered company, distance, and another person’s consciousness. The companion idea is a lovely travel prompt: take the fifth stop and spend the day somewhere unplanned.

• Try measuring art by whether it feels alive. Marlowe Granados rejects the dead language of “good” and “bad” in favor of a quicker test: does the work have pulse, eccentricity, and enough off-center energy to make you want more of it?

Food & places

• The vegetable redemption arc continues. NYT Cooking’s The Veggie collects conversion stories for eggplant, okra, and Brussels sprouts. The pattern is simple: stop boiling vegetables into surrender. Try gochujang-glazed eggplant, roasted okra, cider-glazed sprouts, or shredded sprouts with hot oil, garlic, salt, pepper, and Parmesan.

• Tonight’s reliable dinner: NYT Cooking has turkey meatballs with onion and Parmesan in tomato sauce — about 50 minutes plus chilling — with the useful note that dark-meat turkey brings more flavor. Serve over spaghetti or polenta, or put it in a hero roll.

• Chinatown, heirloom apples, and the community as R&D. Feed Me moves from a Chinatown dinner at the Lee association to a sharp consumer-brand lesson: Saie brought back the spirit of a discontinued Tom Ford “golden peach” eyeshadow after an influencer spent years testing alternatives with her audience. The larger idea is that comment sections can be an early-warning system for what people actually want. Also: whole chickens sold in Chinatown are a freshness signal, and open-source heirloom apples are making a comeback against the five varieties that dominate U.S. production.

Internet oddities

• The fake bird incident. Pirate Wires spends 24 hours at Brooklyn’s Art of Play after Kelly Clarkson complained that the store treated her like she was poor while trying to buy “Molly,” a one-of-a-kind singing-and-dancing bird with a claimed price tag of $15,000. The aftermath includes alleged threats, doxxing, supportive neighbors, Afghan bakery pastries, and a cannabis dispensary dropping off free weed stuff. “Asymmetric social warfare,” indeed.

• Bring back internet beef. Eddie Huang’s Canal Street Dreams takes a 36-minute detour through banned books, Thomas Straker, Keith McNally, Chet Hanks vs. Eric André, Brooklyn teachers in Issey Miyake dupes, and the lost art of public shit-talking.

• The bridge as a gym. Champ tries a three-mile, 45-minute ruck over the Williamsburg Bridge with 30 pounds. The portable lesson: point-to-point routes remove decision fatigue, and the workout’s “slow burn” is the point. The non-portable lesson: do not begin at 30 pounds just because a newsletter editor did.

Ideas to steal

• Make the ad feel like a thing worth watching. Feed Me argues that brands are treating social video more like studio production: polished mini-shows, real casting, deliberate formats, and maybe 95% short film / 5% ad. The goal is to interrupt the feed, not add another piece of disposable iPhone content.

• Build for the threshold, not the demo. Fireside Alpha summarizes OpenAI’s finance pitch: model capability can rise for a long time before a task crosses the “threshold of usefulness,” when review finally costs less than doing the work yourself. Design now for what users will want to control, review, and approve once that threshold arrives.

• Keep the signal alive. From Marlowe Granados: let eccentricity do some of the work. The strange detail is often the part that makes a person, product, room, or piece of writing feel inhabited.

One-liners

• “Culture is not proprietary; trends are not IP.” — WHAT’S ANU

• “The flavor of sadness and slime.” — a reader on zucchini, via The Veggie

• “What are clothes except vehicles for living?” — Marlowe Granados

• The emerging 2027 work habit: keep using whatever just shipped, and keep one small project of your own alive. — Lenny’s Newsletter

entries.body:
Friday, October 16, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 4+ days: how long Katie Zacharia survived as Trump's press secretary. After two brutal Fox News interviews, Trump fired her, setting a new record for the shortest top-spokesman tenure and beating the old 11-day mark.

• 22%: the time-to-exhaustion boost cyclists got from just 10 grams of carbs per hour instead of none. Researchers estimate the real sweet spot is closer to 107 grams per hour.

• 9 watts: the extra power endurance athletes held in a time trial after four hours of cycling when they fueled at 100 grams of carbs per hour instead of 60.

• 90 minutes: the long-run threshold where durable runners separate from fading ones. Runners used to 90-plus-minute sessions lost only about half as much running economy to fatigue as those who ran shorter.

• 3 miles, 45 minutes: Tanner Garrity's ruck across the Williamsburg Bridge, weighted pack and all. The battle prayer of every rucker: "Get this shit off me."

Quotes of the Day

• "Before this movie, you might've been the hottest Nathan Fielder fan. But after this movie ... all the baddies will be on high alert." (Hunter Harris's seatmate Peyton, on You Can See Everything at NYFF)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Explosive CBS News audio: Bari Weiss's handpicked foreign editor Shayndi Raice clashed with reporters, threatened to fire them for "insubordination," and called the Gaza death toll a "magic number." Also in the mix: Lesley Stahl nearly quit "60 Minutes." (Status News)

• "Girls" is coming back to HBO, and the news was so big Hunter Harris discussed it in therapy. (Hung Up)

• What does your drink order say about you? Bartender Dani Brand's field notes from a downtown dive's closing shift have thoughts. Vodka soda, Negroni, Jack and Coke: she's keeping score. (InsideHook)

• Hannah Chamberlain of SpiritedLA on her "exquisitely chilled" martini, her favorite airport bar, and the unlikely establishment where she's a regular. (InsideHook)
