morning.body:
Friday, October 16, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• 63%: wholesale Advent calendar sales are up 63% year over year. Adults now buy most toys for themselves, so a religious countdown has become a month of kidult blind boxes.

• 15%: the yield on CoreWeave's 2031 bonds, after a cofounder's candid comment about the company's debt sent the stock down and rattled the AI trade.

• 60%: the chance of CoreWeave defaulting within five years now priced into credit-default swaps, which hit 1,194 basis points.

• 54,000: residents Los Angeles County lost last year, the most of any county in America, as the mansion tax and housing rules push young people out.

• 100,000,000: Tamagotchis sold as of July, while Bandai revives the digital pets for the toy's 30th anniversary this November.

Quotes of the Day

• "This is what you get when an admin prioritizes loyalty over literacy." (Pirate Wires, on the new White House press secretary's debut press conference)

• "Have you ever opened an exquisite doorknob? A really good doorknob. They don't just appear out of thin air! Somebody sweated over that doorknob for an absurd amount of time." (Hamish Smyth, designer, in the WITI Friday interview)

• "What I eventually had to confront was that those commitments could sometimes be in conflict and that no one ideological movement held all the answers." (John Thomason, The Argument, on falling out of love with dogmatic ideology)

AI & The Machines

• AI hacks are leaving a mess that nobody pays for. Powerful AI models keep causing chaos, but the people getting hit rarely go after the companies behind them. Paresh Dave reports on the victims who are not widely seeking justice, and the AI firms not picking up the tab. (WIRED)

• AI-generated hot girls are stealing comedians' jokes. Fake AI personas are lifting real comedians' bits to juice engagement for their horny content. The punchlines are human. The faces are not. (WIRED)

• Anthropic's growth just flattened. Henry Blodget says the AI lab's growth has really stalled, a sentence that would have been unthinkable six months ago. If the labs stop growing, the whole AI trade has to be repriced. (Regenerator)

Money & Power

• The Tesla Roadster 2 is here, and Musk says it flies. After nearly a decade of delays, Tesla unveiled the new Roadster at a Texas event, claiming 0 to 60 in 0.81 seconds, three trims priced on how much you want it to fly, and production starting in 2028. The FAA will likely have thoughts about a car that leaves the ground. (WIRED)

• The EU is about to lift sanctions on a Chinese firm to save an ASML supplier. Brussels keeps discovering that its supply chains run through the very companies it sanctioned. Industrial policy meets reality. (Bloomberg)

• AI-written speeches are taking over politics. Politicians are letting machines write their words, which raises an awkward question about whose ideas are actually running the country. (The Economist)

The Culture

• The new White House press secretary calls her old employer "sort of a pyramid scheme." WIRED dug through Katie Zacharia's deleted profiles and filled in the missing decade: after returning from China in 2013, she spent time as an affiliate marketer for Beachbody, selling its Shakeology shakes. The company, now BODi, confirmed she was one of about 300,000 independent distributors. She says she quit over the vitamin A content while she was pregnant. (WIRED)

• OpenAI is warning employees about honeypots. The FTC just subpoenaed OpenAI and Anthropic, and the Journal reports foreign spies are hunting for AI secrets. OpenAI's warning to staff: the blonde bombshell at the Linux conference is not into you. She is married to the Motherland. Pirate Wires suggests the spies are wasting their time on engineers and should honeypot the people who actually matter: tech media writers. (Pirate Wires)

• The incentives of the new IRL economy look an awful lot like the old digital one. The Atlantic's piece on the rise of the IRL influencer got Ben Dietz thinking: if in-person gatherings run on the same incentives as content, who pays for them? His answer is that the brands and groups that underwrite the best gatherings, not the most conspicuous ones, will reap the rewards. ([[SIC]](https://sic.substack.com))

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• After an explosive all-hands, CBS News foreign editor Shayndi Raice tried to make amends with her London bureau on an awkward three-hour Thames boat cruise that was supposed to be team-building. (Status)

• Canada has a new apple. The Sunpunch has tropical notes and took 25 years of research and testing. ([[SIC]](https://sic.substack.com))

• First-class amenity kits have become holy-grail collectibles. ([[SIC]](https://sic.substack.com))

• The sneaker bubble is bursting: it is now uncool to wear sneakers in the office, as slouchy sweatpants give way to smarter attire. ([[SIC]](https://sic.substack.com))

• A 100-year magazine study found UK seafood recipes are narrowing. Something fishy about sameness. ([[SIC]](https://sic.substack.com))

• Customer demand for off-network restaurants has created a grey market for food delivery on Facebook Marketplace. ([[SIC]](https://sic.substack.com))

• The new WITI identity was sketched on a bartender's notecard at a Hillstone bar. Designer Hamish Smyth wrote "Why Is This Interesting?" twenty times, underlining different words, until the italics trick clicked. (WITI)

midday.body:
Friday, October 16, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• $3.3 billion: the stock CoreWeave's founders have sold since the IPO, per Bloomberg, landing the same week the company's bonds traded at distress levels.

• $17 billion: Anthropic's third quarter revenue, up 46% from the prior quarter but far below the 100% growth it posted between the first and second quarters. Some investors are now discussing a $1.5 trillion valuation instead of $2 trillion.

• $59 million: Firmus Grid's revenue for fiscal 2026, against the $30 billion valuation it sought at IPO last week before investors balked and the listing was pulled. The Australian data center firm has delivered 46MW of a promised 912MW pipeline, and its CEO previously did time for insider trading.

• 639,000: Republican donors, voters, and supporters whose personal and financial data Jack Smith's office obtained during the Arctic Frost investigation, per a memo released October 14 by Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley. The records included names, addresses, donation amounts as low as $1, and even individual MAGA hat buyers.

• 20,000: suspected noncitizens the Justice Department says sit on California's voter rolls and were sent mail ballots for the November 3 midterms. DOJ sued the state Thursday after California refused a 48 hour review of the federal list.

• 300: data center lawyers top US firms are on pace to hire this year, three times the 2020 figure, per legal intelligence firm Pirical. Kirkland & Ellis and Dentons each have 200-plus lawyers listing data center experience, and hiring has shifted south to Texas where power availability decides whether projects get built.

• $6.5 million: the seed round behind Hometown Equity, the for-profit successor to YC nonprofit New Story. The new company pairs titled land, home construction, and financing, aiming to build 100 "hometowns" across Latin America in 10 years.

Quotes of the Day

• "I think daily how I want to give up because I will never be as cool as them." (Indiana, Los Angeles artist, on the band CocoRosie, Perfectly Imperfect)

• "It's easier to remember pain than happiness." (Na Zhong, writer and translator of Sally Rooney's novels into Chinese, The Drift)

• "If it's not working in story reels, the animation won't save it." (John Lasseter, on Pixar's process, Founder Fridays)

• "We don't have any stock price." (Nobu Torii, Suntory CEO, on the freedom of being private, Semafor)

Power & Accountability

• ICE's body cameras have an off switch, and DHS wants to keep it that way. A congressional watchdog report dated September 15 and made public October 14 finds ICE cannot prove its officers turn cameras on when policy requires it, and zero reprimands were issued for body camera violations from the program's start through September 2025. The fix already exists: Border Patrol uses automated triggers on the same Axon cameras (recording starts when a gun is drawn or lights come on), and DHS's own Science and Technology office tested the feature successfully. DHS agreed with six of seven GAO recommendations and rejected the auto-activation one, warning it could capture informants and bystanders. ICE's camera plan dates to 2024; about 4,800 cameras were in the field as of April 2026 while a hiring surge added roughly 12,000 personnel. (Migrant Insider)

• A shooter entered an Oregon elementary school Thursday and was stopped inside within minutes. The first 911 call came around 12:59pm reporting shots fired into a car outside Silver Rail Elementary in Bend; within a minute, callers reported the person had entered the building and begun shooting. Officers arrived around 1:02pm and the suspect was reported down inside, shot and killed, possibly by a legally armed bystander (police say it is not confirmed who fired). Law enforcement sources told Fox News that three children and one adult were killed; the shooter was described as a 16 year old male with a shotgun. The district closed schools Friday. (NLDR Media)

• Trump wanted the Fort Hood execution livestreamed, then got nervous about how it would look. Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder in the 2009 Fort Hood attack, is scheduled to die by firing squad December 3 at 1pm CT, the first US military execution since 1961 and the first by firing squad since 1945. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be public and livestreamed; Trump reversed that on Truth Social, writing that Hasan "will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed." Jonathan Katz's Racket essay reads the spectacle impulse through 1964 Haiti, where Duvalier bused crowds to a firing squad and propped a rebel's corpse on a lawn chair facing a sign that read "Welcome to Haiti." (The Racket)

Money & The AI Trade

• A nuclear founder is suing his own seed investor over Silicon Valley's unwritten rules. Valar Atomics CEO Isaiah Taylor is enforcing pro-rata rights against Day One Ventures' Masha Bucher after other investors waived theirs when Sequoia invested. Taylor says Bucher sent legal threats via Quinn Emanuel; her side believes she alone was told to give up future rights. Public opinion backed the founder while investors privately sympathized with Bucher, who has ties to suspect Russian investors. (Newcomer)

• Scant retention bonuses killed a Wall Street merger. Perella Weinberg and Piper Sandler were near a handshake when Perella's CEO told roughly 70 partners their retention packages: $2.5 million in combined-company stock for top bankers, tiered down to $500,000 for smaller producers ("offensively low," per one banker). Quit threats helped kill talks that would have built a stronger competitor for a shrinking pool of deals. (Semafor)

• a16z's bull case for OpenAI is distribution, not models. The framework has four levers: get people doing something new, reach lots of users, price to capture value, make switching costly. ChatGPT turned unfamiliar capabilities into everyday behavior, and a broad customer base surfaces problems that become developer building blocks, a learning loop that could produce better models than technical leadership alone. (Founder Fridays)

The Culture

• MIT's Sherry Turkle says chatbots shouldn't get to say "I" or "me." Her new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, warns we are in a state of emergency over our enmeshment with machines posing as tutors, mentors, friends, and lovers. The diminutive professor is taking on a multitrillion dollar industry, aiming for the shelf of Silent Spring and The Jungle. (WIRED)

• The Arthur Jafa retrospective at the New Museum is gloriously uneven. "I Am Tony" runs through January 3: AGHDRA fills a cavernous dark room with an 85 minute floor-to-ceiling projection of digitally animated oceanic waves set to remixed Isley Brothers and Roberta Flack; BEN GAZZARA restages the Taxi Driver finale with Black actors per Paul Schrader's original script, with a Stevie Wonder cameo in one loop. Watching European tourists earnestly decode Michael Blackson and Erykah Badu freestyling "for the D" in The White Album is its own exhibit. (InsideHook)

• Emma Cline's Switzy might be her best book yet. The novel follows David Hastings, a retired executive traveling to Zurich for assisted suicide while his memory deteriorates. Longlisted for the Booker Prize and quieter than The Guest, it is sharply written, contemplative, and unafraid of the totality of a life. (InsideHook)

• Laurel Pantin is done pretending competitiveness is a flaw. The Earl Earl essay traces her shift from twenties jealousy (she skipped bowling because she sucked at it) to competing with herself: skiing, spring tennis lessons, muscle mass, sleep, cardiovascular age. Since turning 40 and getting sober, health (not wellness, not thinness) has become the project. "You only get one short little life." (Earl Earl)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Pablo Manríquez is giving away a 1968 sea-foam-green Brother de Luxe typewriter to his 100th paid subscriber. He has acquired seven machines since July (two to keep, four to sell on eBay) and says typewriting will be an important part of his news work in 2027. (Pablo Reports)

• The Library of Congress dropped nine high-res images on Flickr last night, and at least one newsletter writer is fully obsessed. (Pablo Reports)

• Cameron Winter's Live at Carnegie Hall has been on repeat all week: songs from Heavy Metal plus three new tracks, revamped at the piano, recorded at his mythical December 2025 show. One lyric: "I don't like what happened to Jesus // But I sure do like Saturday morning." (InsideHook)

• A startup founded by crypto enthusiasts is building a real-time Misery Index from prediction-market data. The classic version (unemployment plus inflation) has called presidential elections since LBJ's era, but it runs on backward-looking monthly data. Futures can't be far behind. (Semafor)

• Lex Fridman visited Taiwan with Jensen Huang: huge crowds of engineers, night-market street food, days of conversation, some of it on video. (Founder Fridays)

• Vinegar braised chicken and leeks: sear bone-in thighs, soften leeks and garlic, deglaze with white wine, chicken stock, and sherry vinegar, then finish uncovered in the oven. Serve over rice or crusty bread to catch the sauce. (Side Dish)

: Republican donors, voters, and supporters whose personal and financial data Jack Smith's office obtained during the Arctic Frost investigation, per a memo released October 14 by Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley. The records included names, addresses, donation amounts as low as $1, and even individual MAGA hat buyers.

: suspected noncitizens the Justice Department says sit on California's voter rolls and were sent mail ballots for the November 3 midterms. DOJ sued the state Thursday after California refused a 48 hour review of the federal list.

: data center lawyers top US firms are on pace to hire this year, three times the 2020 figure, per legal intelligence firm Pirical. Kirkland & Ellis and Dentons each have 200-plus lawyers listing data center experience, and hiring has shifted south to Texas where power availability decides whether projects get built.
$6.5 million

: the seed round behind Hometown Equity, the for-profit successor to YC nonprofit New Story. The new company pairs titled land, home construction, and financing, aiming to build 100 "hometowns" across Latin America in 10 years.
Quotes of the Day
"I think daily how I want to give up because I will never be as cool as them." (Indiana, Los Angeles artist, on the band CocoRosie,
Perfectly Imperfect
"It's easier to remember pain than happiness." (Na Zhong, writer and translator of Sally Rooney's novels into Chinese,
The Drift
"If it's not working in story reels, the animation won't save it." (John Lasseter, on Pixar's process,
Founder Fridays
"We don't have any stock price." (Nobu Torii, Suntory CEO, on the freedom of being private,
Semafor
Power & Accountability
ICE's body cameras have an off switch, and DHS wants to keep it that way.

A congressional watchdog report dated September 15 and made public October 14 finds ICE cannot prove its officers turn cameras on when policy requires it, and zero reprimands were issued for body camera violations from the program's start through September 2025. The fix already exists: Border Patrol uses automated triggers on the same Axon cameras (recording starts when a gun is drawn or lights come on), and DHS's own Science and Technology office tested the feature successfully. DHS agreed with six of seven GAO recommendations and rejected the auto-activation one, warning it could capture informants and bystanders. ICE's camera plan dates to 2024; about 4,800 cameras were in the field as of April 2026 while a hiring surge added roughly 12,000 personnel. (
Migrant Insider
A shooter entered an Oregon elementary school Thursday and was stopped inside within minutes.

The first 911 call came around 12:59pm reporting shots fired into a car outside Silver Rail Elementary in Bend; within a minute, callers reported the person had entered the building and begun shooting. Officers arrived around 1:02pm and the suspect was reported down inside, shot and killed, possibly by a legally armed bystander (police say it is not confirmed who fired). Law enforcement sources told Fox News that three children and one adult were killed; the shooter was described as a 16 year old male with a shotgun. The district closed schools Friday. (
NLDR Media
Trump wanted the Fort Hood execution livestreamed, then got nervous about how it would look.

Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder in the 2009 Fort Hood attack, is scheduled to die by firing squad December 3 at 1pm CT, the first US military execution since 1961 and the first by firing squad since 1945. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be public and livestreamed; Trump reversed that on Truth Social, writing that Hasan "will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed." Jonathan Katz's Racket essay reads the spectacle impulse through 1964 Haiti, where Duvalier bused crowds to a firing squad and propped a rebel's corpse on a lawn chair facing a sign that read "Welcome to Haiti." (
The Racket
Money & The AI Trade
A nuclear founder is suing his own seed investor over Silicon Valley's unwritten rules.

Valar Atomics CEO Isaiah Taylor is enforcing pro-rata rights against Day One Ventures' Masha Bucher after other investors waived theirs when Sequoia invested. Taylor says Bucher sent legal threats via Quinn Emanuel; her side believes she alone was told to give up future rights. Public opinion backed the founder while investors privately sympathized with Bucher, who has ties to suspect Russian investors. (
Newcomer
Scant retention bonuses killed a Wall Street merger.

Perella Weinberg and Piper Sandler were near a handshake when Perella's CEO told roughly 70 partners their retention packages: $2.5 million in combined-company stock for top bankers, tiered down to $500,000 for smaller producers ("offensively low," per one banker). Quit threats helped kill talks that would have built a stronger competitor for a shrinking pool of deals. (
Semafor
a16z's bull case for OpenAI is distribution, not models.

The framework has four levers: get people doing something new, reach lots of users, price to capture value, make switching costly. ChatGPT turned unfamiliar capabilities into everyday behavior, and a broad customer base surfaces problems that become developer building blocks, a learning loop that could produce better models than technical leadership alone. (
Founder Fridays
The Culture
MIT's Sherry Turkle says chatbots shouldn't get to say "I" or "me."

Her new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, warns we are in a state of emergency over our enmeshment with machines posing as tutors, mentors, friends, and lovers. The diminutive professor is taking on a multitrillion dollar industry, aiming for the shelf of Silent Spring and The Jungle. (
WIRED
The Arthur Jafa retrospective at the New Museum is gloriously uneven.

"I Am Tony" runs through January 3: AGHDRA fills a cavernous dark room with an 85 minute floor-to-ceiling projection of digitally animated oceanic waves set to remixed Isley Brothers and Roberta Flack; BEN GAZZARA restages the Taxi Driver finale with Black actors per Paul Schrader's original script, with a Stevie Wonder cameo in one loop. Watching European tourists earnestly decode Michael Blackson and Erykah Badu freestyling "for the D" in The White Album is its own exhibit. (
InsideHook
Emma Cline's Switzy might be her best book yet.

The novel follows David Hastings, a retired executive traveling to Zurich for assisted suicide while his memory deteriorates. Longlisted for the Booker Prize and quieter than The Guest, it is sharply written, contemplative, and unafraid of the totality of a life. (
InsideHook
Laurel Pantin is done pretending competitiveness is a flaw.

The Earl Earl essay traces her shift from twenties jealousy (she skipped bowling because she sucked at it) to competing with herself: skiing, spring tennis lessons, muscle mass, sleep, cardiovascular age. Since turning 40 and getting sober, health (not wellness, not thinness) has become the project. "You only get one short little life." (
Earl Earl
Quick Hits & Curiosities

Pablo Manríquez is giving away a 1968 sea-foam-green Brother de Luxe typewriter to his 100th paid subscriber. He has acquired seven machines since July (two to keep, four to sell on eBay) and says typewriting will be an important part of his news work in 2027. (
Pablo Reports
The Library of Congress dropped nine high-res images on Flickr last night, and at least one newsletter writer is fully obsessed. (
Pablo Reports

Cameron Winter's Live at Carnegie Hall has been on repeat all week: songs from Heavy Metal plus three new tracks, revamped at the piano, recorded at his mythical December 2025 show. One lyric: "I don't like what happened to Jesus // But I sure do like Saturday morning." (
InsideHook

A startup founded by crypto enthusiasts is building a real-time Misery Index from prediction-market data. The classic version (unemployment plus inflation) has called presidential elections since LBJ's era, but it runs on backward-looking monthly data. Futures can't be far behind. (
Semafor
Lex Fridman visited Taiwan with Jensen Huang: huge crowds of engineers, night-market street food, days of conversation, some of it on video. (
Founder Fridays

Vinegar braised chicken and leeks: sear bone-in thighs, soften leeks and garlic, deglaze with white wine, chicken stock, and sherry vinegar, then finish uncovered in the oven. Serve over rice or crusty bread to catch the sauce. (
Side Dish

afternoon.body:
Friday, October 16, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

• 13,000: accounts X says it deleted this week that were tied to foreign influence operations aimed at the US midterms, possibly the real reason your feed feels quieter

• 1 billion: ChatGPT's monthly active users, whose chatbot sessions advertisers can now inject ads into, targeted by email, phone number, or the prompts they type

• 100x: the surge in agentic shopping traffic over 45 days, per cybersecurity firm Cheq, as AI shopping assistants go mainstream this holiday season

• $329,000: Gen Z's average art spending, per an Art Basel and UBS survey, more than double the boomers' $156,000 (dealers question the survey, but 13% of young collectors still dropped over $1 million this year)

• 500 million: tokens per week that Meta's Muse sells for $20 a month, a number growth expert Elena Verna calls meaningless because the AI industry prices everything in "arcade money"

• $370: the price of the Home Alone sundae at the Plaza Hotel, available only a few more days before the hotel closes for a four-year facade renovation

• 6 of 8: Gen Z Trump voters in a Navigator Research focus group who now give the president a D or F, with a 29-year-old Floridian saying everything got worse and he will back Democrats

Quotes of the Day

• "You may think you're there to exert control, but you're really there to be SHOP DOMMED, or told what to do by people who know more than you." (Emilia Petrarca, on the power dynamics of luxury retail)

• "Taste is great, but you can buy taste, you can't buy culture." (J Lee, Feed Me's restaurant critic, on why Hudson's new Pocketbook Hotel can never recreate what the late Lil' Deb's Oasis built)

• "People might be doing lowercase to signal that they're not AI." (Adam Aleksic, internet linguist, on why all-lowercase typing is back)

• "I know I didn't commit any crime." (Elizabeth Holmes, in Nathan Fielder's new documentary "You Can See Everything")

• "Mommy and daddy are playing nice again." (Meta's Alexandr Wang, on Meta's new open-weight model running on Apple Macs)

The AI Trade Under Stress

• Character.ai is going bankrupt, and it looks like the AI bubble's first domino. The company burned piles of cash running its product, brought in little revenue, and ran up enormous legal bills after harming users, per its bankruptcy court narrative. Cost-cutting did not save it, and Disney has reportedly offered $20 million to license some of its IP, a year after sending a cease-and-desist. The company was valued at $1 billion in 2023 after a $150 million raise led by a16z. (404 Media)

• Cops can now identify your house from a single interior photo. An AI tool called Raven, made by Graylark Technologies (formerly GeoSpy), pulls from sites like Zillow and Airbnb to match an interior shot to a specific home nearly instantly. The LAPD and Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office already bought access, and Raven just added interior analysis features. It is intelligence-agency tech, now off the shelf for local police. (404 Media)

• AI token spending has been flat for two straight months. Fresh Ramp business-spending data shows growth in AI token spending stalled, likely because frontier prices fell and models got more efficient. New customer growth has dropped sharply, and while OpenAI narrowed Anthropic's lead and xAI got a GrokBot bump, nothing reversed the trend that started this summer. The bulls have a data point to answer. (Newcomer)

• One Semafor columnist says debt will not be what pops the AI bubble. Everything in AI is bottlenecked, from chips to the refrigeration units cooling GPUs, so revenues are held back by supply, not drowned by debt. Efficiency gains keep birthing hungrier use cases, the old Jevons Paradox at work. The columnist even calls Anthropic's claimed 85% gross margins "a cash cow business" that will service its debt. (Semafor)

Power Moves

• A leaked email told immigration judges to keep collecting an asylum fee a judge had already voided. Twenty-one days after a federal court threw out the rules behind the annual asylum fee, Chief Immigration Judge Teresa L. Riley emailed every immigration judge in the country saying the fee "remains in effect." The email's subject line read "injunction - please read," but there was no injunction at all. (Migrant Insider)

How We Live Together

• Homelessness is mostly about collapsed relationships, not the usual three suspects. A 2023 UC San Francisco study found 90% of homeless people are single adults with no friends or family to ask for help, and 63% said social conflict or not wanting to be a burden pushed them out of their last housing. Galloway's read: mental illness, addiction, and cost matter, but the through line is people losing each other. (Prof G)

• Loneliness hits your body like smoking 15 cigarettes a day. That is the Surgeon General's 2023 verdict, with social isolation raising premature-mortality risk 29%. People with strong community ties are 2.6 times more likely to report good physical health and 3.2 times more likely to report good mental health. Meanwhile a Gallup survey finds most Americans feel little responsibility to help their own community. (Prof G)

• A grieving 71-year-old found her way back through baseball and strangers. After losing her 27-year-old son Wyatt to muscular dystrophy, Rhenda Strub bought two Seattle Mariners season tickets and posted on Facebook inviting strangers to join her. Her inbox filled with people carrying similar grief. Now she has a whole community of people who just want to share a hot dog and a ballgame. (Prof G)

Culture & The Zeitgeist

• Sally Rooney's books can no longer be sold in the UK. Her publisher Faber stopped supplying them after Rooney pledged royalties to Palestine Action, a group banned in Britain in July 2025, deciding that paying her could violate the terror ban. Shops can sell the copies they have but cannot reorder. The result: a run on Normal People and Intermezzo at London bookshops. (Feed Me)

• London's oldest restaurant is being preserved as a landmark. The National Trust will safeguard Rules, established in 1798, which has outlasted 9 British monarchs and 45 prime ministers while changing hands only three times. Its game-heavy menu and antler-covered interior are reportedly little changed since the 19th century. (Feed Me)

• Hudson's new design hotel proves taste is the product now, culture still is not. The Pocketbook, in an old textile factory, courts the creative class with Eckhaus Latta robes and a rock on a rope instead of a Do Not Disturb sign. But at $500-plus a night, its restaurant closes Mondays and Tuesdays, leaving fully booked guests to fend for themselves in a sleepy town. (Feed Me)

• Northern Ontario's place names are 9,000 years older than European contact. Abitibi, Temagami, and Temiskaming are Cree and Anishinaabe words from the Nipissing Nation, laid over land that runs deeper still: the Ottawa River cuts through a 400-million-year-old rift valley. Temiskaming itself means "deep water with fast winds." (The Republic of Letters)

• One family's parenting diary survived four countries and a Nazi-era escape. Writer Leah Bhabha inherited a worn book where four generations of women recorded their babies' lives, starting with her great-grandmother Mathilde. Her mother smuggled it out of Nazi Germany tucked into a bag. Births are now logged in Germany, India, England, and the United States. (Spread the Jelly)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• The town of Cobalt was once Canada's biggest silver mine, and the writer's birthplace Timmins one of the largest gold mines in the world, with the scars still visible from the air. (The Republic of Letters)

• Tin Can, a Seattle startup, is building a landline-style Wi-Fi phone for kids, backed by Greylock and Air Mail's viral social lead, on the bet that parents will pay to keep children off smartphones. (Feed Me)

• Graza, the comically oversized olive oil brand, made a 1.3-pound tub of hummus sold only at Costco. (Feed Me)

• Black Christmas (1974), the cozy Christmas slasher, was directed by Bob Clark, the same director behind A Christmas Story. (Tubi)

• The 33,000 photos on Leah Bhabha's phone include her daughters in an estimated 80 to 90 percent of them, a perfect snapshot of how modern parenthood runs on the camera roll. (Spread the Jelly)

evening.body:
Friday, October 16, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 4+ days: how long Katie Zacharia survived as Trump's press secretary. After two brutal Fox News interviews, Trump fired her, setting a new record for the shortest top-spokesman tenure and beating the old 11-day mark.

• 22%: the time-to-exhaustion boost cyclists got from just 10 grams of carbs per hour instead of none. Researchers estimate the real sweet spot is closer to 107 grams per hour.

• 9 watts: the extra power endurance athletes held in a time trial after four hours of cycling when they fueled at 100 grams of carbs per hour instead of 60.

• 90 minutes: the long-run threshold where durable runners separate from fading ones. Runners used to 90-plus-minute sessions lost only about half as much running economy to fatigue as those who ran shorter.

• 3 miles, 45 minutes: Tanner Garrity's ruck across the Williamsburg Bridge, weighted pack and all. The battle prayer of every rucker: "Get this shit off me."

Quotes of the Day

• "Before this movie, you might've been the hottest Nathan Fielder fan. But after this movie ... all the baddies will be on high alert." (Hunter Harris's seatmate Peyton, on You Can See Everything at NYFF)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Explosive CBS News audio: Bari Weiss's handpicked foreign editor Shayndi Raice clashed with reporters, threatened to fire them for "insubordination," and called the Gaza death toll a "magic number." Also in the mix: Lesley Stahl nearly quit "60 Minutes." (Status News)

• "Girls" is coming back to HBO, and the news was so big Hunter Harris discussed it in therapy. (Hung Up)

• What does your drink order say about you? Bartender Dani Brand's field notes from a downtown dive's closing shift have thoughts. Vodka soda, Negroni, Jack and Coke: she's keeping score. (InsideHook)

• Hannah Chamberlain of SpiritedLA on her "exquisitely chilled" martini, her favorite airport bar, and the unlikely establishment where she's a regular. (InsideHook)

full.body:
Friday, October 16, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• 63%: wholesale Advent calendar sales are up 63% year over year. Adults now buy most toys for themselves, so a religious countdown has become a month of kidult blind boxes.

• 15%: the yield on CoreWeave's 2031 bonds, after a cofounder's candid comment about the company's debt sent the stock down and rattled the AI trade.

• 60%: the chance of CoreWeave defaulting within five years now priced into credit-default swaps, which hit 1,194 basis points.

• 54,000: residents Los Angeles County lost last year, the most of any county in America, as the mansion tax and housing rules push young people out.

• 100,000,000: Tamagotchis sold as of July, while Bandai revives the digital pets for the toy's 30th anniversary this November.

Quotes of the Day

• "This is what you get when an admin prioritizes loyalty over literacy." (Pirate Wires, on the new White House press secretary's debut press conference)

• "Have you ever opened an exquisite doorknob? A really good doorknob. They don't just appear out of thin air! Somebody sweated over that doorknob for an absurd amount of time." (Hamish Smyth, designer, in the WITI Friday interview)

• "What I eventually had to confront was that those commitments could sometimes be in conflict and that no one ideological movement held all the answers." (John Thomason, The Argument, on falling out of love with dogmatic ideology)

AI & The Machines

• AI hacks are leaving a mess that nobody pays for. Powerful AI models keep causing chaos, but the people getting hit rarely go after the companies behind them. Paresh Dave reports on the victims who are not widely seeking justice, and the AI firms not picking up the tab. (WIRED)

• AI-generated hot girls are stealing comedians' jokes. Fake AI personas are lifting real comedians' bits to juice engagement for their horny content. The punchlines are human. The faces are not. (WIRED)

• Anthropic's growth just flattened. Henry Blodget says the AI lab's growth has really stalled, a sentence that would have been unthinkable six months ago. If the labs stop growing, the whole AI trade has to be repriced. (Regenerator)

Money & Power

• The Tesla Roadster 2 is here, and Musk says it flies. After nearly a decade of delays, Tesla unveiled the new Roadster at a Texas event, claiming 0 to 60 in 0.81 seconds, three trims priced on how much you want it to fly, and production starting in 2028. The FAA will likely have thoughts about a car that leaves the ground. (WIRED)

• The EU is about to lift sanctions on a Chinese firm to save an ASML supplier. Brussels keeps discovering that its supply chains run through the very companies it sanctioned. Industrial policy meets reality. (Bloomberg)

• AI-written speeches are taking over politics. Politicians are letting machines write their words, which raises an awkward question about whose ideas are actually running the country. (The Economist)

The Culture

• The new White House press secretary calls her old employer "sort of a pyramid scheme." WIRED dug through Katie Zacharia's deleted profiles and filled in the missing decade: after returning from China in 2013, she spent time as an affiliate marketer for Beachbody, selling its Shakeology shakes. The company, now BODi, confirmed she was one of about 300,000 independent distributors. She says she quit over the vitamin A content while she was pregnant. (WIRED)

• OpenAI is warning employees about honeypots. The FTC just subpoenaed OpenAI and Anthropic, and the Journal reports foreign spies are hunting for AI secrets. OpenAI's warning to staff: the blonde bombshell at the Linux conference is not into you. She is married to the Motherland. Pirate Wires suggests the spies are wasting their time on engineers and should honeypot the people who actually matter: tech media writers. (Pirate Wires)

• The incentives of the new IRL economy look an awful lot like the old digital one. Friday, October 16, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• $3.3 billion: the stock CoreWeave's founders have sold since the IPO, per Bloomberg, landing the same week the company's bonds traded at distress levels.

• $17 billion: Anthropic's third quarter revenue, up 46% from the prior quarter but far below the 100% growth it posted between the first and second quarters. Some investors are now discussing a $1.5 trillion valuation instead of $2 trillion.

• $59 million: Firmus Grid's revenue for fiscal 2026, against the $30 billion valuation it sought at IPO last week before investors balked and the listing was pulled. The Australian data center firm has delivered 46MW of a promised 912MW pipeline, and its CEO previously did time for insider trading.

• 639,000: Republican donors, voters, and supporters whose personal and financial data Jack Smith's office obtained during the Arctic Frost investigation, per a memo released October 14 by Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley. The records included names, addresses, donation amounts as low as $1, and even individual MAGA hat buyers.

• 20,000: suspected noncitizens the Justice Department says sit on California's voter rolls and were sent mail ballots for the November 3 midterms. DOJ sued the state Thursday after California refused a 48 hour review of the federal list.

• 300: data center lawyers top US firms are on pace to hire this year, three times the 2020 figure, per legal intelligence firm Pirical. Kirkland & Ellis and Dentons each have 200-plus lawyers listing data center experience, and hiring has shifted south to Texas where power availability decides whether projects get built.

• $6.5 million: the seed round behind Hometown Equity, the for-profit successor to YC nonprofit New Story. The new company pairs titled land, home construction, and financing, aiming to build 100 "hometowns" across Latin America in 10 years.

Quotes of the Day

• "I think daily how I want to give up because I will never be as cool as them." (Indiana, Los Angeles artist, on the band CocoRosie, Perfectly Imperfect)

• "It's easier to remember pain than happiness." (Na Zhong, writer and translator of Sally Rooney's novels into Chinese, The Drift)

• "If it's not working in story reels, the animation won't save it." (John Lasseter, on Pixar's process, Founder Fridays)

• "We don't have any stock price." (Nobu Torii, Suntory CEO, on the freedom of being private, Semafor)

Power & Accountability

• ICE's body cameras have an off switch, and DHS wants to keep it that way. A congressional watchdog report dated September 15 and made public October 14 finds ICE cannot prove its officers turn cameras on when policy requires it, and zero reprimands were issued for body camera violations from the program's start through September 2025. The fix already exists: Border Patrol uses automated triggers on the same Axon cameras (recording starts when a gun is drawn or lights come on), and DHS's own Science and Technology office tested the feature successfully. DHS agreed with six of seven GAO recommendations and rejected the auto-activation one, warning it could capture informants and bystanders. ICE's camera plan dates to 2024; about 4,800 cameras were in the field as of April 2026 while a hiring surge added roughly 12,000 personnel. (Migrant Insider)

• A shooter entered an Oregon elementary school Thursday and was stopped inside within minutes. The first 911 call came around 12:59pm reporting shots fired into a car outside Silver Rail Elementary in Bend; within a minute, callers reported the person had entered the building and begun shooting. Officers arrived around 1:02pm and the suspect was reported down inside, shot and killed, possibly by a legally armed bystander (police say it is not confirmed who fired). Law enforcement sources told Fox News that three children and one adult were killed; the shooter was described as a 16 year old male with a shotgun. The district closed schools Friday. (NLDR Media)

• Trump wanted the Fort Hood execution livestreamed, then got nervous about how it would look. Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder in the 2009 Fort Hood attack, is scheduled to die by firing squad December 3 at 1pm CT, the first US military execution since 1961 and the first by firing squad since 1945. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be public and livestreamed; Trump reversed that on Truth Social, writing that Hasan "will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed." Jonathan Katz's Racket essay reads the spectacle impulse through 1964 Haiti, where Duvalier bused crowds to a firing squad and propped a rebel's corpse on a lawn chair facing a sign that read "Welcome to Haiti." (The Racket)

Money & The AI Trade

• A nuclear founder is suing his own seed investor over Silicon Valley's unwritten rules. Valar Atomics CEO Isaiah Taylor is enforcing pro-rata rights against Day One Ventures' Masha Bucher after other investors waived theirs when Sequoia invested. Taylor says Bucher sent legal threats via Quinn Emanuel; her side believes she alone was told to give up future rights. Public opinion backed the founder while investors privately sympathized with Bucher, who has ties to suspect Russian investors. (Newcomer)

• Scant retention bonuses killed a Wall Street merger. Perella Weinberg and Piper Sandler were near a handshake when Perella's CEO told roughly 70 partners their retention packages: $2.5 million in combined-company stock for top bankers, tiered down to $500,000 for smaller producers ("offensively low," per one banker). Quit threats helped kill talks that would have built a stronger competitor for a shrinking pool of deals. (Semafor)

• a16z's bull case for OpenAI is distribution, not models. The framework has four levers: get people doing something new, reach lots of users, price to capture value, make switching costly. ChatGPT turned unfamiliar capabilities into everyday behavior, and a broad customer base surfaces problems that become developer building blocks, a learning loop that could produce better models than technical leadership alone. (Founder Fridays)

The Culture

• MIT's Sherry Turkle says chatbots shouldn't get to say "I" or "me." Her new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, warns we are in a state of emergency over our enmeshment with machines posing as tutors, mentors, friends, and lovers. The diminutive professor is taking on a multitrillion dollar industry, aiming for the shelf of Silent Spring and The Jungle. (WIRED)

• The Arthur Jafa retrospective at the New Museum is gloriously uneven. "I Am Tony" runs through January 3: AGHDRA fills a cavernous dark room with an 85 minute floor-to-ceiling projection of digitally animated oceanic waves set to remixed Isley Brothers and Roberta Flack; BEN GAZZARA restages the Taxi Driver finale with Black actors per Paul Schrader's original script, with a Stevie Wonder cameo in one loop. Watching European tourists earnestly decode Michael Blackson and Erykah Badu freestyling "for the D" in The White Album is its own exhibit. (InsideHook)

• Emma Cline's Switzy might be her best book yet. The novel follows David Hastings, a retired executive traveling to Zurich for assisted suicide while his memory deteriorates. Longlisted for the Booker Prize and quieter than The Guest, it is sharply written, contemplative, and unafraid of the totality of a life. (InsideHook)

• Laurel Pantin is done pretending competitiveness is a flaw. The Earl Earl essay traces her shift from twenties jealousy (she skipped bowling because she sucked at it) to competing with herself: skiing, spring tennis lessons, muscle mass, sleep, cardiovascular age. Since turning 40 and getting sober, health (not wellness, not thinness) has become the project. "You only get one short little life." (Earl Earl)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Pablo Manríquez is giving away a 1968 sea-foam-green Brother de Luxe typewriter to his 100th paid subscriber. He has acquired seven machines since July (two to keep, four to sell on eBay) and says typewriting will be an important part of his news work in 2027. (Pablo Reports)

• The Library of Congress dropped nine high-res images on Flickr last night, and at least one newsletter writer is fully obsessed. (Pablo Reports)

• Cameron Winter's Live at Carnegie Hall has been on repeat all week: songs from Heavy Metal plus three new tracks, revamped at the piano, recorded at his mythical December 2025 show. One lyric: "I don't like what happened to Jesus // But I sure do like Saturday morning." (InsideHook)

• A startup founded by crypto enthusiasts is building a real-time Misery Index from prediction-market data. The classic version (unemployment plus inflation) has called presidential elections since LBJ's era, but it runs on backward-looking monthly data. Futures can't be far behind. (Semafor)

• Lex Fridman visited Taiwan with Jensen Huang: huge crowds of engineers, night-market street food, days of conversation, some of it on video. (Founder Fridays)

• Vinegar braised chicken and leeks: sear bone-in thighs, soften leeks and garlic, deglaze with white wine, chicken stock, and sherry vinegar, then finish uncovered in the oven. Serve over rice or crusty bread to catch the sauce. (Side Dish)

Friday, October 16, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

• 13,000: accounts X says it deleted this week that were tied to foreign influence operations aimed at the US midterms, possibly the real reason your feed feels quieter

• 1 billion: ChatGPT's monthly active users, whose chatbot sessions advertisers can now inject ads into, targeted by email, phone number, or the prompts they type

• 100x: the surge in agentic shopping traffic over 45 days, per cybersecurity firm Cheq, as AI shopping assistants go mainstream this holiday season

• $329,000: Gen Z's average art spending, per an Art Basel and UBS survey, more than double the boomers' $156,000 (dealers question the survey, but 13% of young collectors still dropped over $1 million this year)

• 500 million: tokens per week that Meta's Muse sells for $20 a month, a number growth expert Elena Verna calls meaningless because the AI industry prices everything in "arcade money"

• $370: the price of the Home Alone sundae at the Plaza Hotel, available only a few more days before the hotel closes for a four-year facade renovation

• 6 of 8: Gen Z Trump voters in a Navigator Research focus group who now give the president a D or F, with a 29-year-old Floridian saying everything got worse and he will back Democrats

Quotes of the Day

• "You may think you're there to exert control, but you're really there to be SHOP DOMMED, or told what to do by people who know more than you." (Emilia Petrarca, on the power dynamics of luxury retail)

• "Taste is great, but you can buy taste, you can't buy culture." (J Lee, Feed Me's restaurant critic, on why Hudson's new Pocketbook Hotel can never recreate what the late Lil' Deb's Oasis built)

• "People might be doing lowercase to signal that they're not AI." (Adam Aleksic, internet linguist, on why all-lowercase typing is back)

• "I know I didn't commit any crime." (Elizabeth Holmes, in Nathan Fielder's new documentary "You Can See Everything")

• "Mommy and daddy are playing nice again." (Meta's Alexandr Wang, on Meta's new open-weight model running on Apple Macs)

The AI Trade Under Stress

• Character.ai is going bankrupt, and it looks like the AI bubble's first domino. The company burned piles of cash running its product, brought in little revenue, and ran up enormous legal bills after harming users, per its bankruptcy court narrative. Cost-cutting did not save it, and Disney has reportedly offered $20 million to license some of its IP, a year after sending a cease-and-desist. The company was valued at $1 billion in 2023 after a $150 million raise led by a16z. (404 Media)

• Cops can now identify your house from a single interior photo. An AI tool called Raven, made by Graylark Technologies (formerly GeoSpy), pulls from sites like Zillow and Airbnb to match an interior shot to a specific home nearly instantly. The LAPD and Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office already bought access, and Raven just added interior analysis features. It is intelligence-agency tech, now off the shelf for local police. (404 Media)

• AI token spending has been flat for two straight months. Fresh Ramp business-spending data shows growth in AI token spending stalled, likely because frontier prices fell and models got more efficient. New customer growth has dropped sharply, and while OpenAI narrowed Anthropic's lead and xAI got a GrokBot bump, nothing reversed the trend that started this summer. The bulls have a data point to answer. (Newcomer)

• One Semafor columnist says debt will not be what pops the AI bubble. Everything in AI is bottlenecked, from chips to the refrigeration units cooling GPUs, so revenues are held back by supply, not drowned by debt. Efficiency gains keep birthing hungrier use cases, the old Jevons Paradox at work. The columnist even calls Anthropic's claimed 85% gross margins "a cash cow business" that will service its debt. (Semafor)

Power Moves

• A leaked email told immigration judges to keep collecting an asylum fee a judge had already voided. Twenty-one days after a federal court threw out the rules behind the annual asylum fee, Chief Immigration Judge Teresa L. Riley emailed every immigration judge in the country saying the fee "remains in effect." The email's subject line read "injunction - please read," but there was no injunction at all. (Migrant Insider)

How We Live Together

• Homelessness is mostly about collapsed relationships, not the usual three suspects. A 2023 UC San Francisco study found 90% of homeless people are single adults with no friends or family to ask for help, and 63% said social conflict or not wanting to be a burden pushed them out of their last housing. Galloway's read: mental illness, addiction, and cost matter, but the through line is people losing each other. (Prof G)

• Loneliness hits your body like smoking 15 cigarettes a day. That is the Surgeon General's 2023 verdict, with social isolation raising premature-mortality risk 29%. People with strong community ties are 2.6 times more likely to report good physical health and 3.2 times more likely to report good mental health. Meanwhile a Gallup survey finds most Americans feel little responsibility to help their own community. (Prof G)

• A grieving 71-year-old found her way back through baseball and strangers. After losing her 27-year-old son Wyatt to muscular dystrophy, Rhenda Strub bought two Seattle Mariners season tickets and posted on Facebook inviting strangers to join her. Her inbox filled with people carrying similar grief. Now she has a whole community of people who just want to share a hot dog and a ballgame. (Prof G)

Culture & The Zeitgeist

• Sally Rooney's books can no longer be sold in the UK. Her publisher Faber stopped supplying them after Rooney pledged royalties to Palestine Action, a group banned in Britain in July 2025, deciding that paying her could violate the terror ban. Shops can sell the copies they have but cannot reorder. The result: a run on Normal People and Intermezzo at London bookshops. (Feed Me)

• London's oldest restaurant is being preserved as a landmark. The National Trust will safeguard Rules, established in 1798, which has outlasted 9 British monarchs and 45 prime ministers while changing hands only three times. Its game-heavy menu and antler-covered interior are reportedly little changed since the 19th century. (Feed Me)

• Hudson's new design hotel proves taste is the product now, culture still is not. The Pocketbook, in an old textile factory, courts the creative class with Eckhaus Latta robes and a rock on a rope instead of a Do Not Disturb sign. But at $500-plus a night, its restaurant closes Mondays and Tuesdays, leaving fully booked guests to fend for themselves in a sleepy town. (Feed Me)

• Northern Ontario's place names are 9,000 years older than European contact. Abitibi, Temagami, and Temiskaming are Cree and Anishinaabe words from the Nipissing Nation, laid over land that runs deeper still: the Ottawa River cuts through a 400-million-year-old rift valley. Temiskaming itself means "deep water with fast winds." (The Republic of Letters)

• One family's parenting diary survived four countries and a Nazi-era escape. Writer Leah Bhabha inherited a worn book where four generations of women recorded their babies' lives, starting with her great-grandmother Mathilde. Her mother smuggled it out of Nazi Germany tucked into a bag. Births are now logged in Germany, India, England, and the United States. (Spread the Jelly)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• The town of Cobalt was once Canada's biggest silver mine, and the writer's birthplace Timmins one of the largest gold mines in the world, with the scars still visible from the air. (The Republic of Letters)

• Tin Can, a Seattle startup, is building a landline-style Wi-Fi phone for kids, backed by Greylock and Air Mail's viral social lead, on the bet that parents will pay to keep children off smartphones. (Feed Me)

• Graza, the comically oversized olive oil brand, made a 1.3-pound tub of hummus sold only at Costco. (Feed Me)

• Black Christmas (1974), the cozy Christmas slasher, was directed by Bob Clark, the same director behind A Christmas Story. (Tubi)

• The 33,000 photos on Leah Bhabha's phone include her daughters in an estimated 80 to 90 percent of them, a perfect snapshot of how modern parenthood runs on the camera roll. (Spread the Jelly)

Friday, October 16, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 4+ days: how long Katie Zacharia survived as Trump's press secretary. After two brutal Fox News interviews, Trump fired her, setting a new record for the shortest top-spokesman tenure and beating the old 11-day mark.

• 22%: the time-to-exhaustion boost cyclists got from just 10 grams of carbs per hour instead of none. Researchers estimate the real sweet spot is closer to 107 grams per hour.

• 9 watts: the extra power endurance athletes held in a time trial after four hours of cycling when they fueled at 100 grams of carbs per hour instead of 60.

• 90 minutes: the long-run threshold where durable runners separate from fading ones. Runners used to 90-plus-minute sessions lost only about half as much running economy to fatigue as those who ran shorter.

• 3 miles, 45 minutes: Tanner Garrity's ruck across the Williamsburg Bridge, weighted pack and all. The battle prayer of every rucker: "Get this shit off me."

Quotes of the Day

• "Before this movie, you might've been the hottest Nathan Fielder fan. But after this movie ... all the baddies will be on high alert." (Hunter Harris's seatmate Peyton, on You Can See Everything at NYFF)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Explosive CBS News audio: Bari Weiss's handpicked foreign editor Shayndi Raice clashed with reporters, threatened to fire them for "insubordination," and called the Gaza death toll a "magic number." Also in the mix: Lesley Stahl nearly quit "60 Minutes." (Status News)

• "Girls" is coming back to HBO, and the news was so big Hunter Harris discussed it in therapy. (Hung Up)

• What does your drink order say about you? Bartender Dani Brand's field notes from a downtown dive's closing shift have thoughts. Vodka soda, Negroni, Jack and Coke: she's keeping score. (InsideHook)

• Hannah Chamberlain of SpiritedLA on her "exquisitely chilled" martini, her favorite airport bar, and the unlikely establishment where she's a regular. (InsideHook)

"I Am Tony" runs through January 3: AGHDRA fills a cavernous dark room with an 85 minute floor-to-ceiling projection of digitally animated oceanic waves set to remixed Isley Brothers and Roberta Flack; BEN GAZZARA restages the Taxi Driver finale with Black actors per Paul Schrader's original script, with a Stevie Wonder cameo in one loop. Watching European tourists earnestly decode Michael Blackson and Erykah Badu freestyling "for the D" in The White Album is its own exhibit. (
InsideHook
Emma Cline's Switzy might be her best book yet.

The novel follows David Hastings, a retired executive traveling to Zurich for assisted suicide while his memory deteriorates. Longlisted for the Booker Prize and quieter than The Guest, it is sharply written, contemplative, and unafraid of the totality of a life. (
InsideHook
Laurel Pantin is done pretending competitiveness is a flaw.

The Earl Earl essay traces her shift from twenties jealousy (she skipped bowling because she sucked at it) to competing with herself: skiing, spring tennis lessons, muscle mass, sleep, cardiovascular age. Since turning 40 and getting sober, health (not wellness, not thinness) has become the project. "You only get one short little life." (
Earl Earl
Quick Hits & Curiosities

Pablo Manríquez is giving away a 1968 sea-foam-green Brother de Luxe typewriter to his 100th paid subscriber. He has acquired seven machines since July (two to keep, four to sell on eBay) and says typewriting will be an important part of his news work in 2027. (
Pablo Reports
The Library of Congress dropped nine high-res images on Flickr last night, and at least one newsletter writer is fully obsessed. (
Pablo Reports

Cameron Winter's Live at Carnegie Hall has been on repeat all week: songs from Heavy Metal plus three new tracks, revamped at the piano, recorded at his mythical December 2025 show. One lyric: "I don't like what happened to Jesus // But I sure do like Saturday morning." (
InsideHook

A startup founded by crypto enthusiasts is building a real-time Misery Index from prediction-market data. The classic version (unemployment plus inflation) has called presidential elections since LBJ's era, but it runs on backward-looking monthly data. Futures can't be far behind. (
Semafor
Lex Fridman visited Taiwan with Jensen Huang: huge crowds of engineers, night-market street food, days of conversation, some of it on video. (
Founder Fridays

Vinegar braised chicken and leeks: sear bone-in thighs, soften leeks and garlic, deglaze with white wine, chicken stock, and sherry vinegar, then finish uncovered in the oven. Serve over rice or crusty bread to catch the sauce. (
Side Dish
Friday, October 16, 2026 - Afternoon Edition
Today's Numbers
: accounts X says it deleted this week that were tied to foreign influence operations aimed at the US midterms, possibly the real reason your feed feels quieter
1 billion
: ChatGPT's monthly active users, whose chatbot sessions advertisers can now inject ads into, targeted by email, phone number, or the prompts they type
: the surge in agentic shopping traffic over 45 days, per cybersecurity firm Cheq, as AI shopping assistants go mainstream this holiday season

: Gen Z's average art spending, per an Art Basel and UBS survey, more than double the boomers' $156,000 (dealers question the survey, but 13% of young collectors still dropped over $1 million this year)
500 million
: tokens per week that Meta's Muse sells for $20 a month, a number growth expert Elena Verna calls meaningless because the AI industry prices everything in "arcade money"
: the price of the Home Alone sundae at the Plaza Hotel, available only a few more days before the hotel closes for a four-year facade renovation
6 of 8
: Gen Z Trump voters in a Navigator Research focus group who now give the president a D or F, with a 29-year-old Floridian saying everything got worse and he will back Democrats
Quotes of the Day

"You may think you're there to exert control, but you're really there to be SHOP DOMMED, or told what to do by people who know more than you." (Emilia Petrarca, on the power dynamics of luxury retail)
"Taste is great, but you can buy taste, you can't buy culture." (J Lee, Feed Me's restaurant critic, on why Hudson's new Pocketbook Hotel can never recreate what the late Lil' Deb's Oasis built)
"People might be doing lowercase to signal that they're not AI." (Adam Aleksic, internet linguist, on why all-lowercase typing is back)
"I know I didn't commit any crime." (Elizabeth Holmes, in Nathan Fielder's new documentary "You Can See Everything")
"Mommy and daddy are playing nice again." (Meta's Alexandr Wang, on Meta's new open-weight model running on Apple Macs)
The AI Trade Under Stress
Character.ai
is going bankrupt, and it looks like the AI bubble's first domino.

The company burned piles of cash running its product, brought in little revenue, and ran up enormous legal bills after harming users, per its bankruptcy court narrative. Cost-cutting did not save it, and Disney has reportedly offered $20 million to license some of its IP, a year after sending a cease-and-desist. The company was valued at $1 billion in 2023 after a $150 million raise led by a16z. (
404 Media
Cops can now identify your house from a single interior photo.

An AI tool called Raven, made by Graylark Technologies (formerly GeoSpy), pulls from sites like Zillow and Airbnb to match an interior shot to a specific home nearly instantly. The LAPD and Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office already bought access, and Raven just added interior analysis features. It is intelligence-agency tech, now off the shelf for local police. (
404 Media
AI token spending has been flat for two straight months.

Fresh Ramp business-spending data shows growth in AI token spending stalled, likely because frontier prices fell and models got more efficient. New customer growth has dropped sharply, and while OpenAI narrowed Anthropic's lead and xAI got a GrokBot bump, nothing reversed the trend that started this summer. The bulls have a data point to answer. (
Newcomer
One Semafor columnist says debt will not be what pops the AI bubble.

Everything in AI is bottlenecked, from chips to the refrigeration units cooling GPUs, so revenues are held back by supply, not drowned by debt. Efficiency gains keep birthing hungrier use cases, the old Jevons Paradox at work. The columnist even calls Anthropic's claimed 85% gross margins "a cash cow business" that will service its debt. (
Semafor
Power Moves
A leaked email told immigration judges to keep collecting an asylum fee a judge had already voided.

Twenty-one days after a federal court threw out the rules behind the annual asylum fee, Chief Immigration Judge Teresa L. Riley emailed every immigration judge in the country saying the fee "remains in effect." The email's subject line read "injunction - please read," but there was no injunction at all. (
Migrant Insider
How We Live Together
Homelessness is mostly about collapsed relationships, not the usual three suspects.

A 2023 UC San Francisco study found 90% of homeless people are single adults with no friends or family to ask for help, and 63% said social conflict or not wanting to be a burden pushed them out of their last housing. Galloway's read: mental illness, addiction, and cost matter, but the through line is people losing each other. (
Prof G
Loneliness hits your body like smoking 15 cigarettes a day.

That is the Surgeon General's 2023 verdict, with social isolation raising premature-mortality risk 29%. People with strong community ties are 2.6 times more likely to report good physical health and 3.2 times more likely to report good mental health. Meanwhile a Gallup survey finds most Americans feel little responsibility to help their own community. (
Prof G
A grieving 71-year-old found her way back through baseball and strangers.

After losing her 27-year-old son Wyatt to muscular dystrophy, Rhenda Strub bought two Seattle Mariners season tickets and posted on Facebook inviting strangers to join her. Her inbox filled with people carrying similar grief. Now she has a whole community of people who just want to share a hot dog and a ballgame. (
Prof G
Culture & The Zeitgeist
Sally Rooney's books can no longer be sold in the UK.

Her publisher Faber stopped supplying them after Rooney pledged royalties to Palestine Action, a group banned in Britain in July 2025, deciding that paying her could violate the terror ban. Shops can sell the copies they have but cannot reorder. The result: a run on Normal People and Intermezzo at London bookshops. (
Feed Me
London's oldest restaurant is being preserved as a landmark.

The National Trust will safeguard Rules, established in 1798, which has outlasted 9 British monarchs and 45 prime ministers while changing hands only three times. Its game-heavy menu and antler-covered interior are reportedly little changed since the 19th century. (
Feed Me
Hudson's new design hotel proves taste is the product now, culture still is not.

The Pocketbook, in an old textile factory, courts the creative class with Eckhaus Latta robes and a rock on a rope instead of a Do Not Disturb sign. But at $500-plus a night, its restaurant closes Mondays and Tuesdays, leaving fully booked guests to fend for themselves in a sleepy town. (
Feed Me
Northern Ontario's place names are 9,000 years older than European contact.

Abitibi, Temagami, and Temiskaming are Cree and Anishinaabe words from the Nipissing Nation, laid over land that runs deeper still: the Ottawa River cuts through a 400-million-year-old rift valley. Temiskaming itself means "deep water with fast winds." (
The Republic of Letters
One family's parenting diary survived four countries and a Nazi-era escape.

Writer Leah Bhabha inherited a worn book where four generations of women recorded their babies' lives, starting with her great-grandmother Mathilde. Her mother smuggled it out of Nazi Germany tucked into a bag. Births are now logged in Germany, India, England, and the United States. (
Spread the Jelly
Quick Hits & Curiosities
The town of Cobalt was once Canada's biggest silver mine, and the writer's birthplace Timmins one of the largest gold mines in the world, with the scars still visible from the air. (
The Republic of Letters

Tin Can, a Seattle startup, is building a landline-style Wi-Fi phone for kids, backed by Greylock and Air Mail's viral social lead, on the bet that parents will pay to keep children off smartphones. (
Feed Me
Graza, the comically oversized olive oil brand, made a 1.3-pound tub of hummus sold only at Costco. (
Feed Me
Black Christmas (1974), the cozy Christmas slasher, was directed by Bob Clark, the same director behind A Christmas Story. (
Tubi
The 33,000 photos on Leah Bhabha's phone include her daughters in an estimated 80 to 90 percent of them, a perfect snapshot of how modern parenthood runs on the camera roll. (
Spread the Jelly
Friday, October 16, 2026 - Evening Edition
Today's Numbers
4+ days

: how long Katie Zacharia survived as Trump's press secretary. After two brutal Fox News interviews, Trump fired her, setting a new record for the shortest top-spokesman tenure and beating the old 11-day mark.
: the time-to-exhaustion boost cyclists got from just 10 grams of carbs per hour instead of none. Researchers estimate the real sweet spot is closer to 107 grams per hour.
9 watts
: the extra power endurance athletes held in a time trial after four hours of cycling when they fueled at 100 grams of carbs per hour instead of 60.
90 minutes
: the long-run threshold where durable runners separate from fading ones. Runners used to 90-plus-minute sessions lost only about half as much running economy to fatigue as those who ran shorter.
3 miles, 45 minutes
: Tanner Garrity's ruck across the Williamsburg Bridge, weighted pack and all. The battle prayer of every rucker: "Get this shit off me."
Quotes of the Day
"Before this movie, you might've been the hottest Nathan Fielder fan. But after this movie ... all the baddies will be on high alert." (Hunter Harris's seatmate Peyton, on
You Can See Everything
at NYFF)
Quick Hits & Curiosities

Explosive CBS News audio: Bari Weiss's handpicked foreign editor Shayndi Raice clashed with reporters, threatened to fire them for "insubordination," and called the Gaza death toll a "magic number." Also in the mix: Lesley Stahl nearly quit "60 Minutes." (
Status News
"Girls" is coming back to HBO, and the news was so big Hunter Harris discussed it in therapy. (
Hung Up
What does your drink order say about you? Bartender Dani Brand's field notes from a downtown dive's closing shift have thoughts. Vodka soda, Negroni, Jack and Coke: she's keeping score. (
InsideHook
Hannah Chamberlain of SpiritedLA on her "exquisitely chilled" martini, her favorite airport bar, and the unlikely establishment where she's a regular. (

entries.title: The Mystery-Price AI, the Cult of Comfort Horror, and the North That Stays in You
entries.description: A strange, excellent Friday: AI companies are charging in imaginary currencies, chatbots are being asked to stop cosplaying as people, Hudson is debating whether taste can manufacture culture, and the internet may have mistaken a bot purge for a bombing story. Meanwhile, there is chili.
entries.body:
A strange, excellent Friday: AI companies are charging in imaginary currencies, chatbots are being asked to stop cosplaying as people, Hudson is debating whether taste can manufacture culture, and the internet may have mistaken a bot purge for a bombing story. Meanwhile, there is chili.

Best links

• AI pricing has entered arcade economics. Lenny’s Newsletter cross-posts Elena Verna’s teardown of Grok, Muse, Lovable, ElevenLabs, ChatGPT, and Anthropic. The shared problem: “100 credits” or “500 million tokens” sound precise while telling a customer almost nothing about what they can actually get done. The useful product lesson is simple: make cost understandable, predictable, and tied to an outcome—not merely to a bigger number.

• Maybe the bot should stop saying “I.” WIRED Backchannel previews Sherry Turkle’s new warning about people becoming dangerously enmeshed with machines posing as tutors, friends, colleagues, and lovers. A good design question hiding inside the polemic: when an interface borrows the voice of a person, what obligations does it create?

• The “Russian bots went quiet because data centers got bombed” story gets a skeptical autopsy. Garbage Day points to a more mundane possibility: X began rolling out liveness checks around the same time, and the platform also deleted thousands of accounts tied to foreign influence operations. The larger takeaway is less cinematic and more unnerving: the people shaping the feed may be the platforms themselves.

Worth reading

• A documentary about Elizabeth Holmes that turns its camera back on the camera. The New Yorker reviews Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything, made after Holmes invited the filmmakers into her home before prison. The review’s hook is the transparency of the transaction: Holmes wants to correct the public narrative; Fielder’s method is to make power, manipulation, and self-deception visible in real time.

• The north that stays in you. The Republic of Letters runs Terrance Lane Millet’s luminous meditation on Northern Ontario, fireweed, family, memory, and the idea that our minds are made of the same mineralities as our bones. Best image: a life’s landscape is like a deep river—what it hides is part of what makes it home.

• Luxury as submission. Emilia Petrarca argues that the fantasy of luxury retail is not control but surrender: the customer enters expecting to command, then lets a store “shop dom” them—provided the store knows enough to give them pleasure. The airborne pizza is merely the decoy.

Food & places

• Go Upstate, apparently immediately. Feed Me makes a case for peak foliage, Rhinebeck’s Sheep and Wool Festival, Hudson’s Red Dot, and the new Pocketbook Hotel. The sharp cultural distinction: taste can be purchased, but culture has to be built. Lil’ Deb’s Oasis did the latter; a perfect Eckhaus Latta robe can only gesture at it.

• The dinner to make when the garden is giving up. Side Dish offers vinegar-braised chicken thighs with leeks, garlic, white wine, stock, sherry vinegar, and butter. Brown the chicken, soften the leeks, make the glossy sauce, finish in a 425°F oven, and serve with something absorbent. It is specifically designed for the late-season abundance of a neglected garden.

• Weekend chili, with a side of logistics. NYT Cooking recommends a slow-cooker chili built around ground beef, beans, paprika, cumin, cayenne, soy sauce, and Worcestershire—big-batch, freezer-friendly, and almost entirely hands-off. Also filed under “ideas worth stealing”: a $100 dinner party with no utensils, anchored by naan, roti, and aloo gosht.

Internet oddities & cultural artifacts

• The free-streaming comfort-horror syllabus. Perfectly Imperfect asked readers for the horror movies they use like weighted blankets, then assembled a Tubi guide. The strongest cluster: Midsommar for beautiful dread, Re-Animator for “classic ’80s homoerotic bromance,” Black Christmas for cozy slasher lighting, Deep Red for stylish practical effects, and Nobuhiko Obayashi’s House for total sensory derangement.

• Cops, Zillow, and the washer-dryer interior. 404 Media reports on Raven, an AI tool that can use clues in an interior photo to identify a specific home, apparently drawing on sites such as Zillow and Airbnb. The same roundup says Character.ai’s bankruptcy is an early warning for an AI business built on expensive inference, weak revenue, and serious legal exposure.

• Smutstep exists. 404 Media’s roundup also points to DARQ DAGR, a dubstep musician whose viral niche is putting horny spoken lines over aggressive beats. The internet continues to reward the person willing to commit hardest to the bit.

One-liners

• “I’m not really selling them 100 units of value. I’m selling them 100 units of mystery.” — Elena Verna, via Lenny’s Newsletter

• “Taste is great, but you can buy taste, you can’t buy culture.” — J Lee, via Feed Me

• “Damn, this outfit is like ten bands.” — a line collected by After School, describing the new “Ball Hog” menswear aesthetic

• “The call is coming from inside the house.” — Garbage Day, on blaming every bad post on Russian bots

• The Plaza’s $370 Home Alone sundae remains an excellent argument for room service as performance art. — Feed Me

entries.title: Zero-click spyware in your ads, Elizabeth Holmes meets Nathan Fielder, gasoline up 9.1% - Saturday, October 17, 2026
entries.body:
Saturday, October 17, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 4,000,000,000: the Android phones and iPhones that get their local time from one text file, the time zone database, kept current in his spare time by Paul Eggert, a UCLA lecturer. Of 251 changes to the file in the last year, 218 were his.

• 5,408 of 5,409: changes to sudo between 2008 and 2018 made by one person, Todd Miller, who has maintained the command that gives you admin rights on a Mac or Linux server since the early 1990s.

• $57: a month, what Denis Pushkarev raised in donations to keep core-js going, the library that lets new JavaScript work in old browsers and runs on about half of the thousand busiest websites.

• 25: years between the line that became Shellshock going into bash and anyone reporting it. Every change in bash's public history is Chet Ramey's.

• 30%: of nineteenth-century cabinet ministers who were Old Etonians. The small elite that ran the biggest empire on earth woke up late, drank copiously, and spent their evenings networking, because that was the work.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Anne Carson won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature, and the LRB rounded up the poems it has published by her since 1993, including one now on vinyl read by Gwendoline Christie (LRB)

• At West Virginia's Green Bank Observatory, the radio telescope is so sensitive that only diesel vehicles are allowed near it, because spark plugs throw off radio interference (Road and Track)
