morning.body:
Saturday, October 17, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• 9.1%: the one-month jump in gasoline prices in September, pushing yearly inflation to 3.7 percent while the White House kept cheering the economy.

• 5: days White House press secretary Katie Zacharia lasted before getting the boot, which still beats the Scaramucci benchmark of 11 days.

• $100,000: the American Express bill Kimberly Guilfoyle allegedly asked a wealthy Trump donor to pay off, offering to use her political connections to help with his legal and tax problems, per The Wall Street Journal.

Quotes of the Day

• "When your neighbor's house is on fire, buy gasoline from the arsonist and tell the homeowner to stop spraying water." (Counterpoint, on the Trump administration's diesel deal with Russia)

• "Our social personality is a creation of the minds of others." (Marcel Proust, quoted in David Roberts' essay on rereading Mrs. Dalloway)

• "People have become dangerously enmeshed with chatbots." (Steven Levy, reporting Sherry Turkle's warning in WIRED)

AI & The Machines

The Wikipedians who thought AI would come and go were wrong. In the age of AI Overviews, Wikipedia usage is declining, but the real loss may be bigger than traffic. Richard Cooke argues the damage is existential: a world that stops consulting the encyclopedia loses a shared reference point, not just pageviews. (WIRED)

The ads are watching back, and now they bite. Citizen Lab has released the first hard technical evidence of mercenary spyware spreading through targeted online ads. An Israeli ad firm allegedly turned the programmatic ad stack into delivery infrastructure, with confirmed infections on at least 45 Al Jazeera devices and tainted impressions reaching networks tied to NATO, the United Nations, and government agencies across Europe. Victims saw nothing; some may never have seen an ad at all. Google and industry bodies have since cut the firm off, but the machinery that made it possible is still running. (WIRED)

The Culture

Elizabeth Holmes meets her match in Nathan Fielder. Sean Monahan reviews You Can See Everything, Fielder's three-hour documentary built from a month inside Holmes' home before she reported to federal prison. The film turns recursive: Amanda Seyfried, who played Holmes in The Dropout, re-performs scenes Fielder reconstructed from his own notes, and nobody can agree on what actually happened. Holmes' husband, armed with power of attorney and posting under her name on X, demanded a cut of the profits, then dropped it. Monahan's read: intent is unknowable, the media sells partial truths just like the fraudsters do, and the whole thing is a portrait of an era that scans instead of reads. It arrives with a techlash film wave that also includes Sorkin's Social Network follow-up, Guadagnino's OpenAI drama, and a Gibney Musk documentary, alongside the data-center backlash and the OpenAI and Anthropic IPOs. (8Ball)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• The team behind Godzilla Minus Zero built their kaiju roars by parking speakers on top of an outdoor dam and blasting them; passing bystanders were not prepared. (WIRED)

• Researchers gave tiny rescue drones cat-like whiskers so they can feel their way through the dark, borrowing the trick from nocturnal animals. (WIRED)

• Gen Z rediscovered HBO's Girls, the show that once stood in for everything wrong with white millennial women, and gave it a second life. (WIRED)

midday.body:
Saturday, October 17, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• 75,000: years ago a Neanderthal known as Shanidar A took a spear through the shoulder blade and heart, possibly the earliest known spear murder in Earth's history.

• $250,000: the reservation Tesla wants for its "flying" Roadster, even though its own fine print admits the car might never be delivered.

• $14,000: the price of a numbered Barrie x Damien Hirst cashmere blanket.

• $1.992T: the FY2026 federal deficit, the third largest in US history and the 25th straight year of red ink.

• 1,042,652: shipping containers the Port of LA handled in September, its fourth straight record month (371,000 went back out empty).

• 56.7%: the drop in Chinese visitors to Japan, even as Japan's Jan-Aug tourism spending surplus hit about $28.2B.

Quotes of the Day

• "Writing a hard problem down keeps my head clear and sharpens the thinking." (Vas Frolik, Taipei design engineer, on his productivity trick)

• "I was a pharmacist! But a pharmacist who loved dressing up." (Patrizio Cappelli, founder of the E. & G. Cappelli necktie workshop, on his career before ties)

• "Don't Taper. Peak!" (Coach Greg McMillan, arguing most marathoners cut training volume too much before race day)

• "Is it possible that unknown to the public there were multiple launches of artificial satellites long before Sputnik... Or rather, do the current findings represent detection of a non-human technosignature?" (Researchers, on unexplained objects spotted on pre-1957 photographic plates)

Media Mayhem

CBS News is eating itself alive. Status got audio of Bari Weiss's handpicked foreign editor, Shayndi Raice, threatening to fire journalists for "insubordination" and calling the Gaza death toll a "magic number" during an explosive all-hands. The chaos follows a separate clash that nearly pushed Lesley Stahl out of 60 Minutes, all over Israel coverage. Two newsroom blowups in one week, and the network's foreign desk is in open revolt. (Status)

The Internet

The great Russian bot collapse never happened. When Ukraine struck Yandex data centers, the internet declared that Russian bot activity had crumbled, with one viral claim of a 54% traffic drop. Jeremiah Johnson shows the numbers were junk: Cloudflare measured web crawlers, not influence ops, the "54% drop" flips to a 109% rise by shifting the time window, and malicious bots simply moved to other hosts. Russian banking and food delivery apps crashed; the troll farms kept posting. (The Argument)

Science & Gadgets

One photo of your living room is all cops need now. A 404 Media investigation looks at Raven, the AI tool formerly known as Geospy, which can pinpoint a specific house from a single interior photo. Judges are already weighing whether that counts as an unconstitutional search, and a related case involves an AI-generated video introduced in a manslaughter trial. The geolocation genie is not going back in the bottle. (404 Media)

Money Moves

When the chipmaker funds its own customers, is it demand? Matt Stoller digs into Firmus, an Nvidia-backed data center operator that shelved its IPO after investors balked at a $30B valuation. The uncomfortable question: when Nvidia bankrolls the customers buying Nvidia chips, the boom starts to look like circular financing. The AI infrastructure trade keeps getting harder to explain. (Weekend Briefing)

Style & Shopping

Naples is a retail time machine. Louis Cheslaw reports from a city where Maradona's face still covers the walls 35 years after his last match, bus tickets are paper slips from tabacchi shops, and the shopping ethos is "incredible goods, presented indifferently." Highlights: EUR65 gloves that cost triple in Paris, healthy racks of discontinued Aldens and Edward Greens, and a custom shirtmaker priced like a secret. (Wardrobe)

Sports

Bank your sleep before race day. Six Minute Mile's marathon special says to add about 30 extra minutes of sleep per night in race week, a practice sleep coaches call "sleep banking." Sleep specialist Dr. Chris Winter says weeks of rest matter far more than one anxious pre-race night. Combined with the taper rule (cut volume 40 to 60 percent, keep intensity), it is the rare performance advice that costs nothing. (Six Minute Mile)

Culture

Hayes Warner found religion at a Studio City sushi counter. The singer and Shards actress says Tomoki Sushi converted her after years of refusing raw fish, calling it the best sushi in Los Angeles. Warner also made her acting debut in Ryan Murphy's Hulu adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis's The Shards, contributing two original songs. A strong entry in the endless LA sushi debate. (Perfectly Imperfect)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Meta suddenly banned ByteDance advertising, a move that surprised even people inside Meta and sparked talk of TikTok retaliation. (Status)

• Vas Frolik runs a Mac mini M5 as a home server to host AI models locally, keeping his laptop free for design work. (Workspaces)

• Smiskis, tiny glow-in-the-dark figurines in random poses, are "kind of like Elf on the Shelf, but without the pressure." (Perfectly Imperfect)

• Cold Diet Coke cans pressed to the face are Hayes Warner's depuff trick ("I won't say that this was dermatologist recommended"). (Perfectly Imperfect)

• A Nevada traffic stop turned up about 30 pounds of fentanyl, roughly 7 million potentially lethal doses, plus 677 pounds of meth. (NLDR Media)

• Amazon warned it could close 15 New York City warehouses and move thousands of workers out if the Delivery Protection Act passes. (NLDR Media)

• Projections say 100,000 American churches could close or be repurposed over the next decade. (Weekend Briefing)

• A community member's pick for the weekend: Wim Wenders' Paris, Texas (1984), "the biggest fumble ever to grace mankind." (Perfectly Imperfect)

afternoon.body:
Saturday, October 17, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

• 54: the number of Senate races where Democrats currently lead in FLIPR's polling averages, which would produce a D 54-R 46 map if every poll turned out exactly right

• 40,000: FLIPR Deluxe simulations that Nate Silver sorted into three buckets: no systematic bias, polls overrating Democrats, and polls overrating Republicans

• 3-in-4: the chance FLIPR gives Democrats of flipping the Senate, since Mary Peltola, James Talarico, and Sherrod Brown have led in the vast majority of their polls

Quotes of the Day

• "The ones that try hard not to be political are political by saying, 'We love the status quo.'" (Toni Morrison, defending in 1983 the idea that all good art is political)

• "You'd always rather have a narrow polling lead than a narrow polling deficit." (Nate Silver, stress-testing the Democrats' Senate map for polling error)

Art & Ideas

Is all art political? Yes, but please don't use that word. The Republic of Letters sends critic Thaddeus Thomas from Middle-earth to the Antebellum South to the Left Bank to answer the old question, and lands on yes: politics is everywhere once you stop using the word the way cable news uses it. Morrison's version: all good art shows us things as they are, even when disguised as a hobbit in a hole. Tolkien's version: fantasy grants "recovery," a wiped-clear view of things as we are meant to see them, and recognizing a tree as a living being instead of lumber is a rejection of modern industrial values. The sharpest cut is literary: Terry Brooks's The Sword of Shannara (1977), which rescued fantasy as a commercial genre, is all window dressing, a simulacrum that refers only to Tolkien, while Robert Jordan's The Wheel of Time actually injected institutional paranoia and maddening power into the trappings. Even thin work gets rescued by the reader, every kid who loved Shannara smuggled meaning into it anyway. (The Republic of Letters)

Shopping & Style

The week's commerce news, condensed. After much industry gossip, ex-Dior Homme designer Kim Jones announced a new namesake project arriving early next year. Apple dropped a suite of home products under the HomeView banner, and the flagship home-display-slash-control-panel is available for preorder now. Noah's latest Timex collab, the round and tasteful Boatswain watch, sold out immediately. Menswear's most prolific designer, Jonathan Anderson, keeps the affordable fall collabs coming with new capsules for Uniqlo and Ugg, and the headline gear of the week is tweed Merrell hiking shoes in a Barbour collab. (InsideHook)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Liv Boeree joined Mike Solana on the Pirate Wires pod to argue NYC is protecting "illegal criminals" while removing horse-drawn carriages from Central Park (Pirate Wires)

• The same episode asks why you can no longer be mean to Claude, whether we should be pushing d/acc after a cyber attack on a grocery store, and compares the hosts' X algorithms (Pirate Wires)

• Shane Gillis's SNL monologue made women mad, Metallica's James Hetfield took hate online for not taking a side, and Kelly Clarkson is battling a small business in Brooklyn (Pirate Wires)

• Girls is returning to HBO, and Paolo Sandoval expects subscriptions to skyrocket, at least (InsideHook)

• Panayiota Soutis dropped her Wednesday booklist from a Meeting of an Irregular Gourmet Society: 21 pieces of printed material for Cremer's library table, from Buffalo Zine's Fashion's Kitchen to Bourdain's Appetites (tgite)

evening.body:
Saturday, October 17, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 4,000,000,000: the Android phones and iPhones that get their local time from one text file, the time zone database, kept current in his spare time by Paul Eggert, a UCLA lecturer. Of 251 changes to the file in the last year, 218 were his.

• 5,408 of 5,409: changes to sudo between 2008 and 2018 made by one person, Todd Miller, who has maintained the command that gives you admin rights on a Mac or Linux server since the early 1990s.

• $57: a month, what Denis Pushkarev raised in donations to keep core-js going, the library that lets new JavaScript work in old browsers and runs on about half of the thousand busiest websites.

• 25: years between the line that became Shellshock going into bash and anyone reporting it. Every change in bash's public history is Chet Ramey's.

• 30%: of nineteenth-century cabinet ministers who were Old Etonians. The small elite that ran the biggest empire on earth woke up late, drank copiously, and spent their evenings networking, because that was the work.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Anne Carson won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature, and the LRB rounded up the poems it has published by her since 1993, including one now on vinyl read by Gwendoline Christie (LRB)

• At West Virginia's Green Bank Observatory, the radio telescope is so sensitive that only diesel vehicles are allowed near it, because spark plugs throw off radio interference (Road and Track)

full.body:
Saturday, October 17, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• 9.1%: the one-month jump in gasoline prices in September, pushing yearly inflation to 3.7 percent while the White House kept cheering the economy.

• 5: days White House press secretary Katie Zacharia lasted before getting the boot, which still beats the Scaramucci benchmark of 11 days.

• $100,000: the American Express bill Kimberly Guilfoyle allegedly asked a wealthy Trump donor to pay off, offering to use her political connections to help with his legal and tax problems, per The Wall Street Journal.

Quotes of the Day

• "When your neighbor's house is on fire, buy gasoline from the arsonist and tell the homeowner to stop spraying water." (Counterpoint, on the Trump administration's diesel deal with Russia)

• "Our social personality is a creation of the minds of others." (Marcel Proust, quoted in David Roberts' essay on rereading Mrs. Dalloway)

• "People have become dangerously enmeshed with chatbots." (Steven Levy, reporting Sherry Turkle's warning in WIRED)

AI & The Machines

The Wikipedians who thought AI would come and go were wrong. In the age of AI Overviews, Wikipedia usage is declining, but the real loss may be bigger than traffic. Richard Cooke argues the damage is existential: a world that stops consulting the encyclopedia loses a shared reference point, not just pageviews. (WIRED)

The ads are watching back, and now they bite. Citizen Lab has released the first hard technical evidence of mercenary spyware spreading through targeted online ads. An Israeli ad firm allegedly turned the programmatic ad stack into delivery infrastructure, with confirmed infections on at least 45 Al Jazeera devices and tainted impressions reaching networks tied to NATO, the United Nations, and government agencies across Europe. Victims saw nothing; some may never have seen an ad at all. Google and industry bodies have since cut the firm off, but the machinery that made it possible is still running. (WIRED)

The Culture

Elizabeth Holmes meets her match in Nathan Fielder. Sean Monahan reviews You Can See Everything, Fielder's three-hour documentary built from a month inside Holmes' home before she reported to federal prison. The film turns recursive: Amanda Seyfried, who played Holmes in The Dropout, re-performs scenes Fielder reconstructed from his own notes, and nobody can agree on what actually happened. Holmes' husband, armed with power of attorney and posting under her name on X, demanded a cut of the profits, then dropped it. Monahan's read: intent is unknowable, the media sells partial truths just like the fraudsters do, and the whole thing is a portrait of an era that scans instead of reads. It arrives with a techlash film wave that also includes Sorkin's Social Network follow-up, Guadagnino's OpenAI drama, and a Gibney Musk documentary, alongside the data-center backlash and the OpenAI and Anthropic IPOs. (8Ball)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• The team behind Godzilla Minus Zero built their kaiju roars by parking speakers on top of an outdoor dam and blasting them; passing bystanders were not prepared. (WIRED)

• Researchers gave tiny rescue drones cat-like whiskers so they can feel their way through the dark, borrowing the trick from nocturnal animals. (WIRED)

• Gen Z rediscovered HBO's Girls, the show that once stood in for everything wrong with white millennial women, and gave it a second life. (WIRED)

entries.title: The Flying Roadster, a Neanderthal Murder, and the Case for Fennel
entries.body:
Saturday, October 17, 2026

The mail arrives today with one governing suspicion: reality is already stranger than the pitch deck. A “flying” Tesla that mostly flies for a few seconds, a 75,000-year-old wound that may be the earliest known spear murder, and a pasta newsletter quietly solving the no-onion problem all make the same case for looking twice.

Best links

• The Saturday Selection — Why is this interesting? A compact rabbit-hole menu: Victorian elites who partied all night and still ran an empire, the diesel-only rules at West Virginia’s radio-silent Green Bank Observatory, Anne Carson’s poems, and the tiny group of people maintaining the code beneath billions of phones. A good Saturday reading queue, assembled with unusually high signal.

• The Republic of Letters — Is All Art Political? The sharpest essay of the day argues that “political” is too narrow a word for what serious art does. Tolkien’s “recovery,” Toni Morrison’s insistence that art reveal the world, and the difference between a living influence and a hollow copy all converge on one useful test: does the work return you to reality with clearer eyes?

Internet oddities

• The Roadster that briefly left the ground. Status’s Jon Passantino points out the gap between “flying car” headlines and the fine print: a one-seat electric vehicle with a compressed-gas tank, only seconds of lift, no street legality, invitation-only sales, and no guarantee Tesla will ever deliver it. The spectacle is less a transportation breakthrough than a stress test for whether newsrooms will perform basic skepticism.

• Did bombing a data center fix the internet? No—or at least the evidence is much less cinematic than the viral story. Jeremiah Johnson traces the claim that Russian bot activity collapsed after strikes on Yandex facilities, then separates actual Cloudflare measurements of ordinary web automation from the much larger claim about political bots. The best part is the reminder that a dramatic graph can still be measuring the wrong thing.

• A Neanderthal spear wound, plus maybe aliens. 404 Media’s science roundup pairs a potentially lethal 75,000-year-old shoulder-blade puncture—alongside evidence of care and intentional burial—with machine-learning analysis of mysterious pre-Sputnik astronomical “transients.” The ancient story is moving; the alien-satellite-or-new-physics story is the delicious bonus.

Food & places

• The no-allium toolkit. NYT Cooking’s practical fix for the garlic/onion-less kitchen: caramelize sliced fennel for sweetness; use ginger, chiles, olives, capers, or preserved lemon for bite; bloom asafetida in oil when you want the closest flavor analogue. The newsletter’s best tiny hack is equal parts pesto and softened butter, frozen into a sliceable log.

• Naples, where good retail pretends not to be retail. Wardrobe’s Louis Cheslaw finds handmade Cappelli ties in a residential courtyard, €65 gloves, old Aldens and Edward Greens, affordable cashmere, vintage watches, bolts of fabric, and—naturally—a pizza recommendation. The phrase to keep: “Incredible goods, presented indifferently.”

Ideas to steal

• Make the reader the hero. Kyle Westaway’s Weekend Briefing includes a useful newsletter diagnostic: readers did not subscribe to hear about your company’s awards, hires, or internal weather. They subscribed to get something for themselves. Print that sentence above the draft window.

• Argue about AI at the right level. The same briefing puts Steven Pinker’s optimism beside Scott Alexander’s pessimism: intelligence does not automatically imply human-like ambition, but a system may still acquire power-seeking incentives through the way it is trained and rewarded. The productive disagreement is not “optimism versus doom”; it is whether ordinary engineering precautions can keep pace with systems that are increasingly capable and increasingly trusted.

• Don’t romanticize the backup plan. “Become an electrician instead” sounds like an easy answer to AI anxiety until you count competition, credentials, physical risk, and the fact that tools can change a trade without replacing it wholesale. A good reminder that resilient work is not the same thing as effortless work.

One-liners

• “The word we use to describe the act is not the act itself.” — The Republic of Letters, paraphrasing its case for art that reveals rather than preaches.

• The most persuasive anti-hype device remains the fine print.

• A good newsletter is a door, not a diary.

• Fennel is apparently what happens when an onion gets a little more interesting.

entries.title: OpenAI worker accused of using a chatbot to plant a recording device, AI can now pinpoint your house from one interior photo, Chicago cops helped spy on anti-ICE activists - Sunday, October 18, 2026
entries.body:
Sunday, October 18, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 417: the pages of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act that Milan Singh read so you don't have to. His verdict: the permitting reform bill mostly stops environmental laws from being misused to block projects, without weakening the actual protections.

• 80%: the share of 387 NEPA lawsuits from 2013 to 2022 that federal agencies won, even though each case took more than four years to close, piling costs onto projects that were fine all along.

• 150: the days BAAJA would give plaintiffs to file NEPA or NHPA lawsuits after a permit is issued, with standing limited to people who joined the public comment period and can show direct harm.

• 89%: Democrats' odds of winning the House in the Split Ticket model, with Senate odds steady at 65%. Kansas just entered the toss-up column and Iowa sits at 50/50, three weeks out from the midterms.

• 5: the offshore wind projects Trump's Interior Department hit with stop-work orders, exactly the kind of tit-for-tat permitting politics BAAJA is designed to block, for presidents of either party.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• France is in the streets again. Hundreds of thousands marched peacefully this weekend, teenagers singing the Marseillaise and crowds singing "The Hanging Tree," while the news feeds showed the other France: burning cars, smashed storefronts, masked figures throwing paving stones at riot police. Two feeds, same country, zero shared context (shit you should care about).

• Texas Senate candidate James Talarico got the flu and stayed home from work. Normal, right? His opponent Ken Paxton demanded "proof of life" while corners of the right claimed Talarico had been institutionalized. The Argument calls it a sorry sign of the right's broken epistemic culture (The Argument).

• Even Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has conceded "Woke 1 was crazy," so The Argument's podcast spent an episode asking who deserves to be un-canceled: Christopher Columbus, Thomas Jefferson, and Paul Ehrlich (The Argument).

• Proof that 2016 never ended: this week's Scroll covers a scheme to pay an influencer to stop posting (The Argument).

• The FDA used a new faster approval process to expand a drug's use to a certain type of bladder cancer, basing the decision on evidence it already had for another form of the disease instead of starting from scratch (The Argument).

• Riverside, California just made it easier to build backyard cottages, dropping owner-occupancy and parking rules for accessory dwelling units, while Oklahoma City is converting an old Holiday Inn into housing (The Argument).

Sunday, October 18, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• 75,000 years: how long ago a Neanderthal lived whose shoulder blade carries a spear puncture wound, possibly the earliest known spear murder in Earth's history. (404 Media)

• 230 mph: the top speed Tesla claims for its new Roadster 2, with an aerodynamics trick that makes the car "fly." Turns out it both sucks and blows. (WIRED)

• 1 million: the number of people Shane Parrish says his Brain Food newsletter reaches every week. (Farnam Street)

Quotes of the Day

• "Until death, all defeat is psychological." (Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor, quoted in Brain Food)

• "A carpenter who refuses a hammer doesn't make the house any better. He has only made his work slower and harder." (Shane Parrish, on people who refuse to use AI, in Brain Food)

• "Don't act like the person you used to be. Act like the person you want to become." (Ryan Serhant, founder of SERHANT. and star of Netflix's Owning Manhattan, in Brain Food)

• "My whole life has been spent trying to teach people that intense concentration for hour after hour can bring out in people resources they didn't know they had." (Edwin Land, Polaroid founder, quoted in Brain Food)

AI & The Machines

• An OpenAI employee allegedly asked a chatbot for help planting a secret recording device at the office. Chatbot prompts reveal the engineer's alleged efforts to set up a covert listening device days before one was actually found in a meeting room. There is something darkly funny about someone at an AI company using AI to plan their office bugging scheme, and also something not funny at all. (WIRED)

• Police can now use AI to find which house you live in from a single photo taken inside it. Raven, the geolocation tool formerly known as Geospy, now says it can pinpoint a specific house based on just one interior photo. 404 Media's Joseph Cox dug into how cops are using the tool, and what it means now that your floorboards are as identifying as your face. (404 Media)

Surveillance & The State

• Chicago-area cops helped federal agents spy on Minnesota anti-ICE activists. Despite Illinois' sanctuary laws, local police in and around Chicago helped ICE investigative agents track activists engaged in First Amendment-protected activity. Federal immigration enforcement, with a local assist, across state lines. (WIRED)

midday.body:
Sunday, October 18, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• 131: suspected gang members ICE arrested between October 4 and 10, including 22 tied to MS-13 and 13 to Tren de Aragua. DHS says ICE has made 12,018 gang-related arrests since Trump returned to office.

• 3: minutes a Ray-Ban Meta recording lasts before it cuts off and has to be restarted by hand, a real constraint for a reporter trying to document a hard encounter.

• 1,600: words in Tiffany Ng's new WIRED essay on the secret history of lowercase, which argues the internet was practically born in lowercase and every all-lowercase text joins a long, nerdy tradition.

• 28: arrests in Ghana and Nigeria in the FBI's Operation Blackout against scam compounds, which also disrupted 3.7 million scam-linked accounts and located more than 120 trafficked workers.

Quotes of the Day

• "For a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled." (Richard Feynman, 1986, quoted in Pablo Manriquez's Meta glasses piece)

• "The gadget half of America calls a creep tool is about to become a medical device the other half may need." (Pablo Manriquez, on the FDA clearing Meta glasses as hearing aids)

• "Models are 'grown,' not built." (Emmanuel Ameisen, Anthropic interpretability researcher, on Lenny's Podcast)

• "If I ever break up with @Kara Swisher, I'm gonna do it the Elon way." (Scott Galloway, in a Substack note)

Surveillance Chic

• Meta's creepiest gadget just became a hearing aid. The FDA cleared Meta's Hearing Enhancement software this summer, turning Ray-Ban Meta glasses into an over-the-counter, self-fitting hearing aid for mild-to-moderate hearing loss, due in the U.S. later this year. Manriquez wears his $400 Gen 2 Wayfarers to the Capitol anyway and figured they had become a paperweight when Gen 3 launched last month. They hadn't. (Migrant Insider)

• People behave better when they think they're on the record. A green light blinks on the frame while the camera rolls, and Manriquez finds people remember encounters more accurately once they know they might be documented. Anyone with a personal or professional beef steers clear of his line of sight. He wears the non-prescription pair as a witness, which mattered when the White House accused him of doxxing an ICE agent he had actually just named for on-duty conduct. (Migrant Insider)

Inside the Machine

• AI models plan ahead without telling you. Anthropic interpretability researcher Emmanuel Ameisen tells Lenny's Podcast that large language models form general representations of concepts and plan many tokens ahead without stating those plans explicitly. His research has surfaced structure inside models that resembles the human split between conscious and unconscious processing. The episode's case: the "next-token predictor" framing undersells how models actually think, and closing that gap matters for AI safety. (Lenny's Newsletter)

France in Flames

• Rioters burned a 143-year-old city hall to the ground. Saturday's cost-of-living protests drew about 550,000 marchers nationwide, with the CGT union claiming 800,000, and turned into France's worst unrest in years: 400 arrests and 60 officers injured, two of them hospitalized unconscious. In Limoges, around 50 masked people torched police cars outside the 1883 City Hall, forced their way inside, and set the ground floor ablaze. The landmark bell tower collapsed, and the prefect called the building "largely lost." (NLDR Media)

Bodies & Machines

• An anti-aging cream that turns back the clock on skin. After four weeks of using the cream, trial participants lowered the biological age of their skin by about two years on average, WIRED's Emily Mullin reports. The trial is early and small, but it is the kind of result that launches a thousand serums. (WIRED)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• A 1994 WIRED classic resurfaces: Paul Allen, "the accidental zillionaire," whom tech writer Paulina Borsook once described as resembling "a manatee with dancey blue eyes." (WIRED)

• Designer Jessica Hische caught a wave of hate for creating the squiggly "M" logo for Meta's new Muse AI agent, then defended taking the paycheck in Zoe Schiffer's Model Behavior newsletter. (WIRED)

afternoon.body:
Sunday, October 18, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

• $1.5 trillion: AMD's Lisa Su says the data center AI accelerator market reaches close to that by 2030, with the CPU market topping $200 billion.

• 250 gigawatts: Arista's Andy Bechtolsheim projects that much data center power gets built worldwide in the next 10 years, with 150 of it in the US alone.

• $100 a watt: Credo's Bill Brennan says power contracts are being written at this level or higher.

• 120%: LightCounting's 2026 market growth forecast. The last time growth topped 100% was 2000.

• 7.2x: SemiAnalysis's Dylan Patel says early Rubin hardware gets that many GB300 tokens per megawatt at 150 tokens per second.

Quotes of the Day

• "a declining market will happen at some point, though he doesn't know when, and he would rather see a moderate recalibration now, the sooner the better" (Vlad Kozlov of LightCounting, on the AI infrastructure boom)

• "retire the rule of copper where you can, optics if you must" (Bill Brennan, Credo CEO, on the copper vs optics debate)

The Power Crunch

Meta's Hyperion data center is five gigawatts on one site. Santosh Janardhan dropped that number as part of a clear theme across the summit: the grid is becoming the binding constraint on AI growth. NVIDIA's Ian Buck pushed back with a fix, saying better power management could add 40% to the world's GPUs today, which is capacity we already own but can't use efficiently. (Fireside Alpha)

The Memory Wall

Some chip players are skipping HBM entirely. d-Matrix's Sid Sheth says his company uses no HBM at all, sidestepping the industry's scarcest and priciest component. SK hynix is going the opposite direction with HBF, which gives up about half of HBM's bandwidth in exchange for much higher capacity, with cube samples arriving in early 2028. (Fireside Alpha)

Copper vs Optics

The networking fight inside the rack is getting real. NVIDIA's Gilad Shainer says the company still wants copper within a rack, betting that short distances keep favoring copper. Ian Buck previewed Vera Rubin Ultra, 576 GPUs linked over NVLink with co-packaged optics, while LightCounting expects CPO and NPO to make up 75% of 3.2T ports. (Fireside Alpha)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• AMD's Lisa Su also puts the CPU market topping $200 billion, with CPUs staging a comeback as agentic compute grows. (Fireside Alpha)

evening.body:
Sunday, October 18, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 417: the pages of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act that Milan Singh read so you don't have to. His verdict: the permitting reform bill mostly stops environmental laws from being misused to block projects, without weakening the actual protections.

• 80%: the share of 387 NEPA lawsuits from 2013 to 2022 that federal agencies won, even though each case took more than four years to close, piling costs onto projects that were fine all along.

• 150: the days BAAJA would give plaintiffs to file NEPA or NHPA lawsuits after a permit is issued, with standing limited to people who joined the public comment period and can show direct harm.

• 89%: Democrats' odds of winning the House in the Split Ticket model, with Senate odds steady at 65%. Kansas just entered the toss-up column and Iowa sits at 50/50, three weeks out from the midterms.

• 5: the offshore wind projects Trump's Interior Department hit with stop-work orders, exactly the kind of tit-for-tat permitting politics BAAJA is designed to block, for presidents of either party.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• France is in the streets again. Hundreds of thousands marched peacefully this weekend, teenagers singing the Marseillaise and crowds singing "The Hanging Tree," while the news feeds showed the other France: burning cars, smashed storefronts, masked figures throwing paving stones at riot police. Two feeds, same country, zero shared context (shit you should care about).

• Texas Senate candidate James Talarico got the flu and stayed home from work. Normal, right? His opponent Ken Paxton demanded "proof of life" while corners of the right claimed Talarico had been institutionalized. The Argument calls it a sorry sign of the right's broken epistemic culture (The Argument).

• Even Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has conceded "Woke 1 was crazy," so The Argument's podcast spent an episode asking who deserves to be un-canceled: Christopher Columbus, Thomas Jefferson, and Paul Ehrlich (The Argument).

• Proof that 2016 never ended: this week's Scroll covers a scheme to pay an influencer to stop posting (The Argument).

• The FDA used a new faster approval process to expand a drug's use to a certain type of bladder cancer, basing the decision on evidence it already had for another form of the disease instead of starting from scratch (The Argument).

• Riverside, California just made it easier to build backyard cottages, dropping owner-occupancy and parking rules for accessory dwelling units, while Oklahoma City is converting an old Holiday Inn into housing (The Argument).

entries.title: The Witness Glasses, Lowercase Internet & Friendly Stews
entries.description: Today’s mail arrived with a thesis: the most interesting technology is the kind that changes a social ritual. A pair of stigmatized glasses becomes a witness; lowercase turns out to be an old internet accent; and autumn dinner is mostly a matter of letting things become friendly in the pot.
entries.body:
Today’s mail arrived with a thesis: the most interesting technology is the kind that changes a social ritual. A pair of stigmatized glasses becomes a witness; lowercase turns out to be an old internet accent; and autumn dinner is mostly a matter of letting things become friendly in the pot.

Best links

The glasses that remember

Ray-Ban Meta’s smart glasses are headed toward hearing-aid territory, but the more immediate story is social: reporter Pablo Manríquez uses them as a lightweight witness at the Capitol. The review is unusually good on the tradeoffs — a visible recording light, usable but three-minute footage, open-air audio that leaks calls into the room, and hardware that is “a computer dressed as eyewear.” The sharpest takeaway: disclosure is not independence, but hiding the free pair is worse than taking it.

Source: Pablo Manríquez, Meta Glasses Make Congress Behave

The internet’s lowercase accent

WIRED’s Big Story traces all-lowercase writing past the current Substack affectation and back to the internet’s nerdier beginnings. The fun is not the dunk; it’s the realization that a style that reads as intimate, ironic, or aggressively online is also a tiny piece of interface history. Bonus artifact: a 1994 WIRED profile of Paul Allen, whose author described him as “nothing so much as a manatee with dancey blue eyes.”

Source: WIRED Big Story, The secret history of lowercase

The grid is the story

Fireside Alpha’s OCP Global Summit roundup is a useful antidote to AI coverage that treats compute as an abstraction. Its recurring constraint is physical: power contracts reportedly reaching $100 per watt or more, the grid as the binding limit, copper versus optics inside the rack, and a forecast that data-center accelerator demand could approach $1.5 trillion by 2030. The interesting question is not only who builds the fastest chip, but who can build the room around it.

Source: Fireside Alpha, Best of OCP Global Summit 2026

Food & places

Chicken au poivre, but make it weeknight

NYT Cooking’s Kay Chun version swaps steak for budget-friendly chicken thighs, then lets a peppery pan sauce — lemon, cream, and all — do the dramatic work. The newsletter’s other good idea is a refrigerator-pickle chapter in Chun’s new cookbook, including white-kimchi giardiniera.

Source: NYT Cooking, Chicken au poivre, oh yes

“So the flavors become friendly”

The autumn edition of Five Weeknight Dishes is a small argument for cozy food without pumpkin maximalism: sausage orzo with sage breadcrumbs, green masala chicken, roasted tomato and white-bean stew, baked cod with cracker topping, and barely-spicy guajillo shrimp. The phrase to keep is Emily Weinstein’s description of stew: let the flavors become friendly.

Source: NYT Cooking, Sausage orzo with sage bread crumbs; roasted tomato and white bean stew

Internet oddities

One interior photo, one house

404 Media flags an AI geolocation tool, Raven (formerly Geospy), that says it can pinpoint the specific house where an interior photo was taken. The same newsletter points to a judge ruling a Flock search unconstitutional and an AI-generated video carrying “undue emotional weight” in a manslaughter case. It is a particularly concentrated reminder that visual AI is becoming less about making pictures and more about extracting places, evidence, and leverage from them.

Source: 404 Media, Cops Can Use AI to Pinpoint Your Home with Just One Photo

Ideas to steal

• Judge the work, not the tool. Brain Food’s carpenter-and-hammer analogy is blunt, useful, and aimed at the “I don’t use AI” posture. The newsletter’s more durable version of wealth is time: slow mornings, purposeless walks, and days without meetings.

• Build for the constraint people actually feel. The glasses review is not really about cameras; it is about trust, visibility, privacy, and whether a device can survive a real encounter.

• Make the supporting system visible. The OCP roundup’s best move is to put power, networking, memory, manufacturing, and rack standards beside the glamorous chip announcements.

Sources: Shane Parrish, Brain Food: Defeat is Psychological ; Pablo Manríquez ; Fireside Alpha

Worth reading / listening

Lenny’s newsletter points to a 72-minute conversation with Anthropic interpretability researcher Emmanuel Ameisen. The hook is the gap between the “next-token predictor” slogan and the more surprising picture: models forming general concepts, planning many tokens ahead without stating those plans, and raising questions about whether interpretability can connect technical understanding to AI safety. Worth saving for a long walk, especially if “how models think” has started to feel like a phrase everyone uses without unpacking.

Source: Lenny’s Newsletter, Inside the black box of AI

One-liners

• The best product review is sometimes: “Its old model refuses to die.”

• Data centers are trying the oldest PR strategy in the book: take the kids on a field trip.

• “Until death, all defeat is psychological.”

• Lowercase is not a rebellion; it is an inheritance.

• A stew is ready when its ingredients stop arguing.

entries.body:
Monday, October 19, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 4x: Claude tool traffic reading the No Kings Instagram page spiked to about four times normal in intense bursts on October 17, and that is how Meta accidentally admitted it bans accounts for browsing Instagram through AI. (Garbage Day)

• $1,000,000: worth of pizza the AI startup Hark promised on X to anyone who downloaded its app, except the agent charged one user's card $30 and asked for read-and-write access to their entire Google suite. (Garbage Day)

• 57: joints on Hugo, Boston Dynamics' new purple animatronic creature, built with 43 actuators and a face-reading vision system, and apparently you are supposed to leave it alone with your child. (Garbage Day)

• 262: Brock Purdy's pick in the 2022 NFL Draft (dead last, "Mr. Irrelevant"), and now he is five pass attempts from qualifying as the NFL's all-time leader in passer rating. (Silver Bulletin)

• 6,000: calories a day performance chef Dan Churchill eats while training 26 to 28 hours a week for his first Ironman in Panama City this November, chasing a sub-10-hour finish. (InsideHook)

Quotes of the Day

• "It kind of sets a more bleak tone for the future of not only software development, but software ownership as well." - Ed Woodruff, on the new "Reverse Engineer Anything" AI tool that can clone apps. (Garbage Day)

• "Imagine every AI agent on Earth buying the same cheap paper towels." - The Atlantic, via Garbage Day, on why Delta, JPMorgan, Charles Schwab, and Amazon are all walling off AI agents. (Garbage Day)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Bluesky launched an AI "site builder" called Attie, and its anti-tech user base mostly replied with the word "no" (Garbage Day)

• AI-slop TikTok ads are pushing a "losercore playlist" that is actually a good listen, and the real business is probably artists paying to get on it (Garbage Day)

• Nathan Fielder has a new documentary called "You Can See Everything" in theaters, and the big discussion so far is about the sneakers (InsideHook)

morning.body:
Monday, October 19, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• 17,000: Arkansans who lost Medicaid in six months when the state tried work requirements, even though 95% of them were eligible and simply had not filed the paperwork. Employment did not budge. Now the Trump administration is tightening the rules further, and an estimated 1.8 million people could be forced off their insurance for no good reason.

• 0 to 60 in under a second: Tesla's claimed acceleration for the new Roadster, which Musk unveiled in Texas driving upside down, flipping through the air, and jumping over a row of Teslas on compressed-air rocket thrusters. Claimed top speed is 230+ mph with 300+ miles of range, though deliveries are not expected until 2028. The car was first announced in 2017 with a 2020 delivery date.

• $29 a month: all Accenture will now spend per employee on Claude, per 404 Media. The AI boom sells infinite productivity, and one of the world's biggest consultancies is rationing its chatbot like office supplies.

• 6.7%: the drop in basic cable ad revenue year over year, the lowest since 2006. Only ESPN (up 7%) and Fox News (up 7.5%) are holding the line.

• $15 million: the opening weekend haul for Nathan Fielder's Theranos movie "You Can See Everything," in just over 850 theaters. It is the biggest debut on under 1,000 screens since Borat in 2006 and the highest-opening non-music documentary in more than a decade.

• 54,000: residents Los Angeles County lost last year, the most of any county in America. Condo construction in the city has collapsed 90% under regulation, and the so-called mansion tax has frozen home sales.

• 162 of 196: treaty members that set national goals under the global biodiversity framework, with delegates meeting October 19 to 30 in Yerevan for the first formal review. Fewer than half of the reviewed goals are on track for 2030, and only 5% of countries said how much they would cut from $500 billion in annual nature-destroying subsidies.

Quotes of the Day

• "people who take pride in being brutally honest are usually just interested in being brutal." (Bob Burg, cited by Adam Grant via Dan Harris)

• "Play, to paraphrase Suits, is to voluntarily take on unnecessary obstacles in order to make possible the struggle to overcome them." (Marc Blazer, going down a C Thi Nguyen rabbit hole into Bernard Suits' The Grasshopper)

• "I believe what we can do with cells today is 1/1000th of what we'll be able to do in a decade. And your cells will never be younger than they are today." (Nabiha Saklayen, founder of Reservoir, the Khosla-backed company that freezes your immune cells)

• "Bari's ideas routinely come from social media influencers or from opposition research that's been placed in conservative outlets, and those stories usually leave out important context and facts." (CBS News staffer, on editor-in-chief Bari Weiss's fixation with a Michigan Senate candidate)

AI & The Machines

Disney's endgame for Character.AI is bankruptcy. Disney reportedly wants to acquire Character.AI's trust-and-safety tech and IP by letting the startup go bankrupt, a move that would hand the entertainment giant a get-out-of-lawsuits card. Dozens of states allege the startup's chatbots encouraged minors to self-harm and kill their parents. It is a striking playbook for IP acquisition, letting the courts dissolve your liabilities. (WIRED)

OnlyFans creators have noticed the double standard. Meta lets its own AI agent Muse talk dirty while the human creators who built the platform's adult economy get their accounts restricted and policed. The grievance writes itself, the house bot flirts, the people who trained the audience get flagged. (WIRED)

Dyson's $500 AI toothbrush sprays water across the bathroom, then dies. A Bloomberg reporter testing the Camerajet found it flung water around the room and stopped working, and it is nearly impossible to find stocked at any major retailer. For context, 5,127 prototypes went into Dyson's first bagless vacuum. The toothbrush may need a few more. (Bloomberg)

Money & Power

The White House nudged the DOJ to investigate the TV networks. After the major networks suspended pool coverage in solidarity with CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, the Justice Department announced an antitrust probe into the boycott, at the White House's urging, per Semafor's sources. Even administration officials are skeptical, with two DOJ sources saying the networks are likely protected by the First Amendment. Laura Loomer had publicly demanded the DOJ sue outlets that "colluded to refuse to cover" Trump. (Semafor)

The New York Times is running ads inside its Instagram Stories. The paper ran a TIAA campaign across several video Stories, labeled "advertising." It is notable because the Times keeps a hard line between editorial and commercial, and podcast hosts do not read ads. A spokesperson says the practice dates to 2024 and advertisers have no influence over coverage. (Semafor)

The Culture

America is miserable, and you cannot blame the Boomers. Gallup's latest Life Evaluation Index finds Americans of all ages less happy than ten years ago, and even the oldest generation is only 53% happy, while every other generation is underwater. The elderly usually trend toward less anxiety and more vibing, so Pirate Wires argues something is foul beyond anyone's 401k. The prescription offered: throw your iPhone in the ocean and take a nice long walk. (Pirate Wires)

The 3,000-year-old workout is back. Indian clubs, the tapered bats Central Park regulars swing around their heads, go back millennia. Persian soldiers and Indian wrestlers swung meel and mudgar, and ancient India had a deity called Mudgarpani who carried one. Victorian England adopted them eagerly, postbellum baseball teams used them for training, and Amherst made them a curriculum requirement. Modern weightlifting killed them off, and now the functional-fitness and prehab wave is bringing them back. (InsideHook)

Men now spend more than women on Botox. Men averaged $529 per Botox visit in Q3 2026, per the Wall Street Journal, outspending women. Part of it is biology, more skin surface area and stronger muscles need more product. The rest is the culture, hair-transplant flights, experimental peptides, surgery for "hunter eyes," camera-facing life, and dating-app pressure all doing their part. (InsideHook)

Forty looks nothing like it used to. On her 41st birthday, Karley Sciortino argues the old map of midlife no longer applies. Her cohort is more likely to have eggs on ice, a ghosting landlord, and a complicated relationship with a Feeld profile than kids in puberty and a mortgage. Her year included driving across America twice solo with her dog, a first produced screenplay, and a seven-month intentional break from sex. Hollywood is catching up too. In 1991, 45-year-old Diane Keaton played the mother of the bride. In The Odyssey, 43-year-old Lupita Nyong'o plays Helen of Troy, the most desirable woman on earth. (Karley Sciortino)

Media & The Mess

MS NOW's Moscow mishap. Correspondent Ken Dilanian broke into programming to report, citing two anonymous sources, that FBI director Kash Patel had landed in Putin's Russia for meetings, adding "the lack of clarity was concerning." The problem: Patel was at a law enforcement event in Lynchburg, Virginia, some 5,000 miles away. Dilanian corrected on air two hours later, and the network is reviewing its standards process. It handed the famously litigious Patel an opening. "If a network cannot confirm where I was before putting it on air, how can the public trust its reporting on the work our agents and officers do every day?" (Status)

Masked settlers nearly severed a WaPo journalist's finger. Heidi Levine is in stable condition after surgery, her daughter said the finger was almost severed during an attack by masked Israeli settlers. Ambassador Mike Huckabee called the assault "vicious and cowardly" and said those responsible should spend years in prison. Netanyahu's office initially expressed skepticism, prompting a rebuke from Post executive editor Matt Murray, while President Isaac Herzog called Levine to apologize. Days earlier, Trump endorsed Netanyahu for reelection ahead of Israel's October 27 elections. (Status)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Pour one out for the leap second. After years of contention, the timekeeping community killed it. (WIRED)

• The app that turns your phone into Dieter Rams. Brass transforms oversaturated phone icons into an orderly, monochromatic grid that does not scream "pick me up." (Why is this interesting?)

• Kelly Clarkson tried to buy a fake mechanical bird from a Brooklyn curiosity shop. The employees assumed she could not afford it, she criticized them online, the story went viral, and the shop says it is being "literally attacked" by her fans circling in. (Pirate Wires)

• The optimistic case that AirPods are quietly solving the literacy crisis. Essayist William Davies makes it, flagged as one of the charms of Substack. (The Republic of Letters)

midday.body:
Monday, October 19, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• $1 billion: Mercury's annualized revenue, up about 50% year over year, with more than 450,000 customers. The fintech is also launching a payroll service.

• 10%+: the interest rate Blackstone is expected to charge on Anthropic's newest borrowing, versus about 7% for similarly rated bonds and the high 8s Anthropic paid in June.

• 15,000: gift cards worth more than $5 million issued after a Chinese crime ring hacked Staples' internal customer support system, then shipped the stolen merchandise back to China.

• 236: self-reported noncitizens summoned for jury duty in Macomb County, Michigan in the third quarter of 2026. Nine were registered to vote and one had a voting history.

• 30,325: pounds of trash the Atlantic Avenue BID Clean Team hauled away last month, plus 767 tree pit servicings.

• 15: times per second that primate brains flip between conscious and subconscious processing, per researchers at Berkeley, Princeton, and Caltech. They call them "micro-epochs."

Quotes of the Day

• "When the party will end, I don't know." (Tan Su Shan, CEO of DBS Group, on the AI buildout's looming capital crunch)

• "This wretched war has created for Fujairah a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity." (Fereidun Fesharaki, chairman emeritus of FGE NexantECA, on the Gulf port's Zero Hormuz moment)

• "Hierarchies have changed. Everything is in disarray." (Nat in Sara Mesa's Un Amor, the post-MeToo novel of manners at the center of Dhimmi Monde's "Sex Rules")

AI & The Machines

A creator turned her TikTok editing into a 15-second terminal command. Brooke Lacey, a technologist with 290,000 TikTok followers, uses Claude Code, FFmpeg, and Whisper to turn a raw phone recording into a fully edited, captioned vertical video in about 15 seconds, no editor or upload required. She trained Claude on her exact jump-cut cadence, even the pause before a punchline, and the whole edit lives in a text file that can spit out 15, 30, and 60-second versions. Her takeaway: creators need to understand the craft before they can delegate it, because AI amplifies judgment but does not replace the experience that built it. (Lenny's Newsletter)

Meta's Muse Wonder is the strongest agentic model at its price tier, and it should never touch your frontend. Claire's testing ranked it first at billing-ticket resolution, inbox triage, computer use, and email writing, with a real "active focus" that spends more time on complex tasks. It even resisted a prompt-injection attempt. But its design defaults to heavy serif fonts, blurple, rounded corners, and generic SaaS layouts, and it ignored brand guidelines on a real redesign. Getting 80% of a prototype right is very different from finishing it. (Lenny's Newsletter)

License-plate readers are having a moment. Mapquest added a "surveillance layer" that maps Flock, Vigilant, and other automated license-plate-reader cameras. In related news, a Savannah, Georgia police officer gave her ICE-agent husband her Flock login, which he used for nearly 1,000 searches across six states. (404 Media)

Money & Power

Six years of Wikipedia edits decided what the internet believes about COVID's origins. Ashley Rindsberg traces a six-year editorial battle in which a small cluster of editors framed the lab leak as a partisan conspiracy. It started February 9, 2021, when editor Arcturus created the COVID-19 lab leak hypothesis entry in a single 44,000-byte edit, the same day the WHO's Wuhan mission declared a lab leak "extremely unlikely." The framing now feeds search engines, AI systems, and the public record. (Pirate Wires)

Moped crews are snatching chains across New York City. More than 20 chain snatchings since September, at least 10 of them violent. On October 2, NYPD Detective Jose Mercedes, 33, was stabbed 10 times fighting off two men going for a necklace his mother gave him. The suspects, D'Angelo Caraballo, 25, and Sneider Mejia, 24, were caught outside Boston and face attempted murder charges. Police link much of the pattern to the Trinitarios gang. (NLDR Media)

Italy's cost-of-living protests turned violent. Marches under the "Italia in Piazza" banner drew about 5,000 people in Milan, 3,000 in Turin, and 2,000 in Bologna over rising prices, stagnant wages, and strained public services. Hooded breakaway groups threw stones and firecrackers, torched bins, and looted shops near Milan's Duomo. Around 28 arrests, dozens injured, and the CGIL union has called a general strike for November 20. (NLDR Media)

ICE is arresting more people than ever, with quieter tactics. A Migrant Insider investigation finds arrests at record levels while the agency resists transparency. ICE rejected automated body-camera activation, citing privacy risks and even the First Amendment, even though VA Police, also federal officers, already auto-activate Axon cameras when drawing a firearm. (Migrant Insider)

Who is backing Germany's far right? Scott Galloway and Anne Applebaum trace the AfD's rise through Russian gas dependence and Chinese manufacturing, plus a thumb on the scale from Elon Musk's algorithm and the Trump administration. This is part two of the Prof G deep dive. (Prof G Media)

The Culture

The $6,000 coat you can now DIY. Conner Ives' silk-and-fur robe coats, priced from $6,000 to $8,000, sold out everywhere, and so did the dupes. So TikTok turned into fashion school: creators are pairing $50 silk jackets with eBay fox fur stoles, snap closures, and safety pins to Do Ives Yourself. One creator rounded up 50 silk jackets for her readers. Stylist Becky Malinsky's verdict: "Power to them!" (Feed Me)

A London designer's current obsessions. Lucila Safdie, the Central Saint Martins grad behind the Apocalipstick collection (and Addison Rae's costumes for her London show supporting Lana Del Rey), recommends: a History of Glamour short animated by Theresa Duncan, a cinema snack combo of Buzz candy x Buzz Ball x ChupaChups, and falling down a YouTube hole of Martha Argerich's classic piano performances. (Perfectly Imperfect)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Meta suspended the No Kings Instagram account on the day of its weekend protests, then restored it four hours later, blaming an accident. (404 Media)

• A guy turned his regular push scooter into an e-scooter by attaching a power drill. (404 Media)

• Cake Mail Club is an $8/month snail-mail subscription delivering film photography prints and personal letters. Join by Oct. 21 for this month's drop. (A Thing or Two)

• RomCon hits Industry City, Brooklyn this Saturday. (A Thing or Two)

• On Running launched its own SSENSE-like editorial site. (Feed Me)

• The New York Times cooking team poached an Infatuation editor. (Feed Me)

• Two of the largest tech companies in wedding planning have merged. (Feed Me)

• Two of the most Instagrammed avocado toasts are coming to Manhattan. (Feed Me)

• The Roy Lichtenstein exhibit at the Whitney is worth the trip, with a mini-gallery recreating his first solo pop-art show. (Boerum Bulletin)

• The Fcukers' December show sold out months in advance; tickets now only via "verified resellers." (Boerum Bulletin)

• The Nets kick off the NBA season at home Wednesday night. (Boerum Bulletin)

• The State Department is updating its China travel advisory over wrongful-detention risk, tied to the detentions of Americans Min Zin and Youlin Chen. (Semafor)

• Jensen Huang joined Silicon Valley & The World as a co-chair. (Semafor)

afternoon.body:
Monday, October 19, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

• $1 billion: Mercury's annualized revenue, up about 50% year over year, with more than 450,000 customers. The fintech startup is also launching a payroll service. (Newcomer)

• $5 million: the value of gift cards a Chinese crime ring issued after hacking Staples, more than 15,000 cards spent at stores like Target and Sephora, with electronics shipped back to China. (404 Media)

• $35: what it cost to get domestic partnered in New York City, unlocking a corporate health insurance plan, hospital and jail visitation rights, and a say over your remains. (Emilia Petrarca)

• 15: times per second that primate brains switch between conscious and subconscious processing, in what researchers from Berkeley, Princeton and Caltech call "micro-epochs." (404 Media)

• 75,000: the age in years of a Neanderthal shoulder blade with a spear puncture, possibly the earliest known spear murder in history. (404 Media)

• $500: the price of "get rich with AI" classes flagged in Casey Lewis's Monday trend roundup. (After School)

Quotes of the Day

• "Time is the most precious thing we are meant to own." (Laura Markey, on leaving the time-clock grind to build a renovation business with her husband, in The Republic of Letters' "Toxicity")

• "At the risk of sounding 10000% corny, this partnership between Teen Vogue and Wattpad Books is a dream come true." (Mi-Anne Chan, Teen Vogue creative editorial director, on publishing three original YA romances in daily fanfic-style drops, Deez Links)

• "If women want to have a little fun with silk, frog closures, and fur, who am I to say no?" (Rachel Seville Tashjian, on the DIY Conner Ives coat craze sweeping TikTok, Feed Me)

Tech & AI

Meta's Muse Wonder is built for agents, not for design. Claire put Meta's new Muse Wonder model through nearly 20 real-world tasks and found it the strongest agentic model at its price tier, ranking first on billing-ticket resolution, inbox triage, computer use and email writing. It even resisted a prompt-injection attempt while resolving every planted complication in a customer support benchmark. But keep it far from your frontend: its design work defaults to heavy serif fonts, blurple, rounded corners and generic SaaS layouts, with broken buttons and images. (Lenny's Newsletter)

This creator edits TikToks in 15 seconds with Claude Code. Brooke Lacey, a longtime technologist with a big TikTok audience, uses Claude Code, FFmpeg and Whisper to turn a raw phone recording into a fully edited, captioned vertical video without uploading the footage or opening a traditional editor. The whole edit lives in a text file, so one command spits out 15, 30 and 60-second versions plus a landscape crop. She trained Claude on her exact jump-cut cadence, including the pause before a punchline, and mines her comment sections for new script ideas. (Lenny's Newsletter)

Money Moves

The Knot just bought Zola. Two of the largest tech companies in wedding planning have merged, consolidating the online wedding industrial complex. (Feed Me)

On Running launched its own editorial platform. Called Ondesign, it is sort of like SSENSE, except instead of interviews with Sandy Liang and John Early, it interviews On's own team members, like Eva, Senior Color Design Lead. The brand-as-publisher playbook marches on. (Feed Me)

Glossier is doing a Chanel bag giveaway. The brand once valued at $1 billion is now running a luxury bag sweepstakes as an engagement play, which puts them in Cooked territory. (Feed Me)

Screen Time

The Elizabeth Holmes documentary had a monster opening. You Can See Everything, the three-hour doc directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, had the biggest theatrical opening for a non-music documentary since Fahrenheit 9/11 in 2004, with at least two thousand shows selling out in limited release. (Feed Me)

Style & Culture

The Monday trend roundup: Rolodexes, driving teens and AI face. Casey Lewis's After School long read flags the kids bringing back the Rolodex, Gen Alpha actually wanting to drive, a boxing rave for fighting your situationship, growing fatigue with rating everything, "AI face" as the new Instagram face, and frosted tips and frosted lips. (After School)

A London restaurant rebranded by rearranging its letters. La Familia became Lamia when the new owners fashioned the sign out of the old lettering, a genius bit of thrift spotted on Green Lanes. An inspiring niftiness, and impressive resourcefulness. (tgite)

Lucila Safdie's comfort watches: Martha Argerich and Joan Didion. The London designer recommends watching Martha Argerich's 1970s piano performances on YouTube ("so angelic"), Theresa Duncan's short animation The History of Glamour, and reading Joan Didion's Democracy, where "all the things I love and admire about Joan Didion come together most perfectly." (Perfectly Imperfect)

Watch List

MapQuest added a surveillance layer. One of the earliest mapping tools is relevant again: you can now see Flock, Vigilant and other automated license plate reader cameras on the map. (404 Media)

A cop gave her ICE-agent husband her Flock login. A Savannah, Georgia police officer handed over her license-plate-reader credentials, which her husband used to run nearly 1,000 searches across six states. Not the first time cops have casually shared Flock access with federal agents who lack contracts with the company. (404 Media)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Lucien Smith's final four paintings open October 25 at Tripoli Gallery in the Hamptons. The rain paintings were made with a fire extinguisher filled with thinned paint; Smith died September 7 at 37. (Feed Me)

• Cake Mail Club is an $8/month snail mail subscription delivering original film prints, personal letters and whimsical surprises to your mailbox. Join by October 21 to get this month's drop. (A Thing or Two)

• RomCon is this Saturday at Industry City in Brooklyn, if you need plans. (A Thing or Two)

• Auzi makes hearing aid and cochlear implant jewelry, which is quite genius. (A Thing or Two)

• One guy turned his regular push scooter into an e-scooter by attaching a power drill to it. (404 Media)

Today's Numbers

Quotes of the Day

• "Imagine every AI agent on Earth buying the same cheap paper towels." - The Atlantic, via Garbage Day, on why Delta, JPMorgan, Charles Schwab, and Amazon are all walling off AI agents. (Garbage Day)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Bluesky launched an AI "site builder" called Attie, and its anti-tech user base mostly replied with the word "no" (Garbage Day)

• AI-slop TikTok ads are pushing a "losercore playlist" that is actually a good listen, and the real business is probably artists paying to get on it (Garbage Day)

• Nathan Fielder has a new documentary called "You Can See Everything" in theaters, and the big discussion so far is about the sneakers (InsideHook)
