full.body:
Monday, October 19, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• 17,000: Arkansans who lost Medicaid in six months when the state tried work requirements, even though 95% of them were eligible and simply had not filed the paperwork. Employment did not budge. Now the Trump administration is tightening the rules further, and an estimated 1.8 million people could be forced off their insurance for no good reason.

• 0 to 60 in under a second: Tesla's claimed acceleration for the new Roadster, which Musk unveiled in Texas driving upside down, flipping through the air, and jumping over a row of Teslas on compressed-air rocket thrusters. Claimed top speed is 230+ mph with 300+ miles of range, though deliveries are not expected until 2028. The car was first announced in 2017 with a 2020 delivery date.

• $29 a month: all Accenture will now spend per employee on Claude, per 404 Media. The AI boom sells infinite productivity, and one of the world's biggest consultancies is rationing its chatbot like office supplies.

• 6.7%: the drop in basic cable ad revenue year over year, the lowest since 2006. Only ESPN (up 7%) and Fox News (up 7.5%) are holding the line.

• $15 million: the opening weekend haul for Nathan Fielder's Theranos movie "You Can See Everything," in just over 850 theaters. It is the biggest debut on under 1,000 screens since Borat in 2006 and the highest-opening non-music documentary in more than a decade.

• 54,000: residents Los Angeles County lost last year, the most of any county in America. Condo construction in the city has collapsed 90% under regulation, and the so-called mansion tax has frozen home sales.

• 162 of 196: treaty members that set national goals under the global biodiversity framework, with delegates meeting October 19 to 30 in Yerevan for the first formal review. Fewer than half of the reviewed goals are on track for 2030, and only 5% of countries said how much they would cut from $500 billion in annual nature-destroying subsidies.

Quotes of the Day

• "people who take pride in being brutally honest are usually just interested in being brutal." (Bob Burg, cited by Adam Grant via Dan Harris)

• "Play, to paraphrase Suits, is to voluntarily take on unnecessary obstacles in order to make possible the struggle to overcome them." (Marc Blazer, going down a C Thi Nguyen rabbit hole into Bernard Suits' The Grasshopper)

• "I believe what we can do with cells today is 1/1000th of what we'll be able to do in a decade. And your cells will never be younger than they are today." (Nabiha Saklayen, founder of Reservoir, the Khosla-backed company that freezes your immune cells)

• "Bari's ideas routinely come from social media influencers or from opposition research that's been placed in conservative outlets, and those stories usually leave out important context and facts." (CBS News staffer, on editor-in-chief Bari Weiss's fixation with a Michigan Senate candidate)

AI & The Machines

Disney's endgame for Character.AI is bankruptcy. Disney reportedly wants to acquire Character.AI's trust-and-safety tech and IP by letting the startup go bankrupt, a move that would hand the entertainment giant a get-out-of-lawsuits card. Dozens of states allege the startup's chatbots encouraged minors to self-harm and kill their parents. It is a striking playbook for IP acquisition, letting the courts dissolve your liabilities. (WIRED)

OnlyFans creators have noticed the double standard. Meta lets its own AI agent Muse talk dirty while the human creators who built the platform's adult economy get their accounts restricted and policed. The grievance writes itself, the house bot flirts, the people who trained the audience get flagged. (WIRED)

Dyson's $500 AI toothbrush sprays water across the bathroom, then dies. A Bloomberg reporter testing the Camerajet found it flung water around the room and stopped working, and it is nearly impossible to find stocked at any major retailer. For context, 5,127 prototypes went into Dyson's first bagless vacuum. The toothbrush may need a few more. (Bloomberg)

Money & Power

The White House nudged the DOJ to investigate the TV networks. After the major networks suspended pool coverage in solidarity with CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, the Justice Department announced an antitrust probe into the boycott, at the White House's urging, per Semafor's sources. Even administration officials are skeptical, with two DOJ sources saying the networks are likely protected by the First Amendment. Laura Loomer had publicly demanded the DOJ sue outlets that "colluded to refuse to cover" Trump. (Semafor)

The New York Times is running ads inside its Instagram Stories. The paper ran a TIAA campaign across several video Stories, labeled "advertising." It is notable because the Times keeps a hard line between editorial and commercial, and podcast hosts do not read ads. A spokesperson says the practice dates to 2024 and advertisers have no influence over coverage. (Semafor)

The Culture

America is miserable, and you cannot blame the Boomers. Gallup's latest Life Evaluation Index finds Americans of all ages less happy than ten years ago, and even the oldest generation is only 53% happy, while every other generation is underwater. The elderly usually trend toward less anxiety and more vibing, so Pirate Wires argues something is foul beyond anyone's 401k. The prescription offered: throw your iPhone in the ocean and take a nice long walk. (Pirate Wires)

The 3,000-year-old workout is back. Indian clubs, the tapered bats Central Park regulars swing around their heads, go back millennia. Persian soldiers and Indian wrestlers swung meel and mudgar, and ancient India had a deity called Mudgarpani who carried one. Victorian England adopted them eagerly, postbellum baseball teams used them for training, and Amherst made them a curriculum requirement. Modern weightlifting killed them off, and now the functional-fitness and prehab wave is bringing them back. (InsideHook)

Men now spend more than women on Botox. Men averaged $529 per Botox visit in Q3 2026, per the Wall Street Journal, outspending women. Part of it is biology, more skin surface area and stronger muscles need more product. The rest is the culture, hair-transplant flights, experimental peptides, surgery for "hunter eyes," camera-facing life, and dating-app pressure all doing their part. (InsideHook)

Forty looks nothing like it used to. On her 41st birthday, Karley Sciortino argues the old map of midlife no longer applies. Her cohort is more likely to have eggs on ice, a ghosting landlord, and a complicated relationship with a Feeld profile than kids in puberty and a mortgage. Her year included driving across America twice solo with her dog, a first produced screenplay, and a seven-month intentional break from sex. Hollywood is catching up too. In 1991, 45-year-old Diane Keaton played the mother of the bride. In The Odyssey, 43-year-old Lupita Nyong'o plays Helen of Troy, the most desirable woman on earth. (Karley Sciortino)

Media & The Mess

MS NOW's Moscow mishap. Correspondent Ken Dilanian broke into programming to report, citing two anonymous sources, that FBI director Kash Patel had landed in Putin's Russia for meetings, adding "the lack of clarity was concerning." The problem: Patel was at a law enforcement event in Lynchburg, Virginia, some 5,000 miles away. Dilanian corrected on air two hours later, and the network is reviewing its standards process. It handed the famously litigious Patel an opening. "If a network cannot confirm where I was before putting it on air, how can the public trust its reporting on the work our agents and officers do every day?" (Status)

Masked settlers nearly severed a WaPo journalist's finger. Heidi Levine is in stable condition after surgery, her daughter said the finger was almost severed during an attack by masked Israeli settlers. Ambassador Mike Huckabee called the assault "vicious and cowardly" and said those responsible should spend years in prison. Netanyahu's office initially expressed skepticism, prompting a rebuke from Post executive editor Matt Murray, while President Isaac Herzog called Levine to apologize. Days earlier, Trump endorsed Netanyahu for reelection ahead of Israel's October 27 elections. (Status)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Pour one out for the leap second. After years of contention, the timekeeping community killed it. (WIRED)

• The app that turns your phone into Dieter Rams. Brass transforms oversaturated phone icons into an orderly, monochromatic grid that does not scream "pick me up." (Why is this interesting?)

• Kelly Clarkson tried to buy a fake mechanical bird from a Brooklyn curiosity shop. The employees assumed she could not afford it, she criticized them online, the story went viral, and the shop says it is being "literally attacked" by her fans circling in. (Pirate Wires)

• The optimistic case that AirPods are quietly solving the literacy crisis. Essayist William Davies makes it, flagged as one of the charms of Substack. (The Republic of Letters)

Monday, October 19, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• $1 billion: Mercury's annualized revenue, up about 50% year over year, with more than 450,000 customers. The fintech is also launching a payroll service.

• 10%+: the interest rate Blackstone is expected to charge on Anthropic's newest borrowing, versus about 7% for similarly rated bonds and the high 8s Anthropic paid in June.

• 15,000: gift cards worth more than $5 million issued after a Chinese crime ring hacked Staples' internal customer support system, then shipped the stolen merchandise back to China.

• 236: self-reported noncitizens summoned for jury duty in Macomb County, Michigan in the third quarter of 2026. Nine were registered to vote and one had a voting history.

• 30,325: pounds of trash the Atlantic Avenue BID Clean Team hauled away last month, plus 767 tree pit servicings.

• 15: times per second that primate brains flip between conscious and subconscious processing, per researchers at Berkeley, Princeton, and Caltech. They call them "micro-epochs."

Quotes of the Day

• "When the party will end, I don't know." (Tan Su Shan, CEO of DBS Group, on the AI buildout's looming capital crunch)

• "This wretched war has created for Fujairah a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity." (Fereidun Fesharaki, chairman emeritus of FGE NexantECA, on the Gulf port's Zero Hormuz moment)

• "Hierarchies have changed. Everything is in disarray." (Nat in Sara Mesa's Un Amor, the post-MeToo novel of manners at the center of Dhimmi Monde's "Sex Rules")

AI & The Machines

A creator turned her TikTok editing into a 15-second terminal command. Brooke Lacey, a technologist with 290,000 TikTok followers, uses Claude Code, FFmpeg, and Whisper to turn a raw phone recording into a fully edited, captioned vertical video in about 15 seconds, no editor or upload required. She trained Claude on her exact jump-cut cadence, even the pause before a punchline, and the whole edit lives in a text file that can spit out 15, 30, and 60-second versions. Her takeaway: creators need to understand the craft before they can delegate it, because AI amplifies judgment but does not replace the experience that built it. (Lenny's Newsletter)

Meta's Muse Wonder is the strongest agentic model at its price tier, and it should never touch your frontend. Claire's testing ranked it first at billing-ticket resolution, inbox triage, computer use, and email writing, with a real "active focus" that spends more time on complex tasks. It even resisted a prompt-injection attempt. But its design defaults to heavy serif fonts, blurple, rounded corners, and generic SaaS layouts, and it ignored brand guidelines on a real redesign. Getting 80% of a prototype right is very different from finishing it. (Lenny's Newsletter)

License-plate readers are having a moment. Mapquest added a "surveillance layer" that maps Flock, Vigilant, and other automated license-plate-reader cameras. In related news, a Savannah, Georgia police officer gave her ICE-agent husband her Flock login, which he used for nearly 1,000 searches across six states. (404 Media)

Money & Power

Six years of Wikipedia edits decided what the internet believes about COVID's origins. Ashley Rindsberg traces a six-year editorial battle in which a small cluster of editors framed the lab leak as a partisan conspiracy. It started February 9, 2021, when editor Arcturus created the COVID-19 lab leak hypothesis entry in a single 44,000-byte edit, the same day the WHO's Wuhan mission declared a lab leak "extremely unlikely." The framing now feeds search engines, AI systems, and the public record. (Pirate Wires)

Moped crews are snatching chains across New York City. More than 20 chain snatchings since September, at least 10 of them violent. On October 2, NYPD Detective Jose Mercedes, 33, was stabbed 10 times fighting off two men going for a necklace his mother gave him. The suspects, D'Angelo Caraballo, 25, and Sneider Mejia, 24, were caught outside Boston and face attempted murder charges. Police link much of the pattern to the Trinitarios gang. (NLDR Media)

Italy's cost-of-living protests turned violent. Marches under the "Italia in Piazza" banner drew about 5,000 people in Milan, 3,000 in Turin, and 2,000 in Bologna over rising prices, stagnant wages, and strained public services. Hooded breakaway groups threw stones and firecrackers, torched bins, and looted shops near Milan's Duomo. Around 28 arrests, dozens injured, and the CGIL union has called a general strike for November 20. (NLDR Media)

ICE is arresting more people than ever, with quieter tactics. A Migrant Insider investigation finds arrests at record levels while the agency resists transparency. ICE rejected automated body-camera activation, citing privacy risks and even the First Amendment, even though VA Police, also federal officers, already auto-activate Axon cameras when drawing a firearm. (Migrant Insider)

Who is backing Germany's far right? Scott Galloway and Anne Applebaum trace the AfD's rise through Russian gas dependence and Chinese manufacturing, plus a thumb on the scale from Elon Musk's algorithm and the Trump administration. This is part two of the Prof G deep dive. (Prof G Media)

The Culture

The $6,000 coat you can now DIY. Conner Ives' silk-and-fur robe coats, priced from $6,000 to $8,000, sold out everywhere, and so did the dupes. So TikTok turned into fashion school: creators are pairing $50 silk jackets with eBay fox fur stoles, snap closures, and safety pins to Do Ives Yourself. One creator rounded up 50 silk jackets for her readers. Stylist Becky Malinsky's verdict: "Power to them!" (Feed Me)

A London designer's current obsessions. Lucila Safdie, the Central Saint Martins grad behind the Apocalipstick collection (and Addison Rae's costumes for her London show supporting Lana Del Rey), recommends: a History of Glamour short animated by Theresa Duncan, a cinema snack combo of Buzz candy x Buzz Ball x ChupaChups, and falling down a YouTube hole of Martha Argerich's classic piano performances. (Perfectly Imperfect)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Meta suspended the No Kings Instagram account on the day of its weekend protests, then restored it four hours later, blaming an accident. (404 Media)

• A guy turned his regular push scooter into an e-scooter by attaching a power drill. (404 Media)

• Cake Mail Club is an $8/month snail-mail subscription delivering film photography prints and personal letters. Join by Oct. 21 for this month's drop. (A Thing or Two)

• RomCon hits Industry City, Brooklyn this Saturday. (A Thing or Two)

• On Running launched its own SSENSE-like editorial site. (Feed Me)

• The New York Times cooking team poached an Infatuation editor. (Feed Me)

• Two of the largest tech companies in wedding planning have merged. (Feed Me)

• Two of the most Instagrammed avocado toasts are coming to Manhattan. (Feed Me)

• The Roy Lichtenstein exhibit at the Whitney is worth the trip, with a mini-gallery recreating his first solo pop-art show. (Boerum Bulletin)

• The Fcukers' December show sold out months in advance; tickets now only via "verified resellers." (Boerum Bulletin)

• The Nets kick off the NBA season at home Wednesday night. (Boerum Bulletin)

• The State Department is updating its China travel advisory over wrongful-detention risk, tied to the detentions of Americans Min Zin and Youlin Chen. (Semafor)

• Jensen Huang joined Silicon Valley & The World as a co-chair. (Semafor)

Monday, October 19, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

Claire put Meta's new Muse Wonder model through nearly 20 real-world tasks and found it the strongest agentic model at its price tier, ranking first on billing-ticket resolution, inbox triage, computer use and email writing. It even resisted a prompt-injection attempt while resolving every planted complication in a customer support benchmark. But keep it far from your frontend: its design work defaults to heavy serif fonts, blurple, rounded corners and generic SaaS layouts, with broken buttons and images. (Lenny's Newsletter)

This creator edits TikToks in 15 seconds with Claude Code. Brooke Lacey, a longtime technologist with a big TikTok audience, uses Claude Code, FFmpeg and Whisper to turn a raw phone recording into a fully edited, captioned vertical video without uploading the footage or opening a traditional editor. The whole edit lives in a text file, so one command spits out 15, 30 and 60-second versions plus a landscape crop. She trained Claude on her exact jump-cut cadence, including the pause before a punchline, and mines her comment sections for new script ideas. (Lenny's Newsletter)

Money Moves

The Knot just bought Zola. Two of the largest tech companies in wedding planning have merged, consolidating the online wedding industrial complex. (Feed Me)

On Running launched its own editorial platform. Called Ondesign, it is sort of like SSENSE, except instead of interviews with Sandy Liang and John Early, it interviews On's own team members, like Eva, Senior Color Design Lead. The brand-as-publisher playbook marches on. (Feed Me)

Glossier is doing a Chanel bag giveaway. The brand once valued at $1 billion is now running a luxury bag sweepstakes as an engagement play, which puts them in Cooked territory. (Feed Me)

Screen Time

The Elizabeth Holmes documentary had a monster opening. You Can See Everything, the three-hour doc directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, had the biggest theatrical opening for a non-music documentary since Fahrenheit 9/11 in 2004, with at least two thousand shows selling out in limited release. (Feed Me)

Style & Culture

The Monday trend roundup: Rolodexes, driving teens and AI face. Casey Lewis's After School long read flags the kids bringing back the Rolodex, Gen Alpha actually wanting to drive, a boxing rave for fighting your situationship, growing fatigue with rating everything, "AI face" as the new Instagram face, and frosted tips and frosted lips. (After School)

A London restaurant rebranded by rearranging its letters. La Familia became Lamia when the new owners fashioned the sign out of the old lettering, a genius bit of thrift spotted on Green Lanes. An inspiring niftiness, and impressive resourcefulness. (tgite)

Lucila Safdie's comfort watches: Martha Argerich and Joan Didion. The London designer recommends watching Martha Argerich's 1970s piano performances on YouTube ("so angelic"), Theresa Duncan's short animation The History of Glamour, and reading Joan Didion's Democracy, where "all the things I love and admire about Joan Didion come together most perfectly." (Perfectly Imperfect)

Watch List

MapQuest added a surveillance layer. One of the earliest mapping tools is relevant again: you can now see Flock, Vigilant and other automated license plate reader cameras on the map. (404 Media)

A cop gave her ICE-agent husband her Flock login. A Savannah, Georgia police officer handed over her license-plate-reader credentials, which her husband used to run nearly 1,000 searches across six states. Not the first time cops have casually shared Flock access with federal agents who lack contracts with the company. (404 Media)

• Lucien Smith's final four paintings open October 25 at Tripoli Gallery in the Hamptons. The rain paintings were made with a fire extinguisher filled with thinned paint; Smith died September 7 at 37. (Feed Me)

• RomCon is this Saturday at Industry City in Brooklyn, if you need plans. (A Thing or Two)

• Auzi makes hearing aid and cochlear implant jewelry, which is quite genius. (A Thing or Two)

• One guy turned his regular push scooter into an e-scooter by attaching a power drill to it. (404 Media)

: Arkansans who lost Medicaid in six months when the state tried work requirements, even though 95% of them were eligible and simply had not filed the paperwork. Employment did not budge. 0 to 60 in under a second

: Tesla's claimed acceleration for the new Roadster, which Musk unveiled in Texas driving upside down, flipping through the air, and jumping over a row of Teslas on compressed-air rocket thrusters. Claimed top speed is 230+ mph with 300+ miles of range, though deliveries are not expected until 2028. The car was first announced in 2017 with a 2020 delivery date.
$29 a month

: all Accenture will now spend per employee on Claude, per 404 Media. The AI boom sells infinite productivity, and one of the world's biggest consultancies is rationing its chatbot like office supplies.
: the drop in basic cable ad revenue year over year, the lowest since 2006. Only ESPN (up 7%) and Fox News (up 7.5%) are holding the line.
$15 million

: the opening weekend haul for Nathan Fielder's Theranos movie "You Can See Everything," in just over 850 theaters. It is the biggest debut on under 1,000 screens since Borat in 2006 and the highest-opening non-music documentary in more than a decade.

: residents Los Angeles County lost last year, the most of any county in America. Condo construction in the city has collapsed 90% under regulation, and the so-called mansion tax has frozen home sales.

: treaty members that set national goals under the global biodiversity framework, with delegates meeting October 19 to 30 in Yerevan for the first formal review. Fewer than half of the reviewed goals are on track for 2030, and only 5% of countries said how much they would cut from $500 billion in annual nature-destroying subsidies.

"people who take pride in being brutally honest are usually just interested in being brutal." (
Bob Burg

Semafor

Gallup's latest Life Evaluation Index finds Americans of all ages less happy than ten years ago, and even the oldest generation is only 53% happy, while every other generation is underwater. Victorian England adopted them eagerly, postbellum baseball teams used them for training, and Amherst made them a curriculum requirement. Tuesday, October 20, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 91%: the chance Democrats would have of taking the Senate under a naive coin-flip model that treats every race as independent. Nate Silver's FLIPR model, which assumes polling misses are correlated, puts the real odds in the mid-70s instead.

• 54-46: the Senate majority Democrats would hold based on current state polls alone, though Silver notes many of those leads are modest and the fundamentals push several races back toward 50/50.

• $190 million: outside spending behind Ken Paxton's Texas Senate campaign, per Hill Heat. Rival James Talarico told voters in Denton: "Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He is trying to buy Texas."

• 30%: the odds Silver's model gave Donald Trump of winning in 2016, while some competitors put it at literally 1%, a reminder that serious forecasters have baked systematic polling error into their math for a decade.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Walking works for knees: people with knee arthritis who walked for exercise were less likely to develop new pain or worsening joint damage over two years, per a Washington Post piece flagged by Six Minute Mile (Washington Post).

• Alexander Chee on Netflix's East of Eden: Zoe Kazan enlisted the novelist to write Lee, the character he calls "almost a unicorn" of Asian American literature, for episode five (Book Gossip).

• BAAJA, the data-centers-everywhere fast-tracking bill (S. 5653), is moving through a lame-duck Congress, per Hill Heat (Hill Heat).

• A Bushwick pop-up worth seeing: Chicago's Deadly Prey Gallery works with Ghanaian artists to keep alive the tradition of hand-painted movie posters once made for mobile cinema screenings (InsideHook).

• Agave wine is having a moment: ferment the agave plant with yeast and fortify it like sherry and you get a tequila-adjacent spirit that bartenders are now mixing into low-ABV cocktails, including a lighter margarita (InsideHook).

morning.body:
Tuesday, October 20, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• $15 million: the opening-weekend take for Nathan Fielder's Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything" from just 855 US theaters, the biggest debut for a non-music or concert doc since 2004's "Fahrenheit 9/11," and the largest opening for any movie on under 1,000 screens since "Borat" in 2006.

• 178: "life-changing" nonfiction recommendations crowd-sourced from Maybe Baby readers and collected into one big shared spreadsheet. Patrick Radden Keefe is the most recommended author by far.

• 70%: Coca-Cola's share of US fountain sales by volume. Pepsi's slice of the carbonated soft drink market fell from just over 13.6% in 2000 to a little over 8% last year, and KFC just became the latest fast food chain to defect from Pepsi to Coke.

• 5%: of Anthropic's shares committed to its Public Benefit Fund, announced Sunday. The fund could make giant donations to traditional non-profits or direct donations to specific populations. Details are vague.

• $1 billion: worth of shares the CoreWeave CEO has offloaded since the IPO in March 2025, after the stock slumped almost 25% last week.

• 32: states where election offices have received suspicious letters ahead of the midterms, according to WIRED's survey of officials in all 50 states plus DC.

Quotes of the Day

• "the AI boom has resulted in a race between available supply and surging demand in certain categories of goods - and so far, demand is winning" (John Williams, NY Fed president, quoted in The Housing Frame)

• "After more than 43 years at CNN, Christiane has decided that the time is right to begin a new chapter" (Mark Thompson, CNN chief, announcing Christiane Amanpour's exit)

• "Women should absolutely not be having sex out of politeness." (Maibritt Henkel, The Argument)

• "Russia, Russia, Russia! What Can I Do for You Today?" (Counterpoint, on Trump's transformation)

AI & The Machines

The Fed is now trying to cool the AI boom. For most of this year, the debate over the AI buildout was tech companies and investors on one side and the public on the other. That changed in the past three weeks, because now markets and the Federal Reserve are questioning the speed and intensity of it. Conor Sen lays out three paths for AI financing in 2027: "Boomflation" (October's turbulence was a hiccup, the Fed hikes through mid-2027, and 7.50% mortgages become the base case), "Weeding Out the Weaker Balance Sheets" (the aggressive spenders dependent on external financing pull back and Meta and Alphabet get the chips instead), and "Subprime-ish" (the weakness in CoreWeave equity and bond prices is the start of something bigger). None of the three is great for housing, and all keep mortgage rates elevated. (The Housing Frame)

WhatsApp's help pages leaked hidden instructions for a Meta chatbot. Around 80 pages on WhatsApp's website exposed instructions that were designed for its chatbot, including a section literally labeled "WHAT NOT TO SAY." Meta says a bug caused the issue. (WIRED)

A physicist explains how Tesla's flying Roadster actually works. Elon Musk's new car hops, glides, and supposedly sticks upside down. Rhett Allain walks through the friction and force needed to understand how that is even possible. It is a neat little lesson in physics hiding inside a car story. (WIRED)

Money & Power

Elon Musk wants to give every American child a share of SpaceX. Musk announced plans to give every American child a single share of SpaceX next year, which amounts to around $10.5 billion worth of stock at its current valuation. The plan is to do it via Trump Accounts, the new kid-focused savings accounts. That came right as Anthropic announced it will commit at least 5% of its shares to its Public Benefit Fund. We are entering the robo-socialism era, and everyone has a different theory about who should get the check. (CNBC)

Apple's foldable iPhone Duo is already sold through January. Within 30 minutes of preorders opening, estimated delivery dates for the iPhone Duo shifted from October 23, 2026 to January 25, 2027, according to MacRumors. That is either huge demand or a paper launch, and Apple is not saying which. (MacRumors)

The OpenAI engineer accused of spying on executives stays behind bars. A judge ordered Abdulrahman Alfozan to remain in custody, likening the Saudi government's offer to secure the former OpenAI engineer's release to a "blank check." Alfozan is accused of planting a recording device to spy on OpenAI's executives. (WIRED)

A Democratic senator is threatening to jail Trump staffers. Speaking at the University of Chicago, Sen. Elissa Slotkin said she hopes to prosecute not just Trump but also those who "enabled" him. The threat prompted calls for Trump to preemptively pardon his entire administration. It is a normal week in the American political system. (Pirate Wires)

The Culture

A busy day in the media business. Christiane Amanpour is leaving CNN after 43 years, Jon Stewart is staying at Comedy Central, Netflix fired Dan Lin, and Laurene Powell Jobs invested $250 million in Skydance. Old media is not dying, it is just changing addresses. (Status)

They fled Trump's America. Now they regret it. The internet told a wave of Americans that Europe was a social paradise, so they moved. Turns out the trains are awful, the health care is not free, and people can be really mean. Sarah Manavis reports on the expats who are having second thoughts. (WIRED)

Kevin Bacon lost a box of '90s clothes and it went around the world. The 68-year-old actor posted an Instagram video detailing the weeks-long journey of a box of "old boots, old jeans, and old hats" through New York, Memphis, France, Germany, Israel, and England. He seemed to call out FedEx as the offending courier, and a FedEx spokesperson has since confirmed they are in direct contact with his team. Six degrees of baggage claim. (People)

Kelly Clarkson vs. a Brooklyn curiosity shop. Clarkson tried to buy a mechanical bird at Art of Play, an "adult toy store" in Brooklyn, and alleges the employees assumed she was too poor to afford it and then called her a liar after she criticized them on social media. The shop says it is being "literally attacked" by the singer's upset fans. Pirate Wires sent Harris Sockel to check the vibe. (Pirate Wires)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Dr Pepper is actually the oldest of America's three most popular soft beverages. The "pepper soda" was first sold in 1885, a year before Coca-Cola and about eight years before Pepsi, which was then called "Brad's Drink." (Snacks)

• Japan's JAXA is leading an international mission to reach Mars' moon Phobos and bring soil back to Earth. If it works, it could unlock new clues about the history of the solar system. (WIRED)

• The Orionids are peaking this week, so look up. (WIRED)

• Ashley Rindsberg on how a handful of Wikipedia editors rewrote the story of COVID's origins to depict "lab leak" as a racist conspiracy, even as the FBI, CIA, and leading scientists say they believe the virus likely came from a lab. (Pirate Wires)

• Mary Anne Franks, who has spent years fighting online abuse, on why sexual assault is a free speech issue: "When people are abused with impunity, the message becomes 'We do not care about women's voices.'" (WIRED)

• On the earnings calendar today: GE Aerospace, RTX, Hasbro, and GM report premarket. SpaceX releases results after the close. (Snacks)

midday.body:
Tuesday, October 20, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• 342,000: GitHub stars for "Reverse Engineer Anything," the viral open-source project that uses AI to deconstruct features in other software so you can clone them yourself.

• 20,000: cars Waymo plans to have on the road by the end of 2027, up from 4,000 today, funded by $5 billion in fresh debt with no explicit Alphabet backstop.

• 12 billion: social impressions generated by the 6,000 creators Disney is working with this year, up 30% from 2025 (via the LA Times).

• $138 million: revenue Baseball Lifestyle 101 pulled in last year off its melting-cone patterns, as Gen Alpha decks out youth baseball with custom cleats and Cuban link chains (via Yahoo).

• 75%: of investors under 30 who have changed or are considering changing their portfolios before the midterms, compared with 17% of boomers (via Bloomberg).

• 543 miles: Elon Musk's wealth visualized as a stack of $100 bills. For comparison, $5 million is nearly 18 feet.

• 200: packets of Zyn that director Lance Oppenheim sent Robert Pattinson to convince him to star in his film "Primetime."

Quotes of the Day

• "90% (!) of a great restaurant has nothing to do with how it looks." (Christine Gachot, AD100 designer)

• "This is why I am celibate... It's because I'm calling in a fucking king." (Kesha, on Alex Cooper's podcast)

• "There have been four times the software industry has been doubted, and this is one of them. Every other time, it's boomed after it's been doubted. People got it wrong. It'll be the same thing this time." (Orlando Bravo, Thoma Bravo chief)

• "jumping out of its lane" (Austan Goolsbee, Chicago Fed president, on inflation spreading from AI-linked sectors into the rest of the economy)

AI & The Machines

The government is kicking DeepSeek out of its own buildings. DHS ordered federal civilian agencies to remove and stop buying products from Chinese AI developer DeepSeek and its parent company, per an order filed for Tuesday's Federal Register. Agencies can request exceptions only with 60 days' notice and a "compelling justification." The decision was actually made back in June; it's only going public now. (NLDR Media)

The AI doomers have a sex problem. Jane Gatsby's essay links the AI-doom movement to unconventional sex in rationalist circles, from polyamory to hardcore BDSM. On Sept 5, Aella, the self-styled "whorelord" of the Bay Area, offered to throw a "reverse gangbang" for any OpenAI employee who publicly resigned, whistleblew, and called for a criminal investigation. On Sept 8, ex-employee Jacob Coxon's first-ever X post explaining his resignation pulled 170 million views overnight, and it ended with tech CEOs pledging internal safety controls and independent audits after meeting Trump. (Pirate Wires)

A programming language designed to be hostile to AI. Dominik Picheta built "Killswitch," an esoteric language that LLMs and coding agents can't use, stuffed with "hidden lies which humans are unlikely to read, or which they are likely to recognize as lies." As AI learns to reverse-engineer anything, some coders are building fortresses it can't enter. (404 Media)

Money & Power

France is scaring the whole Eurozone. The gap between French 10-year bonds and the German benchmark is at its widest since 2012, stoking fears that France's political and fiscal crisis could infect the broader economy. Violent protests, a huge debt burden, and a possible far-right presidency are all in the mix. (Semafor)

The great startup buyout is quietly reversing. Unilever is selling Welly (acquired 2021), Pepsi admitted the $2 billion Poppi deal isn't making enough to earn its M&A bonus, and Coca-Cola is looking to unwind Costa. Even Nestle is trimming back, with 11% of its products driving 80% of revenue. The rare winners: Liquid IV and SkinnyPop. (Semafor)

Trump signed a women's health executive order. At a Rose Garden ceremony with Melania Trump, he directed NIH to set up a Women's Health Division within 90 days, covering heart disease, cancer, Alzheimer's, endometriosis, infertility, and menopause. The task force is co-chaired by RFK Jr. and Susie Wiles, and the order revokes earlier women's health research actions. (NLDR Media)

Young men can't stop betting. As long as they feel anxious about falling behind, young men keep turning to gambling, crypto, and get-rich-quick schemes. Some are betting on women's college volleyball, a sport they've never watched, just to have something to bet on. "With a couple of Eagles parlays, I have a chance of making [that $10,000] into $100,000... Now I have a down payment," says gambling policy lead Jonathan Cohen. (After School, via Politico)

The Culture

The NBA won the internet by giving it away. Twenty years ago the NFL threatened to come to your house over a Tom Brady photo while the NBA put clips on YouTube with a liberal take on fair use. The result: the most internet-native league in sports, where House of Highlights now shapes how all sports media operates and ESPN talks in memes. Defector's "Nothing But Respect" (100+ episodes) treats basketball as a critical text for understanding America. (InsideHook)

The drumming collective that outlasted the icons. Olodum, Brazil's activist drumming collective, played in Michael Jackson's Spike Lee-directed favela video (authorities tried to ban the shoot, fearing it would hurt Rio's 2004 Olympics bid). Paul Simon recorded them on Salvador's streets with an eight-track in 1990 and opened his 1991 Central Park concert with them. Decades later, with Jackson disgraced and Simon retired, Olodum still plays weekly in Pelourinho's streets. (Why Is This Interesting?)

Work & Ideas

Netflix's top hiring skill isn't what you'd guess. Its Chief Product and Technology Officer says systems thinking is the most important competency they screen for. The World Economic Forum agrees it's a core skill on the rise, and there's a growing gap between how much it matters and how many people actually have it. (The Critical Path)

We're automating the ladder out from under the next generation. The Aspen Institute's "Last Masters Problem": if AI does the junior-level tasks, young workers never build the expertise those tasks used to teach. The system looks more efficient while quietly losing the people who know how it works. (The Critical Path)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Scammers cloned a Florida sheriff's voice with AI and left residents a voicemail pretending to be him. (404 Media)

• Ukraine used a giant drone to rescue a wounded soldier in combat, believed to be the first time it's ever happened. (404 Media)

• YouTuber ThroatyMumbo ported Doom to VHS, with the tape itself running the game code. (404 Media)

• At the NYC Wine & Food Festival's Burger Bash, the crowd picked Nowon and the judges picked Gotham Burger Social Club. (On the House)

• Lila Drew finally watched Bong Joon-Ho's "Memories of Murder" and learned the real-life killer watched it too, which makes it even creepier. (Perfectly Imperfect)

Tuesday, October 20, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• $15 million: the opening-weekend take for Nathan Fielder's Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything" from just 855 US theaters, the biggest debut for a non-music or concert doc since 2004's "Fahrenheit 9/11," and the largest opening for any movie on under 1,000 screens since "Borat" in 2006.

• 178: "life-changing" nonfiction recommendations crowd-sourced from Maybe Baby readers and collected into one big shared spreadsheet. Patrick Radden Keefe is the most recommended author by far.

• 70%: Coca-Cola's share of US fountain sales by volume. Pepsi's slice of the carbonated soft drink market fell from just over 13.6% in 2000 to a little over 8% last year, and KFC just became the latest fast food chain to defect from Pepsi to Coke.

• 5%: of Anthropic's shares committed to its Public Benefit Fund, announced Sunday. The fund could make giant donations to traditional non-profits or direct donations to specific populations. Details are vague.

• $1 billion: worth of shares the CoreWeave CEO has offloaded since the IPO in March 2025, after the stock slumped almost 25% last week.

• 32: states where election offices have received suspicious letters ahead of the midterms, according to WIRED's survey of officials in all 50 states plus DC.

Quotes of the Day

• "the AI boom has resulted in a race between available supply and surging demand in certain categories of goods - and so far, demand is winning" (John Williams, NY Fed president, quoted in The Housing Frame)

• "After more than 43 years at CNN, Christiane has decided that the time is right to begin a new chapter" (Mark Thompson, CNN chief, announcing Christiane Amanpour's exit)

• "Women should absolutely not be having sex out of politeness." (Maibritt Henkel, The Argument)

• "Russia, Russia, Russia! What Can I Do for You Today?" (Counterpoint, on Trump's transformation)

AI & The Machines

The Fed is now trying to cool the AI boom. For most of this year, the debate over the AI buildout was tech companies and investors on one side and the public on the other. That changed in the past three weeks, because now markets and the Federal Reserve are questioning the speed and intensity of it. Conor Sen lays out three paths for AI financing in 2027: "Boomflation" (October's turbulence was a hiccup, the Fed hikes through mid-2027, and 7.50% mortgages become the base case), "Weeding Out the Weaker Balance Sheets" (the aggressive spenders dependent on external financing pull back and Meta and Alphabet get the chips instead), and "Subprime-ish" (the weakness in CoreWeave equity and bond prices is the start of something bigger). None of the three is great for housing, and all keep mortgage rates elevated. (The Housing Frame)

WhatsApp's help pages leaked hidden instructions for a Meta chatbot. Around 80 pages on WhatsApp's website exposed instructions that were designed for its chatbot, including a section literally labeled "WHAT NOT TO SAY." Meta says a bug caused the issue. (WIRED)

A physicist explains how Tesla's flying Roadster actually works. Elon Musk's new car hops, glides, and supposedly sticks upside down. Rhett Allain walks through the friction and force needed to understand how that is even possible. It is a neat little lesson in physics hiding inside a car story. (WIRED)

Money & Power

Elon Musk wants to give every American child a share of SpaceX. Musk announced plans to give every American child a single share of SpaceX next year, which amounts to around $10.5 billion worth of stock at its current valuation. The plan is to do it via Trump Accounts, the new kid-focused savings accounts. That came right as Anthropic announced it will commit at least 5% of its shares to its Public Benefit Fund. We are entering the robo-socialism era, and everyone has a different theory about who should get the check. (CNBC)

Apple's foldable iPhone Duo is already sold through January. Within 30 minutes of preorders opening, estimated delivery dates for the iPhone Duo shifted from October 23, 2026 to January 25, 2027, according to MacRumors. That is either huge demand or a paper launch, and Apple is not saying which. (MacRumors)

The OpenAI engineer accused of spying on executives stays behind bars. A judge ordered Abdulrahman Alfozan to remain in custody, likening the Saudi government's offer to secure the former OpenAI engineer's release to a "blank check." Alfozan is accused of planting a recording device to spy on OpenAI's executives. (WIRED)

A Democratic senator is threatening to jail Trump staffers. Speaking at the University of Chicago, Sen. Elissa Slotkin said she hopes to prosecute not just Trump but also those who "enabled" him. The threat prompted calls for Trump to preemptively pardon his entire administration. It is a normal week in the American political system. (Pirate Wires)

The Culture

A busy day in the media business. Christiane Amanpour is leaving CNN after 43 years, Jon Stewart is staying at Comedy Central, Netflix fired Dan Lin, and Laurene Powell Jobs invested $250 million in Skydance. Old media is not dying, it is just changing addresses. (Status)

They fled Trump's America. Now they regret it. The internet told a wave of Americans that Europe was a social paradise, so they moved. Turns out the trains are awful, the health care is not free, and people can be really mean. Sarah Manavis reports on the expats who are having second thoughts. (WIRED)

Kevin Bacon lost a box of '90s clothes and it went around the world. The 68-year-old actor posted an Instagram video detailing the weeks-long journey of a box of "old boots, old jeans, and old hats" through New York, Memphis, France, Germany, Israel, and England. He seemed to call out FedEx as the offending courier, and a FedEx spokesperson has since confirmed they are in direct contact with his team. Six degrees of baggage claim. (People)

Kelly Clarkson vs. a Brooklyn curiosity shop. Clarkson tried to buy a mechanical bird at Art of Play, an "adult toy store" in Brooklyn, and alleges the employees assumed she was too poor to afford it and then called her a liar after she criticized them on social media. The shop says it is being "literally attacked" by the singer's upset fans. Pirate Wires sent Harris Sockel to check the vibe. (Pirate Wires)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Dr Pepper is actually the oldest of America's three most popular soft beverages. The "pepper soda" was first sold in 1885, a year before Coca-Cola and about eight years before Pepsi, which was then called "Brad's Drink." (Snacks)

• Japan's JAXA is leading an international mission to reach Mars' moon Phobos and bring soil back to Earth. If it works, it could unlock new clues about the history of the solar system. (WIRED)

• The Orionids are peaking this week, so look up. (WIRED)

• Ashley Rindsberg on how a handful of Wikipedia editors rewrote the story of COVID's origins to depict "lab leak" as a racist conspiracy, even as the FBI, CIA, and leading scientists say they believe the virus likely came from a lab. (Pirate Wires)

• Mary Anne Franks, who has spent years fighting online abuse, on why sexual assault is a free speech issue: "When people are abused with impunity, the message becomes 'We do not care about women's voices.'" (WIRED)

• On the earnings calendar today: GE Aerospace, RTX, Hasbro, and GM report premarket. SpaceX releases results after the close. (Snacks)

Tuesday, October 20, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• 342,000: GitHub stars for "Reverse Engineer Anything," the viral open-source project that uses AI to deconstruct features in other software so you can clone them yourself.

• 20,000: cars Waymo plans to have on the road by the end of 2027, up from 4,000 today, funded by $5 billion in fresh debt with no explicit Alphabet backstop.

• 12 billion: social impressions generated by the 6,000 creators Disney is working with this year, up 30% from 2025 (via the LA Times).

• $138 million: revenue Baseball Lifestyle 101 pulled in last year off its melting-cone patterns, as Gen Alpha decks out youth baseball with custom cleats and Cuban link chains (via Yahoo).

• 75%: of investors under 30 who have changed or are considering changing their portfolios before the midterms, compared with 17% of boomers (via Bloomberg).

• 543 miles: Elon Musk's wealth visualized as a stack of $100 bills. For comparison, $5 million is nearly 18 feet.

• 200: packets of Zyn that director Lance Oppenheim sent Robert Pattinson to convince him to star in his film "Primetime."

Quotes of the Day

• "90% (!) of a great restaurant has nothing to do with how it looks." (Christine Gachot, AD100 designer)

• "This is why I am celibate... It's because I'm calling in a fucking king." (Kesha, on Alex Cooper's podcast)

• "There have been four times the software industry has been doubted, and this is one of them. Every other time, it's boomed after it's been doubted. People got it wrong. It'll be the same thing this time." (Orlando Bravo, Thoma Bravo chief)

• "jumping out of its lane" (Austan Goolsbee, Chicago Fed president, on inflation spreading from AI-linked sectors into the rest of the economy)

AI & The Machines

The government is kicking DeepSeek out of its own buildings. DHS ordered federal civilian agencies to remove and stop buying products from Chinese AI developer DeepSeek and its parent company, per an order filed for Tuesday's Federal Register. Agencies can request exceptions only with 60 days' notice and a "compelling justification." The decision was actually made back in June; it's only going public now. (NLDR Media)

The AI doomers have a sex problem. Jane Gatsby's essay links the AI-doom movement to unconventional sex in rationalist circles, from polyamory to hardcore BDSM. On Sept 5, Aella, the self-styled "whorelord" of the Bay Area, offered to throw a "reverse gangbang" for any OpenAI employee who publicly resigned, whistleblew, and called for a criminal investigation. On Sept 8, ex-employee Jacob Coxon's first-ever X post explaining his resignation pulled 170 million views overnight, and it ended with tech CEOs pledging internal safety controls and independent audits after meeting Trump. (Pirate Wires)

A programming language designed to be hostile to AI. Dominik Picheta built "Killswitch," an esoteric language that LLMs and coding agents can't use, stuffed with "hidden lies which humans are unlikely to read, or which they are likely to recognize as lies." As AI learns to reverse-engineer anything, some coders are building fortresses it can't enter. (404 Media)

Money & Power

France is scaring the whole Eurozone. The gap between French 10-year bonds and the German benchmark is at its widest since 2012, stoking fears that France's political and fiscal crisis could infect the broader economy. Violent protests, a huge debt burden, and a possible far-right presidency are all in the mix. (Semafor)

The great startup buyout is quietly reversing. Unilever is selling Welly (acquired 2021), Pepsi admitted the $2 billion Poppi deal isn't making enough to earn its M&A bonus, and Coca-Cola is looking to unwind Costa. Even Nestle is trimming back, with 11% of its products driving 80% of revenue. The rare winners: Liquid IV and SkinnyPop. (Semafor)

Trump signed a women's health executive order. At a Rose Garden ceremony with Melania Trump, he directed NIH to set up a Women's Health Division within 90 days, covering heart disease, cancer, Alzheimer's, endometriosis, infertility, and menopause. The task force is co-chaired by RFK Jr. and Susie Wiles, and the order revokes earlier women's health research actions. (NLDR Media)

Young men can't stop betting. As long as they feel anxious about falling behind, young men keep turning to gambling, crypto, and get-rich-quick schemes. Some are betting on women's college volleyball, a sport they've never watched, just to have something to bet on. "With a couple of Eagles parlays, I have a chance of making [that $10,000] into $100,000... Now I have a down payment," says gambling policy lead Jonathan Cohen. (After School, via Politico)

The Culture

The NBA won the internet by giving it away. Twenty years ago the NFL threatened to come to your house over a Tom Brady photo while the NBA put clips on YouTube with a liberal take on fair use. The result: the most internet-native league in sports, where House of Highlights now shapes how all sports media operates and ESPN talks in memes. Defector's "Nothing But Respect" (100+ episodes) treats basketball as a critical text for understanding America. (InsideHook)

The drumming collective that outlasted the icons. Olodum, Brazil's activist drumming collective, played in Michael Jackson's Spike Lee-directed favela video (authorities tried to ban the shoot, fearing it would hurt Rio's 2004 Olympics bid). Paul Simon recorded them on Salvador's streets with an eight-track in 1990 and opened his 1991 Central Park concert with them. Decades later, with Jackson disgraced and Simon retired, Olodum still plays weekly in Pelourinho's streets. (Why Is This Interesting?)

Work & Ideas

Netflix's top hiring skill isn't what you'd guess. Its Chief Product and Technology Officer says systems thinking is the most important competency they screen for. The World Economic Forum agrees it's a core skill on the rise, and there's a growing gap between how much it matters and how many people actually have it. (The Critical Path)

We're automating the ladder out from under the next generation. The Aspen Institute's "Last Masters Problem": if AI does the junior-level tasks, young workers never build the expertise those tasks used to teach. The system looks more efficient while quietly losing the people who know how it works. (The Critical Path)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Scammers cloned a Florida sheriff's voice with AI and left residents a voicemail pretending to be him. (404 Media)

• Ukraine used a giant drone to rescue a wounded soldier in combat, believed to be the first time it's ever happened. (404 Media)

• YouTuber ThroatyMumbo ported Doom to VHS, with the tape itself running the game code. (404 Media)

• At the NYC Wine & Food Festival's Burger Bash, the crowd picked Nowon and the judges picked Gotham Burger Social Club. (On the House)

• Lila Drew finally watched Bong Joon-Ho's "Memories of Murder" and learned the real-life killer watched it too, which makes it even creepier. (Perfectly Imperfect)

entries.body:
The day’s mail offered a very 2026 collision: AI infrastructure straining under its own weight, ordinary people resurrecting locked-down gadgets with AI, a mechanical crustacean disguised as a PlayStation, and a white chicken chili that solves dinner with pantry staples. Plus: Olodum’s drums outlasting the pop stars who borrowed them.

Front page

• The AI story has split in two. Ethan Mollick says the tools have leapt from four-minute tasks to work measured in hours—and perhaps weeks—while Ed Zitron argues the financial scaffolding underneath the boom requires near-perfect, perpetual growth. Same exponential; radically different mood. One Useful Thing · Where’s Your Ed At

Best links

• AI as repair kit, not magic wand. 404 Media’s “Reverse Engineer Anything” dispatch describes people using AI to strip ads from TVs, revive bricked hardware, turn a picture frame into a calendar, and rebuild software they never had source code for. It is simultaneously liberation, plagiarism, and a maintenance nightmare. 404 Media

• A playlist with a thesis. The New York Times assembled eight songs named for actresses, from “Bette Davis Eyes” and “Drew Barrymore” to “Lee Remick,” two “Clara Bow”s, Frances Farmer, and Adéla’s “Nicole Kidman.” The best mini-argument: stars fade, but the supporting cast can keep the song alive. The Amplifier

• The percussion that keeps returning. “Why is this interesting?” traces the drumming on Paul Simon’s “The Obvious Child” back to Olodum, the Brazilian activist collective also featured in Michael Jackson’s “They Don’t Care About Us.” Jackson and Simon recede; Olodum keeps playing the streets of Salvador and even made the 2014 World Cup opening ceremony. Why is this interesting?

Worth reading

• The risk of an AI detector deciding who sounds human. Book Gossip examines accusations that an award-winning Zimbabwean writer used AI, and the concern that imperfect detection tools can reproduce racial and linguistic bias—especially when the person under suspicion is an emerging writer of color. The issue also recommends You Don’t Need a Smartphone and Yiyun Li’s Music Against the Night. Book Gossip

• The novel as a diagram of the machine. The Republic of Letters makes Tom McCarthy’s The Rhyl Poster sound like a bureaucratic fever dream: a protagonist who is less a self than a node in law, language, war, and files. The sharpest idea is that the post-systems novel should not recreate an incomprehensible network; it should reveal it through the institutions that give its invisible mass a shape. The Republic of Letters

Food & places

• Tonight’s move: white chicken chili that gets its body by mashing some of the white beans instead of reaching immediately for cream cheese. Rotisserie chicken, canned chiles, seeded jalapeños, tortilla chips, avocado, pickled jalapeños: a modular dinner with a heat dial. NYT Cooking

• Luxury is now a banana-bread category. Feed Me reports on Gone Bananas Bread beside Rockefeller Center, whose ingredient list answers “Not telling you!” and whose calorie count is simply “It’s better you don’t know.” The same issue’s more practical flight luxury: a Delta One suite with a purse hook, glasses hook, wireless charging, side sauces, and a dessert cart with dairy-free sorbet and Amarena cherries. Feed Me

Internet oddities

• The Playstacean: an orange PlayStation 1 with legs and claws attached. Today in Tabs also serves up an exquisite-corpse “Frankenmodel,” a Wendy’s emo record, a programming language designed to be adversarial to LLMs, and a correction for a theory about Russian bot traffic that turns out not to have been true. The newsletter’s real gift is treating all of these as one coherent ecology. Today in Tabs

• The soda cold war gets a new front. KFC has switched from Pepsi to Coke in the U.S.; the issue notes Pepsi’s U.S. carbonated-soft-drink share has fallen from above 13% in the early 2000s to a little over 8%, while Dr Pepper has overtaken it. Also: Dr Pepper is older than both Coke and Pepsi. Snacks

Ideas to steal

• Use the “conjurer” model. Mollick’s useful term for the agentic era: summon agents, assign them work, evaluate what comes back. The upside is leverage; the danger is losing track of how the answer was made. His own test was a set of charts, layouts, images, research, and citations produced from a few sentences of direction.

• Design for the tiny relief. Delta’s purse hook and glasses hook are a good product lesson: a minor piece of hardware can communicate more care than a grand promise. The same goes for pre-ordering a meal up to 18 hours before departure—or skipping breakfast for coffee and a croissant.

• Let the supporting cast become the story. Olodum, Lee in East of Eden, the workers who maintain “luxury” households, and the anonymous people rebuilding abandoned devices all make today’s mail more interesting than its marquee names.

One-liners

• “Ball hog” is apparently the deep-fried zoomer equivalent of the millennial hypebeast aesthetic. — Today in Tabs

• A $5 million fortune is nearly 18 feet of stacked hundred-dollar bills; Elon Musk’s is 543 miles. — 404 Media

• The most unsettling AI metric today: a model can be superhuman at math and still be a bad long-form writer. — One Useful Thing

• Sad-dish protocol: gelato with a splash of booze on top. — Feed Me

Compiled from today’s Gmail messages labeled Newsletters, October 20, 2026.

entries.title: OpenAI bets on brain implant cancer startup, Anthropic braces for recursive self-improvement, Girls returns for season 7 - Wednesday, October 21, 2026
entries.body:
Wednesday, October 21, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 3,500: individual samples stitched together to make Since I Left You, The Avalanches' genre-defining debut. After a 15-year creative block, the Australian duo is back with a fourth album, No Bad Memories, and James Jung sat down with them to write about aging alongside the music you love.

• 13: days until the midterm elections, and the White House blame game has already started. Trump aides are hunting for a scapegoat for expected House and Senate losses, but GOP operatives privately say "Clearly it's the president's fault."

• 32: states where election offices have received suspicious letters ahead of the midterms, per WIRED's Inner Loop.

• One month: the length of Jack's school suspension. The Long Island senior, a former hometown-fair standout and self-described post-SoundCloud kid, turns 18 on Monday, works at Stop & Shop, and says his dream is "just being content. Waking up in the morning and feeling good."

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• The first rule of Greek island-hopping: get on the right ferry. InsideHook's new guide maps nine days across Naxos, Paros, and Ios, with three nights per island as the minimum to absorb each one's distinct character. (InsideHook)

• Instagram's Rings awards honor creators outside the billion-follower cohort, with the 2026 judges including Donatella Versace, Isamaya Ffrench, and Finneas. IG's fashion head Eva Chen says the most important muscle for a creator is pressing publish, because you never know how your voice might come back to you ten times bigger. (Biz Sherbert)

morning.body:
Wednesday, October 21, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• $45 million: the seed round for Coherence Neuro, a startup building a coin-sized brain implant that listens for tumor signals and may also deliver targeted stimulation. OpenAI's venture arm and Peter Thiel's Founders Fund are among the backers, the latest sign that AI labs see brain data as the next training frontier. The device was tested in three patients in June and aims for first chronic human implants in 2027, with glioblastoma in its sights.

• $29: the monthly cap Accenture has reportedly put on employee spending on Claude, per 404 Media. The relationship between AI companies and their corporate customers is starting to show cracks.

• 1,000: the number of people Netflix laid off last week, about 6% of its workforce, with the stock down more than 40% over the past year.

• 92%: the chance prediction markets give Democrats of taking the House in the midterms, with 65% for the Senate and a 97% chance of Roy Cooper flipping North Carolina.

• $30,000: the payout the White House's new whistleblower tip line offers if a tip leads to a fraud conviction.

Quotes of the Day

• "Do we want to build a world in which we don't actually matter?" (Jon Stewart, after an OpenAI researcher told The Daily Show he expects "no jobs" and universal high income)

• "I hope that we make recursive self-improvement illegal before you get there." (Kelsey Piper, closing her dispatch from inside Anthropic's San Francisco headquarters)

• "Close to 100%." (United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby, saying the U.S. should have an inheritance tax close to 100%, and that he would happily pay it)

• "They're on TV, dummy!" (Hunter Harris, on viewers who complain TV characters would not still be friends in real life)

AI & The Machines

Anthropic's plan to save humanity from AI is mostly hope and guesswork. Kelsey Piper spent a day at Anthropic's San Francisco headquarters, where researchers briefed outsiders on bioweapon risk, recursive self-improvement, and charts showing Claude's growing mastery. The most striking detail: when Anthropic tested Claude planning a bioweapon attack on its own, the model did better than a human aided by Claude. The lab says recursive self-improvement, the point at which Claude can independently build the next, more powerful Claude, could arrive next year. Piper's takeaway is that the company knows what it does not want (extinction, concentrated power, irrelevance), but the positive vision is thin, and its lobbying bill looks like a normal company protecting its interests. (The Argument)

An AI agent wandered into a listserv of top internet researchers, and the reply-all chaos is still unfolding. A 7,500-person group of internet experts melted down over the agent's appearance, a flare-up that WIRED's Olivia Snow says reveals how outdated their notions of privacy really are. It is a small preview of a bigger problem: we keep deploying agents into human spaces with human expectations, then acting shocked when the humans freak out. (WIRED)

Europe wants the data centers, but its climate goals keep getting in the way. A German plan to funnel the heat given off by data centers into nearby homes has run aground, and policymakers across the continent are weighing AI ambitions against climate objectives. Everyone wants the compute; nobody wants the carbon bill. (WIRED)

Money & Power

Zuck's Muse has a lot to prove. Meta reports earnings after the bell today, expected to show $41.1 billion in quarterly capital expenditures and $9.4 billion in negative free cash flow, which would mark its first cash-flow-negative quarter since 2012. The bright spot is Muse, the personal AI agent launched September 8 with a furry mascot that is equal parts cute and unsettling, which passed 5 million downloads in its first three weeks. Investors are asking two questions of every AI spender: how much more money will you borrow, and when does any of this make money? (Sherwood Snacks)

Investors are buying default insurance on the AI boom. Trading in credit default swaps tied to the bonds of Oracle, SpaceX, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Broadcom, and Nvidia surged from under $2 billion a week in July to a much heavier clip in September, per Morgan Stanley research cited by the Financial Times. The cost of protection on AI names, especially the rattled CoreWeave, keeps rising as the market hedges against mountains of AI-fueled debt. (Reuters)

The Culture

Girls is coming back, and TV's best writers have notes. The series returns for a five-episode seventh season on HBO Max in 2027, and Hunter Harris asked a dozen writers what they want from it. The pitches are gloriously unhinged: Marnie running a gentle-parenting Substack from a renovated Saratoga Springs farmhouse while cheating with the farmhand, Shosh founding The RealReal, Jessa hosting ayahuasca retreats for new mothers in Marin County, and Hannah back in school for a marriage and family therapy degree. Harris's own ask is simpler: she wants it to feel like "Beach House" on replay, five weeks straight. (Hung Up)

The Americans who fled to Europe over Trump are quietly admitting it is not better. WIRED reports that self-exiled liberals are "sheepishly confessing" that quality of life is lower across the Atlantic: dishwashers and dryers are rare luxuries, Britain's "free" healthcare is not exactly free, and one Berlin transplant misses "freedom of speech." Most spoke anonymously, fearing backlash from Americans who would call them fascist for missing capitalism. Pirate Wires calls it Scared Straight for leftists. (Pirate Wires)

The DEA's star crypto detective followed the blockchain straight to her own family. Lili Infante fled a chaotic Russian childhood to become an American law enforcement prodigy, pioneering the DEA's dark-web investigations. She never suspected who she would find hiding in the ledger. The full story reads like a prestige thriller with a real blockchain. (WIRED)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• That "brain-penetrating" magnesium on your supplement label probably does not reach your brain. Biology is not in the habit of respecting marketing claims. (WIRED)

• Ultra Right Beer, the "woke-free" brew launched for Bud Light boycotters in 2023, has vanished from the internet with many deliveries unfulfilled. The culture war has a supply chain problem. (WIRED)

• GM's board approved a $20 billion stock buyback plan. (The Wall Street Journal)

• A Texas woman is suing Torchy's Tacos for $250,000 after nearly swallowing a cow tooth hidden in her barbacoa taco. She was, per reports, "grossed out and sickened." (Inc.)

• Snack fact: cows do not have upper front teeth. They have a tough dental pad that tears grass from the ground. (Sherwood Snacks)

• Brazil registered a record fall in deforestation ahead of Sunday's presidential runoff, where Lula faces Flavio Bolsonaro. (BBC)

midday.body:
Wednesday, October 21, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• 4: the entire private key of eMudhra, an Indian certifying authority that issues digital security signatures, was literally the number 4

• 333: infected Tor exit nodes found by a Swedish researcher, roughly 10 percent of the entire network, which the Tor Project then took down

• $100 million: the opportunities fund MVP Ventures is raising to double down on its best bets; the five-year-old firm holds early stakes in Palmer Luckey's Anduril, Erebor, and ModRetro

• 40%: how far Netflix shares have fallen since April, as slowing revenue growth, layoffs, and a leadership shakeup hit the streaming king

• 300,000: visas the State Department says have been revoked since January 2025, a faster pace than any administration in history

Quotes of the Day

• "if you buy a hi record 45 from the 70's, it's probably good. They put the good songs on the 45's." (J Mascis, on digging for Hi Records singles) (Perfectly Imperfect)

• "The President is not popular, so all messaging should be focused on local politics and needs." (left behind in an AI prompt on the live website of GOP congressional candidate Eric Pratt) (404 Media)

• "I don't want to just compete for the sake of competing on terms that someone else has set." (Satya Nadella, on Microsoft settling into AI fast follower life) (Semafor)

• "At least five people this week said nice jacket. In all the ads online, in all the stores it's called a shirt. How come when I wear it everybody calls it a jacket?" (J Mascis, on his favorite "shirt") (Perfectly Imperfect)

Trees Vs. Terabytes
A tiny grove of endangered American chestnut trees is the newest front in the data center wars. In Mason County, West Virginia, the former Clements State Nursery holds historic American chestnut trees, descendants of a species nearly wiped out by a blight that killed as many as four billion trees after 1904. Now a UK startup called Nscale wants to build its 2,250 acre Monarch Compute Campus there, a project tied to Anthropic, Nvidia, and Microsoft. A little over an acre of old trees has become a site of resistance as communities nationwide push back against hyperscale builds over noise, pollution, and property values. (404 Media)

The Phone That Wipes Itself
A DHS alert flagged a Stop Cop City activist as a suspected "terrorist" at the airport, and he was carrying a phone designed to disappear. In January 2025, Customs and Border Protection stopped Samuel Tunick; he handed over a code that wiped his GrapheneOS phone. Newly filed court records include a screenshot of the alert and photos of the interrogation. Officials now claim they wanted to search the phone for child abuse material. Tunick is being criminally charged for the wipe, in what may become one of the most high profile tech civil rights cases in recent memory. (404 Media)

The $2,000 Fold
Joanna Stern folded the iPhone Duo 32,000 times with a robot she built alongside a hardware designer, and the hinge survived. Apple's first folding phone has a matte folding screen that's impressive outdoors and turns the phone into a tablet, an alarm clock, or a tiny laptop depending on how you position it. It's also buggy, occasionally maddening, and full of first generation compromises. Stern calls it one of the most exciting and frustrating iPhones she's tested in years. But should you spend two grand to get there early? That's the harder question. (New Things)

The MAGA Whisperer Exits
Meta's Republican policy chief is leaving just as the political pendulum swings the other way.
