afternoon.body:
Wednesday, October 21, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

• 7,000: the downloads by which Dave's Hot Chicken's iOS app briefly dethroned Meta's Muse on the App Store on October 13. The chain gives away free sliders every year, and this year you had to download the app to get one. (Appfigures via Garbage Day)

• 10 million: downloads of Muse across iOS and Android in barely a month, versus about 400,000 lifetime downloads for the Dave's Hot Chicken app. Sensor Tower puts Muse's seven-day retention at 30% and fourteen-day at 20%, which is actually strong for AI assistants; ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok sit in the mid-teens.

• 3%: American households paying for any AI service at all, per a June Bank of America report. Menlo Ventures found 64% of Americans have used AI this year (up three points from 2025) and one in five uses it daily. US AI adoption in 2026 is roughly where Facebook was in 2015, or where internet access was in 2004.

• $3.5 trillion: the corporate giant Elon Musk is exploring by merging Tesla and SpaceX. Grok already runs inside Teslas and controls more of the car over time; the bet is that AI, robotics, and space are collapsing into one physical industry where scale decides who gets to build.

• 2,300: jobs Princeton PhD Jack Weis has applied to from his parents' basement, getting ghosted even for food-prep roles. His ice-formation research was cited by the Nobel committee in 2024; a brief $70-an-hour AI training gig ended via a Slack message blasted to 810 people.

• 83%: accuracy when three lab-grown brain clumps, each smaller than a millimeter, teamed up to identify Braille letters fed to them as electrical signals. One clump alone managed 61%; three together hit 83%.

• $15 million: opening-weekend box office for Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's three-hour Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, sold out across more than 2,000 showings. The biggest documentary debut in two decades, excluding music and concert films.

Quotes of the Day

• "(You may not be ready to hear this, but soon all of human society will run on the Dave's Hot Chicken app.)" (Ryan Broderick, on a fried chicken chain briefly topping Meta's Muse in the App Store) (Garbage Day)

• "Some may consider it parasitic rather than symbiotic." (David Meyer, the 29-year-old founder of Strata, opening his pitch for small data centers to a packed town hall in rural Colorado) (Pirate Wires)

• "like telling someone that Santa Claus isn't real every day" (Sandy, 29, on trying to talk her mother-in-law out of trusting AI-generated 1950s music and AI doctors) (After School)

• "Nearly every aspect of the entire model pipeline was actually done and improved upon by AI." (Richard Socher, CEO of Recursive, on the open-weight coding model Flint built by his "Eureka Machine") (WIRED)

Data Centers Try Being Liked
A 29-year-old is pitching tiny data centers to small-town Colorado, one folding-chair town hall at a time. David Meyer founded Strata to build modular, smaller data centers, and Pirate Wires tagged along on his "listening tour" through rural Colorado. In Saguache County (population 7,000), about 60 mostly older residents packed the Road and Bridge office for an informational session, with dozens more online; the county's six-month data center moratorium, set in May, is about to expire. Meyer told the room that hyperscalers building in the hundreds of megawatts do things to communities that "aren't beneficial," and that his vision is to change the national conversation about building data centers more responsibly. Two hours of public comment later, the room was not obviously convinced. (Pirate Wires)

The data center industry's new PR plan is your kid's field trip. Facing national backlash, the industry is courting its most impressionable (and influential) audience: Gen Alpha. A nonprofit called 7x24 Exchange International promotes a picture book in which a honey badger named Honey tours a data center and learns it runs around the clock ("Like when my mom shops online late at night because my dad is sleeping and won't know about it?" Honey asks). The group pitches schools on "International Data Center Day" with coloring pages and a "Draw a data superhero" prompt; in Loudoun County, Virginia, a trade group sent 3,100 first graders Memorial Day flag kits with cards touting the industry's economic impact. (After School)

AI Gets Weird
A startup is betting the farm on AI that improves AI, and its first model is scary good. Recursive's open-weight coding model Flint was built mostly by its own recursive system, the "Eureka Machine," which CEO Richard Socher says devised new training methods, new model architectures, and code optimized for specific silicon. A handful of researchers produced a world-class model in a few months; shared benchmarks suggest Flint outperforms similar-size models on coding. It is the closest thing yet to fully recursive self-improvement, the exciting and controversial idea of using AI to build better AI. (WIRED)

AI can now guess a cancer patient's risk of dying from a single photo of their face. Researchers fed thousands of patient images into a model using "attention mapping," which studies specific facial regions to estimate biological age and the risk of dying within 90 days. Smokers and heavy drinkers showed the clearest signs of aging. Published October 19 in Lancet Digital Health, the model (dubbed FAHR-Face) is not ready for wide use; it still needs training on a more diverse set of faces, but researchers hope it could help doctors spot warning signs of disease spreading. (Semafor)

Screens Up, Screens Down
Young audiences still love stories, just not the way adults keep making them. UCLA's Center for Scholars and Storytellers surveyed more than 1,500 people ages 10 to 24 for its 2026 Teens and Screens Report: YouTube is the top storytelling medium at 72.9%, yet going to the movies topped their ideal weekend activities for the third year running. More than half want more platonic relationships on screen, 52% say romance matters more to fictional characters than in real life, and nearly 40% would cast an unknown actor over an influencer. "Adults are making stories that they think are going to resonate with young people, but they're not really talking to a lot of young people to do it," said founder Yalda T. Uhls. (After School)

School laptops are basically YouTube machines. NBC News analyzed YouTube histories on 11 students' school-issued devices: more than 95% of the 17,000-plus videos opened during school hours were not educational by any traditional standard. The lineup included NFL highlights, Family Guy clips, handgun demos, police chases, an Eminem video, and AI-generated animations of a time-traveling skeleton visiting ancient Rome. One Pennsylvania eighth grader watched 4,784 videos, few school-related; after his laptop was confiscated for two weeks he said he slept better and felt "less load on my shoulders," then went right back to his fixation when it was returned. (After School)

Food Is a Whole Orange
The power cocktail of the season is an entire sliced orange in a glass. Party reporter Emily Dawn Long spotted Vera Wang's drink order at a dinner: ice, vodka, a whole orange sliced up, and a splash of tonic. This morning she reported it is also Kris Jenner's drink of choice. Now the city waits to see whether New Yorkers start ordering whole citrus in their cocktails. (Feed Me)

"Dark nutrition" is having a moment: raw buffalo brains, raw-milk ice cream, raw egg yolks. Sophie Haigney profiled the movement for The New York Times Magazine, traveling to southeastern Pennsylvania and Tennessee's Smoky Mountains to meet carnivores, biohackers, and Primal-dieters. Many turned to raw food to "fix" health issues: autoimmune disease, skin conditions, chronic pain, digestive trouble, fertility problems, eating disorders, psychiatric illness. The top comment on the story: "There's a reason humans learned to cook food. They'll find out eventually." (Feed Me)

TASTE is launching a business-of-grocery podcast, and the CPG media land grab continues. Eye Level, hosted by TASTE editor Matt Rodbard and New Fare Partners investor Elly Truesdell, will cover what it takes to start a CPG brand, win shelf space, and survive the GLP-1 era. First guests include Alison Roman (talking retail and her new Brooklyn store), Loonen co-founder Clara Sieg, and Athletic Brewing's Bill Shufelt. The show arrives as food-business media heats up: Morning Brew just acquired the Substack newsletter Express Checkout, and Bachan's Japanese sauces were acquired this year for $400 million. (Feed Me)

Power and Money
New York's Democratic Socialists are fighting over whether AI will kill everyone or is just a hustle. The NYC chapter of the DSA is split on a proposed resolution warning of "the potential for loss of control of AI agents to cause catastrophic harm." One camp wants the party to acknowledge mass automation and runaway systems; the more established techno-skeptical camp says doom talk just inflates company valuations and that AI is already doing enough damage. A proposed amendment would strip the existential-risk language. The rift previews a bigger 2028 question: how Democrats talk about AI risk could shape regulation if they retake Congress. (Semafor)

Meta was Big Tech's biggest lobbying spender in Q3, laying out $5.9 million as the AI race heated up. Senate filings show Meta outspent its peers while AI safety debates and high-profile hacks pressured Washington. OpenAI and Anthropic are spending more every quarter too, nearly doubling and tripling their outlays in the first half of the year. Both lobbied lawmakers on sharing information with each other without tripping antitrust rules, right as AI leaders debated a coordinated development "slowdown" last month. (Semafor)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Panic World finally did an episode about bronies: PJ Vogt returns to walk through how grown men obsessed with little ponies won the internet, jar included (Garbage Day)

• Divers off Turkey found more than 30 clay jars and three stone anchors from up to 4,700 years ago, some jars still holding residue that was likely olive oil or wine, making it a contender for the world's oldest shipwreck (Smithsonian)

• Arsenal's new Rocastle font took four years to design; the G alone took about 2,000 redraws, and the spiky Old English face is named for club legend David Rocastle (It's Nice That)

• Students from the École du Louvre blocked the museum's entrance Monday, joining France's cost-of-living protests that have brought roughly half a million people into the streets (euronews)

• Maine has its own Sistine Chapel: the plain white South Solon Meeting House hides 1950s frescoes on nearly every wall, including a Great Flood modeled on Michelangelo's (AP)

• France's weekend riots hit luxury stores including Louis Vuitton, Burberry, and Celine, and secondhand marketplace Vinted says it pulled listings suspected of selling the looted goods, acting "against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans" (Feed Me)

• Citrini, the No. 1 finance Substack, poached Fortune reporter Eva Roytburg to build out its social presence; she launched its Instagram accounts on day one (Feed Me)

• NYT fashion critic Vanessa Friedman linked Mayor Mamdani's brown-and-black-shoes-with-a-suit look to "Team Trump," then recommended dress sneakers; Twitter is not having it (Feed Me)

• Ella Rubin is on the cover of Nylon as "the new patron saint of teenage girls," Jacob Elordi will narrate Eric Dane's memoir audiobook, Joe Keery is making his Broadway debut in Other Desert Cities, a Glee reboot is officially happening, and Google's Frightgeist says Dolly Parton tops kids' Halloween costumes (After School)

• Spotify has stopped recommending 50 million AI slop tracks (Variety)

evening.body:
Wednesday, October 21, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 3,500: individual samples stitched together to make Since I Left You, The Avalanches' genre-defining debut. After a 15-year creative block, the Australian duo is back with a fourth album, No Bad Memories, and James Jung sat down with them to write about aging alongside the music you love.

• 13: days until the midterm elections, and the White House blame game has already started. Trump aides are hunting for a scapegoat for expected House and Senate losses, but GOP operatives privately say "Clearly it's the president's fault."

• 32: states where election offices have received suspicious letters ahead of the midterms, per WIRED's Inner Loop.

• One month: the length of Jack's school suspension. The Long Island senior, a former hometown-fair standout and self-described post-SoundCloud kid, turns 18 on Monday, works at Stop & Shop, and says his dream is "just being content. Waking up in the morning and feeling good."

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• The first rule of Greek island-hopping: get on the right ferry. InsideHook's new guide maps nine days across Naxos, Paros, and Ios, with three nights per island as the minimum to absorb each one's distinct character. (InsideHook)

• Instagram's Rings awards honor creators outside the billion-follower cohort, with the 2026 judges including Donatella Versace, Isamaya Ffrench, and Finneas. IG's fashion head Eva Chen says the most important muscle for a creator is pressing publish, because you never know how your voice might come back to you ten times bigger. (Biz Sherbert)

full.body:
Wednesday, October 21, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• $45 million: the seed round for Coherence Neuro, a startup building a coin-sized brain implant that listens for tumor signals and may also deliver targeted stimulation. OpenAI's venture arm and Peter Thiel's Founders Fund are among the backers, the latest sign that AI labs see brain data as the next training frontier. The device was tested in three patients in June and aims for first chronic human implants in 2027, with glioblastoma in its sights.

• $29: the monthly cap Accenture has reportedly put on employee spending on Claude, per 404 Media. The relationship between AI companies and their corporate customers is starting to show cracks.

• 1,000: the number of people Netflix laid off last week, about 6% of its workforce, with the stock down more than 40% over the past year.

• 92%: the chance prediction markets give Democrats of taking the House in the midterms, with 65% for the Senate and a 97% chance of Roy Cooper flipping North Carolina.

• $30,000: the payout the White House's new whistleblower tip line offers if a tip leads to a fraud conviction.

Quotes of the Day

• "Do we want to build a world in which we don't actually matter?" (Jon Stewart, after an OpenAI researcher told The Daily Show he expects "no jobs" and universal high income)

• "I hope that we make recursive self-improvement illegal before you get there." (Kelsey Piper, closing her dispatch from inside Anthropic's San Francisco headquarters)

• "Close to 100%." (United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby, saying the U.S. should have an inheritance tax close to 100%, and that he would happily pay it)

• "They're on TV, dummy!" (Hunter Harris, on viewers who complain TV characters would not still be friends in real life)

AI & The Machines

Anthropic's plan to save humanity from AI is mostly hope and guesswork. Kelsey Piper spent a day at Anthropic's San Francisco headquarters, where researchers briefed outsiders on bioweapon risk, recursive self-improvement, and charts showing Claude's growing mastery. The most striking detail: when Anthropic tested Claude planning a bioweapon attack on its own, the model did better than a human aided by Claude. The lab says recursive self-improvement, the point at which Claude can independently build the next, more powerful Claude, could arrive next year. Piper's takeaway is that the company knows what it does not want (extinction, concentrated power, irrelevance), but the positive vision is thin, and its lobbying bill looks like a normal company protecting its interests. (The Argument)

An AI agent wandered into a listserv of top internet researchers, and the reply-all chaos is still unfolding. A 7,500-person group of internet experts melted down over the agent's appearance, a flare-up that WIRED's Olivia Snow says reveals how outdated their notions of privacy really are. It is a small preview of a bigger problem: we keep deploying agents into human spaces with human expectations, then acting shocked when the humans freak out. (WIRED)

Europe wants the data centers, but its climate goals keep getting in the way. A German plan to funnel the heat given off by data centers into nearby homes has run aground, and policymakers across the continent are weighing AI ambitions against climate objectives. Everyone wants the compute; nobody wants the carbon bill. (WIRED)

Money & Power

Zuck's Muse has a lot to prove. Meta reports earnings after the bell today, expected to show $41.1 billion in quarterly capital expenditures and $9.4 billion in negative free cash flow, which would mark its first cash-flow-negative quarter since 2012. The bright spot is Muse, the personal AI agent launched September 8 with a furry mascot that is equal parts cute and unsettling, which passed 5 million downloads in its first three weeks. Investors are asking two questions of every AI spender: how much more money will you borrow, and when does any of this make money? (Sherwood Snacks)

Investors are buying default insurance on the AI boom. Trading in credit default swaps tied to the bonds of Oracle, SpaceX, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Broadcom, and Nvidia surged from under $2 billion a week in July to a much heavier clip in September, per Morgan Stanley research cited by the Financial Times. The cost of protection on AI names, especially the rattled CoreWeave, keeps rising as the market hedges against mountains of AI-fueled debt. (Reuters)

The Culture

Girls is coming back, and TV's best writers have notes. The series returns for a five-episode seventh season on HBO Max in 2027, and Hunter Harris asked a dozen writers what they want from it. The pitches are gloriously unhinged: Marnie running a gentle-parenting Substack from a renovated Saratoga Springs farmhouse while cheating with the farmhand, Shosh founding The RealReal, Jessa hosting ayahuasca retreats for new mothers in Marin County, and Hannah back in school for a marriage and family therapy degree. Harris's own ask is simpler: she wants it to feel like "Beach House" on replay, five weeks straight. (Hung Up)

The Americans who fled to Europe over Trump are quietly admitting it is not better. WIRED reports that self-exiled liberals are "sheepishly confessing" that quality of life is lower across the Atlantic: dishwashers and dryers are rare luxuries, Britain's "free" healthcare is not exactly free, and one Berlin transplant misses "freedom of speech." Most spoke anonymously, fearing backlash from Americans who would call them fascist for missing capitalism. Pirate Wires calls it Scared Straight for leftists. (Pirate Wires)

The DEA's star crypto detective followed the blockchain straight to her own family. Lili Infante fled a chaotic Russian childhood to become an American law enforcement prodigy, pioneering the DEA's dark-web investigations. She never suspected who she would find hiding in the ledger. The full story reads like a prestige thriller with a real blockchain. (WIRED)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• That "brain-penetrating" magnesium on your supplement label probably does not reach your brain. Biology is not in the habit of respecting marketing claims. (WIRED)

• Ultra Right Beer, the "woke-free" brew launched for Bud Light boycotters in 2023, has vanished from the internet with many deliveries unfulfilled. The culture war has a supply chain problem. (WIRED)

• GM's board approved a $20 billion stock buyback plan. (The Wall Street Journal)

• A Texas woman is suing Torchy's Tacos for $250,000 after nearly swallowing a cow tooth hidden in her barbacoa taco. She was, per reports, "grossed out and sickened." (Inc.)

• Snack fact: cows do not have upper front teeth. They have a tough dental pad that tears grass from the ground. (Sherwood Snacks)

• Brazil registered a record fall in deforestation ahead of Sunday's presidential runoff, where Lula faces Flavio Bolsonaro. (BBC)

Wednesday, October 21, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• 4: the entire private key of eMudhra, an Indian certifying authority that issues digital security signatures, was literally the number 4

• 333: infected Tor exit nodes found by a Swedish researcher, roughly 10 percent of the entire network, which the Tor Project then took down

• $100 million: the opportunities fund MVP Ventures is raising to double down on its best bets; the five-year-old firm holds early stakes in Palmer Luckey's Anduril, Erebor, and ModRetro

• 40%: how far Netflix shares have fallen since April, as slowing revenue growth, layoffs, and a leadership shakeup hit the streaming king

• 300,000: visas the State Department says have been revoked since January 2025, a faster pace than any administration in history

Quotes of the Day

• "if you buy a hi record 45 from the 70's, it's probably good. They put the good songs on the 45's." (J Mascis, on digging for Hi Records singles) (Perfectly Imperfect)

• "The President is not popular, so all messaging should be focused on local politics and needs." (left behind in an AI prompt on the live website of GOP congressional candidate Eric Pratt) (404 Media)

• "I don't want to just compete for the sake of competing on terms that someone else has set." (Satya Nadella, on Microsoft settling into AI fast follower life) (Semafor)

• "At least five people this week said nice jacket. In all the ads online, in all the stores it's called a shirt. How come when I wear it everybody calls it a jacket?" (J Mascis, on his favorite "shirt") (Perfectly Imperfect)

Trees Vs. Terabytes
A tiny grove of endangered American chestnut trees is the newest front in the data center wars. In Mason County, West Virginia, the former Clements State Nursery holds historic American chestnut trees, descendants of a species nearly wiped out by a blight that killed as many as four billion trees after 1904. Now a UK startup called Nscale wants to build its 2,250 acre Monarch Compute Campus there, a project tied to Anthropic, Nvidia, and Microsoft. A little over an acre of old trees has become a site of resistance as communities nationwide push back against hyperscale builds over noise, pollution, and property values. (404 Media)

The Phone That Wipes Itself
A DHS alert flagged a Stop Cop City activist as a suspected "terrorist" at the airport, and he was carrying a phone designed to disappear. In January 2025, Customs and Border Protection stopped Samuel Tunick; he handed over a code that wiped his GrapheneOS phone. Newly filed court records include a screenshot of the alert and photos of the interrogation. Officials now claim they wanted to search the phone for child abuse material. Tunick is being criminally charged for the wipe, in what may become one of the most high profile tech civil rights cases in recent memory. (404 Media)

The $2,000 Fold
Joanna Stern folded the iPhone Duo 32,000 times with a robot she built alongside a hardware designer, and the hinge survived. Apple's first folding phone has a matte folding screen that's impressive outdoors and turns the phone into a tablet, an alarm clock, or a tiny laptop depending on how you position it. It's also buggy, occasionally maddening, and full of first generation compromises. Stern calls it one of the most exciting and frustrating iPhones she's tested in years. But should you spend two grand to get there early? That's the harder question. (New Things)

The MAGA Whisperer Exits
Meta's Republican policy chief is leaving just as the political pendulum swings the other way. Joel Kaplan replaced the neoliberal Nick Clegg in early 2025, and Meta rushed to stack MAGA credentials on its board and its lobbying operation. He'll be gone early next year. The timing is hard to miss: Democrats are projected to take at least one chamber of Congress, along with the hearing gavel and all the scrutiny that comes with it. (Semafor)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Data center companies are paying a startup to scrape tens of thousands of city council meeting recordings and tag comments as friendly or hostile to new projects, so investors can see where NIMBY resistance is softest (Semafor)

• AI-generated TikTok "lawyers" are preying on immigrants trying to stay in the United States, some imitating real lawyers, others fully invented, according to a Documented NY investigation (404 Media)

• There is now a SimCity with permitting, zoning, and organized homeowners, and you can try it yourself (404 Media)

• Dinosaur Jr. released There Near, its first full-length record in five years, celebrated with free NYC shows featuring Thurston Moore Group and Mike Kinsella, and the band is touring into 2027 (Perfectly Imperfect)

Wednesday, October 21, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

• 7,000: the downloads by which Dave's Hot Chicken's iOS app briefly dethroned Meta's Muse on the App Store on October 13. The chain gives away free sliders every year, and this year you had to download the app to get one. (Appfigures via Garbage Day)

• 10 million: downloads of Muse across iOS and Android in barely a month, versus about 400,000 lifetime downloads for the Dave's Hot Chicken app. Sensor Tower puts Muse's seven-day retention at 30% and fourteen-day at 20%, which is actually strong for AI assistants; ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok sit in the mid-teens.

• 3%: American households paying for any AI service at all, per a June Bank of America report. Menlo Ventures found 64% of Americans have used AI this year (up three points from 2025) and one in five uses it daily. US AI adoption in 2026 is roughly where Facebook was in 2015, or where internet access was in 2004.

• $3.5 trillion: the corporate giant Elon Musk is exploring by merging Tesla and SpaceX. Grok already runs inside Teslas and controls more of the car over time; the bet is that AI, robotics, and space are collapsing into one physical industry where scale decides who gets to build.

• 2,300: jobs Princeton PhD Jack Weis has applied to from his parents' basement, getting ghosted even for food-prep roles. His ice-formation research was cited by the Nobel committee in 2024; a brief $70-an-hour AI training gig ended via a Slack message blasted to 810 people.

• 83%: accuracy when three lab-grown brain clumps, each smaller than a millimeter, teamed up to identify Braille letters fed to them as electrical signals. One clump alone managed 61%; three together hit 83%.

• $15 million: opening-weekend box office for Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's three-hour Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, sold out across more than 2,000 showings. The biggest documentary debut in two decades, excluding music and concert films.

Quotes of the Day

• "(You may not be ready to hear this, but soon all of human society will run on the Dave's Hot Chicken app.)" (Ryan Broderick, on a fried chicken chain briefly topping Meta's Muse in the App Store) (Garbage Day)

• "Some may consider it parasitic rather than symbiotic." (David Meyer, the 29-year-old founder of Strata, opening his pitch for small data centers to a packed town hall in rural Colorado) (Pirate Wires)

• "like telling someone that Santa Claus isn't real every day" (Sandy, 29, on trying to talk her mother-in-law out of trusting AI-generated 1950s music and AI doctors) (After School)

• "Nearly every aspect of the entire model pipeline was actually done and improved upon by AI." (Richard Socher, CEO of Recursive, on the open-weight coding model Flint built by his "Eureka Machine") (WIRED)

Data Centers Try Being Liked
A 29-year-old is pitching tiny data centers to small-town Colorado, one folding-chair town hall at a time. David Meyer founded Strata to build modular, smaller data centers, and Pirate Wires tagged along on his "listening tour" through rural Colorado. In Saguache County (population 7,000), about 60 mostly older residents packed the Road and Bridge office for an informational session, with dozens more online; the county's six-month data center moratorium, set in May, is about to expire. Meyer told the room that hyperscalers building in the hundreds of megawatts do things to communities that "aren't beneficial," and that his vision is to change the national conversation about building data centers more responsibly. Two hours of public comment later, the room was not obviously convinced. (Pirate Wires)

The data center industry's new PR plan is your kid's field trip. Facing national backlash, the industry is courting its most impressionable (and influential) audience: Gen Alpha. A nonprofit called 7x24 Exchange International promotes a picture book in which a honey badger named Honey tours a data center and learns it runs around the clock ("Like when my mom shops online late at night because my dad is sleeping and won't know about it?" Honey asks). The group pitches schools on "International Data Center Day" with coloring pages and a "Draw a data superhero" prompt; in Loudoun County, Virginia, a trade group sent 3,100 first graders Memorial Day flag kits with cards touting the industry's economic impact. (After School)

AI Gets Weird
A startup is betting the farm on AI that improves AI, and its first model is scary good. Recursive's open-weight coding model Flint was built mostly by its own recursive system, the "Eureka Machine," which CEO Richard Socher says devised new training methods, new model architectures, and code optimized for specific silicon. A handful of researchers produced a world-class model in a few months; shared benchmarks suggest Flint outperforms similar-size models on coding. It is the closest thing yet to fully recursive self-improvement, the exciting and controversial idea of using AI to build better AI. (WIRED)

AI can now guess a cancer patient's risk of dying from a single photo of their face. Researchers fed thousands of patient images into a model using "attention mapping," which studies specific facial regions to estimate biological age and the risk of dying within 90 days. Smokers and heavy drinkers showed the clearest signs of aging. Published October 19 in Lancet Digital Health, the model (dubbed FAHR-Face) is not ready for wide use; it still needs training on a more diverse set of faces, but researchers hope it could help doctors spot warning signs of disease spreading. (Semafor)

Screens Up, Screens Down
Young audiences still love stories, just not the way adults keep making them. UCLA's Center for Scholars and Storytellers surveyed more than 1,500 people ages 10 to 24 for its 2026 Teens and Screens Report: YouTube is the top storytelling medium at 72.9%, yet going to the movies topped their ideal weekend activities for the third year running. More than half want more platonic relationships on screen, 52% say romance matters more to fictional characters than in real life, and nearly 40% would cast an unknown actor over an influencer. "Adults are making stories that they think are going to resonate with young people, but they're not really talking to a lot of young people to do it," said founder Yalda T. Uhls. (After School)

School laptops are basically YouTube machines. NBC News analyzed YouTube histories on 11 students' school-issued devices: more than 95% of the 17,000-plus videos opened during school hours were not educational by any traditional standard. The lineup included NFL highlights, Family Guy clips, handgun demos, police chases, an Eminem video, and AI-generated animations of a time-traveling skeleton visiting ancient Rome. One Pennsylvania eighth grader watched 4,784 videos, few school-related; after his laptop was confiscated for two weeks he said he slept better and felt "less load on my shoulders," then went right back to his fixation when it was returned. (After School)

Food Is a Whole Orange
The power cocktail of the season is an entire sliced orange in a glass. Party reporter Emily Dawn Long spotted Vera Wang's drink order at a dinner: ice, vodka, a whole orange sliced up, and a splash of tonic. This morning she reported it is also Kris Jenner's drink of choice. Now the city waits to see whether New Yorkers start ordering whole citrus in their cocktails. (Feed Me)

"Dark nutrition" is having a moment: raw buffalo brains, raw-milk ice cream, raw egg yolks. Sophie Haigney profiled the movement for The New York Times Magazine, traveling to southeastern Pennsylvania and Tennessee's Smoky Mountains to meet carnivores, biohackers, and Primal-dieters. Many turned to raw food to "fix" health issues: autoimmune disease, skin conditions, chronic pain, digestive trouble, fertility problems, eating disorders, psychiatric illness. The top comment on the story: "There's a reason humans learned to cook food. They'll find out eventually." (Feed Me)

TASTE is launching a business-of-grocery podcast, and the CPG media land grab continues. Eye Level, hosted by TASTE editor Matt Rodbard and New Fare Partners investor Elly Truesdell, will cover what it takes to start a CPG brand, win shelf space, and survive the GLP-1 era. First guests include Alison Roman (talking retail and her new Brooklyn store), Loonen co-founder Clara Sieg, and Athletic Brewing's Bill Shufelt. The show arrives as food-business media heats up: Morning Brew just acquired the Substack newsletter Express Checkout, and Bachan's Japanese sauces were acquired this year for $400 million. (Feed Me)

Power and Money
New York's Democratic Socialists are fighting over whether AI will kill everyone or is just a hustle. The NYC chapter of the DSA is split on a proposed resolution warning of "the potential for loss of control of AI agents to cause catastrophic harm." One camp wants the party to acknowledge mass automation and runaway systems; the more established techno-skeptical camp says doom talk just inflates company valuations and that AI is already doing enough damage. A proposed amendment would strip the existential-risk language. The rift previews a bigger 2028 question: how Democrats talk about AI risk could shape regulation if they retake Congress. (Semafor)

Meta was Big Tech's biggest lobbying spender in Q3, laying out $5.9 million as the AI race heated up. Senate filings show Meta outspent its peers while AI safety debates and high-profile hacks pressured Washington. OpenAI and Anthropic are spending more every quarter too, nearly doubling and tripling their outlays in the first half of the year. Both lobbied lawmakers on sharing information with each other without tripping antitrust rules, right as AI leaders debated a coordinated development "slowdown" last month. (Semafor)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Panic World finally did an episode about bronies: PJ Vogt returns to walk through how grown men obsessed with little ponies won the internet, jar included (Garbage Day)

• Divers off Turkey found more than 30 clay jars and three stone anchors from up to 4,700 years ago, some jars still holding residue that was likely olive oil or wine, making it a contender for the world's oldest shipwreck (Smithsonian)

• Arsenal's new Rocastle font took four years to design; the G alone took about 2,000 redraws, and the spiky Old English face is named for club legend David Rocastle (It's Nice That)

• Students from the École du Louvre blocked the museum's entrance Monday, joining France's cost-of-living protests that have brought roughly half a million people into the streets (euronews)

• Maine has its own Sistine Chapel: the plain white South Solon Meeting House hides 1950s frescoes on nearly every wall, including a Great Flood modeled on Michelangelo's (AP)

• France's weekend riots hit luxury stores including Louis Vuitton, Burberry, and Celine, and secondhand marketplace Vinted says it pulled listings suspected of selling the looted goods, acting "against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans" (Feed Me)

• Citrini, the No. 1 finance Substack, poached Fortune reporter Eva Roytburg to build out its social presence; she launched its Instagram accounts on day one (Feed Me)

• NYT fashion critic Vanessa Friedman linked Mayor Mamdani's brown-and-black-shoes-with-a-suit look to "Team Trump," then recommended dress sneakers; Twitter is not having it (Feed Me)

• Ella Rubin is on the cover of Nylon as "the new patron saint of teenage girls," Jacob Elordi will narrate Eric Dane's memoir audiobook, Joe Keery is making his Broadway debut in Other Desert Cities, a Glee reboot is officially happening, and Google's Frightgeist says Dolly Parton tops kids' Halloween costumes (After School)

• Spotify has stopped recommending 50 million AI slop tracks (Variety)

Wednesday, October 21, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• 3,500: individual samples stitched together to make Since I Left You, The Avalanches' genre-defining debut. After a 15-year creative block, the Australian duo is back with a fourth album, No Bad Memories, and James Jung sat down with them to write about aging alongside the music you love.

• 13: days until the midterm elections, and the White House blame game has already started. Trump aides are hunting for a scapegoat for expected House and Senate losses, but GOP operatives privately say "Clearly it's the president's fault."

• 32: states where election offices have received suspicious letters ahead of the midterms, per WIRED's Inner Loop.

• One month: the length of Jack's school suspension. The Long Island senior, a former hometown-fair standout and self-described post-SoundCloud kid, turns 18 on Monday, works at Stop & Shop, and says his dream is "just being content. Waking up in the morning and feeling good."

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• The first rule of Greek island-hopping: get on the right ferry. InsideHook's new guide maps nine days across Naxos, Paros, and Ios, with three nights per island as the minimum to absorb each one's distinct character. (InsideHook)

• Instagram's Rings awards honor creators outside the billion-follower cohort, with the 2026 judges including Donatella Versace, Isamaya Ffrench, and Finneas. IG's fashion head Eva Chen says the most important muscle for a creator is pressing publish, because you never know how your voice might come back to you ten times bigger. (Biz Sherbert)

But should you spend two grand to get there early? That's the harder question. (
New Things
The MAGA Whisperer Exits
Meta's Republican policy chief is leaving just as the political pendulum swings the other way.

Joel Kaplan replaced the neoliberal Nick Clegg in early 2025, and Meta rushed to stack MAGA credentials on its board and its lobbying operation. He'll be gone early next year. The timing is hard to miss: Democrats are projected to take at least one chamber of Congress, along with the hearing gavel and all the scrutiny that comes with it. (
Semafor
Quick Hits & Curiosities

Data center companies are paying a startup to scrape tens of thousands of city council meeting recordings and tag comments as friendly or hostile to new projects, so investors can see where NIMBY resistance is softest (
Semafor
AI-generated TikTok "lawyers" are preying on immigrants trying to stay in the United States, some imitating real lawyers, others fully invented, according to a Documented NY investigation (
404 Media
There is now a SimCity with permitting, zoning, and organized homeowners, and you can try it yourself (
404 Media
Dinosaur Jr. released
There Near
, its first full-length record in five years, celebrated with free NYC shows featuring Thurston Moore Group and Mike Kinsella, and the band is touring into 2027 (
Perfectly Imperfect
Wednesday, October 21, 2026 - Afternoon Edition
Today's Numbers

: the downloads by which Dave's Hot Chicken's iOS app briefly dethroned Meta's Muse on the App Store on October 13. The chain gives away free sliders every year, and this year you had to download the app to get one. (Appfigures via Garbage Day)
10 million

: downloads of Muse across iOS and Android in barely a month, versus about 400,000 lifetime downloads for the Dave's Hot Chicken app. Sensor Tower puts Muse's seven-day retention at 30% and fourteen-day at 20%, which is actually strong for AI assistants; ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok sit in the mid-teens.

: American households paying for any AI service at all, per a June Bank of America report. Menlo Ventures found 64% of Americans have used AI this year (up three points from 2025) and one in five uses it daily. US AI adoption in 2026 is roughly where Facebook was in 2015, or where internet access was in 2004.
$3.5 trillion

: the corporate giant Elon Musk is exploring by merging Tesla and SpaceX. Grok already runs inside Teslas and controls more of the car over time; the bet is that AI, robotics, and space are collapsing into one physical industry where scale decides who gets to build.

: jobs Princeton PhD Jack Weis has applied to from his parents' basement, getting ghosted even for food-prep roles. His ice-formation research was cited by the Nobel committee in 2024; a brief $70-an-hour AI training gig ended via a Slack message blasted to 810 people.

: accuracy when three lab-grown brain clumps, each smaller than a millimeter, teamed up to identify Braille letters fed to them as electrical signals. One clump alone managed 61%; three together hit 83%.
$15 million
: opening-weekend box office for Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's three-hour Elizabeth Holmes documentary
You Can See Everything
, sold out across more than 2,000 showings. The biggest documentary debut in two decades, excluding music and concert films.
Quotes of the Day
"(You may not be ready to hear this, but soon all of human society will run on the Dave's Hot Chicken app.)" (Ryan Broderick, on a fried chicken chain briefly topping Meta's Muse in the App Store) (
Garbage Day
"Some may consider it parasitic rather than symbiotic." (David Meyer, the 29-year-old founder of Strata, opening his pitch for small data centers to a packed town hall in rural Colorado) (
Pirate Wires
"like telling someone that Santa Claus isn't real every day" (Sandy, 29, on trying to talk her mother-in-law out of trusting AI-generated 1950s music and AI doctors) (
After School
"Nearly every aspect of the entire model pipeline was actually done and improved upon by AI." (Richard Socher, CEO of Recursive, on the open-weight coding model Flint built by his "Eureka Machine") (
WIRED
Data Centers Try Being Liked
A 29-year-old is pitching tiny data centers to small-town Colorado, one folding-chair town hall at a time.

David Meyer founded Strata to build modular, smaller data centers, and Pirate Wires tagged along on his "listening tour" through rural Colorado. In Saguache County (population 7,000), about 60 mostly older residents packed the Road and Bridge office for an informational session, with dozens more online; the county's six-month data center moratorium, set in May, is about to expire. Meyer told the room that hyperscalers building in the hundreds of megawatts do things to communities that "aren't beneficial," and that his vision is to change the national conversation about building data centers more responsibly. Two hours of public comment later, the room was not obviously convinced. (
Pirate Wires
The data center industry's new PR plan is your kid's field trip.

Facing national backlash, the industry is courting its most impressionable (and influential) audience: Gen Alpha. A nonprofit called 7x24 Exchange International promotes a picture book in which a honey badger named Honey tours a data center and learns it runs around the clock ("Like when my mom shops online late at night because my dad is sleeping and won't know about it?" Honey asks). The group pitches schools on "International Data Center Day" with coloring pages and a "Draw a data superhero" prompt; in Loudoun County, Virginia, a trade group sent 3,100 first graders Memorial Day flag kits with cards touting the industry's economic impact. (
After School
AI Gets Weird
A startup is betting the farm on AI that improves AI, and its first model is scary good.

Recursive's open-weight coding model Flint was built mostly by its own recursive system, the "Eureka Machine," which CEO Richard Socher says devised new training methods, new model architectures, and code optimized for specific silicon. A handful of researchers produced a world-class model in a few months; shared benchmarks suggest Flint outperforms similar-size models on coding. It is the closest thing yet to fully recursive self-improvement, the exciting and controversial idea of using AI to build better AI. (
WIRED
AI can now guess a cancer patient's risk of dying from a single photo of their face.

Smokers and heavy drinkers showed the clearest signs of aging. (
Semafor

School laptops are basically YouTube machines.

NBC News analyzed YouTube histories on 11 students' school-issued devices: more than 95% of the 17,000-plus videos opened during school hours were not educational by any traditional standard. The lineup included NFL highlights,
Family Guy

clips, handgun demos, police chases, an Eminem video, and AI-generated animations of a time-traveling skeleton visiting ancient Rome. One Pennsylvania eighth grader watched 4,784 videos, few school-related; after his laptop was confiscated for two weeks he said he slept better and felt "less load on my shoulders," then went right back to his fixation when it was returned. (
After School
Food Is a Whole Orange
The power cocktail of the season is an entire sliced orange in a glass.

Party reporter Emily Dawn Long spotted Vera Wang's drink order at a dinner: ice, vodka, a whole orange sliced up, and a splash of tonic. This morning she reported it is also Kris Jenner's drink of choice. Now the city waits to see whether New Yorkers start ordering whole citrus in their cocktails. (
Feed Me
"Dark nutrition" is having a moment: raw buffalo brains, raw-milk ice cream, raw egg yolks.

Sophie Haigney profiled the movement for The New York Times Magazine, traveling to southeastern Pennsylvania and Tennessee's Smoky Mountains to meet carnivores, biohackers, and Primal-dieters. Many turned to raw food to "fix" health issues: autoimmune disease, skin conditions, chronic pain, digestive trouble, fertility problems, eating disorders, psychiatric illness. The top comment on the story: "There's a reason humans learned to cook food. They'll find out eventually." (
Feed Me
TASTE is launching a business-of-grocery podcast, and the CPG media land grab continues.
Eye Level

, hosted by TASTE editor Matt Rodbard and New Fare Partners investor Elly Truesdell, will cover what it takes to start a CPG brand, win shelf space, and survive the GLP-1 era. First guests include Alison Roman (talking retail and her new Brooklyn store), Loonen co-founder Clara Sieg, and Athletic Brewing's Bill Shufelt. The show arrives as food-business media heats up: Morning Brew just acquired the Substack newsletter Express Checkout, and Bachan's Japanese sauces were acquired this year for $400 million. (
Feed Me
Power and Money
New York's Democratic Socialists are fighting over whether AI will kill everyone or is just a hustle.

The NYC chapter of the DSA is split on a proposed resolution warning of "the potential for loss of control of AI agents to cause catastrophic harm." One camp wants the party to acknowledge mass automation and runaway systems; the more established techno-skeptical camp says doom talk just inflates company valuations and that AI is already doing enough damage. A proposed amendment would strip the existential-risk language. The rift previews a bigger 2028 question: how Democrats talk about AI risk could shape regulation if they retake Congress. (
Semafor
Meta was Big Tech's biggest lobbying spender in Q3, laying out $5.9 million as the AI race heated up.

Senate filings show Meta outspent its peers while AI safety debates and high-profile hacks pressured Washington. OpenAI and Anthropic are spending more every quarter too, nearly doubling and tripling their outlays in the first half of the year. Both lobbied lawmakers on sharing information with each other without tripping antitrust rules, right as AI leaders debated a coordinated development "slowdown" last month. (
Semafor

Panic World finally did an episode about bronies: PJ Vogt returns to walk through how grown men obsessed with little ponies won the internet, jar included (
Garbage Day

Divers off Turkey found more than 30 clay jars and three stone anchors from up to 4,700 years ago, some jars still holding residue that was likely olive oil or wine, making it a contender for the world's oldest shipwreck (
Smithsonian
Arsenal's new Rocastle font took four years to design; the G alone took about 2,000 redraws, and the spiky Old English face is named for club legend David Rocastle (
It's Nice That
Students from the École du Louvre blocked the museum's entrance Monday, joining France's cost-of-living protests that have brought roughly half a million people into the streets (
euronews
Maine has its own Sistine Chapel: the plain white South Solon Meeting House hides 1950s frescoes on nearly every wall, including a Great Flood modeled on Michelangelo's (
AP

France's weekend riots hit luxury stores including Louis Vuitton, Burberry, and Celine, and secondhand marketplace Vinted says it pulled listings suspected of selling the looted goods, acting "against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans" (

Citrini, the No. 1 finance Substack, poached Fortune reporter Eva Roytburg to build out its social presence; she launched its Instagram accounts on day one (
Feed Me
NYT fashion critic Vanessa Friedman linked Mayor Mamdani's brown-and-black-shoes-with-a-suit look to "Team Trump," then recommended dress sneakers; Twitter is not having it (

Ella Rubin is on the cover of Nylon as "the new patron saint of teenage girls," Jacob Elordi will narrate Eric Dane's memoir audiobook, Joe Keery is making his Broadway debut in
Other Desert Cities
, a Glee reboot is officially happening, and Google's Frightgeist says Dolly Parton tops kids' Halloween costumes (

Spotify has stopped recommending 50 million AI slop tracks (

: individual samples stitched together to make Since I Left You, The Avalanches' genre-defining debut. After a 15-year creative block, the Australian duo is back with a fourth album, No Bad Memories, and James Jung sat down with them to write about aging alongside the music you love.

The first rule of Greek island-hopping: get on the right ferry. InsideHook's new guide maps nine days across Naxos, Paros, and Ios, with three nights per island as the minimum to absorb each one's distinct character. (

Instagram's Rings awards honor creators outside the billion-follower cohort, with the 2026 judges including Donatella Versace, Isamaya Ffrench, and Finneas. entries.title: The Chicken App, the Chestnut Grove, and the Curry Brick
entries.description: Today's mail assembled a strange triptych: AI needs a fast-food giveaway to prove its popularity, data-center builders are doing town-by-town diplomacy, and the best dinner idea is ground-beef curry from boxed roux.
entries.body:
Today's mail assembled a strange triptych: AI needs a fast-food giveaway to prove its popularity, data-center builders are doing town-by-town diplomacy, and the best dinner idea is ground-beef curry from boxed roux.

Best links

• AI's popularity test is a free slider. Garbage Day noticed Meta's Muse briefly lost the iOS App Store top spot to Dave's Hot Chicken, whose free-slider promotion drove downloads. Muse is still vastly larger, but the episode makes a sharp point: for a platform company with billions of existing users, the appearance of AI momentum may matter almost as much as durable use. The newsletter cites roughly 30% seven-day retention and 20% two-week retention for Muse, versus mid-teens rates for several rival assistants.

• The data-center fight is becoming intensely local. Pirate Wires followed 29-year-old Strata founder David Meyer into Saguache County, Colorado, where about 60 residents packed a room to hear a pitch for smaller, supposedly more responsible facilities—and then spent two hours explaining why they were unconvinced. 404 Media finds a parallel fight in West Virginia, where a proposed 2,250-acre Nscale campus would sit near an endangered American chestnut grove. AI infrastructure has entered its small-town-meeting era.

• Recursive self-improvement leaves the lab notebook. WIRED's Will Knight profiles Recursive, whose open-weight Flint coding model was developed with an in-house “Eureka Machine” that reportedly automated much of the model pipeline—training methods, architecture work, and chip-specific optimization included. The interesting question is not just whether Flint benchmarks well; it is whether a small research team can use AI to compress the entire route from idea to model.

Worth reading

• A tradition worth rescuing. The Republic of Letters runs Elisabeth Becker's defense of a German-Jewish universalist tradition built around argument, solidarity across difference, peace, beauty, and “real utopias.” Her cast—Walter Benjamin, Hannah Arendt, Albert Einstein, Max Liebermann, and Mascha Kaléko—turns “home” into something that can exist between people, places, and texts rather than inside a single nation.

• The field trip industrial complex. After School spots a new data-center PR strategy: picture books, coloring pages, “International Data Center Day,” and even school kits. In the same dispatch, an analysis of school-issued YouTube histories found that more than 95% of 17,000-plus videos watched during school hours were not educational by conventional standards. The newsletter's best phrase is “screenagers”—parents now policing the feeds of their TikTok-absorbed elders.

• The $2,000 iPhone as a glimpse, not a verdict. Joanna Stern's New Things review put the folding iPhone Duo through 32,000 hinge cycles. Her verdict: beautiful, surprisingly durable, genuinely flexible—and buggy, maddening, full of first-generation compromises, and very expensive. It sounds less like a recommendation than a dispatch from the future.

Food & places

• Dinner answer: Japanese ground-beef curry, one skillet, 50 minutes. Potatoes, carrots, peas, and store-bought curry roux do the heavy lifting; serve it over rice, udon, lo mein, or beside a breaded pork cutlet.

• The anti-gadget kitchen. InsideHook's Kendra Vaculin argues for a short, durable kit: a tri-ply stainless skillet, one sharp 8-inch chef's knife, a Dutch oven, and two properly sized cutting boards. The useful principle is less “buy these brands” than “buy fewer things that can survive decades.”

• The drink of the moment may be an entire orange. Feed Me reports that Vera Wang and Kris Jenner both favor a glass with ice, vodka, a whole sliced orange, and a splash of tonic. Elsewhere in the issue: a retro portrait studio in Greenpoint, a new grocery-and-CPG podcast called Eye Level, and a warning that “dark nutrition” has taken raw buffalo brains and raw-milk ice cream mainstream-adjacent.

Internet oddities

• J Mascis recommends a life assembled from tiny enthusiasms: soy-free eggs, a real Superfuzz pedal, cowboy shirts that everyone insists are jackets, Hi Records 45s, and homemade yogurt. It is a perfect anti-algorithmic shopping list: specific, slightly cranky, and impossible to optimize.

• Patch PHP; distrust the polished page. 404 Media also flags major PHP vulnerabilities, 333 infected Tor exit nodes, AI-generated “lawyers” targeting immigrants on TikTok, and a Republican congressional candidate who accidentally left an AI prompt visible on his campaign site. The web remains a place where the strangest detail is usually the most important one.

Ideas to steal

• Make the infrastructure argument human-sized. If you are selling something enormous, show up in the room where 60 people are folding chairs—and listen for two hours.

• Build the useful version of a media niche. Feed Me's Eye Level is aimed at people who want the machinery behind grocery and CPG: shelf negotiations, buyer behavior, distribution, acquisition costs, and what actually makes a product defensible.

• Prefer the tool that changes the way you work. One great knife, one good pan, one pot that can braise, bake, simmer, and serve.

One-liners

“The appearance of success is what’s really important.” — Garbage Day on Muse

“Social nonconformism is the sine qua non of intellectual achievement.” — Hannah Arendt, quoted in The Republic of Letters

“It makes me happy to look at it.” — J Mascis on his Superfuzz pedal

“You don’t need a ton of stuff, just a handful of nice things that work well and make you look like you know your way around a braise (which is hot).” — Kendra Vaculin

“The band is always the same, and awesome. they just parade in different singers who are also all awesome.” — J Mascis on Hi Records 45s

entries.title: Anthropic's $16.3B S-1 leak, GTA VI's $1B sick-out, Ghost of Uncle Joe's returns - Thursday, October 22, 2026
entries.body:
Thursday, October 22, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• $90,000: the asking price on a Galliano-era Dior newsprint dress The RealReal just listed. Vintage fashion has officially entered high art territory.

• 10: years since The Strategist launched online as a holiday pop-up blog. Emilia Petrarca talks with co-founder Alexis Swerdloff about how e-commerce went from the Wild West to the default way everyone shops.

• 40: recipes in Rosie Grant's new cookbook "To Die For", all carved into gravestones or tied to graves with stories to tell. She spent five and a half years visiting cemeteries and cooking with the families left behind.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• InsideHook's bartender-reporter breaks down what your drink order says about you: Long Island drinkers are feared, beer-and-shot regulars are a bartender's dream, martini people should stop at three, and an espresso martini is a weapon. (InsideHook)

• Elin Strong refuses the "momfluencer" label, even though mom content built her whole audience. There is a difference, she writes, between writing about being a mom and being branded as one. (Spread the Jelly)

• "On The Fence", a quiz built by a Massey University team, matches first-time voters to parties by comparing their answers on the issues. A solid starting point if voting still feels like homework. (shit you should care about)

• Intrepid Travel's 2027 "Not Hot List" points travelers at places the algorithm hasn't found yet: Dili in Timor-Leste ("what Bali looked like before the influencers"), Samburu in Kenya, and Mestia in Georgia. (shit you should care about)

• People are buying wagyu beef and groceries on Whatnot, the live shopping platform, and the trend is only getting weirder. (Emilia Petrarca)

• Priya Krishna digs into what happens to beloved restaurants after private equity money arrives. Her take: the money can be good for owners, but flavorless burgers and soggy fries are the risk. (The New York Times)

morning.body:
Thursday, October 22, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• $16.3 billion: Anthropic's revenue for the first half of 2026, up from $1.1 billion a year earlier. The Wall Street Journal got hold of a draft S-1 for the AI company's Wall Street debut, which could value it around $2 trillion. The same filing shows an $80 billion net loss and $450 billion in locked-in cloud computing deals it cannot back out of.

• $1 billion: the predicted hit to U.S. GDP on the day GTA VI drops next month, as more than a million Americans are forecast to call out sick to play. Economists are actually modeling this.

• 7.5%: how much wearing a necktie can reduce blood flow to the brain, according to a 2018 study.

• $60,000: the bet a restaurant group near Dodger Stadium placed on Kalshi that the Dodgers would not advance. The trade doubled in value after Milwaukee swept LA, filling the revenue hole left by the missing World Series crowds.

• 300,000: seasonal and full-time workers Amazon says it will hire for the holidays, its biggest holiday hiring surge yet.

Quotes of the Day

• "My conscious brain is really bad at playing goalie. I have to let my unconscious brain do the work because it reacts a lot quicker. Today was unconscious. Like, don't think about anything. If you asked me how I made a save, I'd be like 'I have no idea.'" (Devin Cooley, Calgary Flames goalkeeper, after a 34-save game)

• "If you went looking for the Democratic Party's weakest point, you might start with education, income, or race. But I'd give you a different answer: religion." (Lakshya Jain, The Argument, on polling that shows religion as the left's biggest electoral problem)

• "It's the political equivalent of blaming your neighbor for a kitchen fire in Paris because you don't like his lawn signs." (Counterpoint, on Trump blaming Democrats for France's cost-of-living protests)

• "Put down the bottle, ladies. The republic won't survive." (Pirate Wires, on politicians openly discussing jailing their rivals' staffers)

AI & The Machines

Hugging Face built an AI that speaks the language of DNA. The new open-source biology model can chat about genetic changes and help researchers understand how those changes affect gene activity and health. Think of it as a translator for the language of life, aimed at working scientists. (WIRED)

Hackers beat the patch on the internet-melting PHP bugs. Amazon Web Services logged attempts to exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities four days before the fixes were released. The bugs are now being broadly exploited across the internet. (WIRED)

Money & Power

CBS's Election Night coverage will be sponsored by DraftKings. Executives at CBS's owned-and-operated stations learned their election coverage now carries sports-gambling branding straight through Election Night. The deal stirred angst and irritation at the sales team that sold it. The line between the news desk and the betting window keeps getting thinner. (Status)

Meta's ad business is slowing in Europe now that users can pick less-personalized ads. An earnings briefing revealed ad revenue has softened since the EU introduced the Less-Personalized Ads model at the start of the year. Given the choice, people are choosing fewer creepy ads. (WIRED)

Health & Habits

Hims wants to put every dude on testosterone. The telehealth giant plans to offer testosterone replacement therapy, its first prescription of a controlled substance. Unlike its other meds, this one requires a video call with a physician first, and it is being offered to cisgender men only. (WIRED)

The Culture

Moviegoing has quietly become a wellness activity. InsideHook's Tanner Garrity saw four films in four days (Naza, Primetime, You Can See Everything, and the Palme d'Or winner Fjord), each in a packed theater, and came out convinced that communal moviegoing is old-school social connection worth protecting. Nobody checks their phone. Nobody spoils the ending. (InsideHook)

San Francisco's "hot girl bubble" might be an economic warning sign. Multiple sources tell Pirate Wires that gorgeous women are flocking to the city, many of them effectively paid by cash-flush companies to woo business prospects. When venture money starts hiring baddies again, it is usually a bubble tell. (Pirate Wires)

Around Hoboken

The Ghost of Uncle Joe's is back this weekend. One of Jersey City's biggest Halloween traditions returns to Harsimus Cemetery on Friday and Saturday, with local musicians dressing as famous artists and playing tribute sets. This year's lineup includes Pink Floyd, KISS, Prince, Christina Aguilera, Dolly Parton, Fleetwood Mac, and Green Day, with proceeds benefiting the historic cemetery. (The Hoboken Girl)

• Airbnb hosts are furious they can no longer make guests do their chores. Guests, meanwhile, are celebrating. (WIRED)

• Hoboken was just named the most walkable city in the U.S. in a new ranking. (The Hoboken Girl)

• Lisa's Deli in Hoboken is under new ownership and will reopen soon. (The Hoboken Girl)

• Hoboken Pizza Fest returns on 11/14, with the participating spots announced. (The Hoboken Girl)

• After 90 years, Journal Square's iconic Boulevard Drinks is moving to a new location. (The Hoboken Girl)

• Meta was hit with a $25 billion penalty in a New Mexico case. (Status)

• Trump barred CNN from Air Force One, again. (Status)

• The White House threatened POLITICO over its staff stories. (Status)

• The yield on 10-year French government bonds hit 5% as borrowing costs spiked amid mass unrest. (Snacks)

midday.body:
Thursday, October 22, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• 72 million: Americans who watched Seinfeld through August of this year, roughly a fifth of the country, for a show that stopped production in 1998. The business spine of Acquired's new 3.5-hour episode: a one-off NBC special slipped past every gatekeeper and left its creators owning a $7 billion asset.

• $42 million: in SNAP fraud targeted by the DOJ's first national benefits-fraud enforcement surge, announced Wednesday in Cincinnati by JD Vance; 40+ defendants hit since September 1.

• $107.6 million: what an anonymous guarantor paid for Brancusi's 113-year-old "Danaïde" at Christie's, making it the second-most expensive sculpture ever sold.

• 7-2: the Supreme Court vote refusing to let the Trump administration stop gender-transition care for federal inmates, affecting about 1,000 people.

• 183.2 million: Americans who spent time outdoors in 2025, a record, though growth slowed year over year, partly because young adults are broke.

• 1,600%: how much assaults on ICE officers are up, per the agency itself (vehicle attacks up 3,300%, death threats up 8,000%).

Quotes of the Day

• "Drill, baby, drill is basically drill as much as you can to commit economic suicide." (Kaes Van't Hof, Diamondback Energy CEO, in Semafor, on why Permian oil bosses won't pump more)

• "In a world of infinite 'content,' information, media, the value of a distinct perspective is going to the moon." (Chris Best, Substack CEO, in a Feed Me reader interview, on why he's "extremely AI-pilled")

• "You can force virality but you can't force fandom." (Casey Lewis, After School, on creators building talent pipelines, from MrBeast's programming hire to Alex Cooper's Unwell University)

• "things to be unequivocally real" (Blake Korengold, 17, in After School, on why he films wildlife with trail cams: tired of "doomscrolling and AI slop")

• "It used to be technology was like this train, and all we had to do is get on the train and ride it into the promised land of progress. Now people feel like they're on the train tracks." (Brian Chesky, Airbnb cofounder, on Semafor's The CEO Signal, on the populist backlash against AI)

Fraud & Power

A Massachusetts marriage ring charged $38,000 to $40,000 per wedding. Jennifer Gonzalez, 43, of Fall River allegedly arranged 18 to 20 sham marriages a year for over a decade, mostly for Brazilian men, pulling in more than $6 million. She reportedly staged couples' photos to fool immigration officials and told a cooperating witness she paused the business in 2025 because enforcement under Trump got "a little harsh." She also collected about $124,500 in SNAP benefits without reporting income. (NLDR Media)

A scammer opened a CashApp in her name. She spent three nights in jail. Amanda Smith of upstate Pennsylvania was arrested on a computer-fraud warrant out of Arkansas, a state she had never visited. A scammer had used her Social Security number and date of birth to open a CashApp account, then tricked a Facebook Marketplace buyer into sending $1,000 to it. CashApp then refused to share any information about the account because Smith couldn't prove she owned it. (404 Media)

Mattel invited an activist inside to stop the activists. Hours after Semafor reported that Southeastern Asset Management was preparing a boardroom fight, Mattel signed a cooperation agreement with EdgePoint Investment Group, putting one of the Canadian firm's top partners on its board. That locks about 18% of the stock in friendly hands and neutralizes Southeastern plus others pushing for a sale. Scoreboard: Mattel 1, activists 0. (Semafor)

Tech Money

Meta is minting nonvoting stock so Zuckerberg never has to share control. Semafor scooped that Meta is creating a new class of nonvoting shares, letting Zuckerberg issue stock for acquisitions, giant pay packages for OpenAI and Anthropic recruits, or plain cash raises, without diluting his grip on the company he founded 22 years ago. One motivator: a possible California billionaire tax that could force him to sell shares (he reportedly told the board he planned to list his Palo Alto house for sale publicly). Shareholders absorbed the snub; the stock rose 2% in after-hours trading. (Semafor)

No venture firm owns more than 2% of Anthropic. Newcomer's Tom Dotan reports that Iconiq, Menlo and Lightspeed are set to be the biggest venture winners in the upcoming IPO, with Dario Amodei ringing the NASDAQ bell next month. But every firm stayed under 2%, by design: Anthropic told investors it wanted no single investor with outsized control, after years of VCs passing on the company over its unusual structure and its fixation on safety over commercialization. (Newcomer)

CoreWeave is Wall Street's AI Rorschach test. Goldman Sachs upgraded the compute provider this week while HSBC cut its price target, with yields on its riskiest bonds sitting around 15% after an investor selloff. Even Meta's A-rated bonds for its Hyperion data center in Louisiana dipped to 91 cents on the dollar. "When have we overbuilt?" (Semafor)

The Culture

Toyota is exporting restraint. The Century, Japan's chauffeured-limo institution since 1967, is now a standalone brand and comes to the US in 2028 through a small club of upgraded Lexus dealers. Only three generations in nearly 60 years: the 1997 car carried Toyota's only passenger-car V12, with hand-cut wood grain and a crystal dashboard clock. The phoenix hood emblem takes about six weeks to hand-carve. If it lands here, it will be luxury sold as the absence of friction. (Why Is This Interesting?)

Miami's Monkey Jungle cages the humans. At the thirty-acre park, visitors stand inside an enormous cage while hundreds of primates roam free outside, gathering on top for craisins dropped into a metal bowl and hoisted up on a chain. The founder's son figured out how to breed squirrel monkeys reliably: separate them by gender most of the year, like "a young teenage dance party." (The Drift)

"Abracadabra" comes from an Aramaic phrase meaning "as I speak, I create." The Drift's new short story by Chidima Anekwe follows a Nigerian-American linguistics student whose attractive peer mentor plans to work on LLMs after graduation, a discovery that scrambles everything she thought she knew about language, identity and politics. (The Drift)

The Zeitgeist

Young adults are posting classified ads for friends. A 33-year-old vintage-store owner in Indiana made a TikTok "friendship application" to find "other weirdos" and met two of her closest friends in the comments; they have since been to a Hilary Duff concert together. Another poster got more than 800 comments offering baked goods and made exactly one friend. "Nobody is really trying to get past that small-talk phase." (After School)

Brazilian pop fandoms are campaigning for Lula. More than 600 fan accounts for Billie Eilish, Lady Gaga and Harry Styles have rallied behind President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead of the October 25 vote against Flávio Bolsonaro. At a São Paulo rally this month, Lula joked he wasn't sure whether to address the crowd as "comrades" or "fandoms from all over Brazil." (After School)

EA laid off around 400 workers weeks after its $55 billion take-private. Vanity Fair reports the cuts followed the August closing of the all-cash deal with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners. Hey, at least shareholder value was created. (404 Media)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Barclays plans to cut 5,000 jobs in an AI push. (Semafor)

• DeepSeek is targeting an IPO. (Semafor)

• The US pulled diplomats from Saudi Arabia. (Semafor)

• A federal intelligence center warned police that city council meetings about Flock cameras "may be viewed by extremists as a desirable target." (404 Media)

• San Diego's city council voted to end its Flock surveillance contract (still needs confirmation). (404 Media)

• Automattic CEO Matt Mullenweg is laying off more staff across comms, social, WordPress.com and VIP. (404 Media)

• The Mediterranean has too many yachts; Europe is running out of places to park them. (Semafor)

• The UN met this week to discuss autonomous weapons; the ICRC's legal warfare chief says the technology is developing at "a pace that is very concerning." (404 Media)

afternoon.body:
Thursday, October 22, 2026 - Afternoon Edition

Today's Numbers

• $15.6 million: what You Can See Everything made on 855 screens in its opening weekend. It goes wide to 2,500+ screens this weekend, and with a production and marketing budget under $20 million, A24 is already headed for a profit.

• $500 million: what Obsession (2026) has grossed worldwide. The Blair Witch-style horror flick sold for just $15 million at TIFF, making it one of the biggest distribution deals in recent memory.

• 0.6 points: the average Democratic lean of Wedgewood Polls' fabricated numbers. The fake firm confessed it invented its data as an "experiment," and Nate Silver says the explanation is bullshit.

• 11: pollsters permanently banned from Nate Silver's FLIPR database. Wedgewood just joined a club that already includes the fakes Strategic Vision and Research 2000.

• $160,000: roughly what "Rachel," a blue-eyed brunette, earns a year selling data centers in San Francisco. Pirate Wires treats the influx of women into SF as the city's newest economic warning sign.

Quotes of the Day

• "If your company can only win by requiring everyone to work 996, maybe the problem isn't that your employees lack ambition. Maybe your company hasn't figured out how to prioritize." (Elena Verna, head of growth at Lovable, on why she refuses the 996 grind)

• "The reason I like the artists I like is that I'm interested in their point of view... AI doesn't have a point of view, so it can't show me one." (Rick Rubin, talking AI and creativity with Substack's Chris Best)

• "My opinion is that Wedgewood's explanation is bullshit, a pathetic attempt to get ahead of the story." (Nate Silver, on the fake polling firm caught fabricating data)

• "We expect our children, grandchildren and great grandchildren to live in a New York City which will still be the Number One city in the world in all activities of the human body, mind and soul." (Former Mayor Abe Beame, in a 1976 letter found in a time capsule opened by Mayor Zohran Mamdani)

Film & TV

Nathan Fielder is everywhere this week, and WIRED has the full dossier. There is an exclusive interview with the comic auteur ahead of his first feature film, a deep dive into "Theranos 2.0" (Elizabeth Holmes' husband Billy Evans is apparently a key figure in Fielder's new documentary and may be working on a second blood-testing company), and a guide for newcomers to Fielder's strange universe. (WIRED)

George Saunders has a new short story out in The New Yorker. "Appeasement, Ohio" comes with an author interview about the story behind it. Sample dialogue: an Ohio family argues over a headline reading "Gettysburg Archaeology Proves No Battle" next to a photo of a metal detector leaning against a palm tree ("Zero palm trees in Pennsylvania," Carl says. "That you know of," Kip says). (The New Yorker)

Tech & AI

Cybersecurity people are bracing for a "Black October." Experts warn an AI-powered black-swan event could be coming: a sudden flood of new vulnerabilities as AI agents discover and exploit bugs nobody knew about. The same week, the UN convened on autonomous weapons, and the Red Cross legal warfare chief Laurent Gisel said, "The technology is developing at a pace that is very concerning." (404 Media)

Surveillance & Power

The feds got warrants to use fake cell towers to hunt down Don Lemon's producer. Investigators deployed cell-site simulators, the invasive surveillance tech that mimics phone towers, and sought the same tool against journalist Georgia Fort and a Minnesota state Senate candidate. (WIRED)

A federal intelligence center warned police that city council meetings about Flock cameras "may be viewed by extremists as a desirable target." The bulletin told cops to watch for "emotional confrontations" between anti-surveillance residents and officials. Meanwhile San Diego voted to end its Flock camera contract, a notable loss for the company given Darth Vader's famous backing there. (404 Media)

Creators

The biggest creators are building their own talent pipelines. MrBeast is hiring a head of programming at $170,000 to $230,000 plus bonus and equity to "define the next generation of creator-led programming" for his $5 billion company, a move meant to solve the "God King" key-man risk. Colin Rosenblum and Samir Chaudry handed $25,000 from their Adobe-backed Big Idea Fund to two rising filmmakers, Kai Cenat is taking Streamer University to Europe, and Alex Cooper's Unwell University added 103 student creators. (After School)

Style & Shopping

Alison Roman's tomato sauce company is now just "Roman's." Same sauce, new labels designed by Polonsky & Friends. She is also going wholesale through Faire, launched cookwithromans.com, and offers free shipping on orders over $70 with same-day NYC delivery on orders placed by 3pm. (Alison Roman)

Lightweight jackets are on sale everywhere. Huckberry has the Flint and Tinder Dry Wax Trucker down to $108 from $198 and the Knickerbocker Catskills Canvas Coat at $202 from $450, plus Adsum's Fall/Winter fleece drop, a restock of the sold-out Noah x Timex collab watch, a Madewell capsule with the New York Public Library, and a fresh update to the New Balance 990. (InsideHook)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Art Basel Paris is closing Friday at 7pm instead of the end of the weekend because of planned protests in Paris. Security barriers are already going up around the Grand Palais. (Feed Me)

• Cardi B launched her hair-care line Good Grow at independently owned beauty supply stores instead of Ulta or Sephora: "This is where I used to be and I still am." (Feed Me)

• Airbnb now bans hosts from requiring guests to do dishes, take out the trash, or follow flush rules. Hosts are not happy. (404 Media)

• LinkedIn removed its "Rewrite with AI" button and added a "Report as AI slop" option. (On Substack)

• Olivia Colman's new Sundance hit Wicker has her handcrafting a wicker husband, played by Alexander Skarsgard. (Feed Me)

• A fist fight broke out in the cigar lounge at Aman New York on Mother's Day last year. (Feed Me)

• Apollo is delaying PE associate interviews until banking analysts have at least a year under their belts. (Feed Me)

• Metrograph is screening Oldboy (2003), Rosemary's Baby on 35mm, and The Blair Witch Project this weekend. (Feed Me)
