Thursday, October 22, 2026 - Evening Edition

Today's Numbers

• $90,000: the asking price on a Galliano-era Dior newsprint dress The RealReal just listed. Vintage fashion has officially entered high art territory.

• 10: years since The Strategist launched online as a holiday pop-up blog. Emilia Petrarca talks with co-founder Alexis Swerdloff about how e-commerce went from the Wild West to the default way everyone shops.

• 40: recipes in Rosie Grant's new cookbook "To Die For", all carved into gravestones or tied to graves with stories to tell. She spent five and a half years visiting cemeteries and cooking with the families left behind.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• InsideHook's bartender-reporter breaks down what your drink order says about you: Long Island drinkers are feared, beer-and-shot regulars are a bartender's dream, martini people should stop at three, and an espresso martini is a weapon. (InsideHook)

• Elin Strong refuses the "momfluencer" label, even though mom content built her whole audience. There is a difference, she writes, between writing about being a mom and being branded as one. (Spread the Jelly)

• "On The Fence", a quiz built by a Massey University team, matches first-time voters to parties by comparing their answers on the issues. A solid starting point if voting still feels like homework. (shit you should care about)

• Intrepid Travel's 2027 "Not Hot List" points travelers at places the algorithm hasn't found yet: Dili in Timor-Leste ("what Bali looked like before the influencers"), Samburu in Kenya, and Mestia in Georgia. (shit you should care about)

• People are buying wagyu beef and groceries on Whatnot, the live shopping platform, and the trend is only getting weirder. (Emilia Petrarca)

• Priya Krishna digs into what happens to beloved restaurants after private equity money arrives. Her take: the money can be good for owners, but flavorless burgers and soggy fries are the risk. (The New York Times)

full.body:
Thursday, October 22, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• $16.3 billion: Anthropic's revenue for the first half of 2026, up from $1.1 billion a year earlier. The Wall Street Journal got hold of a draft S-1 for the AI company's Wall Street debut, which could value it around $2 trillion. The same filing shows an $80 billion net loss and $450 billion in locked-in cloud computing deals it cannot back out of.

• $1 billion: the predicted hit to U.S. GDP on the day GTA VI drops next month, as more than a million Americans are forecast to call out sick to play. Economists are actually modeling this.

• 7.5%: how much wearing a necktie can reduce blood flow to the brain, according to a 2018 study.

• $60,000: the bet a restaurant group near Dodger Stadium placed on Kalshi that the Dodgers would not advance. The trade doubled in value after Milwaukee swept LA, filling the revenue hole left by the missing World Series crowds.

• 300,000: seasonal and full-time workers Amazon says it will hire for the holidays, its biggest holiday hiring surge yet.

Quotes of the Day

• "My conscious brain is really bad at playing goalie. I have to let my unconscious brain do the work because it reacts a lot quicker. Today was unconscious. Like, don't think about anything. If you asked me how I made a save, I'd be like 'I have no idea.'" (Devin Cooley, Calgary Flames goalkeeper, after a 34-save game)

• "If you went looking for the Democratic Party's weakest point, you might start with education, income, or race. But I'd give you a different answer: religion." (Lakshya Jain, The Argument, on polling that shows religion as the left's biggest electoral problem)

• "It's the political equivalent of blaming your neighbor for a kitchen fire in Paris because you don't like his lawn signs." (Counterpoint, on Trump blaming Democrats for France's cost-of-living protests)

• "Put down the bottle, ladies. The republic won't survive." (Pirate Wires, on politicians openly discussing jailing their rivals' staffers)

AI & The Machines

Hugging Face built an AI that speaks the language of DNA. The new open-source biology model can chat about genetic changes and help researchers understand how those changes affect gene activity and health. Think of it as a translator for the language of life, aimed at working scientists. (WIRED)

Hackers beat the patch on the internet-melting PHP bugs. Amazon Web Services logged attempts to exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities four days before the fixes were released. The bugs are now being broadly exploited across the internet. (WIRED)

Money & Power

CBS's Election Night coverage will be sponsored by DraftKings. Executives at CBS's owned-and-operated stations learned their election coverage now carries sports-gambling branding straight through Election Night. The deal stirred angst and irritation at the sales team that sold it. The line between the news desk and the betting window keeps getting thinner. (Status)

Meta's ad business is slowing in Europe now that users can pick less-personalized ads. An earnings briefing revealed ad revenue has softened since the EU introduced the Less-Personalized Ads model at the start of the year. Given the choice, people are choosing fewer creepy ads. (WIRED)

Health & Habits

Hims wants to put every dude on testosterone. The telehealth giant plans to offer testosterone replacement therapy, its first prescription of a controlled substance. Unlike its other meds, this one requires a video call with a physician first, and it is being offered to cisgender men only. (WIRED)

The Culture

Moviegoing has quietly become a wellness activity. InsideHook's Tanner Garrity saw four films in four days (Naza, Primetime, You Can See Everything, and the Palme d'Or winner Fjord), each in a packed theater, and came out convinced that communal moviegoing is old-school social connection worth protecting. Nobody checks their phone. Nobody spoils the ending. (InsideHook)

San Francisco's "hot girl bubble" might be an economic warning sign. Multiple sources tell Pirate Wires that gorgeous women are flocking to the city, many of them effectively paid by cash-flush companies to woo business prospects. When venture money starts hiring baddies again, it is usually a bubble tell. (Pirate Wires)

Around Hoboken

The Ghost of Uncle Joe's is back this weekend. One of Jersey City's biggest Halloween traditions returns to Harsimus Cemetery on Friday and Saturday, with local musicians dressing as famous artists and playing tribute sets. This year's lineup includes Pink Floyd, KISS, Prince, Christina Aguilera, Dolly Parton, Fleetwood Mac, and Green Day, with proceeds benefiting the historic cemetery. (The Hoboken Girl)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Airbnb hosts are furious they can no longer make guests do their chores. Guests, meanwhile, are celebrating. (WIRED)

• Hoboken was just named the most walkable city in the U.S. in a new ranking. (The Hoboken Girl)

• Lisa's Deli in Hoboken is under new ownership and will reopen soon. (The Hoboken Girl)

• Hoboken Pizza Fest returns on 11/14, with the participating spots announced. (The Hoboken Girl)

• After 90 years, Journal Square's iconic Boulevard Drinks is moving to a new location. (The Hoboken Girl)

• Meta was hit with a $25 billion penalty in a New Mexico case. (Status)

• Trump barred CNN from Air Force One, again. (Status)

• The White House threatened POLITICO over its staff stories. (Status)

• The yield on 10-year French government bonds hit 5% as borrowing costs spiked amid mass unrest. (Snacks)

Thursday, October 22, 2026 - Midday Edition

Today's Numbers

• 72 million: Americans who watched Seinfeld through August of this year, roughly a fifth of the country, for a show that stopped production in 1998. The business spine of Acquired's new 3.5-hour episode: a one-off NBC special slipped past every gatekeeper and left its creators owning a $7 billion asset.

• $42 million: in SNAP fraud targeted by the DOJ's first national benefits-fraud enforcement surge, announced Wednesday in Cincinnati by JD Vance; 40+ defendants hit since September 1.

• $107.6 million: what an anonymous guarantor paid for Brancusi's 113-year-old "Danaïde" at Christie's, making it the second-most expensive sculpture ever sold.

• 7-2: the Supreme Court vote refusing to let the Trump administration stop gender-transition care for federal inmates, affecting about 1,000 people.

• 183.2 million: Americans who spent time outdoors in 2025, a record, though growth slowed year over year, partly because young adults are broke.

• 1,600%: how much assaults on ICE officers are up, per the agency itself (vehicle attacks up 3,300%, death threats up 8,000%).

Quotes of the Day

• "Drill, baby, drill is basically drill as much as you can to commit economic suicide." (Kaes Van't Hof, Diamondback Energy CEO, in Semafor, on why Permian oil bosses won't pump more)

• "In a world of infinite 'content,' information, media, the value of a distinct perspective is going to the moon." (Chris Best, Substack CEO, in a Feed Me reader interview, on why he's "extremely AI-pilled")

• "You can force virality but you can't force fandom." (Casey Lewis, After School, on creators building talent pipelines, from MrBeast's programming hire to Alex Cooper's Unwell University)

• "things to be unequivocally real" (Blake Korengold, 17, in After School, on why he films wildlife with trail cams: tired of "doomscrolling and AI slop")

• "It used to be technology was like this train, and all we had to do is get on the train and ride it into the promised land of progress. Now people feel like they're on the train tracks." (Brian Chesky, Airbnb cofounder, on Semafor's The CEO Signal, on the populist backlash against AI)

Fraud & Power

A Massachusetts marriage ring charged $38,000 to $40,000 per wedding. Jennifer Gonzalez, 43, of Fall River allegedly arranged 18 to 20 sham marriages a year for over a decade, mostly for Brazilian men, pulling in more than $6 million. She reportedly staged couples' photos to fool immigration officials and told a cooperating witness she paused the business in 2025 because enforcement under Trump got "a little harsh." She also collected about $124,500 in SNAP benefits without reporting income. (NLDR Media)

A scammer opened a CashApp in her name. She spent three nights in jail. Amanda Smith of upstate Pennsylvania was arrested on a computer-fraud warrant out of Arkansas, a state she had never visited. A scammer had used her Social Security number and date of birth to open a CashApp account, then tricked a Facebook Marketplace buyer into sending $1,000 to it. CashApp then refused to share any information about the account because Smith couldn't prove she owned it. (404 Media)

Mattel invited an activist inside to stop the activists. Hours after Semafor reported that Southeastern Asset Management was preparing a boardroom fight, Mattel signed a cooperation agreement with EdgePoint Investment Group, putting one of the Canadian firm's top partners on its board. That locks about 18% of the stock in friendly hands and neutralizes Southeastern plus others pushing for a sale. Scoreboard: Mattel 1, activists 0. (Semafor)

Tech Money

Meta is minting nonvoting stock so Zuckerberg never has to share control. Semafor scooped that Meta is creating a new class of nonvoting shares, letting Zuckerberg issue stock for acquisitions, giant pay packages for OpenAI and Anthropic recruits, or plain cash raises, without diluting his grip on the company he founded 22 years ago. One motivator: a possible California billionaire tax that could force him to sell shares (he reportedly told the board he planned to list his Palo Alto house for sale publicly). Shareholders absorbed the snub; the stock rose 2% in after-hours trading. (Semafor)

No venture firm owns more than 2% of Anthropic. Newcomer's Tom Dotan reports that Iconiq, Menlo and Lightspeed are set to be the biggest venture winners in the upcoming IPO, with Dario Amodei ringing the NASDAQ bell next month. But every firm stayed under 2%, by design: Anthropic told investors it wanted no single investor with outsized control, after years of VCs passing on the company over its unusual structure and its fixation on safety over commercialization. (Newcomer)

CoreWeave is Wall Street's AI Rorschach test. Goldman Sachs upgraded the compute provider this week while HSBC cut its price target, with yields on its riskiest bonds sitting around 15% after an investor selloff. Even Meta's A-rated bonds for its Hyperion data center in Louisiana dipped to 91 cents on the dollar. "When have we overbuilt?" (Semafor)

The Culture

Toyota is exporting restraint. The Century, Japan's chauffeured-limo institution since 1967, is now a standalone brand and comes to the US in 2028 through a small club of upgraded Lexus dealers. Only three generations in nearly 60 years: the 1997 car carried Toyota's only passenger-car V12, with hand-cut wood grain and a crystal dashboard clock. The phoenix hood emblem takes about six weeks to hand-carve. If it lands here, it will be luxury sold as the absence of friction. (Why Is This Interesting?)

Miami's Monkey Jungle cages the humans. At the thirty-acre park, visitors stand inside an enormous cage while hundreds of primates roam free outside, gathering on top for craisins dropped into a metal bowl and hoisted up on a chain. The founder's son figured out how to breed squirrel monkeys reliably: separate them by gender most of the year, like "a young teenage dance party." (The Drift)

"Abracadabra" comes from an Aramaic phrase meaning "as I speak, I create." The Drift's new short story by Chidima Anekwe follows a Nigerian-American linguistics student whose attractive peer mentor plans to work on LLMs after graduation, a discovery that scrambles everything she thought she knew about language, identity and politics. (The Drift)

The Zeitgeist

Young adults are posting classified ads for friends. A 33-year-old vintage-store owner in Indiana made a TikTok "friendship application" to find "other weirdos" and met two of her closest friends in the comments; they have since been to a Hilary Duff concert together. Another poster got more than 800 comments offering baked goods and made exactly one friend. "Nobody is really trying to get past that small-talk phase." (After School)

Brazilian pop fandoms are campaigning for Lula. More than 600 fan accounts for Billie Eilish, Lady Gaga and Harry Styles have rallied behind President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead of the October 25 vote against Flávio Bolsonaro. At a São Paulo rally this month, Lula joked he wasn't sure whether to address the crowd as "comrades" or "fandoms from all over Brazil." (After School)

EA laid off around 400 workers weeks after its $55 billion take-private. Vanity Fair reports the cuts followed the August closing of the all-cash deal with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners. Hey, at least shareholder value was created. (404 Media)

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Barclays plans to cut 5,000 jobs in an AI push. (Semafor)

• DeepSeek is targeting an IPO. (Semafor)

• The US pulled diplomats from Saudi Arabia. (Semafor)

• A federal intelligence center warned police that city council meetings about Flock cameras "may be viewed by extremists as a desirable target." (404 Media)

• San Diego's city council voted to end its Flock surveillance contract (still needs confirmation). (404 Media)

• Automattic CEO Matt Mullenweg is laying off more staff across comms, social, WordPress.com and VIP. (404 Media)

• The Mediterranean has too many yachts; Europe is running out of places to park them. (Semafor)

• The UN met this week to discuss autonomous weapons; the ICRC's legal warfare chief says the technology is developing at "a pace that is very concerning." (404 Media)

"It's the political equivalent of blaming your neighbor for a kitchen fire in Paris because you don't like his lawn signs." (Counterpoint, on Trump blaming Democrats for France's cost-of-living protests)
"Put down the bottle, ladies. The republic won't survive." (Pirate Wires, on politicians openly discussing jailing their rivals' staffers)
AI & The Machines
Hugging Face built an AI that speaks the language of DNA.

The new open-source biology model can chat about genetic changes and help researchers understand how those changes affect gene activity and health. Think of it as a translator for the language of life, aimed at working scientists. (
WIRED
Hackers beat the patch on the internet-melting PHP bugs.
Amazon Web Services logged attempts to exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities four days before the fixes were released. The bugs are now being broadly exploited across the internet. (
WIRED
Money & Power
CBS's Election Night coverage will be sponsored by DraftKings.

Executives at CBS's owned-and-operated stations learned their election coverage now carries sports-gambling branding straight through Election Night. The deal stirred angst and irritation at the sales team that sold it. The line between the news desk and the betting window keeps getting thinner. (
Status
Meta's ad business is slowing in Europe now that users can pick less-personalized ads.
An earnings briefing revealed ad revenue has softened since the EU introduced the Less-Personalized Ads model at the start of the year. Given the choice, people are choosing fewer creepy ads. (
WIRED
Health & Habits
Hims wants to put every dude on testosterone.

The telehealth giant plans to offer testosterone replacement therapy, its first prescription of a controlled substance. Unlike its other meds, this one requires a video call with a physician first, and it is being offered to cisgender men only. (
WIRED
The Culture
Moviegoing has quietly become a wellness activity.

InsideHook's Tanner Garrity saw four films in four days (Naza, Primetime, You Can See Everything, and the Palme d'Or winner Fjord), each in a packed theater, and came out convinced that communal moviegoing is old-school social connection worth protecting. Nobody checks their phone. Nobody spoils the ending. (
InsideHook
San Francisco's "hot girl bubble" might be an economic warning sign.

Multiple sources tell Pirate Wires that gorgeous women are flocking to the city, many of them effectively paid by cash-flush companies to woo business prospects. When venture money starts hiring baddies again, it is usually a bubble tell. (
Pirate Wires
Around Hoboken
The Ghost of Uncle Joe's is back this weekend.

One of Jersey City's biggest Halloween traditions returns to Harsimus Cemetery on Friday and Saturday, with local musicians dressing as famous artists and playing tribute sets. This year's lineup includes Pink Floyd, KISS, Prince, Christina Aguilera, Dolly Parton, Fleetwood Mac, and Green Day, with proceeds benefiting the historic cemetery. (
The Hoboken Girl
Quick Hits & Curiosities
Airbnb hosts are furious they can no longer make guests do their chores. Guests, meanwhile, are celebrating. (
WIRED
Hoboken was just named the most walkable city in the U.S. in a new ranking. (
The Hoboken Girl
Lisa's Deli in Hoboken is under new ownership and will reopen soon. (
The Hoboken Girl
Hoboken Pizza Fest returns on 11/14, with the participating spots announced. (
The Hoboken Girl
After 90 years, Journal Square's iconic Boulevard Drinks is moving to a new location. (
The Hoboken Girl
Meta was hit with a $25 billion penalty in a New Mexico case. (
Status
Trump barred CNN from Air Force One, again. (
Status
The White House threatened POLITICO over its staff stories. (
Status
The yield on 10-year French government bonds hit 5% as borrowing costs spiked amid mass unrest. (
Snacks
Thursday, October 22, 2026 - Midday Edition
Today's Numbers
72 million

: Americans who watched Seinfeld through August of this year, roughly a fifth of the country, for a show that stopped production in 1998. The business spine of Acquired's new 3.5-hour episode: a one-off NBC special slipped past every gatekeeper and left its creators owning a $7 billion asset.
$42 million
: in SNAP fraud targeted by the DOJ's first national benefits-fraud enforcement surge, announced Wednesday in Cincinnati by JD Vance; 40+ defendants hit since September 1.
$107.6 million
: what an anonymous guarantor paid for Brancusi's 113-year-old "Danaïde" at Christie's, making it the second-most expensive sculpture ever sold.
: the Supreme Court vote refusing to let the Trump administration stop gender-transition care for federal inmates, affecting about 1,000 people.
183.2 million
: Americans who spent time outdoors in 2025, a record, though growth slowed year over year, partly because young adults are broke.
: how much assaults on ICE officers are up, per the agency itself (vehicle attacks up 3,300%, death threats up 8,000%).
Quotes of the Day
"Drill, baby, drill is basically drill as much as you can to commit economic suicide." (Kaes Van't Hof, Diamondback Energy CEO, in Semafor, on why Permian oil bosses won't pump more)

"In a world of infinite 'content,' information, media, the value of a distinct perspective is going to the moon." (Chris Best, Substack CEO, in a Feed Me reader interview, on why he's "extremely AI-pilled")
"You can force virality but you can't force fandom." (Casey Lewis, After School, on creators building talent pipelines, from MrBeast's programming hire to Alex Cooper's Unwell University)
"things to be unequivocally real" (Blake Korengold, 17, in After School, on why he films wildlife with trail cams: tired of "doomscrolling and AI slop")

"It used to be technology was like this train, and all we had to do is get on the train and ride it into the promised land of progress. Now people feel like they're on the train tracks." (Brian Chesky, Airbnb cofounder, on Semafor's The CEO Signal, on the populist backlash against AI)
Fraud & Power
A Massachusetts marriage ring charged $38,000 to $40,000 per wedding.

Jennifer Gonzalez, 43, of Fall River allegedly arranged 18 to 20 sham marriages a year for over a decade, mostly for Brazilian men, pulling in more than $6 million. She reportedly staged couples' photos to fool immigration officials and told a cooperating witness she paused the business in 2025 because enforcement under Trump got "a little harsh." She also collected about $124,500 in SNAP benefits without reporting income. (
NLDR Media
A scammer opened a CashApp in her name. She spent three nights in jail.

Amanda Smith of upstate Pennsylvania was arrested on a computer-fraud warrant out of Arkansas, a state she had never visited. A scammer had used her Social Security number and date of birth to open a CashApp account, then tricked a Facebook Marketplace buyer into sending $1,000 to it. CashApp then refused to share any information about the account because Smith couldn't prove she owned it. (
404 Media
Mattel invited an activist inside to stop the activists.

Hours after Semafor reported that Southeastern Asset Management was preparing a boardroom fight, Mattel signed a cooperation agreement with EdgePoint Investment Group, putting one of the Canadian firm's top partners on its board. That locks about 18% of the stock in friendly hands and neutralizes Southeastern plus others pushing for a sale. Scoreboard: Mattel 1, activists 0. (
Semafor
Tech Money
Meta is minting nonvoting stock so Zuckerberg never has to share control.

Semafor scooped that Meta is creating a new class of nonvoting shares, letting Zuckerberg issue stock for acquisitions, giant pay packages for OpenAI and Anthropic recruits, or plain cash raises, without diluting his grip on the company he founded 22 years ago. One motivator: a possible California billionaire tax that could force him to sell shares (he reportedly told the board he planned to list his Palo Alto house for sale publicly). Shareholders absorbed the snub; the stock rose 2% in after-hours trading. (
Semafor
No venture firm owns more than 2% of Anthropic.

Newcomer's Tom Dotan reports that Iconiq, Menlo and Lightspeed are set to be the biggest venture winners in the upcoming IPO, with Dario Amodei ringing the NASDAQ bell next month. But every firm stayed under 2%, by design: Anthropic told investors it wanted no single investor with outsized control, after years of VCs passing on the company over its unusual structure and its fixation on safety over commercialization. (
Newcomer
CoreWeave is Wall Street's AI Rorschach test.

Goldman Sachs upgraded the compute provider this week while HSBC cut its price target, with yields on its riskiest bonds sitting around 15% after an investor selloff. Even Meta's A-rated bonds for its Hyperion data center in Louisiana dipped to 91 cents on the dollar. "When have we overbuilt?" (
Semafor
The Culture
Toyota is exporting restraint.

The Century, Japan's chauffeured-limo institution since 1967, is now a standalone brand and comes to the US in 2028 through a small club of upgraded Lexus dealers. Only three generations in nearly 60 years: the 1997 car carried Toyota's only passenger-car V12, with hand-cut wood grain and a crystal dashboard clock. The phoenix hood emblem takes about six weeks to hand-carve. If it lands here, it will be luxury sold as the absence of friction. (
Why Is This Interesting?
Miami's Monkey Jungle cages the humans.

At the thirty-acre park, visitors stand inside an enormous cage while hundreds of primates roam free outside, gathering on top for craisins dropped into a metal bowl and hoisted up on a chain. The founder's son figured out how to breed squirrel monkeys reliably: separate them by gender most of the year, like "a young teenage dance party." (
The Drift
"Abracadabra" comes from an Aramaic phrase meaning "as I speak, I create."

The Drift's new short story by Chidima Anekwe follows a Nigerian-American linguistics student whose attractive peer mentor plans to work on LLMs after graduation, a discovery that scrambles everything she thought she knew about language, identity and politics. (
The Drift
The Zeitgeist
Young adults are posting classified ads for friends.

A 33-year-old vintage-store owner in Indiana made a TikTok "friendship application" to find "other weirdos" and met two of her closest friends in the comments; they have since been to a Hilary Duff concert together. Another poster got more than 800 comments offering baked goods and made exactly one friend. "Nobody is really trying to get past that small-talk phase." (
After School
Brazilian pop fandoms are campaigning for Lula.

More than 600 fan accounts for Billie Eilish, Lady Gaga and Harry Styles have rallied behind President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead of the October 25 vote against Flávio Bolsonaro. At a São Paulo rally this month, Lula joked he wasn't sure whether to address the crowd as "comrades" or "fandoms from all over Brazil." (
After School
EA laid off around 400 workers weeks after its $55 billion take-private.

Vanity Fair reports the cuts followed the August closing of the all-cash deal with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners. Hey, at least shareholder value was created. (
404 Media
Quick Hits & Curiosities
Barclays plans to cut 5,000 jobs in an AI push. (
Semafor
DeepSeek is targeting an IPO. (
Semafor
The US pulled diplomats from Saudi Arabia. (
Semafor
A federal intelligence center warned police that city council meetings about Flock cameras "may be viewed by extremists as a desirable target." (
404 Media
San Diego's city council voted to end its Flock surveillance contract (still needs confirmation). (
404 Media
Automattic CEO Matt Mullenweg is laying off more staff across comms, social,
WordPress.com
and VIP. (
404 Media
The Mediterranean has too many yachts; Europe is running out of places to park them. (
Semafor
The UN met this week to discuss autonomous weapons; the ICRC's legal warfare chief says the technology is developing at "a pace that is very concerning." (
404 Media
Thursday, October 22, 2026 - Afternoon Edition
Today's Numbers
$15.6 million
: what
You Can See Everything
made on 855 screens in its opening weekend. It goes wide to 2,500+ screens this weekend, and with a production and marketing budget under $20 million, A24 is already headed for a profit.
$500 million
: what
Obsession
(2026) has grossed worldwide. The Blair Witch-style horror flick sold for just $15 million at TIFF, making it one of the biggest distribution deals in recent memory.
0.6 points
: the average Democratic lean of Wedgewood Polls' fabricated numbers. The fake firm confessed it invented its data as an "experiment," and Nate Silver says the explanation is bullshit.
: pollsters permanently banned from Nate Silver's FLIPR database. Wedgewood just joined a club that already includes the fakes Strategic Vision and Research 2000.
: roughly what "Rachel," a blue-eyed brunette, earns a year selling data centers in San Francisco. Pirate Wires treats the influx of women into SF as the city's newest economic warning sign.
Quotes of the Day

"If your company can only win by requiring everyone to work 996, maybe the problem isn't that your employees lack ambition. Maybe your company hasn't figured out how to prioritize." (Elena Verna, head of growth at Lovable, on why she refuses the 996 grind)

"The reason I like the artists I like is that I'm interested in their point of view... AI doesn't have a point of view, so it can't show me one." (Rick Rubin, talking AI and creativity with Substack's Chris Best)
"My opinion is that Wedgewood's explanation is bullshit, a pathetic attempt to get ahead of the story." (Nate Silver, on the fake polling firm caught fabricating data)

"We expect our children, grandchildren and great grandchildren to live in a New York City which will still be the Number One city in the world in all activities of the human body, mind and soul." (Former Mayor Abe Beame, in a 1976 letter found in a time capsule opened by Mayor Zohran Mamdani)
Film & TV
Nathan Fielder is everywhere this week, and WIRED has the full dossier.

There is an exclusive interview with the comic auteur ahead of his first feature film, a deep dive into "Theranos 2.0" (Elizabeth Holmes' husband Billy Evans is apparently a key figure in Fielder's new documentary and may be working on a second blood-testing company), and a guide for newcomers to Fielder's strange universe. (
WIRED
George Saunders has a new short story out in The New Yorker.

"Appeasement, Ohio" comes with an author interview about the story behind it. Sample dialogue: an Ohio family argues over a headline reading "Gettysburg Archaeology Proves No Battle" next to a photo of a metal detector leaning against a palm tree ("Zero palm trees in Pennsylvania," Carl says. "That you know of," Kip says). (
The New Yorker
Tech & AI
Cybersecurity people are bracing for a "Black October."

Experts warn an AI-powered black-swan event could be coming: a sudden flood of new vulnerabilities as AI agents discover and exploit bugs nobody knew about. The same week, the UN convened on autonomous weapons, and the Red Cross legal warfare chief Laurent Gisel said, "The technology is developing at a pace that is very concerning." (
404 Media
Surveillance & Power
The feds got warrants to use fake cell towers to hunt down Don Lemon's producer.

Investigators deployed cell-site simulators, the invasive surveillance tech that mimics phone towers, and sought the same tool against journalist Georgia Fort and a Minnesota state Senate candidate. (
WIRED
A federal intelligence center warned police that city council meetings about Flock cameras "may be viewed by extremists as a desirable target."

The bulletin told cops to watch for "emotional confrontations" between anti-surveillance residents and officials. Meanwhile San Diego voted to end its Flock camera contract, a notable loss for the company given Darth Vader's famous backing there. (
404 Media
Creators
The biggest creators are building their own talent pipelines.

MrBeast is hiring a head of programming at $170,000 to $230,000 plus bonus and equity to "define the next generation of creator-led programming" for his $5 billion company, a move meant to solve the "God King" key-man risk. Colin Rosenblum and Samir Chaudry handed $25,000 from their Adobe-backed Big Idea Fund to two rising filmmakers, Kai Cenat is taking Streamer University to Europe, and Alex Cooper's Unwell University added 103 student creators. (
After School
Style & Shopping
Alison Roman's tomato sauce company is now just "Roman's."
Same sauce, new labels designed by Polonsky & Friends. She is also going wholesale through Faire, launched
cookwithromans.com
, and offers free shipping on orders over $70 with same-day NYC delivery on orders placed by 3pm. (
Alison Roman
Lightweight jackets are on sale everywhere.

Huckberry has the Flint and Tinder Dry Wax Trucker down to $108 from $198 and the Knickerbocker Catskills Canvas Coat at $202 from $450, plus Adsum's Fall/Winter fleece drop, a restock of the sold-out Noah x Timex collab watch, a Madewell capsule with the New York Public Library, and a fresh update to the New Balance 990. (
InsideHook
Quick Hits & Curiosities
Art Basel Paris is closing Friday at 7pm instead of the end of the weekend because of planned protests in Paris. Security barriers are already going up around the Grand Palais. (
Feed Me
Cardi B launched her hair-care line Good Grow at independently owned beauty supply stores instead of Ulta or Sephora: "This is where I used to be and I still am." (
Feed Me
Airbnb now bans hosts from requiring guests to do dishes, take out the trash, or follow flush rules. Hosts are not happy. (
404 Media
LinkedIn removed its "Rewrite with AI" button and added a "Report as AI slop" option. (
On Substack
Olivia Colman's new Sundance hit
Wicker
has her handcrafting a wicker husband, played by Alexander Skarsgard. (
Feed Me
A fist fight broke out in the cigar lounge at Aman New York on Mother's Day last year. (
Feed Me
Apollo is delaying PE associate interviews until banking analysts have at least a year under their belts. (
Feed Me
Metrograph is screening
Oldboy
Rosemary's Baby
on 35mm, and
The Blair Witch Project
this weekend. (
Feed Me
Thursday, October 22, 2026 - Evening Edition
Today's Numbers
: the asking price on a Galliano-era Dior newsprint dress The RealReal just listed. Vintage fashion has officially entered high art territory.

: years since The Strategist launched online as a holiday pop-up blog. Emilia Petrarca talks with co-founder Alexis Swerdloff about how e-commerce went from the Wild West to the default way everyone shops.

: recipes in Rosie Grant's new cookbook "To Die For", all carved into gravestones or tied to graves with stories to tell. She spent five and a half years visiting cemeteries and cooking with the families left behind.
Quick Hits & Curiosities

InsideHook's bartender-reporter breaks down what your drink order says about you: Long Island drinkers are feared, beer-and-shot regulars are a bartender's dream, martini people should stop at three, and an espresso martini is a weapon. (
InsideHook
Elin Strong refuses the "momfluencer" label, even though mom content built her whole audience. There is a difference, she writes, between writing about being a mom and being branded as one. (
Spread the Jelly
"On The Fence", a quiz built by a Massey University team, matches first-time voters to parties by comparing their answers on the issues. A solid starting point if voting still feels like homework. (
shit you should care about

Intrepid Travel's 2027 "Not Hot List" points travelers at places the algorithm hasn't found yet: Dili in Timor-Leste ("what Bali looked like before the influencers"), Samburu in Kenya, and Mestia in Georgia. (
shit you should care about
People are buying wagyu beef and groceries on Whatnot, the live shopping platform, and the trend is only getting weirder. (
Emilia Petrarca
Priya Krishna digs into what happens to beloved restaurants after private equity money arrives. Her take: the money can be good for owners, but flavorless burgers and soggy fries are the risk. (
The New York Times

entries.title: The Century, the Soup Swap, and the 996 Line
entries.body:
Front page

Today’s mail had a theme: the good life is less about maximal output than deliberate texture. Toyota is bringing an ultra-discreet chauffeur’s car to America; an AI operator is drawing a hard line against 996; a soup newsletter turns pantry inventory into a social event; and a Cash App identity-theft story reads like Kafka with push notifications.

Best links

• Luxury’s quietest flex: Toyota’s Century—Japan’s hand-finished, V12-era symbol of conservative power—is coming to the U.S. in 2028 through a deliberately tiny Lexus dealer network. The pitch is not spectacle; it is the absence of friction. Why is this interesting? calls it “exporting restraint at a serious premium.”

• A better way to pick a ballot: shit you should care about surfaced On The Fence, a Massey University questionnaire that lets first-time voters compare their views with political parties’ answers without pretending to tell them what to think. Useful civic UX: orient, don’t dictate.

• A city in close-up: Feed Me recommends Metro, Sarah Koenig’s new New York Times podcast, whose first episode follows the person who polishes Grand Central’s railings, doors, and ticket windows. The city, reduced to one job and one voice.

Worth reading

• George Saunders, in the Ohio uncanny valley: “Appeasement, Ohio” opens with eggs, Civil War buttons, a Dell, and a fake Gettysburg archaeology headline featuring a palm tree. The excerpt’s joke is simple and lethal: every argument arrives wearing the costume of evidence. New Yorker Substack also includes an interview about the story.

• The human cost of being impersonated: 404 Media follows Amanda Smith, arrested after a scammer opened a Cash App in her name and used it to receive stolen money. The bureaucratic nightmare is that Cash App refuses to explain the account because she cannot prove she owns it.

• The anti-996 manifesto: Elena Verna’s essay, cross-posted by Lenny’s Newsletter, argues that extreme hours are not ambition; they are a company borrowing against employees’ future health, relationships, and capacity. Her practical tool is the five-year regret test: when work and life collide, which choice will you regret more later?

Food & places

• The soup bucket list: NYT Cooking’s The Veggie starts with a pantry inventory—black beans, lentils, chickpeas, one lonely can of coconut milk—and builds outward into charred cabbage and lentil soup, curried coconut and red lentil soup, tomato-and-bean soups, and a borscht learned from Ebon Moss-Bachrach’s Ukrainian mother-in-law. This is recipe planning as domestic archaeology.

• Steal this gathering: a soup swap is a cookie swap with more heft: everyone makes one soup, then trades portions and leaves with several dinners. The kind of potluck that improves the week instead of merely occupying an evening.

• A sauce company grows up: Alison Roman renamed “A Very Good Tomato Sauce” to Roman’s, kept the sauce, redesigned the labels, and opened wholesale distribution. A neat little lesson in knowing when a cheeky placeholder name has done its job.

Internet oddities

• Survival and chill: After School found an audience of indoor workers watching people build snow caves, cook in Alaskan blizzards, and sit around virtual campfires. The genre is an antidote to the manosphere—and to synthetic internet sludge—because the appeal is slow, physical, and “unequivocally real.”

• The comment-to-link economy: Feed Me describes the now-common ritual where an apartment, recipe, or outfit is hidden behind “comment HOME.” The newsletter’s counter-move: search the listings yourself, save three minutes of performative engagement, and discover the kitchen is comically small.

Ideas to steal

• Make boundaries legible. Don’t hide family time behind a mysterious “focus block”; say what it is. People cannot respect a boundary they cannot see.

• Use the five-year regret test. Work is excellent at manufacturing urgency. Family, health, and the rest of life are less noisy—and easier to postpone forever.

• Design for texture. A Century, a soup swap, a handwritten civic questionnaire, a trail camera: the memorable things in today’s mail all replace frictionless scale with a little more craft, locality, or reality.

One-liners

• “996 is not a competitive advantage.” — Elena Verna, via Lenny’s Newsletter.

• AI may eliminate a lot of work while eliminating very little working.

• The Century’s real luxury is making the passenger feel that nothing required effort.

• “Things that are unequivocally real” is a pretty good editorial brief for the next year of the internet.

entries.title: Luckey's $200M war dogs, Netflix's Indian summer, SF's hot girl bubble - Friday, October 23, 2026
entries.body:
Friday, October 23, 2026 - Morning Edition

Today's Numbers

• $200M: Palmer Luckey's Warhound just came out of stealth with $200 million in funding to build genetically modified "elite working dogs" equipped with advanced body armor.

• 31%: Trump's approval rating has sunk to 31% in a new Reuters/Ipsos poll, as Americans fume over rising prices and his handling of the economy.

• $30B: Norway's sovereign wealth fund lost $30 billion last quarter, mostly on its government bond portfolio, yet it is still worth about $2.3 trillion.

• 63%: Waymo robotaxis crash about 63% less per mile than human drivers, per WaPo reporting, which makes the shadowy anti-robotaxi group in DC look even more suspicious.

• 15%: 15% of Americans now order groceries online every week, up from just 4% less than a decade ago, while trips to restaurants and stores sit at their lowest since Gallup started asking.

Quotes of the Day

• "We did so not in spite of, but because of our commitment to free expression." (president of the Columbia Open Discourse Alliance, on canceling a panel about press freedom)

• "Nothing looks worse than when a brand's fake honeycomb knee fades are landing half-way down your calves, or anywhere it's obvious your own leg doesn't actually bend." (Andrew Chen of 3Sixteen, on why his denim shop will never sell artificial distressing)

• "No one actually knows what they're doing." (Panayiota Soutis, from a night of ten big ideas shared with friends)

• "Boredom breeds good ideas. Being in nature breeds great ideas." (Panayiota Soutis, same night, on where ideas come from)

AI & The Machines

• Casey Newton and Kevin Roose just launched a new AI podcast with NPR, and it is deliberately neither doomer nor booster. Machine Gods drops twice a week and plants its flag on what they call "AI realism": take the safety warnings seriously, but also ask what could go right. The second episode hands the mic to two recently fired OpenAI safety researchers to tell their side of the story. (Platformer)

• Meta is pulling its share links feature after researchers showed how easily it exposed strangers' private chats with Muse, Meta's AI assistant. Ars Technica's reporting for WIRED found the design flaw let snoops read conversations other users had shared with the chatbot. (WIRED)

Money & Power

• The housing market is in a split the industry has never seen, and the closest parallel is 1966. Rentals are improving on nearly every data point while the for-sale market keeps sinking: September pending home sales hit a record low, homebuilder sentiment sits at a 14-year low, and mortgage purchase applications are down 18% from a year ago. The 1966 lesson is that a crowding-out slump can reverse fast, but only once prices meet buyers where they are. (The Housing Frame)
